topics.name: TypeScript setup and configuration

beginner.content:
Introduction to TypeScript and JavaScript vs TypeScript

• TypeScript (TS) is JavaScript plus a type system. Think of Java: you declare that a variable is a String, and the compiler refuses to put a number in it. TS does the same for JavaScript, then compiles (transpiles) to plain JavaScript that browsers run. Types vanish at runtime.
• JavaScript vs TypeScript: every valid JS file is valid TS. TS adds type annotations, interfaces, generics, enums, access modifiers and decorators, and catches mistakes like typos or calling a method on undefined while you type, not when users click. Angular is written in TS and requires it.

Installation and the first compile

• Install Node.js, then TypeScript in your project: npm install -D typescript. Compile with npx tsc. In Angular projects the CLI already installs and runs TypeScript for you; you never call tsc yourself.
codeExamples:
# terminal
npm install -D typescript
npx tsc --init            # creates tsconfig.json
npx tsc                   # compiles *.ts to *.js using tsconfig.json
npx tsc --noEmit          # only type-check (what CI usually does)

intermediate.content:
tsconfig.json and compiler configuration

• tsconfig.json tells the compiler what to compile and how. Key compiler options: target (output JS version), module (ES modules), lib (available APIs, e.g. DOM), outDir, sourceMap, moduleResolution, paths (import aliases), experimentalDecorators, and the strict family.
• Angular projects have a base tsconfig.json plus tsconfig.app.json and tsconfig.spec.json that extend it, and an angularCompilerOptions block for the template type checker.

Strict type checking

• strict: true enables: noImplicitAny (no silent any), strictNullChecks (null/undefined are separate types, the most valuable flag), strictFunctionTypes, strictBindCallApply, strictPropertyInitialization (class fields must be set), noImplicitThis, useUnknownInCatchVariables, alwaysStrict.
• Always start new projects strict. Migrating a legacy codebase: turn flags on one at a time.
codeExamples:
let name: string = 'Asha';
name = null;                // error under strictNullChecks
let maybe: string | null = null;    // you must say so explicitly
console.log(maybe.length);          // error: possibly null
console.log(maybe?.length);         // ok

expert.content:
Internals and version notes

• TypeScript uses structural typing (compatible shape = compatible type) unlike Java's nominal typing, and the type system is erased: you cannot check an interface with instanceof at runtime.
• The Angular CLI compiles through the esbuild-based application builder (default since v17); TypeScript only type-checks and emits, bundling is separate. Each Angular version supports a narrow TypeScript range (the CLI refuses unsupported ones): do not upgrade TS independently.
• isolatedModules and verbatimModuleSyntax matter for fast transpilers; use import type for type-only imports. skipLibCheck speeds builds by not checking .d.ts files of dependencies.
• target ES2022 with useDefineForClassFields changes how class field initialisation order works, which affects Angular code that reads inject()ed fields; the CLI sets a compatible default.
• Prefer noUncheckedIndexedAccess for safer array access in strict teams.

interviewQA: What is TypeScript and why use it with Angular?
A typed superset of JavaScript compiled to JS. Types catch errors at build time, give IDE completion and refactoring, and Angular's API (decorators, DI, templates) is designed around it.
Does TypeScript exist at runtime?
No. Types are erased during compilation; only the generated JavaScript runs, so runtime checks need real code.
What does strictNullChecks do?
It makes null and undefined distinct types, so a string cannot be null unless declared string | null, eliminating a large class of null-reference errors.
What is tsconfig.json for?
It marks the project root and holds compiler options (target, module, strict, paths) and file selection; Angular extends a base file per build target.
What is structural typing?
Types are compatible if their shapes match, regardless of declared names, unlike Java's nominal types.

topics.name: Basic types

beginner.content:
Type annotations, inference and primitives

• A type annotation labels a variable like a name tag on a jar: let age: number = 30;. With type inference the compiler reads the value and fills the tag for you, so let age = 30 is already a number. Annotate function parameters and public APIs; let inference handle locals.
• Primitive data types: string, number (all numbers, no int/double), boolean, bigint, symbol, null, undefined. Use lowercase names, never String or Number objects.

Arrays, tuples and enums

• An array is a list of one type: number[] or Array<number>. A tuple is a fixed-length array whose positions have their own types, like a row (name, age). An enum names a set of constants.

intermediate.content:
any, unknown, never and void

TypeMeaningUse
anySwitches type checking offAvoid; migration only
unknownCould be anything; must be checked before useSafe replacement for any (parsed JSON, catch errors)
voidFunction returns nothingEvent handlers
neverNever returns or value impossibleFunctions that throw; exhaustive checks

Enum alternatives

• Plain numeric enums allow assigning any number and emit runtime code. Many teams prefer a union of string literals or a const object with as const instead; they are tree-shakable and print readably in JSON.

expert.content:
Details and pitfalls

• Inference widens mutable values (let x = 'a' is string) but keeps literals for const; as const freezes an object/array to readonly literal types. Annotate return types of exported functions to keep API stable and speed up the compiler.
• any is contagious: it silently disables checks downstream. Ban it with the ESLint rule no-explicit-any; use unknown at boundaries (HTTP, JSON.parse, catch) and validate (a schema library like zod, or hand-written guards).
• void vs undefined: a callback typed () => void may return a value that is ignored. never powers exhaustiveness checks in switch statements, valuable when adding enum values.
• const enums are inlined but problematic with isolatedModules; regular enums create an object at runtime. Numeric enums have reverse mapping (Role[0] is 'Student').
• number is a 64-bit float; money should use integers (cents) or a decimal library.

interviewQA: any vs unknown?
any disables checking; unknown accepts any value but forces you to narrow it before use, so it is type-safe.
What is a tuple?
A fixed-length array whose elements have individually declared types, such as [string, number].
When is never used?
For functions that never return (throw/infinite loop) and for exhaustive checks, where a leftover union member is assigned to never.
When should you annotate and when rely on inference?
Annotate function parameters, return types of public functions and empty initialisers; let inference handle obvious local values.
String enum vs union of literals?
Both restrict values. Enums emit runtime objects and are nominal; literal unions are erased, tree-shake and are simpler, so many teams prefer them.
What is the difference between null and undefined?
undefined means a value was never assigned; null is an explicit empty value. Under strictNullChecks both must be declared in the type.

topics.name: Composing types

beginner.content:
Union, intersection and literal types

• A union type (A | B) says "one of these", like a form field that accepts either a number or text. An intersection type (A & B) says "all of these at once", merging shapes. A literal type is an exact value: 'asc' | 'desc' is a tidy alternative to magic strings.

Type aliases, interfaces, optional and readonly properties

• A type alias gives any type a name (type Id = number | string). An interface describes an object shape, like a Java interface but for data. Mark a property optional with ? and readonly to forbid reassignment.

intermediate.content:
Interface vs type alias

interfacetype
Object shapesYesYes
Unions, tuples, primitivesNoYes
Extendingextendsintersection &
Declaration mergingYesNo
Implemented by classesYesYes (object types)
• Convention: interface for object models and public contracts, type for unions and computed types.
Index signatures and readonly collections

expert.content:
Design guidance

• Discriminated unions (a shared literal field such as kind or status) are the idiomatic way to model states like loading / success / error; the compiler narrows on the tag and checks exhaustiveness.
• readonly is compile-time only; it does not freeze objects at runtime (use Object.freeze). Prefer readonly inputs to catch accidental mutation, which also helps OnPush and signals.
• Intersections of conflicting property types collapse to never; prefer interface extends which reports conflicts clearly.
• Excess property checks apply only to fresh object literals; a variable with extra properties is assignable (structural typing).
• Large unions slow the compiler; keep them reasonable. Use satisfies (TS 4.9+) to validate a value against a type without widening it.
codeExamples:
const routes = { home: '/', about: '/about' } satisfies Record<string, string>;
routes.home;      // still the literal key set, not widened to string index

interviewQA: Union vs intersection types?
A union value is one of the member types; an intersection value has all properties of all member types.
Interface vs type alias?
Both describe object shapes. Interfaces can be extended and merged; type aliases can also name unions, tuples and mapped/conditional types.
What are literal types useful for?
Restricting a value to exact constants such as 'asc' | 'desc' and enabling discriminated unions.
What does readonly guarantee?
Compile-time protection against reassigning the property; it does not freeze the object at runtime.
What is a discriminated union?
A union whose members share a literal-typed tag property; checking the tag narrows the union to one member.

topics.name: Functions

beginner.content:
Functions, parameters and return types

• A function in TS declares parameter types and a return type. Think of a vending machine: you must insert the right coins (parameters) and know what comes out (return type).
• Optional parameters use ? (and must come last); default parameters use =; rest parameters (...args) gather extra arguments into an array.

Arrow functions and callbacks

• An arrow function is a short function: (a, b) => a + b. A callback is a function you hand to another function to call later (click handlers, array methods, setTimeout). Angular code is full of them.

intermediate.content:
Function types, overloads and this

• Describe function shapes with function types and reuse them with aliases. Overloads give one function several call signatures. Arrow functions capture this lexically, which is why class methods used as callbacks are often arrows.
Typing callbacks and async functions

expert.content:
Pitfalls and best practices

• Prefer default parameters over optional ones when a sensible default exists, and an options object (named properties) over many positional parameters.
• Regular functions have a dynamic this; arrows do not. Passing a class method as a callback (btn.onclick = this.save) loses this; use an arrow property, bind, or wrap it in an arrow in the template.
• Parameter bivariance: method parameters are checked bivariantly even in strict mode (a known soundness hole); property-style function types are checked strictly.
• Return types: annotate exported functions; for callbacks like array map let inference work. A function declared () => void accepts a callback returning anything.
• Excess closures in templates (arrow functions in event handlers) are not allowed in templates, so keep handlers as methods. In Angular templates do not call heavy functions on every change detection run: use computed signals or pipes.

interviewQA: Optional vs default parameters?
Optional (p?: T) may be undefined and must come last; default (p = value) supplies a value when omitted and makes the parameter optional.
What are rest parameters?
A final parameter prefixed with ... that collects remaining arguments into a typed array.
How does this behave in arrow functions?
Arrow functions capture this from the enclosing scope and cannot rebind it, unlike regular functions where this depends on the caller.
What is a callback?
A function passed to another function to be invoked later, for example an event handler or the argument of map().
How do you type a function that takes a callback?
Declare the callback type in the parameter: done: (data: string) => void, or alias it with type.

topics.name: Classes and OOP

beginner.content:
Classes, objects and constructors

• A class is a blueprint (like a house plan); an object is a house built from it. As in Java, a class has fields, a constructor and methods. TypeScript adds parameter properties: put an access modifier on a constructor parameter and TS creates and assigns the field for you.

Access modifiers, encapsulation, getters and setters

• public (default), protected (class and subclasses) and private (class only) control visibility. Encapsulation means hiding state and exposing safe methods. Getters and setters look like properties but run code, so you can validate on assignment.

intermediate.content:
Inheritance, abstract classes, polymorphism, static members

• Inheritance: extends reuses a parent; call super() first in a subclass constructor; override marks overridden methods (required with noImplicitOverride). An abstract class cannot be instantiated and may declare abstract methods subclasses must implement. Polymorphism: code written against the parent type works with any subclass. Static members belong to the class itself.
• Classes can also implement interfaces (many allowed), just like Java.
Protected and runtime privacy

expert.content:
Differences from Java and Angular usage

• TS private is compile-time only; the field still exists in the emitted JS. For real privacy use #field. A class has one constructor body (overloads are signatures only).
• Structural typing: an object literal with the right shape is assignable to a class type unless the class has private/protected members.
• Prefer composition over inheritance. Angular components and services rarely extend others; shared behaviour goes into services, directives, or host directives. Where inheritance is used for components, the base class needs its own decorator metadata (@Directive abstract) for inputs/outputs to be inherited.
• Parameter properties are how Angular DI classes are written: constructor(private http: HttpClient) {}. Modern code uses inject() field initialisers instead (see the DI module).
• With useDefineForClassFields, a field declared in a subclass can overwrite a parent-initialised value; initialise via constructor or avoid redeclaring.
• Getters in templates run on every change detection; keep them cheap or use computed signals.

interviewQA: public, private and protected?
public is visible everywhere (default); protected in the class and subclasses; private only inside the class. All three are compile-time checks in TS.
Abstract class vs interface?
An abstract class can hold implementation and state and is single-inherited; an interface only describes a contract, has no runtime presence, and a class can implement many.
What are parameter properties?
Constructor parameters with an access modifier or readonly; TypeScript declares and assigns the field automatically.
What do getters and setters give you?
Property syntax with method logic: validation, computed values and read-only views, while keeping the field private.
What is a static member?
A field or method on the class itself, shared by all instances and accessed as ClassName.member.
TS private vs #private?
private is erased at runtime and can be bypassed; #name is enforced by the JavaScript engine.

topics.name: Generics and type operators

beginner.content:
Generics

• Generics let one piece of code work with many types while staying type safe: like a box labelled "holds T" where T is decided when you use it. Java developers know them from List<String>. In Angular you meet them everywhere: Observable<User[]>, http.get<Course>(), signal<number>(0).

Generic constraints

• A constraint limits T with extends, like Java's T extends Comparable, so you can use the members you promised.

intermediate.content:
Utility types

UtilityResult
Partial<T>All properties optional (patch objects)
Required<T>All properties required
Readonly<T>All properties readonly
Pick<T, K>Only the listed keys
Omit<T, K>Everything except the listed keys
Record<K, V>Object with keys K and values V
ReturnType<F>, Parameters<F>Types taken from a function
NonNullable<T>, Awaited<T>Remove null / unwrap a Promise

keyof and typeof

• keyof T is the union of T's property names. typeof value (in a type position) is the type of an existing value. Together they type safe property access.

expert.content:
Mapped and conditional types

• A mapped type builds a new type by looping over keys: that is how Partial and Readonly are written. A conditional type chooses a type with T extends U ? X : Y; infer captures a type inside the check.
Real Angular examples

interviewQA: What problem do generics solve?
They let you write reusable, type-safe code without duplicating it per type or falling back to any.
Partial vs Pick vs Omit?
Partial makes all properties optional; Pick keeps selected keys; Omit removes selected keys.
What does keyof return?
A union of the string/number/symbol keys of a type; combined with generics it types safe property access.
What is a mapped type?
A type created by iterating over the keys of another type, transforming each property (for example making all optional or readonly).
What does infer do?
In a conditional type it declares a type variable captured from the matched position, e.g. extracting the element type of an array or the result of a Promise.
Difference between typeof in JS and TS?
In expressions typeof returns a runtime string; in type positions typeof gets the compile-time type of a value.

topics.name: Narrowing, guards and modules

beginner.content:
Type narrowing, guards and assertions

• Type narrowing: inside a check, the compiler knows more. After if (typeof x === 'string'), x is a string in that block. The checks that narrow are type guards: typeof, instanceof, in, equality, truthiness, and your own functions. A type assertion (as) simply tells the compiler "trust me"; it performs no runtime check.

Import and export, modules and namespaces

• A module is a file with import or export. Each file has its own scope, like a Java class file with imports. Namespaces (the namespace keyword) are an older internal-module style; in modern code use ES modules and avoid namespaces.

intermediate.content:
Custom type guards and discriminated unions

• A user-defined guard returns x is T; an assertion function returns asserts x is T. Use them to validate untyped data from HTTP.

Decorators

• A decorator is a function that adds metadata or behaviour to a class, method or property, written @Name; like Java annotations. Angular's @Component, @Injectable, @Input, @Directive and @Pipe are decorators, and the Angular compiler reads their metadata. They need no configuration inside Angular projects (the CLI enables them).

expert.content:
Safety and module details

• Assertions are not casts: x as T never checks at runtime and silences errors. Prefer guards, validation, or satisfies. The double assertion (as unknown as T) is a last resort. The non-null assertion value! is also unchecked; use it rarely.
• Narrowing does not cross function boundaries or survive assignments in callbacks; copy to a const first. Use exhaustive switch with never.
• Decorators: Angular still uses the experimentalDecorators (legacy) implementation, enabled by the CLI. TC39 standard decorators (TS 5.0) are different and not interchangeable. Parameter decorators like @Inject exist only in the legacy form.
• Modules: with the bundler, circular imports cause undefined at startup; keep dependency direction one way. Barrel files (index.ts) can defeat tree shaking and slow builds in big repos. Use import type to keep type-only imports out of the output. Dynamic import() creates a lazy chunk, which Angular uses for lazy routes.

interviewQA: What is type narrowing?
The compiler refining a broad type to a specific one inside a conditional check such as typeof, instanceof, in, or equality.
Type assertion vs type guard?
An assertion (as) only changes the compile-time type without checking; a guard performs a runtime check that the compiler also uses to narrow.
What are decorators and how does Angular use them?
Functions prefixed with @ that attach metadata/behaviour to classes and members. Angular reads @Component, @Injectable, @Input and others to configure rendering and DI.
Named export vs default export?
Named exports are imported by name, enable refactoring and tree shaking; a default export is imported under any name. Angular style guides prefer named exports.
What does import type do?
It imports only for type checking and is erased from the output, avoiding unneeded runtime imports and circular-dependency issues.

topics.name: Async code and errors

beginner.content:
Promises and async/await

• A Promise is an IOU for a value that arrives later (a network response). It is pending, then fulfilled or rejected. async/await lets you write that code top-to-bottom like normal code. An async function always returns a Promise.

Error handling

• Use try/catch/finally around risky code. Anything can be thrown, so the caught value is unknown in strict TS and must be narrowed. You can create custom error classes.

intermediate.content:
Concurrency with Promises

• Await sequentially only when steps depend on each other. For independent calls start them together with Promise.all (fails fast), Promise.allSettled (never rejects) or Promise.race.

Promises vs Observables in Angular

• A Promise has one value and starts immediately; an RxJS Observable can emit many values, is lazy and cancellable. Angular's HttpClient returns Observables. Convert with firstValueFrom(obs$) when you want await, or with toSignal. (RxJS is covered in a later module.)
codeExamples:
import { firstValueFrom } from 'rxjs';
const course = await firstValueFrom(this.http.get<Course>('/api/courses/1'));

expert.content:
Pitfalls

• Unhandled rejections: a promise without catch or await in try fails silently or crashes. Never leave a floating promise: await it, return it, or mark intentional with void. Enable the ESLint rule no-floating-promises.
• forEach(async ...) does not await its callbacks; use for...of or Promise.all with map.
• Event loop: promise callbacks are microtasks and run before timers. Zone.js patches promises and timers so Angular knows when to run change detection; native async/await used to be down-levelled to promises for Zone, one reason Angular CLI targets ES2022 with a special transform. Zoneless apps (stable in 20+) do not rely on this.
• Errors inside async code do not propagate to the caller unless awaited. In Angular, route a global handler through ErrorHandler.
• Always rethrow or log unknown errors; swallowing exceptions hides bugs. Use finally for cleanup such as loading flags.
• Cancellation: promises cannot be cancelled; use AbortController with fetch, or Observables with switchMap.

interviewQA: What are the states of a Promise?
Pending, then either fulfilled with a value or rejected with an error; once settled it never changes.
Promise.all vs Promise.allSettled?
all rejects immediately if any promise rejects; allSettled waits for all and reports each outcome without rejecting.
Why is the catch variable unknown?
Any value can be thrown in JavaScript, so under useUnknownInCatchVariables (part of strict) you must narrow it before use.
What does async/await compile to?
Syntactic sugar over Promises: an async function returns a Promise and await suspends it until the awaited promise settles.
How do Promises differ from Observables?
Promises are eager and deliver one value; Observables are lazy, can emit many values over time, and can be cancelled or transformed with operators.
Why does forEach with async callbacks misbehave?
forEach ignores returned promises, so it neither waits for them nor catches their errors; use for...of or Promise.all.

topics.name: What Angular is

beginner.content:
What is Angular?

• Angular is an open-source framework from Google for building single-page applications (SPAs) with TypeScript. A SPA loads one HTML page and then updates it with JavaScript as the user navigates, so it feels like a desktop app.
• Analogy: React and Vue are engines; Angular is the whole car. It ships a router, forms, an HTTP client, dependency injection, testing tools and a CLI, all designed together.
• Angular architecture in one picture: the browser loads index.html, which contains your root component; the root component's template contains other components; services supply data; the router swaps components by URL.
codeExamples:
<!-- index.html -->
<body>
  <app-root></app-root>          <!-- the root component is mounted here -->
</body>

// app.component.ts
@Component({
  selector: 'app-root',
  template: '<app-header /><router-outlet /><app-footer />'   // tree of components
})
export class AppComponent {}

beginner.content:
Angular use cases and history

• Typical uses: enterprise dashboards, admin portals, banking and insurance front ends, e-commerce back offices, internal tools, large apps with many developers.
• History: AngularJS 1.x (2010, JavaScript, now end of life) was replaced by a complete rewrite, Angular 2 (2016, TypeScript, components). Versions then moved to 4, 5 ... with a regular schedule. Recent milestones: Ivy renderer (v9), standalone components (v14-15), signals (v16-17), new control flow and the esbuild builder (v17), zoneless support (v18-20+).

intermediate.content:
Architecture: the building blocks

PartJobJava/Spring analogy
ComponentTemplate + class for one UI pieceView + controller
TemplateHTML with bindings and control flowThymeleaf page
Directive / PipeBehaviour on elements / value formattingTag library / formatter
Service + DIShared logic provided by injection@Service beans + IoC
RouterURL to component mapping@RequestMapping
HttpClientREST callsRestTemplate / WebClient
Signals / RxJSReactive state and async streamsReactor / CompletableFuture

Angular vs React vs Vue

AngularReactVue
TypeFull frameworkUI libraryProgressive framework
LanguageTypeScriptJS or TS (JSX)JS or TS (SFC)
TemplatesHTML + Angular syntaxJSXHTML-like templates
ReactivitySignals, RxJSState + hooksRefs/reactive proxies
Built-inRouter, forms, HTTP, DI, i18nChoose librariesOfficial router and store
Learning curveSteeper, then consistentGentle start, many choicesGentle
Best fitLarge teams, long-lived enterprise appsFlexible products, large ecosystemSmall to medium apps

expert.content:
Angular versions and release cycle

• A major release arrives about every six months (May and November). Each major gets 6 months of active support and then 12 months of long-term support (security fixes). Minor releases add features roughly monthly; patches come weekly. Deprecations are announced at least two majors before removal, and ng update migrates code with schematics.
• Notable versions: v14 standalone preview and inject(); v16 signals preview; v17 built-in control flow (@if/@for), @defer, esbuild builder, standalone in ng new schematics; v17.1-17.3 signal inputs, model(), output(); v18 stable control flow, zoneless experiment; v19 standalone is the default (standalone: true no longer needed), linkedSignal/resource experimental, incremental hydration preview; v20 signals APIs (effect, toSignal, linkedSignal) stable, zoneless in developer preview, new style guide with shorter file names; later versions continue to make zoneless and signal forms mainstream. Always read the current release notes on angular.dev.

Choosing Angular

• Pick Angular when you need strong conventions across a big team, built-in solutions for everything, TypeScript-first tooling and a predictable upgrade path (the CLI migrates your code). Pick something lighter for small marketing sites or when SEO-first content frameworks fit better.
• Java developers adapt quickly: classes, interfaces, decorators (like annotations), dependency injection and layering all feel familiar. The new ideas are asynchronous reactive code and the browser as an untrusted environment.
• Rendering: Angular supports client-side rendering, server-side rendering, prerendering and hydration; the component model is the same.

interviewQA: What is Angular?
An open-source TypeScript framework from Google for building single-page applications, with components, templates, DI, routing, forms and HTTP built in.
AngularJS vs Angular?
AngularJS (1.x) is the old JavaScript framework with controllers and scope, now end of life. Angular 2+ is a TypeScript, component-based rewrite.
Why choose Angular over React?
Opinionated structure, batteries included (router, forms, HTTP, DI), TypeScript by default and consistent code across large teams; React offers more freedom but needs you to assemble the stack.
How often is Angular released?
A major version about every six months, with 6 months active and 12 months long-term support per major.
What are good use cases for Angular?
Enterprise dashboards, admin and back-office tools, data-heavy forms, and large applications maintained by many developers over years.
What is a single-page application?
An app that loads one HTML document and updates the view in the browser through JavaScript and API calls instead of full page reloads.

topics.name: Setup, CLI and project structure

beginner.content:
Node.js, npm and the Angular CLI

• Angular tooling runs on Node.js (install the current LTS from nodejs.org; each Angular version lists the Node versions it supports). npm comes with Node and downloads libraries into node_modules. The Angular CLI is the command-line tool ng that creates, runs, builds and tests projects.
codeExamples:
# check tools
node -v
npm -v

# install the CLI globally, create and run a project
npm install -g @angular/cli
ng version
ng new school-app          # answer the prompts (stylesheet format, SSR: no for now)
cd school-app
ng serve --open            # dev server at http://localhost:4200

beginner.content:
Angular project structure

• After ng new you get a workspace. The files you will touch most: src/app (your components and services), src/main.ts (bootstrap), src/index.html, src/styles.css (global styles), and public/ or src/assets (static files).
codeExamples:
school-app/
  angular.json            workspace and build configuration
  package.json            dependencies and npm scripts
  tsconfig.json           TypeScript options (plus tsconfig.app.json, tsconfig.spec.json)
  public/                 static files copied as-is (favicon, images)
  src/
    index.html            the single HTML page with <app-root>
    main.ts               bootstrapApplication(...)
    styles.css            global styles
    app/
      app.component.ts    root component (app.ts in the newest style guide)
      app.config.ts       providers: router, http, etc.
      app.routes.ts       route table

intermediate.content:
angular.json, package.json and tsconfig.json

• angular.json defines projects and their architect targets (build, serve, test) with options per configuration (production, development): entry file, assets, global styles, budgets, file replacements.
• package.json lists dependencies (@angular/core, rxjs, zone.js, tslib), devDependencies (@angular/cli, typescript) and scripts (start = ng serve, build, test). Commit package-lock.json.
• tsconfig.json sets compiler and strictness options; angularCompilerOptions.strictTemplates turns on template type checking.

The development server and CLI commands

• ng serve builds in memory, serves at port 4200 and reloads on save (hot module replacement for styles; full or partial reload for code). Options: --port, --open, --host, --configuration, --proxy-config (to forward /api to Spring Boot at 8080 and avoid CORS during development).
CommandPurpose
ng newCreate a workspace
ng serveDev server
ng generate (g) component|service|directive|pipe|guard|interceptorScaffold code
ng buildCompile to dist/
ng testRun unit tests
ng addInstall and configure a library (Material)
ng updateUpgrade Angular with migrations
ng lint, ng e2eRun configured linters / e2e tools (after adding them)

expert.content:
Workspace practices

• Keep the Node version fixed per team (.nvmrc or the engines field) and use npm ci in CI for reproducible installs from the lockfile. Do not install the CLI globally in CI; use npx ng or a local script so each repo uses its own version.
• Version alignment: all @angular/* packages must share the same major; upgrade one major at a time with ng update @angular/core @angular/cli, commit between steps, and read the update guide on angular.dev/update-guide.
• Budgets in angular.json fail the build when bundles grow too large. fileReplacements or environment files swap settings per configuration (see the deployment module).
• Monorepos: angular.json can hold many projects (apps and libraries) in one workspace; target a project with ng build my-lib.
• Analytics prompt in ng new can be disabled with ng analytics disable; set NG_CLI_ANALYTICS=false in CI.
• The dev server serves unminified code with source maps; never deploy it. Use ng build and static hosting (covered in the deployment module).

interviewQA: How do you create and run an Angular app?
Install Node.js, run npm install -g @angular/cli, then ng new app-name and ng serve to open http://localhost:4200.
What is angular.json?
The workspace configuration file listing projects and their build/serve/test targets with options per configuration (production, development).
What does package.json contain in an Angular project?
Dependencies (Angular packages, RxJS, zone.js), dev dependencies (CLI, TypeScript, test tools) and npm scripts such as start and build.
What does ng serve do?
Builds the app in memory, serves it with live reload on port 4200 and rebuilds on every change.
How do you avoid CORS problems in development?
Use the dev-server proxy (--proxy-config) so /api calls are forwarded to the backend from the same origin.
How do you upgrade Angular safely?
Use ng update one major version at a time, review the official update guide, run tests, and commit after each step.

topics.name: Builds, rendering and module styles

beginner.content:
Angular compilation

• Browsers cannot read Angular templates. The Angular compiler converts your templates and decorators into plain JavaScript. With AOT (ahead-of-time) this happens during the build, so users download ready code. It also checks template types, catching errors like a misspelled property before release. Think of translating a book before printing instead of translating while reading.
• Development vs production builds: ng serve and the development configuration are quick and readable (no minification, source maps). ng build (production by default) does AOT, tree shaking, minification, hashing of file names and budgets, producing a small dist/ folder.
codeExamples:
ng build                                  # production by default (since v12)
ng build --configuration development      # fast, readable build
# output: dist/school-app/browser/ with main-XXXX.js, styles-XXXX.css, index.html

beginner.content:
Standalone components and NgModules

• A standalone component lists what its template needs in its own imports array: no NgModule required. This is the modern default (v19+ ng new, and standalone: true is implied).
• NgModules (@NgModule with declarations, imports, exports, providers, bootstrap) are the legacy module-based way. You will find them in older projects; they still work and mix with standalone code, and migrations exist (ng generate @angular/core:standalone).

intermediate.content:
Rendering fundamentals

• Each component template is compiled into a template function with two modes: a create pass that builds DOM nodes once, and an update pass that re-evaluates bindings and writes only what changed. This is the Ivy renderer (default since v9); there is no virtual DOM.
• Change detection decides when the update pass runs: after browser events and async tasks in zone-based apps, or when a signal read by the template changes. Components using signals and OnPush are only refreshed when needed.
• The bootstrap sequence: main.ts calls bootstrapApplication, creating the platform and an application injector with the providers from app.config.ts, then creates the root component and attaches it to the element matching its selector.

Standalone vs NgModule: migration points

AspectStandaloneNgModule
DependenciesComponent imports arrayModule imports, shared via exports
BootstrapbootstrapApplicationbootstrapModule
ProvidersprovideXxx() functions in app.configModule providers and forRoot()
Lazy loadingloadComponent / loadChildren routesloadChildren with a module
BoilerplateLowHigher

expert.content:
Build internals and pitfalls

• Builders: the default application builder uses esbuild and Vite for the dev server (v17+), giving much faster builds than the older webpack browser builder. It supports SSR and prerendering output. Hybrid code with webpack-only plugins needs migration (ng update offers it).
• Tree shaking removes unused exports; providedIn: 'root' services are tree-shakable, module-level providers are not. Lazy routes become separate chunks. Check bundle contents with ng build --stats-json and a visualiser.
• AOT vs JIT: JIT compiled in the browser at startup (no longer used by default; only in some tests). AOT enables template type checking, smaller bundles and faster startup. strictTemplates is highly recommended.
• Hydration and zoneless: with SSR, hydration reuses server-rendered DOM instead of recreating it. Zoneless change detection (provideZonelessChangeDetection(), developer preview in v20 and promoted after) removes zone.js for smaller bundles and clearer updates, requiring signals/markForCheck.
• Legacy NgModule apps: schematics can convert them to standalone gradually; mixing both in one app is supported (a standalone component can import a module, and an NgModule can import a standalone component).

interviewQA: What is AOT compilation?
Ahead-of-time compilation turns templates and decorators into JavaScript during the build, enabling template type checks, smaller bundles and faster startup.
Development vs production build?
Development is quick with source maps and no minification; production adds AOT, tree shaking, minification, hashed file names and budgets for small, cacheable output.
What is a standalone component?
A component that declares its own template dependencies in its imports array and needs no NgModule; the default style in modern Angular.
Why are NgModules called legacy?
They add indirection (declarations/exports) that standalone components make unnecessary, though existing module-based apps remain supported and can be migrated.
How does Angular render without a virtual DOM?
The Ivy compiler generates instructions per template that create DOM once and update only changed bindings during change detection.
Where does an Angular app start?
main.ts calls bootstrapApplication(RootComponent, appConfig); the root selector in index.html is where the component mounts.

topics.name: Component anatomy

beginner.content:
What is a component?

• A component is a LEGO brick of your UI: a TypeScript class (data and behaviour), an HTML template (what is shown) and optional CSS (how it looks). A page is a tree of components: an app shell contains a header, a course list, and each course card is a component too. This is the component architecture of Angular.
• The @Component decorator marks a class as a component and carries its metadata. The selector is the custom HTML tag you write to place it.

Creating components with the CLI

• ng generate component courses/course-card (short: ng g c) creates the ts, html, css and spec files in one step. Add --inline-template or --inline-style to keep them in the class, and --skip-tests to omit the spec.
codeExamples:
ng g c courses/course-card
# creates src/app/courses/course-card/course-card.component.ts / .html / .css / .spec.ts
ng g c shared/badge --inline-template --inline-style --skip-tests

intermediate.content:
Inline vs external templates and styles, metadata

• Inline (template, styles) suits tiny components of a few lines. External (templateUrl, styleUrl) keeps real templates readable and gets editor HTML support. Since v17 use styleUrl (single) and styleUrls (list).
• Important component metadata: selector, template/templateUrl, styles/styleUrl, imports, changeDetection (OnPush), encapsulation, providers (component-level services), host (bindings on the host element), and standalone (default true from v19).

Selectors and standalone imports

• Selectors may be an element name (the usual, with a prefix like app-), an attribute ([appTooltip]) or a class; but components should normally use element selectors, attribute selectors fit directives. The selector must be unique and kebab-case.
• Component imports: anything the template uses must be imported: other standalone components, directives (NgClass), pipes (DatePipe), or legacy NgModules (FormsModule). A missing import gives a compile error "is not a known element" in strict templates.
codeExamples:
<!-- if the import is forgotten -->
<!-- error NG8001: 'app-course-card' is not a known element -->

@Component({ selector: 'app-demo', imports: [CourseCardComponent, NgClass, FormsModule], template: '...' })
export class DemoComponent {}

expert.content:
Standalone components and conventions

• Standalone components (v14+, default v19+) carry their own dependency list, so they are tree-shakable and lazy-loadable one by one with loadComponent. In Angular 17 to 18 write standalone: true explicitly; from 19 it is implied and the ng update migration removes it (add standalone: false for NgModule-declared ones).
• Angular 20's style guide drops the type suffix from file and class names for new projects (course-card.ts with class CourseCard); the older .component.ts naming remains common and fully valid. Be consistent within a project.
• Keep components thin: presentation and event wiring in the component, data access and business rules in services. Inject with inject() instead of constructor parameters in new code.
• Prefix selectors per feature area (app-, admin-) and enforce with ESLint @angular-eslint/component-selector. Do not use the CLI's default styles inline for larger components; extracting them improves diffs and reuse.
• Template compilation: AOT turns the template into a function evaluated by change detection. Complex expressions and method calls in templates run on every check, so prefer fields, signals and computed values.

interviewQA: What is an Angular component?
A class decorated with @Component that combines a template, styles and logic into a reusable UI building block with its own selector.
Inline vs external template?
Inline puts HTML in the template property (fine for tiny components); external uses templateUrl for larger templates with better tooling.
What does the selector do?
It defines the HTML tag (or attribute) that Angular replaces with the component's rendered view.
What is the imports array of a standalone component?
The list of components, directives, pipes or NgModules that the component's template uses.
How do you create a component with the CLI?
ng generate component path/name (ng g c), optionally with --inline-template, --inline-style or --skip-tests.
Why use OnPush for components?
It limits change detection to when inputs change by reference, an event fires inside, or a signal/async pipe notifies, improving performance and predictability.

topics.name: Parent-child communication

beginner.content:
Parent and child components, composition and reuse

• A parent component places a child in its template with the child's selector, just like using an HTML tag. Composition means building big screens from small components (page, list, card, button). A reusable component gets its data from inputs rather than hard-coding it, and reports user actions through outputs.
• Rule of thumb: data flows down (parent to child through inputs) and events flow up (child to parent through outputs). Think of a manager giving a task (input) and the worker reporting back (output).

intermediate.content:
@Input(), @Output() and EventEmitter (decorator style)

• Before signals, communication used decorators: @Input() marks a property the parent can set; @Output() marks an EventEmitter the child fires with emit(). This style is not deprecated and appears in most existing code; new code prefers input() and output() (they give signals, required inputs, transforms and better typing).

Model inputs and two-way component binding

• model() (Angular 17.2+) declares an input that the child can also write back to. The parent uses the banana-in-a-box syntax [(value)]. It is the signal replacement for the pattern of an @Input() value plus an @Output() valueChange.

Communication options at a glance

SituationUse
Parent to childinput() / @Input()
Child to parentoutput() / @Output() with EventEmitter
Both directions, one valuemodel() / [(value)]
Parent calls child methodtemplate reference or viewChild()
Siblings or distant componentsA shared service with signals or Subjects
Deep subtreesDependency injection (providers in a component)

expert.content:
Signal inputs in depth and design rules

• Signal inputs are read-only signals (value()), so computed() and effect() react to them without ngOnChanges. Options: input(0, { alias: 'count', transform: numberAttribute }). Required inputs have no default and fail the build if missing. In tests set them with fixture.componentRef.setInput('value', 3).
• Input signals cannot be assigned inside the child; if a child needs local edits use model() or copy into a linkedSignal. Never mutate an object received via input: it breaks OnPush and surprises the parent. Treat inputs as immutable.
• output() returns an OutputEmitterRef (not an Observable subclass like EventEmitter). It can be subscribed programmatically with .subscribe() and auto-cleans up. outputFromObservable() and outputToObservable() bridge to RxJS. Do not call .subscribe on EventEmitter in the child to emit; EventEmitter's only supported use is @Output().
• Reusability guidance: smart (container) components fetch data and manage state; presentational components only take inputs and emit outputs. Keep the API small, name outputs as verbs without the on prefix ((save), not (onSave)), do not reach into parents via injection of the parent component, and support ARIA and keyboard use.
• Versions: input() 17.1, model() and signal queries 17.2, output() 17.3; all stable since v19.

interviewQA: How does a parent pass data to a child?
Through an input: bind with [name]="value" in the parent template, where the child declares input() or @Input().
How does a child notify a parent?
By emitting an output: output() with .emit(value), or @Output() EventEmitter; the parent listens with (name)="handler($event)".
What is EventEmitter?
The RxJS-based class used with @Output(); calling emit() sends a value to the parent's event handler.
What does model() do?
It creates a writable input (Angular 17.2+) enabling two-way binding [(value)] between parent and child without a manual valueChange output.
Difference between input() and @Input()?

input() returns a read-only signal, supports required inputs and transforms with better typing, and works with computed/effect; @Input() is a decorated property updated by Angular and observed through ngOnChanges.
How do two sibling components communicate?
Through a shared service (holding signals or subjects) or through their common parent passing inputs and handling outputs.

topics.name: Queries, projection and dynamic components

beginner.content:
Template reference variables

• A template reference variable is a name tag you attach with #name. It refers to the DOM element (or the component/directive instance) inside the same template, so you can use it without writing TypeScript.
codeExamples:
<input #nameInput type="text" placeholder="Name">
<button (click)="greet(nameInput.value)">Greet</button>        <!-- read the input directly -->

<app-timer #timer />
<button (click)="timer.start()">Start</button>                    <!-- call a child's public method -->

beginner.content:
Content projection with ng-content

• Content projection lets a parent put its own markup inside your component, like a picture frame that shows whatever photo you slide in. You mark the hole with <ng-content>. Multi-slot projection uses several ng-content tags with a select attribute (CSS selector).

intermediate.content:
ViewChild, ViewChildren, ContentChild, ContentChildren

• ViewChild / ViewChildren query things in the component's own template. ContentChild / ContentChildren query things that the parent projected into ng-content. Modern code uses the signal functions viewChild(), viewChildren(), contentChild(), contentChildren() (17.2+), which return signals; the decorators (@ViewChild etc.) still work.
• Results are available after the view is created (the signal is simply undefined until then; with the decorator form, read in ngAfterViewInit).

Dynamic components

• Dynamic components are created at runtime, chosen by data: wizards, widget dashboards, plugin UIs. The simple way is the NgComponentOutlet directive. The flexible way is ViewContainerRef.createComponent(), which returns a ComponentRef so you can set inputs and destroy it.

expert.content:
Timing, pitfalls and tips

• Projection is not creation: projected content is created by the parent even if the child never renders the slot (for example inside an @if that is false). The elements are instantiated and run their constructors regardless. To create content lazily, pass an ng-template and render it with ngTemplateOutlet.
• Static vs dynamic queries: a ViewChild inside @if or @for resolves later (use the signal form or ngAfterViewInit). Query options: read (get ElementRef, ViewContainerRef or a different token), descendants for ContentChildren (default false, direct children only), static in decorator form.
• Do not read or mutate the DOM in the constructor or ngOnInit: the view is not ready. Use afterNextRender / afterRender (SSR-safe, runs only in the browser) rather than setTimeout hacks.
• Reaching into a child via ViewChild to call methods tightly couples components; prefer inputs and outputs, and use queries for genuinely imperative needs (focus, scroll, measurements, coordinating tab groups).
• Default content for ng-content is not supported in older versions; Angular 18+ allows fallback content inside ng-content tags. A template can contain only one ng-content without a select as the catch-all slot. ngProjectAs lets an element pretend to match another selector.
• Dynamic components must be standalone (or declared) and the inputs must be set through setInput (so OnPush and signal inputs update); assigning instance properties directly skips change notification. Always call destroy() or rely on the ViewContainerRef being destroyed to avoid leaks.

interviewQA: What is a template reference variable?
A #name tag on an element, component or ng-template that gives other parts of the same template access to that instance.
ViewChild vs ContentChild?
ViewChild queries nodes declared in the component's own template; ContentChild queries nodes the parent projected into it via ng-content.
When are ViewChild results available?
After the view is initialised: ngAfterViewInit for decorator queries; with viewChild() signals the value updates automatically and is read when needed.
What is content projection?
Passing markup from a parent into a child's ng-content slot(s) so the child provides structure and the parent the content.
How do you build multi-slot projection?
Use several ng-content elements with a select attribute (CSS selector), plus one unselected default slot.
How do you create a component dynamically?
With NgComponentOutlet in a template, or ViewContainerRef.createComponent() in code, then setInput() and destroy() on the returned ComponentRef.

topics.name: Lifecycle, change detection and styling

beginner.content:
Component lifecycle and destruction

• Every component has a life: it is created, shown, updated and destroyed. Angular calls lifecycle hooks at each stage, like a theatre calling the actor at the right cue. The most used: ngOnInit (once, after inputs are set; load data here), ngOnChanges (an input changed), ngAfterViewInit (view ready), and ngOnDestroy (cleanup).
• Component destruction: when a component is removed (route change, @if false) Angular calls ngOnDestroy. Use it to unsubscribe, stop timers and remove listeners. Modern alternative: inject(DestroyRef).onDestroy(...).

Change detection and styling basics

• Change detection is how Angular notices that data changed and updates the screen. By default it checks every component after any event; with OnPush or signals it checks only components whose inputs or signals changed.
• Component CSS is scoped to its own template by default (emulated encapsulation): a style for h3 in one component does not leak into others.

intermediate.content:
Change detection strategies

StrategyChecks the component when
DefaultAnything async happens anywhere (every check pass)
OnPushAn input reference changes, an event handler in it runs, an async pipe or signal read by the template updates, or markForCheck() is called

Styling and view encapsulation

• ViewEncapsulation.Emulated (default): Angular adds unique attributes so styles apply only to this component. None: styles become global. ShadowDom: real shadow DOM. Special selectors: :host (the component's own element), :host-context(), and ::ng-deep (deprecated; avoid). Pass theme values through CSS custom properties, which pierce encapsulation.

expert.content:
Best practices for reusable components

• Make components small and single-purpose; use OnPush plus signal inputs; keep templates declarative with computed values instead of method calls; name selectors with a prefix; provide good defaults and document inputs.
• Accessibility: native elements (button, not div), labels, keyboard handling, focus management, ARIA only where needed. Style via CSS variables and :host, never depend on a parent's global CSS.
• Avoid hidden dependencies: do not inject the parent component; take data by inputs and emit outputs. Provide customisation via content projection (templates for headers, empty states) instead of a flood of boolean flags.
• Clean up everything you start: subscriptions (use takeUntilDestroyed() or the async pipe), timers, event listeners.
• Test through the public API (inputs, outputs, DOM), not internals.

Lifecycle and change detection internals

• Order for one component: constructor, ngOnChanges, ngOnInit, ngDoCheck, ngAfterContentInit, ngAfterContentChecked, ngAfterViewInit, ngAfterViewChecked, and later ngOnDestroy. The constructor should only wire dependencies (inject). Details of every hook are in the dedicated lifecycle module.
• Zone.js patches browser async APIs and triggers a change detection pass after each task; signals mark just the consuming views dirty and enable zoneless apps (provideZonelessChangeDetection, stable in recent versions). Never mutate state inside ngAfterViewChecked in dev mode: it triggers ExpressionChangedAfterItHasBeenChecked.
• With ViewEncapsulation.None two components can clash in CSS; global styles belong in styles.css, library themes via custom properties. Shadow DOM encapsulation blocks global CSS entirely, including utility frameworks like Tailwind.
• Prefer afterNextRender/afterEveryRender (v17+; stable v19) over ngAfterViewInit for DOM measurement because they run only in the browser, which keeps SSR safe.

interviewQA: What is the difference between constructor and ngOnInit?
The constructor runs at instantiation (dependency wiring only) before inputs are set; ngOnInit runs once after the first inputs are bound and is where initialisation logic belongs.
Why implement ngOnDestroy?
To release resources the component started: unsubscribe from Observables, clear timers and remove event listeners, preventing memory leaks.
What does OnPush change?
The component is checked only when an input reference changes, an event fires in it, an async pipe/signal updates, or it is marked for check, instead of on every pass.
What are the view encapsulation modes?
Emulated (default, attribute-scoped), None (global styles) and ShadowDom (native shadow root).
How can a parent restyle a child component?
Through CSS custom properties the child exposes, host classes the child supports, or ng-content; ::ng-deep is deprecated.
What makes a component reusable?
A clear input/output API, no hidden dependencies on parents, projection for customisation, OnPush, accessibility and styling through variables.

interviewQA: How should I use the module overview?

topics.name: Template syntax and core bindings

beginner.content:
Angular template syntax and interpolation

• An Angular template is HTML with superpowers. It is the view of a component, and everything dynamic is written with a few special symbols. Think of a mail-merge letter: the fixed text is HTML and the placeholders are bindings filled with data from the class.
• Interpolation {{ expression }} prints a value (converted to text) into the page.

Property, event and two-way binding

• Property binding [property]="expression" pushes data from the class to an element or child component (class to view). Event binding (event)="statement" sends user actions from the view to the class. Two-way data binding [(x)] combines both: banana in a box.
• The [(ngModel)] syntax is the classic two-way binding for form inputs; it needs FormsModule in the component imports.
codeExamples:
You typed: {{ name }}

// component imports: [FormsModule] <- required for ngModel // class: name = ''; photoUrl = 'a.png'; valid = true; save() { ... }

intermediate.content:
Property binding vs interpolation, and the three directions

SyntaxDirectionExample
{{ }}class to view (text)<p>{{ title }}</p>
[ ]class to view (property)<img [src]="url">
( )view to class<button (click)="save()">
[( )]both<input [(ngModel)]="name">
• Binding to the property (not the HTML attribute) is the key idea: [value] sets the live DOM property, while the attribute only sets the initial value. Interpolation inside attributes (title="Hi {{ name }}") is just sugar for property binding.
• Use property binding to pass non-string data to child components: <app-rating [value]="4"> passes a number; value="4" would pass the string "4".

Two-way binding without ngModel, template reference variables

• [(x)] is shorthand for [x]="v" (xChange)="v = $event". A component supports it when it has an input x and an output xChange (or a model() input). Use template reference variables (#box) to read values without TypeScript.
codeExamples:
<!-- the long form of [(ngModel)] -->
<input [ngModel]="name" (ngModelChange)="name = $event">

<!-- reference variable -->
<input #city placeholder="City">
<button (click)="search(city.value)">Search</button>

<!-- signals : two-way binding to a signal works directly -->
<input [(ngModel)]="query">       <!-- class: query = signal(''); -->

intermediate.content:
Template expressions and statements

• A template expression (inside {{ }} and [ ]) is a small JavaScript-like expression: property access, method calls, operators, ternary, pipes (value | date), safe navigation (user?.name), non-null assertion (user!.name) and nullish coalescing (??).
• A template statement (inside ( )) responds to an event: it may assign (count = count + 1), call methods, use $event, and chain with semicolons.
codeExamples:
{{ user?.address?.city ?? "Unknown" }}

{{ total | currency }}

expert.content:
Expression restrictions and how the engine evaluates

• Expression restrictions: no assignment (in expressions), no new, no ++/--, no bitwise operators, no chaining with commas, no access to globals such as window, document, console or Math (expose them via class members), no template literal syntax in older versions, no arrow functions or regular expression literals in expressions. Template-literal strings are supported from v19.2; check your version.
• Expressions must be fast and side-effect free: change detection may run them many times per second. A method call like {{ expensive() }} executes on every pass; use a field, a computed signal or a pure pipe instead.
• The pipe operator has the lowest precedence: {{ a + b | number }} pipes the sum; use parentheses when needed.
• Interpolation output is escaped and bindings to dangerous properties (innerHTML, href=javascript:, style) are sanitised: Angular protects against XSS by default. Bypass APIs (DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrust...) are dangerous and should be avoided.
• Two-way binding with signals: [(ngModel)]="sig" and [(value)]="sig" accept a WritableSignal directly (since v17.2). Unwrap with sig() in read-only places.
• Reference variable scope: it is visible in the whole template including children, but not inside separate ng-templates declared elsewhere (structural scoping). Reference variables on a component give the instance; on a plain element the DOM element; #f="ngForm" exports a directive.

interviewQA: Difference between interpolation and property binding?
Interpolation renders a value as text and is sugar for binding a string; property binding [prop] sets any DOM or component property with its real type (number, boolean, object).
What does [(ngModel)] expand to?
[ngModel]="value" (ngModelChange)="value = $event"; it needs FormsModule.
What is a template statement?
The code in an event binding (click)="..."; it can assign values and call methods, and can use $event.
Why avoid method calls in template expressions?
They run on every change detection pass; use fields, computed signals or pure pipes to avoid repeated work.
How does Angular protect against XSS in templates?
Interpolation escapes text and property bindings sanitise untrusted values for HTML, styles and URLs; bypassSecurityTrust* disables that and must be avoided.
What is the safe navigation operator?
?. stops evaluation and yields undefined when the left side is null or undefined, as in user?.address?.city.

topics.name: Attribute, class, style and event bindings

beginner.content:
Binding HTML attributes, class and style

• Some attributes have no matching DOM property (aria-label, colspan, data-*). Bind them with [attr.name]. To toggle a CSS class use class binding ([class.active]="isOn"); to set an inline style use style binding ([style.width.px]="w"). Think of switches on a control panel that you flip from your data.
codeExamples:
...
  • {{ c.title }}
    • ...

beginner.content:
Event binding, $event and common events

• Event binding uses parentheses. $event is the event object (for DOM events) or the emitted value (for component outputs). Event handling usually calls a component method.
codeExamples:
<button (click)="onSave()">Save</button>
<input (input)="onType($event)">
<form (submit)="onSubmit($event)">...</form>

// onType(event: Event) {
//   const value = (event.target as HTMLInputElement).value;   // typed access to the input
// }

intermediate.content:
Keyboard, mouse and form events with modifiers

• Keyboard events (keydown, keyup) accept key filters: (keyup.enter), (keydown.escape), combinations such as (keydown.control.s). Mouse events: click, dblclick, mouseenter, mouseleave, mousedown, mouseup, contextmenu. Form events: input (every keystroke), change (on commit), submit, focus, blur, reset.
• Event modifiers in other frameworks (.prevent, .stop) do not exist in Angular: call $event.preventDefault() or stopPropagation() in the handler. Pseudo-events (window:resize), (document:keydown) listen on global targets; Angular removes the listener when the component is destroyed.
codeExamples:
Hover me
Open
...
// open(e: Event) { e.preventDefault(); this.router.navigate(['/x']); }

intermediate.content: Typed handlers and performance-friendly input

expert.content:
How bindings really work and pitfalls

• Class and style bindings merge: [class] and [class.x] from different sources (template, host bindings, directives) are combined with a defined precedence (template over directive over component host), so you rarely clash. Use [class]="{active: isOn, 'is-new': isNew}" with an object or array for several classes at once. The ngClass/ngStyle directives still work but native bindings are faster and preferred.
• [attr.x] removes the attribute when the value is null or undefined; a boolean attribute bound with property binding works as expected ([disabled]="flag"), while [attr.disabled]="false" still leaves "false" string present, a common bug.
• Event plumbing: handlers registered by Angular run inside the Angular zone and trigger change detection; high-frequency events (mousemove, scroll, resize) can cause many passes. Use eventCoalescing, debounce, or register outside the zone with NgZone.runOutsideAngular. Passive listeners are not configurable in templates; use fromEvent or Renderer2 when needed.
• Key names in filters follow DOM KeyboardEvent.key lowercase (enter, escape, arrowdown, space), and modifiers (alt, control, meta, shift) are dot-separated in alphabetical order. IME composition (Asian languages) fires keyup.enter prematurely; for search boxes use (input) plus debounce.
• Avoid $any() except where typing is truly impractical. Prefer handlers with typed parameters or reference variables ((input)="onChange(box.value)" with #box).
• Do not bind a click on non-interactive elements (div); use button or add role, tabindex and key handlers for accessibility.

interviewQA: Attribute vs property binding?
Attributes are the initial HTML values; properties are the live DOM state. [prop] sets the property; [attr.x] sets an attribute for cases with no property (aria-*, colspan).
How do you toggle a CSS class conditionally?
Use [class.name]="condition" or [class]="expr" (string, array or object); ngClass is the older equivalent.
How do you handle the Enter key in an input?
(keyup.enter)="handler()" or (keydown.enter) using the key filter syntax.
What is $event?
In DOM event bindings, the native event object; for component outputs, the emitted value.
How do you prevent default browser behaviour?
Call $event.preventDefault() in the handler; Angular has no .prevent modifier. (ngSubmit on a form already prevents the native submit.)
How do you listen to window or document events?
Use global targets in the binding: (window:resize), (document:keydown), which Angular cleans up automatically.

topics.name: Built-in control flow

beginner.content:
Conditional rendering with @if and @else

• Conditional rendering shows markup only when a condition is true. The built-in @if block (Angular 17+) replaces the old *ngIf. Add @else if and @else for other branches. It reads like normal code and needs no imports.

List rendering with @for, track and @empty

• List rendering repeats markup for each item with @for. The track expression is required: it tells Angular how to recognise each item (use a unique id) so it can reuse DOM nodes when the list changes. @empty shows when the list is empty.
codeExamples:
@for (c of courses; track c.id; let i = $index, last = $last) {
  • {{ i + 1 }}. {{ c.title }}
    • } @empty {
  • No courses yet
    • }

intermediate.content:
@switch and template variables

• @switch chooses one branch by value with @case and @default (no fall-through, no break needed). Template variables include the implicit @for variables $index, $count, $first, $last, $even, $odd and the @let declaration (Angular 18.1+, stable 19) to store an expression once.

Choosing track correctly

• track item.id is best for objects with ids; track $index is acceptable only for static lists; track item works for lists of primitives. Never track by a new object each time. Angular logs a warning (NG0955) for duplicate keys.
codeExamples: @for (u of users(); track u.id) { } @for (tag of tags; track tag) { {{ tag }} }

intermediate.content:
Migrating from legacy structural directives

Legacy (NgModule era)Built-in control flow
*ngIf="x; else tpl"@if (x) { } @else { }
*ngFor="let i of items; trackBy: fn"@for (i of items; track i.id) { }
[ngSwitch] / *ngSwitchCase@switch / @case
• Run the automatic migration: ng generate @angular/core:control-flow.

expert.content:
Internals, performance and gotchas

• Control flow is compiler syntax, not directives: it compiles into optimised template instructions, with no extra imports and a smaller bundle. In benchmarks the new @for is faster than *ngFor thanks to a better diffing algorithm, and track is mandatory because a wrong default (identity) caused performance bugs.
• A good track keeps DOM, component instances and their local state when data refreshes from the server with new object instances. With track $index, inserting at the front re-binds every row; with a wrong key you may keep stale child state.
• @for iterates any Iterable (arrays, Sets, Maps' entries via a helper), not plain objects; use the keyvalue pipe for objects. Large lists (thousands of rows) should use pagination or CDK virtual scroll, not just @for.
• Block content creates its own scope: @let variables are visible in the same and nested blocks, not outside. @let is not reassignable and, unlike a signal, is just an alias evaluated each pass.
• @if with as aliases also acts as a type guard in strict templates (the variable is narrowed to the truthy type), a main reason to prefer it over *ngIf for typing nullable data. Alias example: @if (user(); as u).
• @defer (also compiler control flow, covered in the performance module) lazily loads blocks; @placeholder/@loading/@error accompany it.
• Version: control flow ships as developer preview in 17 and stable from 18; *ngIf, *ngFor and NgSwitch are officially deprecated from v20 and slated for eventual removal, but remain functional.

interviewQA: What replaces *ngIf in modern Angular?
The built-in @if block (Angular 17+) with optional @else if and @else branches; no import is needed.
Why is track required in @for?
It lets Angular identify items so it reuses DOM and component instances on updates instead of re-creating the whole list; a missing key was a common performance bug with *ngFor.
What should be used in track?
A stable unique identifier like item.id; $index only for static lists; the item itself for primitives.
What does @empty do?
It renders its content when the iterated collection is empty.
What is @let?
A template declaration (Angular 18.1+, stable in 19) that stores an expression result in a read-only variable for reuse in the same template.
How do you migrate from *ngFor to @for?
Run ng generate @angular/core:control-flow, then ensure each loop has a proper track expression instead of trackBy.

topics.name: Template fragments and type checking

beginner.content:
ng-template, ng-container and ngTemplateOutlet

• An ng-template is a blueprint that Angular does not draw by itself, like an unused stamp. It renders only when something instantiates it. An ng-container is an invisible wrapper that groups things without adding an element to the DOM. ngTemplateOutlet says "draw this template here".
codeExamples:
No data available

 @if (items.length) { } @else { }

Title

Body

beginner.content:
Template fragments

• A template fragment is a chunk of markup you reuse within one component, defined once with ng-template (or an @let value) and rendered in several places. This avoids copy-paste when creating a whole component would be overkill.

intermediate.content:
Templates with context

• ngTemplateOutlet can pass a context object; inside the template read it with let- variables. This is how you build reusable list or table pieces where the parent supplies the row layout.
codeExamples:
{{ i + 1 }}{{ user.name }} @for (u of users; track u.id; let n = $index) { }
// component imports: [NgTemplateOutlet]

intermediate.content:
Passing templates into components

• A child can accept a template from its parent using content projection with a contentChild of type TemplateRef, then render it with its own data. This keeps data logic in the child and layout decisions in the parent.

Template type checking

• The Angular compiler can type-check templates like TypeScript checks code: wrong property names, wrong input types or calling a missing method become build errors. Enable it with "strictTemplates": true in tsconfig angularCompilerOptions (default in new projects).

expert.content:
Details and pitfalls

• ng-container is also how you place a structural directive or control flow without a wrapper element, and the host for *ngComponentOutlet. With built-in control flow you need it less often (the old *ngIf plus *ngFor on one element problem is gone: nest blocks instead).
• ng-template vs ng-content: ng-content projects already-created parent content; ng-template defers creation until you instantiate it, can be instantiated multiple times and accepts context. Templates declared in one place and rendered elsewhere keep the injector and scope of where they were declared.
• Context typing: add a static guard so strict templates know the shape: static ngTemplateContextGuard(dir: MyDirective, ctx: unknown): ctx is MyContext { return true; } in the directive that owns the template, or the template's let- variables are any. This is how NgFor/ngIf typed their variables in the legacy form.
• Strict template checking levels: basic mode checks only top-level expressions; fullTemplateTypeCheck checks embedded views; strictTemplates adds input and output typing, DOM event typing, safe-navigation inference and pipe argument checks. Sub-options (strictInputTypes, strictNullInputTypes, strictDomEventTypes, strictAttributeTypes and others) can be relaxed individually when migrating. Use $any() as a deliberate, searchable escape hatch.
• Diagnostic errors appear in the editor through the Angular Language Service, in ng build and ng serve, and in CI (ng build). Treat them as failing builds.
• Fragments rendered with ngTemplateOutlet are created and destroyed with their outlet view, so state in the fragment is lost if the outlet is toggled by @if.

interviewQA: ng-template vs ng-container?
ng-template is a non-rendered blueprint that you instantiate later (with outlets or structural directives); ng-container is an actual grouping node that renders its children but adds no DOM element.
What does ngTemplateOutlet do?
It stamps an ng-template into the DOM at that location and can provide a context object read with let- variables.
How can a parent customise part of a child's layout?
It passes an ng-template which the child captures with contentChild and renders using ngTemplateOutlet with its own context.
What is strictTemplates?
A compiler option that type-checks template expressions, inputs, outputs and events strictly, turning binding mistakes into build errors.
What is $any() for?
It casts an expression to any inside a template to bypass type checking when typing is impractical; use sparingly.
Why use ng-container instead of a div?
It groups or hosts directives without adding an extra element that could break CSS layout or semantics.
