topics.name: Built-in directives

beginner.content:
What are directives?

• A directive is a class that teaches an HTML element new tricks, like a sticker that says "turn red on hover". Angular has three directive types:
• Component directives: a directive with a template (every component is one).
• Attribute directives: change appearance or behaviour of an existing element (ngClass, ngStyle, ngModel).
• Structural directives: add or remove elements from the DOM (the legacy *ngIf, *ngFor; today replaced by @if and @for control flow).
codeExamples:
Attribute directive

Styled with ngStyle
A component is also a directive

beginner.content:
Legacy structural directives

• *ngIf, *ngFor and ngSwitch are the legacy way to branch and loop. You still meet them in most existing projects; new code uses @if, @for and @switch. The star (*) is shorthand for wrapping the element in an ng-template.
codeExamples:
Welcome back

Please log in
  • {{ i }} {{ c.title }}
    • Admin User

intermediate.content:
ngClass, ngStyle, ngModel

• ngClass accepts a string, array or object of class names ({ active: isOn }). ngStyle accepts an object of style names and values. For one or two classes or styles the native [class.x] and [style.x] are simpler and faster. ngModel (from FormsModule) two-way binds a form control and tracks its state (valid, touched).

ngTemplateOutlet and ngComponentOutlet

• ngTemplateOutlet renders a TemplateRef (with context); ngComponentOutlet renders a component class chosen at runtime, optionally with inputs and a custom injector.
codeExamples:
<ng-container *ngTemplateOutlet="tpl; context: { $implicit: user }" />
<ng-container *ngComponentOutlet="widget; inputs: { title: 'Sales' }" />
// class: widget: Type<unknown> = SalesWidgetComponent;

intermediate.content:
Built-in control flow vs legacy structural directives

Topic@if / @for / @switch*ngIf / *ngFor / ngSwitch
Import neededNoYes (NgIf, NgFor...)
PerformanceFaster, built into the compilerRuntime directives
Loop identitytrack requiredtrackBy optional
Empty state@empty blockelse template
ReadabilityReads like codeMicrosyntax
StatusRecommended (v17+), stable v18Legacy, deprecated since v20

expert.content:
Internals and tips

• Structural directives work with TemplateRef and ViewContainerRef: the star syntax *ngIf="x" is desugared by the compiler into <ng-template [ngIf]="x">. The directive decides when to createEmbeddedView or clear it. The built-in control flow skips directives completely and compiles to template instructions, which is why it needs no imports and is faster and more type-friendly.
• ngClass/ngStyle performance: they diff objects on every change detection; binding [class]/[style] directly is cheaper. ngStyle with unit keys ('width.px') is supported. Prefer CSS classes over many inline styles.
• ngTemplateOutlet context gets $implicit as the default let- value; an injector option can be passed too. ngComponentOutlet supports inputs (16.2+), injector, content (projectable nodes) and environmentInjector; inputs set through it are applied with setInput so signal inputs work.
• ngModel inside a form needs a name attribute or [ngModelOptions]="{standalone: true}"; it is part of template-driven forms (see the forms module). The directive in FormsModule is not tree-shaken away if you import the whole module; standalone imports can list only NgModel.
• Migrate with ng generate @angular/core:control-flow. *ngFor's trackBy functions should become inline track expressions.
• All directives need to be imported in standalone components; forgetting NgClass gives "Can't bind to 'ngClass' since it isn't a known property".

interviewQA: What are the three kinds of directives?
Components (with a template), attribute directives (alter an element's behaviour or look) and structural directives (add or remove DOM).
ngClass vs [class.x]?
ngClass handles many classes from an object, array or string; [class.x] binds one class and is lighter. Prefer native class bindings when possible.
What does the asterisk in *ngIf mean?
Shorthand: Angular wraps the element in an ng-template and passes the expression to the directive.
Why is @for preferred over *ngFor?
It is built into the compiler (no imports), faster, has an @empty block, and requires track for correct DOM reuse.
What is ngComponentOutlet used for?
Rendering a component whose class is chosen at runtime, with optional inputs and injector.
Are *ngIf and *ngFor removed?
No, they still work but are deprecated in recent versions (v20) in favour of control flow; migrate with the provided schematic.

topics.name: Custom attribute directives

beginner.content:
Creating custom attribute directives

• Make your own directive when you want to reuse behaviour on many elements without a template. Example: a highlight directive that colours any element on hover. Create it with ng generate directive highlight.
• The host element is the element carrying the directive (here the <p>). The selector in square brackets [appHighlight] means "match elements with this attribute".

intermediate.content:
Host bindings and host listeners the modern way

• Host bindings set properties, classes, styles and attributes of the host element from the directive; host listeners handle host events. The recommended place is the host metadata property (the @HostBinding and @HostListener decorators still work).

Directive selectors and inputs/outputs

• Selector forms: [attr], [attr=value], element, .class, input[type=text], a comma list [a], [b] and exclusion :not(.skip). Directives cannot have element selectors that clash with components on the same tag. Use a unique prefix (app-, or your library's).
• Directive inputs configure behaviour; use an alias equal to the selector (as above) to allow [appHighlight]="color" as a single attribute. Outputs notify the host component. Use the same input()/output() functions as components.

expert.content:
Best practices and pitfalls

• Do not use ElementRef.nativeElement for styling if you can bind: prefer host bindings (declarative, SSR-safe). If you must touch the DOM, use Renderer2 or guard with afterNextRender, because on the server there is no real DOM. Direct innerHTML writes bypass sanitisation and invite XSS.
• Host listeners are registered once and removed automatically on destroy. Global targets are available: '(window:scroll)': 'onScroll()'. High-frequency events trigger change detection; consider running outside the zone.
• Specificity: host class bindings merge with template bindings; host styles lose against template bindings on the same element. Host element attributes written by a directive are visible to CSS ([aria-busy=true]), a nice hook for styling.
• Directives are standalone by default (v19); for older code add standalone: true. An unused import of a directive produces a compiler warning.
• Keep directives single-purpose and prefix names; document the selector and inputs. For behaviour shared by several components consider the composition API (next lesson) instead of inheritance.
• Testing: create a small host component with TestBed, apply the directive, dispatch events with triggerEventHandler or dispatchEvent, and assert on the DOM.

interviewQA: What is an attribute directive?
A directive attached to an existing element via an attribute selector that changes its appearance or behaviour without altering the DOM structure.
What is the host element?
The element in the template on which the directive (or component) is applied.
@HostBinding vs @HostListener?
@HostBinding binds a property/class/style of the host to a directive field; @HostListener subscribes to events on the host (or window/document). The host metadata property supports both.
How can a directive be configured?
With inputs (input()/@Input), optionally aliased to the selector name, and it can notify with outputs.
How do you get the host element in a directive?
Inject ElementRef (inject(ElementRef)) and use nativeElement, or better use host bindings or Renderer2.
Which selectors can a directive use?
Attribute, element, class and combined selectors, comma lists and :not(), e.g. input[appTrim].

topics.name: Structural directives, composition and injection

beginner.content:
Creating custom structural directives

• A custom structural directive decides whether to show a piece of template. It receives a TemplateRef (the blueprint) and a ViewContainerRef (the place to draw). Example: *appHasRole="'ADMIN'" shows content only for admins (a UI convenience; the backend still enforces permissions).

intermediate.content:
Directive injection and host directives

• Directive injection: directives use DI like any class: inject(ElementRef), services, and other directives on the same element (inject(NgControl, { optional: true })) or on a parent element (inject(ParentDirective, { host: true })).
• The directive composition API (Angular 15+) lets you build behaviour from small directives. With host directives a component or directive lists directives in hostDirectives; they are applied to its host automatically, and you choose which inputs and outputs to expose. This replaces most use of inheritance for sharing behaviour.
A structural directive with template context

expert.content:
Deep dive

• Desugaring: *appHasRole="'ADMIN'" becomes <ng-template [appHasRole]="'ADMIN'">...</ng-template>. The microsyntax (*appX="expr; let item; as alias") maps to inputs prefixed with the selector (appXAs etc.). Add a static ngTemplateContextGuard and ngTemplateGuard_appHasRole for strict template typing and type narrowing.
• Host directive rules: host directives must be standalone, run before the host component (their constructors and inputs initialise first), can themselves have host directives, and their outputs/inputs are hidden unless exposed. You cannot host-compose a directive twice. Lifecycle hooks on the host directive run alongside.
• Injection context: inject() works only in constructors and field initialisers (the injection context). A directive can read the closest NgControl or form container; using { self: true } or { host: true } restricts the lookup. For ControlValueAccessor wiring a host directive is a clean extension point.
• Security: UI role directives are cosmetic. Anything hidden by a directive remains in the JavaScript bundle and can be called from the console; the Spring Boot API must authorise every request.
• Performance: creating and clearing views on every effect run is expensive; only recreate when the condition actually flips (compare previous state). Using effect() inside a directive requires the injection context and writes to the view container synchronously during change detection of the host; for simple cases an @if on a computed signal is better.
• Comparison: mixins and inheritance share code but tightly couple; host directives compose at runtime, keep each unit testable and let consumers choose the exposed API.

interviewQA: How does a structural directive work?
It injects TemplateRef and ViewContainerRef and creates or clears an embedded view from the template depending on its inputs; the * syntax wraps the element in an ng-template.
What are host directives?
Directives listed in a component or directive's hostDirectives metadata; Angular applies them to the host element, optionally exposing selected inputs and outputs.
What is the directive composition API good for?
Reusing behaviour (disabled state, tooltips, focus handling) through composition instead of inheritance or duplicated code.
How can a directive get another directive on the same element?
inject(OtherDirective) (use optional: true when not guaranteed) in the injection context.
Is hiding a button with *appHasRole secure?
No. It is only a UI convenience; the server must enforce authorisation because client code can be bypassed.
What is ngTemplateContextGuard?
A static method on a directive that tells the strict template checker the type of its template context so let- variables are typed.

topics.name: Formatting pipes

beginner.content:
What are pipes? Built-in pipes

• A pipe takes a value, changes how it looks, and returns the result, like a coffee filter between the raw data and the screen. It never changes the original value. You write it with the pipe character: {{ value | pipeName }}.
• Angular ships built-in pipes in @angular/common: DatePipe, UpperCasePipe, LowerCasePipe, TitleCasePipe, CurrencyPipe, DecimalPipe, PercentPipe, JsonPipe, SlicePipe, KeyValuePipe, AsyncPipe and more. In a standalone component list the ones you use in imports.

intermediate.content:
DatePipe, CurrencyPipe, DecimalPipe, PercentPipe in detail

PipeSignatureNotes
datedate:format:timezone:localePresets: short, medium, long, fullDate, shortTime. Accepts Date, ISO string, ms number
currencycurrency:code:display:digitsInfo:localedisplay: symbol, code, symbol-narrow; digitsInfo like 1.0-0
numbernumber:"minInt.minFrac-maxFrac"Rounds half away from zero; uses locale separators
percentpercent:digitsInfoMultiplies by 100: 0.256 gives 26%
uppercase / lowercase / titlecaseno argumentsStrings only; null returns null
codeExamples:
{{ order.createdAt | date:"fullDate" }}

{{ order.createdAt | date:"shortTime":"+0530" }}

{{ order.total | currency:"USD":"symbol":"1.0-0" }}

{{ order.total | currency:"EUR":"code" }}

{{ 1234567.891 | number:"1.0-1" }}

{{ 0.256 | percent:"1.1-1" }}

intermediate.content:
Locale and default currency

• Pipes format using the application locale (default en-US). To use another locale, register its data once and provide LOCALE_ID. The default currency code can be set with DEFAULT_CURRENCY_CODE. See the internationalisation module for full details.

expert.content:
Pitfalls and good practice

• Dates: JSON delivers dates as strings; DatePipe parses ISO-8601 strings, but a string without a time zone is interpreted in local time, a classic off-by-one-day source. Without a timezone argument the pipe uses the browser's zone. Prefer sending ISO instants (UTC with Z) from Spring Boot (Instant/OffsetDateTime) and formatting at the edge.
• Format strings are case-sensitive: yyyy year, MM month (mm is minutes), dd day of month, HH 24-hour (hh is 12-hour), Y is week-based year (a bug source around new year). Invalid input throws NG02100 (InvalidPipeArgument) which breaks rendering, so guard nulls with @if or ?? '' or validate upstream.
• Money: floating-point numbers are not exact. Keep amounts as integer minor units or as strings/decimals from the backend (BigDecimal serialised as string) and only format for display. CurrencyPipe does not convert currencies; it only formats.
• number pipe uses Intl-like rules from the locale data bundled by Angular, not Intl.NumberFormat; for exotic needs (compact notation) format in a service or custom pipe using Intl.
• Pipes in templates are tree-shakable standalone classes; importing CommonModule pulls them all in and is discouraged in new code.
• Pipes take any expression as an argument, including component fields, but arguments are re-evaluated on each check; keep them primitive for pure-pipe caching to work.

interviewQA: What is a pipe in Angular?
A function-like template construct used with | that transforms a value for display without modifying the underlying data.
How do you format a date as 20/10/2026?
Use the DatePipe: {{ value | date:"dd/MM/yyyy" }}; remember MM is month and mm is minutes.
Does CurrencyPipe convert currencies?
No. It only formats a number as money for a given currency code and locale; conversion must be done in code or by the backend.
How do you change the locale used by pipes?
Register the locale data with registerLocaleData and provide LOCALE_ID, or pass a locale argument to the pipe.
Why might a date appear one day off?
Date-only strings or missing time zones are parsed in local time; send ISO instants with offset or format with an explicit timezone.
Where do you import built-in pipes in standalone components?
In the component's imports array (DatePipe, CurrencyPipe...), or all at once via CommonModule, which is discouraged in new code.

topics.name: Data pipes, async and chaining

beginner.content:
JsonPipe, SlicePipe, KeyValuePipe

• JsonPipe prints an object as formatted JSON: the quickest debugging tool in a template. SlicePipe returns a part of an array or string (like substring/slice). KeyValuePipe turns an object or Map into a list of { key, value } so you can loop over it.
codeExamples:
{{ user | json }}

{{ title | slice:0:20 }}...

@for (c of courses | slice:0:3; track c.id) {

{{ c.title }}

} @for (entry of scores | keyvalue; track entry.key) {

{{ entry.key }}: {{ entry.value }}

}

beginner.content:
AsyncPipe, chaining and parameters

• AsyncPipe subscribes to an Observable (or Promise) for you, shows the latest value, and unsubscribes automatically when the component is destroyed: no manual subscribe, no memory leaks. Chaining pipes applies them left to right. Pipe parameters follow colons.

intermediate.content:
Working with the async pipe properly

• One subscription per | async. If the template uses the same stream twice, either alias it once with @if (data$ | async; as data) or use @let, otherwise HTTP observables fire several requests.
• AsyncPipe also works with Promises; it returns null until the first emission, so type it as T | null. With signals you no longer need it: bind the signal directly or use toSignal(obs$).

Pipe parameters and chaining rules

• Parameters are separated with colons and can be literals, fields or expressions: value | date:format:tz. Pipe precedence is lower than the ternary operator, so wrap in parentheses: {{ (cond ? a : b) | uppercase }}. Chaining order matters: {{ amount | currency | uppercase }} works because currency returns a string.
codeExamples:
{{ today | date:"EEEE" | uppercase }}                    <!-- TUESDAY -->
{{ (isAdmin ? "admin" : "user") | titlecase }}            <!-- parentheses required -->
{{ items | slice:start:end }}                              <!-- parameters from fields -->

expert.content:
Details worth knowing

• AsyncPipe internals: it is an impure pipe that stores the latest value and calls markForCheck() when a new value arrives, which is why it works with OnPush. It handles resubscribing when the source reference changes; do not create a new Observable in the template (obs$ = this.getData() as a method call re-subscribes every check). Create streams once as fields.
• Errors: if the observable errors, AsyncPipe rethrows into Angular's ErrorHandler; handle errors upstream with catchError returning a fallback or an error state object.
• KeyValuePipe sorts entries by key by default (a stable compare); pass a comparator function to preserve insertion order: obj | keyvalue: originalOrder. It is an impure pipe that diffs the object internally and returns a new array only when entries change. SlicePipe is pure and returns a new array when input or arguments change; a mutated array (push) will not refresh it, so use immutable updates.
• JsonPipe is impure and runs JSON.stringify every check: use only for debugging, never in production lists.
• Pipes execute only in templates. In code call the class directly: new DatePipe('en-US').transform(d, 'short') or inject it by listing it in providers.
• With signals, prefer computed() for derived values and use pipes for presentation formatting only.

interviewQA: What does the async pipe do?
It subscribes to an Observable or Promise, renders the latest value, triggers change detection when new values arrive and unsubscribes automatically on destroy.
How do you avoid multiple subscriptions with async?
Subscribe once and alias the value: @if (obs$ | async; as value) or @let value = obs$ | async, or convert with toSignal.
How do you loop over an object's properties?
Use the keyvalue pipe: @for (e of obj | keyvalue; track e.key) and read e.key and e.value.
In what order are chained pipes applied?
Left to right: the output of each pipe is the input of the next, e.g. value | slice:0:5 | uppercase.
What is the json pipe used for?
Debug printing of objects; it stringifies on every check, so it should not be used in production views.
Why do you need parentheses around a ternary before a pipe?
The pipe operator has lower precedence than the conditional operator, so without parentheses the pipe would apply only to the last branch.

topics.name: Custom pipes

beginner.content:
Creating custom pipes

• When no built-in pipe fits, write your own: a small class with the @Pipe decorator and a transform method. Example: show "5 minutes ago" or shorten text with "...". Create one with ng generate pipe shared/truncate.

intermediate.content:
Parameterized custom pipes and pure vs impure

• Extra arguments in the template map to extra parameters of transform, in order. A pure pipe (default) runs only when its input value or arguments change by reference/primitive value; Angular caches the result. An impure pipe (pure: false) runs on every change detection pass; use it only when the output depends on something outside the arguments (such as a service or mutated array), and keep it extremely cheap.
Injecting services and using a pipe in code

expert.content:
Pipe performance and best practices for custom pipes

• Pure pipes are memoised per call site: each place the pipe is used keeps the last arguments and result. That makes a pure pipe an ideal cheap place for derived display data instead of a template method call.
• Pipe performance pitfalls: filtering or sorting arrays in an impure pipe runs the work on every check, thousands of times per second on large lists. Instead filter in a computed() signal or in the service, and keep pipes for formatting. Pure pipes cannot see mutation of an array/object argument, so update state immutably (list = [...list, x]).
• Best practices: pure by default, no side effects, no HTTP calls, no random or time reads without an explicit parameter (as in timeAgo, where you pass a ticking now to refresh), return a stable type, handle null and undefined, give a clear lower camel-case name, keep pipes in a shared folder, write a unit test calling transform directly, and prefer a computed() or a function for logic that is not about presentation.
• Typing: use generics and overload-like unions so strict templates catch misuse, and declare nullable inputs (string | null | undefined) so it composes with the async pipe.
• Standalone pipes are tree-shakable (standalone: true before v19, implicit later). Do not mark a pipe providedIn root; list it in providers if you need it in a class.
• Do not use pipes to sort or filter for large tables; combine with pagination, @for track and virtual scrolling.

interviewQA: How do you create a custom pipe?
Decorate a class with @Pipe({ name: "x" }), implement PipeTransform.transform(value, ...args) and import it in the components that use it.
Pure vs impure pipe?
Pure pipes re-run only when their inputs change (cached); impure pipes (pure: false) run every change detection cycle and can hurt performance.
Why does a pure filter pipe not update after array.push()?
The array reference is unchanged, so the pure pipe sees identical inputs; replace the array immutably or do the filtering in a computed signal.
When is an impure pipe justified?
When the result depends on mutable external state that cannot be passed as an argument, such as AsyncPipe; keep the work minimal.
Pipe or method call in a template?
A pure pipe is cached and only re-runs on input changes; a method call is evaluated on every check, so the pipe (or computed signal) is better.
How do you test a pipe?
Instantiate it (or use TestBed for DI) and call transform with various inputs, including null and edge cases.

topics.name: Services and DI fundamentals

beginner.content:
What is a service? Service architecture

• A service is an ordinary TypeScript class that holds logic or data that more than one component needs: calling APIs, storing the logged-in user, calculating prices. Think of it as a shared kitchen: components are dining tables; they should not each cook the food.
• Service architecture: keep components thin (display and user events) and put business logic and data access in services. It is exactly the Spring layering of controller, service and repository, applied to the browser.
• Generate with ng generate service courses/course (short ng g s), which creates course.service.ts with @Injectable.

Dependency Injection fundamentals

• Dependency Injection (DI) means a class does not create the objects it needs with new; it asks for them and the framework supplies them. The restaurant analogy: you do not grow vegetables, you order and the waiter brings them. Spring developers know this as the IoC container with @Autowired.
• @Injectable() marks a class that can be injected (and itself receive dependencies). The token is the key you ask for; usually the class itself.

intermediate.content:
Constructor-based injection vs inject()

• Constructor-based injection lists dependencies as constructor parameters (the style known from Java and older Angular). The inject() function (Angular 14+) does the same in field initialisers and is the modern recommendation: shorter, works in functional guards/interceptors/resolvers, and avoids long constructors and super() problems in inheritance.
A realistic service layer

Dependency injection tokens

• Every dependency is looked up by a token. For a class the class itself is the token. For things that are not classes (a config object, a string, an interface, which does not exist at runtime) use an InjectionToken (see the provider types lesson).

expert.content:
How the injector works

• The injector is a map from token to provider plus a cache of created instances. When you inject a token, Angular finds the provider, runs its factory once, stores the instance and returns it on later requests (singleton per injector). Instances are created lazily on first request.
• @Injectable metadata is required so the compiler emits the parameter metadata for constructor injection; with inject() the decorator is still needed if you use providedIn, and is conventional for every service.
• Injection context: calling inject() outside it throws NG0203. Wrap code with runInInjectionContext(injector, () => ...) when you must call it later (for example in a callback), or capture dependencies up front.
• Circular dependencies (A needs B needs A) throw NG0200; break the cycle by extracting a third service, injecting lazily through the Injector (injector.get(Token) when needed) or restructuring responsibilities.
• Decorator injection with inheritance: constructor injection forces subclasses to repeat all parent parameters; inject() fields avoid that, a major reason to prefer it.
• Compare with Spring: @Service ≈ @Injectable, @Autowired ≈ inject(), @Bean method ≈ useFactory provider, @Qualifier ≈ separate InjectionToken, @Scope("prototype") ≈ providing in a component. Angular injectors are hierarchical and the same class can have different instances at different levels.

interviewQA: What is a service in Angular?
A class (usually @Injectable) that encapsulates reusable logic or data access and is provided to components and other services through dependency injection.
What is dependency injection and why use it?
A class receives its collaborators from the framework instead of constructing them, which decouples code, enables sharing instances and makes testing with mocks easy.
inject() vs constructor injection?

Both ask the injector for a token. inject() works in field initialisers and functions (guards, interceptors), reads shorter, and simplifies inheritance; constructor injection is the classic form and still supported.
What does @Injectable do?
Marks a class as participating in DI and can set providedIn so the class registers itself with an injector.
Where can inject() be called?
Only in an injection context: constructors, field initialisers, provider factories, functional guards/resolvers/interceptors, or inside runInInjectionContext.
How do Angular services relate to Spring beans?
Both are container-managed singletons by default; @Injectable with providedIn root corresponds to a singleton @Service bean, and inject() to @Autowired.

topics.name: Providers and the injector hierarchy

beginner.content:
Provider configuration and providedIn: 'root'

• A provider tells the injector how to create a token. The shortest provider is the class itself. With @Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' }) the service registers in the root injector: one instance for the whole app, created only if somebody uses it (so unused services are tree-shaken out of the bundle). This is the default choice for most services.

Component-level providers

• Put a service in a component's providers array and each instance of that component gets its own service instance (and so do its child components). Use it for per-component state, like a form wizard's draft.

intermediate.content:
Route-level providers and environment injectors

• Route-level providers: the providers property of a route creates an environment injector for that route and its children. The service is created when the route is first activated and lives as long as the route's injector, ideal for feature state in lazy-loaded areas.
• Environment injectors hold services of modules/app/routes. There are: the platform injector, the root (application) injector, and child environment injectors for lazy routes. createEnvironmentInjector() can create one by hand.

Hierarchical Dependency Injection

• Injectors form a tree that mirrors your app. A request for a token starts at the element injector of the requesting component, walks up the parents (directives, components, host elements), then continues through the environment injectors (route injectors, root), and finally the platform. The first provider found wins; if none, a NullInjectorError (NG0201) is thrown.
codeExamples:
Resolution order for inject(Token) in a component:
  1. the component's own providers / viewProviders
  2. parent component / directive element injectors (walking up the DOM tree)
  3. route environment injector(s) (lazy route providers)
  4. root environment injector (providedIn: 'root', app config)
  5. platform injector
  -> not found: NullInjectorError (unless optional: true)

intermediate.content:
providers vs viewProviders

• providers on a component are visible to its view and to projected content; viewProviders are visible only to the component's own view (not to content children projected via ng-content). Use viewProviders to keep a service private from projected content.

expert.content:
Choosing the right scope

ScopeUse forLifetime
providedIn: 'root'Auth, API clients, global stateWhole app
Route providersFeature-area state, per-feature configWhile the route injector lives (lazy chunk, normally for the session)
Component providersPer-instance state (wizard, table, dialog)Component instance
Dynamic environment injectorPlugin or micro-frontend isolationUntil destroyed

Pitfalls and internals

• Duplicate singletons: providing a root service again in a component or lazy route silently creates a second instance, so state is not shared and bugs appear (the classic "my service has two copies"). Provide a stateful service in exactly one place.
• Lifetime of route injectors: a lazy route injector is created once and kept for the lifetime of the app (it is not destroyed on navigation away), so route-level services behave like singletons per route tree, not per visit. Component-level providers are destroyed with the component, and their ngOnDestroy is called (services can implement OnDestroy).
• Tree shaking: only providedIn and InjectionToken factories are tree-shakable; services listed in app providers always ship. providedIn: 'platform' shares across multiple Angular apps on one page; 'any' (deprecated) creates one per lazy module.
• NgModule world (legacy): module providers arrays, forRoot() / forChild() patterns to avoid duplicates, and eager modules share the root injector while lazy modules get a child injector. Standalone code uses provideXxx() functions instead, which return EnvironmentProviders (only allowed in environment contexts, not component providers).
• The root injector is created at bootstrap, so root services that do work in constructors run lazily on first inject; use provideAppInitializer() (v19+; older APP_INITIALIZER) to run startup code such as loading configuration before the app renders.

interviewQA: What does providedIn: 'root' mean?
The service is registered in the root injector as a single shared instance for the app and is tree-shakable if never used.
How do you get a new service instance per component?
List the service in the component's providers array; each component instance and its children get a separate instance.
What are route-level providers?
Providers declared in a route config that create an environment injector for that route and its children, handy for lazy-loaded feature services.
Explain hierarchical DI.
Injectors form a tree; a token is resolved from the requesting element upward through parent element injectors, route/root environment injectors and the platform, using the first matching provider.
providers vs viewProviders?
providers are visible to a component's view and projected content; viewProviders only to its own view.
How can a service end up with two instances?
By providing it in more than one injector (for example root plus a component or lazy route); each injector creates its own instance.

topics.name: Provider types and tokens

beginner.content:
InjectionToken and value providers

• Interfaces and primitives do not exist at runtime, so Angular cannot use them as keys. An InjectionToken is a unique key object you create for them. A value provider (useValue) supplies a ready-made value, like a config object or a constant.

intermediate.content:
Class, factory and existing providers

• Class provider (useClass): "when someone asks for X, create Y": swap implementations (real vs mock, like a Spring profile). Factory provider (useFactory): run code to build the value, with deps or inject() inside. Existing provider (useExisting): make one token an alias of another so both return the same instance.

Multi providers

• With multi: true several providers contribute to one token, and injecting it gives an array. Angular itself uses this for HTTP_INTERCEPTORS and APP_INITIALIZER. It is a plugin mechanism.

expert.content:
Design notes and pitfalls

ProviderKeySpring analogy
useClassclass to instantiate@Component bean / @Primary alternative
useValueexisting value@Value / constant bean
useFactoryfunction returning value@Bean method
useExistinganother tokenAlias / bean reference
multi: truecollectionInjecting a List of beans
• Abstract classes as tokens: since interfaces vanish, an abstract class is the idiomatic way to inject by abstraction (as with Logger). An InjectionToken typed with an interface is the alternative and can hold function values.
• Tree-shakable tokens: give an InjectionToken a providedIn: 'root' and a factory, so it has a default and costs nothing when unused; override it in tests or per environment with a normal provider.
• Multi providers and ordering: the array order equals provider registration order, which for interceptors defines execution order; mixing multi and non-multi providers for the same token is an error. Provider arrays in lower injectors replace, not merge with, higher ones.
• useFactory with deps (legacy form: deps: [Http, APP_CONFIG]) is equivalent to calling inject() in the factory; prefer inject() style. Factories run in an injection context.
• useValue is shared: mutating the object affects every consumer; freeze it (Object.freeze) or expose it read-only.
• Do not read environment values deep inside services; provide them as a token so tests can override. For secrets: nothing in a browser bundle is secret.
• The older @Inject(TOKEN) parameter decorator is the constructor-injection counterpart of inject(TOKEN).

interviewQA: Why do we need InjectionToken?
Interfaces, strings and plain objects are not valid runtime keys; an InjectionToken is a unique runtime key (with type information) for injecting such values.
useClass vs useExisting?
useClass creates a new instance of the given class for the token; useExisting aliases the token to another token so both resolve to the same instance.
When do you use useFactory?
When the value needs logic or other dependencies to create, such as choosing an implementation by environment.
What does multi: true do?
Lets several providers register under one token; injection returns an array of all values, used for plugins and interceptors.
How do you inject by interface?
Define an abstract class or InjectionToken as the key and provide an implementation with useClass or useValue.
How would you swap a real service for a mock in tests?
Provide { provide: RealService, useClass: MockService } or useValue with a stub in TestBed.configureTestingModule.

topics.name: Resolution modifiers

beginner.content:
Optional dependencies

• Normally if a token has no provider Angular throws an error. Mark the dependency optional and you get null instead, like a guest who may not show up. Useful for plugins or components that work with or without a parent.

Self, SkipSelf and Host

• self: look only in the current element's own injector. skipSelf: start looking in the parent, ignoring the current one. host: stop the search at the host element of the current component (do not go beyond). Combine with optional.

intermediate.content:
Host and Optional decorators (constructor parameter decorators)

• Before inject() options existed the same ideas were parameter decorators: @Optional(), @Self(), @SkipSelf(), @Host(). They are fully supported in constructor injection and common in older libraries.

A practical use: nested tree nodes

• A tree node that registers itself with its parent node: skip itself to find the parent, optional so the root node works.

expert.content:
Rules, pitfalls and migration

• Modifier combinations: { self: true, optional: true } is the common safe check for "is it provided right here". self and skipSelf cannot be combined. host bounds the search at the host element, important for content/view providers: it lets a child directive find the component whose template it sits in without leaking into unrelated ancestors.
• Optional only handles missing providers; errors thrown while constructing an existing provider still propagate.
• The legacy decorators and the options object are equivalent; ng generate @angular/core:inject migrates constructor injection to inject(), preserving modifiers (v19+). The inject() flags enum (InjectFlags) is deprecated in favour of the options object.
• Where it matters: Angular's own ControlContainer, NgControl and MatFormField lookups use these modifiers; custom form controls and compound components (tabs, accordions, menus) are the usual consumers.
• Prefer explicit inputs or a dedicated token to reaching for the parent via DI when the relationship is a feature of your API; DI-based parent lookup couples child and parent implicitly.
• Self-injection loops: providing a token with useExisting that points to itself yields a cyclic dependency error.

interviewQA: What does @Optional() / { optional: true } do?
Returns null instead of throwing when no provider is found for the token.
@Self vs @SkipSelf?
@Self restricts lookup to the current element injector; @SkipSelf skips the current injector and starts at its parent.
What does @Host do?
Limits the lookup at the host element of the current component, so providers beyond the component boundary are not used.
Which is the modern syntax for these modifiers?
The options object of inject(): inject(Token, { optional, self, skipSelf, host }).
Give a use case for skipSelf.
A recursive component or tree node that needs its parent instance of the same type, skipping its own provider.

topics.name: Service patterns, communication and testing

beginner.content:
Shared services and communication between components

• A shared service is one instance injected into many components, so they can share data without being parent and child, like a notice board in the hall. Use a signal inside the service to hold state; every component that reads it updates automatically.

Singleton service patterns

• Singleton: providedIn: 'root' gives one instance per application: the standard way. Never write your own static getInstance(); the injector already guarantees the singleton, and tests can replace it. Keep singletons stateless where possible or hold only well-owned state.

intermediate.content:
Communication patterns compared

MechanismWhen
Signals in a serviceDefault for shared state (modern)
BehaviorSubject / Observable in a serviceStreams, existing RxJS code, async sources
Subject / event busFire-and-forget events (toast, logout notification)
Inputs and outputsDirect parent and child
Router (params, state)Passing identifiers between pages
NgRx / signal storeLarge, complex app-wide state

Service testing

• Services are easy to test because their dependencies are injected. For a service without dependencies just create it with new. With dependencies use TestBed, provide fakes, and for HTTP use provideHttpClientTesting() and HttpTestingController.

expert.content:
Dependency Injection best practices

• Single responsibility: one service, one purpose (CourseApi for HTTP, CartState for state, ToastService for messages). Avoid "god" services.
• Expose less: keep writable signals/subjects private and publish read-only views (asReadonly(), asObservable()); mutate only through methods so invariants hold.
• Depend on abstractions: tokens and abstract classes for things that vary (logging, storage, payment); concrete classes for the rest. Do not over-abstract single implementations.
• Prefer inject() in new code, put dependencies in readonly fields, and avoid the service-locator anti-pattern (injecting Injector everywhere and calling get() dynamically) except for plugin scenarios.
• Services must clean up: implement OnDestroy for component-scoped services, and use DestroyRef and takeUntilDestroyed() for subscriptions in root services' long-lived streams only when really needed.
• No UI in services: no direct DOM access; if you need the DOM use Renderer2 or the DOCUMENT token (inject(DOCUMENT)), which also keeps SSR safe. Browser globals (window, localStorage) should be wrapped in a service behind a token so tests and SSR can substitute them.
• Testing: configure only what the unit needs, fake HTTP with HttpTestingController, override providers with useValue, and test signals by reading them after calling methods (computed values update synchronously). Use TestBed.runInInjectionContext to test functions that call inject().
• Singleton pitfalls: state in root services lives for the whole session; in SSR a root singleton is shared across requests only if the injector is shared. Angular creates a fresh application injector per request, but module-level variables are shared, so never keep user data in module scope.
• Version note: inject() since v14, standalone provideXxx functions v14+, provideAppInitializer v19, ng generate @angular/core:inject migration v19.

interviewQA: How do two unrelated components share state?
Through a shared root service that holds the state (signals or a BehaviorSubject); both inject the same instance.
How do you make a service a singleton?
Register it in the root injector with providedIn: 'root' (or in app providers); Angular then creates one instance for the app.
How do you unit test a service that uses HttpClient?
Provide provideHttpClient() and provideHttpClientTesting(), inject HttpTestingController, trigger the call, then expectOne(url).flush(data) and verify().
Why expose asReadonly() or asObservable() instead of the writable source?
To stop consumers from changing state directly; changes go through service methods so rules stay in one place.
What is a service locator and why avoid it?
Fetching dependencies dynamically from an Injector instead of declaring them; it hides dependencies and hurts testability and tree shaking.
How do you replace a dependency in a test?
In TestBed.configureTestingModule({ providers: [{ provide: Real, useValue: fake }] }) or useClass with a stub class.

beginner.content:
What this module covers

A component is born, updated, rendered and destroyed. Angular calls lifecycle hooks at each step so you can run code at the right moment.

interviewQA: How should I use this checklist?
Work through the lessons in order, tick each item once you can explain it and write a small example from memory. The last column tells you which lesson to revisit.

topics.name: Lifecycle overview, constructor and the first hooks

beginner.content:
The life of a component

• Think of a component like an employee: hired (created), onboarded (inputs set), working (views rendered and updated), and finally leaves (destroyed). Angular's component lifecycle lets you run code at each of those moments through lifecycle hooks: methods with fixed names such as ngOnInit.
• The constructor is plain TypeScript (like a Java constructor). It runs first, before Angular has set any @Input. Use it only to receive dependencies (or use inject()) and set simple fields.
• ngOnInit() runs once, after the first inputs are set. This is where you load data and start work.
• To use a hook, implement its interface (OnInit) and add the method. Interfaces are optional but catch typos.

intermediate.content:
The hooks in order, and constructor vs ngOnInit

Lifecycle ordering for one component:
1. constructor, 2. ngOnChanges (only if it has bound inputs; runs before ngOnInit and again on every input change), 3. ngOnInit (once), 4. ngDoCheck (every change detection pass), 5. ngAfterContentInit (once), 6. ngAfterContentChecked (every pass), 7. ngAfterViewInit (once), 8. ngAfterViewChecked (every pass), 9. ngOnDestroy (once).

HookRunsTypical use
ngOnChangesBefore init, then on each input changeReact to a changed @Input with old and new values
ngOnInitOnceFetch data, set up subscriptions
ngDoCheckEvery CD passCustom change detection (rare)
ngAfterContentInit / CheckedOnce / every passWork with projected content (ContentChild)
ngAfterViewInit / CheckedOnce / every passWork with ViewChild, third-party widgets
ngOnDestroyOnceCleanup

ngOnChanges and ngOnInit in practice

• ngOnChanges(changes: SimpleChanges) gives a SimpleChange per changed input with previousValue, currentValue and firstChange. It only fires when the input reference changes: mutating an object in place does not trigger it.
• ngOnInit is the right place for initial data loading because the inputs are ready. The constructor must stay free of logic so the component is easy to test.

expert.content:
ngDoCheck, internals and version notes

• ngDoCheck runs on every change detection pass of the component (and for OnPush components it still runs when the parent is checked, even if the component itself is skipped). Use it only to detect changes Angular cannot see, such as in-place mutation of an input object, and keep it extremely cheap (compare a version number or use KeyValueDiffers / IterableDiffers).
• Angular calls ngOnChanges, ngOnInit and ngDoCheck during the parent's template update, per child, in template order. Hooks are not called on every component instance for free: Angular only calls hooks that exist, resolved at compile time (Ivy).
• Signal-era note: with input() signals you usually do not need ngOnChanges. Use computed() for derived values and effect() for side effects (see Module 13). The classic hooks remain fully supported.
• Prefer inject() or constructor injection for dependencies, ngOnInit for startup work, and afterNextRender() / afterRenderEffect() (newer APIs) for DOM work that must run in the browser only.

interviewQA: Constructor vs ngOnInit: what goes where?

The constructor is for dependency injection and trivial field setup; at that time inputs are not set and the view does not exist. ngOnInit runs after the first ngOnChanges with inputs available, so it hosts initial data loading and subscription setup.
In what order do the lifecycle hooks run?

constructor, ngOnChanges (if inputs), ngOnInit, ngDoCheck, ngAfterContentInit, ngAfterContentChecked, ngAfterViewInit, ngAfterViewChecked, and finally ngOnDestroy. Init hooks run once; DoCheck and the Checked hooks run on every change detection pass.
When does ngOnChanges fire?
Before ngOnInit and whenever a bound input gets a new reference (or primitive value). Mutating an object or array in place does not trigger it.
What is ngDoCheck for and what is the danger?
It lets you run custom change detection logic on every pass, for example to detect in-place mutations. Because it runs so often, expensive code there degrades performance of the whole app.
Is ngOnChanges still needed with signal inputs?
Usually not. input() returns a signal, so you derive values with computed() and react with effect(). ngOnChanges still works for decorator-based @Input.

topics.name: Content and view hooks

beginner.content:
Content vs view

• Imagine a photo frame. The frame (your component) has its own parts (its view: template and child components). Someone can also slide a picture into it from outside (content projected with <ng-content>).
• ngAfterContentInit() runs once after the projected content is ready. ngAfterViewInit() runs once after the component's own template and its children are rendered.
• The Checked variants (ngAfterContentChecked, ngAfterViewChecked) run after every change detection pass, so they run very often.
• Rule of thumb: need a @ViewChild element? Use ngAfterViewInit. Not before: it is undefined in ngOnInit (unless static: true).

intermediate.content:
Content hooks with projected content

• ngAfterContentInit is where @ContentChild / @ContentChildren (or signal contentChild()) are first populated. Typical for tabs, accordions and menu components that inspect their projected children.
• ngAfterContentChecked runs after Angular checked the projected content on each pass. Use it very rarely.

View hooks with third-party widgets

• ngAfterViewInit is the place to hand a DOM element to a charting or map library, measure sizes, or call scrollIntoView.
• Do not change bound state in the view hooks: it triggers the dev-mode error ExpressionChangedAfterItHasBeenChecked because the view was already checked.

expert.content:
Internals, pitfalls and modern replacements

• Queries resolve in a fixed order: static queries before ngOnInit, content queries before ngAfterContentInit, view queries before ngAfterViewInit. Dynamic queries (inside @if / @for) update after each pass and are visible in the Checked hooks.
• ngAfterViewChecked / ngAfterContentChecked fire after every pass, even when nothing changed. Putting DOM reads there causes layout thrashing. Prefer signal queries viewChild() and contentChild() with effect(), or afterNextRender() / afterEveryRender() (v17.x-19, the render hooks API is stable from v19 under the names afterNextRender and afterEveryRender; earlier versions had afterRender).
• Under SSR, ngAfterViewInit also runs on the server where there is no real DOM. Guard browser-only code with afterNextRender or isPlatformBrowser.
• To change state after the view was checked, either schedule it (afterNextRender, Promise.resolve().then) or call cdr.detectChanges(), but first ask if the state belongs in a signal.

interviewQA: Difference between ngAfterContentInit and ngAfterViewInit?
Content hooks concern nodes projected into the component through ng-content (declared by the parent). View hooks concern the component own template and its child components. Content hooks fire first.
Why is my @ViewChild undefined in ngOnInit?
The view is not rendered yet. View queries are resolved before ngAfterViewInit; only { static: true } queries (elements not inside @if/@for) are available in ngOnInit.
What causes ExpressionChangedAfterItHasBeenChecked and how do you fix it?

Changing a bound value after Angular already checked it in the same pass, often in ngAfterViewInit or a child hook. Fix by deriving state correctly, moving the change earlier, using signals, or deferring it to the next render.
Why are the Checked hooks dangerous?
They run after every change detection pass for every instance. Heavy or DOM-reading logic there hurts performance and can cause loops.
How do you safely run browser-only code after render in SSR apps?
Use afterNextRender / afterEveryRender or guard with isPlatformBrowser, because lifecycle hooks such as ngAfterViewInit also execute on the server.

topics.name: Destruction and cleanup

beginner.content:
Cleaning up after yourself

• When a component is removed (route change, @if turns false) Angular calls ngOnDestroy() once. Like Java's close() in try-with-resources, this is where you release things: stop timers, unsubscribe, close sockets.
• If you forget, the timer or subscription keeps running in memory: a memory leak, and sometimes code keeps updating a component that no longer exists.

intermediate.content:
DestroyRef and takeUntilDestroyed()

• DestroyRef (v16+) is an injectable that lets you register cleanup callbacks with onDestroy(fn) right where you create the resource, so no separate ngOnDestroy is needed. It works in components, directives, services and environment injectors.
• takeUntilDestroyed() (from @angular/core/rxjs-interop) is an RxJS operator that completes the stream when the current injection context is destroyed. Call it with no argument in a constructor or field initialiser, or pass a DestroyRef elsewhere.

expert.content:
Patterns, pitfalls and what not to clean

• The classic pattern before v16 was a destroy$ = new Subject() with takeUntil(this.destroy$) and destroy$.next() in ngOnDestroy. It still works, but takeUntilDestroyed() removes the boilerplate.
• You do not need to unsubscribe from: the async pipe (it cleans itself), HttpClient calls that complete, router paramMap of the same component, template event listeners, and toSignal() (it unsubscribes with its owner).
• You must clean: interval/fromEvent/Subject subscriptions, addEventListener on window/document, WebSocket/SSE connections, third-party widgets, ResizeObserver/IntersectionObserver.
• takeUntilDestroyed() without argument throws NG0203 outside an injection context. Put it before subscribe and, when combined with other completing operators, place it last in the pipe to avoid leaks from inner observables (same rule as takeUntil).
• Service destruction: root services live as long as the app; component-provided services are destroyed with the component and their ngOnDestroy runs too.

interviewQA: When is ngOnDestroy called and what belongs there?

Just before Angular removes the component or directive (route change, @if false, @for item removed). Put cleanup there: timers, manual subscriptions, event listeners, sockets, third-party widget disposal.
What is DestroyRef?
An injectable (v16+) that exposes onDestroy(callback), letting you register cleanup logic at the place where you create the resource, in components, directives and services.
How does takeUntilDestroyed work and where can you call it?
It completes an observable when the surrounding injection context is destroyed. With no argument it must run in an injection context (constructor or field initialiser); elsewhere pass a DestroyRef.
Which subscriptions do not need manual unsubscription?
Async pipe subscriptions, completing HttpClient observables, toSignal subscriptions, and template event bindings. Infinite streams like interval, fromEvent and Subjects do need cleanup.
What was the older pattern and why replace it?
A destroy$ Subject with takeUntil(destroy$) and next()/complete() in ngOnDestroy. It works but is boilerplate and easy to forget; takeUntilDestroyed does the same automatically.

topics.name: Parent-child behavior, input changes and mistakes

beginner.content:
Parents and children together

• A parent creates its children while rendering. The parent's constructor and ngOnInit run before the children are created; the children then run their hooks; and the parent's ngAfterViewInit runs only after all children finished theirs. Destruction goes parent first, then children.
• When a parent changes a bound value, Angular updates the child input and calls the child's ngOnChanges. That is how input changes reach lifecycle hooks.

intermediate.content:
Input changes and the hooks

• With several children, hooks interleave in template order: ngOnChanges/ngOnInit/ngDoCheck for child A, then child B, while the After* hooks run once the whole view subtree is created.
• Primitive inputs trigger ngOnChanges when the value differs; object inputs when the reference differs. Use immutable updates in the parent.
• With OnPush children, ngDoCheck still runs, but the child view is skipped unless an input reference changed, an event fired inside it, or a signal it reads changed.

expert.content:
Avoiding expensive lifecycle operations

• Anything in ngDoCheck, ngAfterContentChecked, ngAfterViewChecked and template method calls runs on each pass; for a list of 1000 rows that is thousands of calls per click. Keep them O(1), or move work to computed(), pure pipes or OnPush.
• Do heavy startup work lazily (@defer, route lazy loading) rather than blocking ngOnInit; never make ngOnInit block on synchronous heavy loops.
• Avoid reading layout (offsetWidth) and writing the DOM in the same hook: it forces synchronous reflow.

Common lifecycle mistakes

MistakeConsequenceFix
Fetching data or reading @Input in the constructorInputs are undefined, hard to testUse ngOnInit
Using @ViewChild in ngOnInitundefinedngAfterViewInit or signal viewChild()
Forgetting to unsubscribe from infinite streamsMemory leak, ghost updatestakeUntilDestroyed / async pipe
Changing bound state in ngAfterViewInitExpressionChangedAfterItHasBeenCheckedDerive earlier, use signals, afterNextRender
Mutating an input objectngOnChanges and OnPush do not fireImmutable updates
Heavy code in ngDoCheck / *CheckedSlow appcomputed, pure pipe, OnPush
Browser APIs (window, document) in hooks under SSRServer crashafterNextRender, isPlatformBrowser
Calling ngOnInit manuallyRuns twiceNever call hooks yourself

Version notes and design guidance

• Order guarantee: for a parent P with child C, PreOrder hooks (OnChanges, OnInit, DoCheck) go P then C; AfterContent/AfterView hooks go C then P (post-order). OnDestroy is invoked for the parent and then its descendants.
• In zoneless apps (stable from v20.2, developer preview in v18-20.1) hooks still run, but change detection is scheduled by signals, markForCheck, events and the async pipe rather than zone.js.
• Prefer reactive wiring (signals, computed, effect) over hook choreography: fewer ordering bugs. Keep hooks thin and delegate to services or pure functions so they are testable: in tests fixture.detectChanges() triggers the first ngOnInit.

interviewQA: In what order do parent and child hooks run?

Parent constructor, ngOnInit and ngDoCheck first; then each child runs its constructor, ngOnChanges, ngOnInit, ngDoCheck and view hooks; the parent AfterViewInit runs after all children are initialised.
How does an input change reach a child?
The parent binding changes, Angular sets the child input and calls ngOnChanges (or updates the input signal). Only a new value or reference counts; in-place mutation is not detected.
Name common lifecycle mistakes.
Logic in the constructor, ViewChild in ngOnInit, leaked subscriptions, state changes in AfterViewInit, mutated inputs, heavy code in DoCheck/Checked hooks, and browser APIs used under SSR.
How do you keep lifecycle work cheap?
Keep per-pass hooks O(1), memoise with computed or pure pipes, use OnPush, track in @for, lazy load with @defer, and move heavy work out of ngOnInit.
