interviewQA: How should I use this checklist?
Work through the lessons in order, tick each item once you can explain it and write a small example from memory. The last column tells you which lesson to revisit.

topics.name: Router basics and configuration

beginner.content:
What is routing?

• An Angular app is a single page application: the browser loads index.html once. Routing swaps which component is shown when the URL changes, without a full page reload, like changing TV channels while the TV stays on.
• Java comparison: Spring MVC maps a URL to a controller method on the server; the Angular Router maps a URL to a component in the browser.
• Three pieces: a routes array (the map), <router-outlet> (where the page appears) and RouterLink (clickable links).

intermediate.content:
Using the router building blocks

• provideRouter(routes, ...features) replaces RouterModule.forRoot. Features are added as arguments: withComponentInputBinding(), withRouterConfig(), withPreloading(), withInMemoryScrolling(), withViewTransitions(), withDebugTracing().
• RouterLink accepts a string, an array of segments ([ '/users', user.id ]), plus [queryParams], fragment and relativeTo. It renders a real href, so open in new tab and SEO work.
• RouterLinkActive adds one or more CSS classes when the link URL matches the current URL; use [routerLinkActiveOptions]="{ exact: true }" for the home link, otherwise "/" is always active.
• Named outlets (<router-outlet name="side">) allow auxiliary routes.

expert.content:
Router architecture internals

• The Router service holds the current RouterState, a tree of ActivatedRouteSnapshot/ActivatedRoute objects mirroring the matched route tree. Each RouterOutlet renders the component of the route at its depth. URL parsing is done by UrlSerializer into a UrlTree.
• Matching: recognize walks the config depth-first, applies CanMatch, applies the first matching route, and builds the state. Then guards, resolvers and activation run (see lifecycle lesson).
• URL strategy: PathLocationStrategy (HTML5 pushState, needs server fallback to index.html; in Spring Boot add a forward from unknown paths to /index.html) or HashLocationStrategy (withHashLocation(), works without server rules).
• Route reuse: navigating to the same route with different params reuses the component instance, so ngOnInit does not re-run. Subscribe to paramMap or use input binding (see next lesson). A custom RouteReuseStrategy can cache components.
• Version notes: RouterModule.forRoot is legacy but supported. Since v16 withComponentInputBinding; v17 added view transitions; v18-19 introduced redirectTo as function.

interviewQA: What is the Angular Router and what are its core parts?

It maps URL paths to components inside a single page app. Core parts: the Routes configuration, the Router service, RouterOutlet where components render, RouterLink for links, and ActivatedRoute for reading route information.
How do you set up routing in a standalone app?
Define a Routes array and pass it to provideRouter(routes) in the application config providers, then place <router-outlet> in a template.
Why use routerLink rather than href?
routerLink navigates through the Router without reloading the page and still renders a real href. A plain href triggers a full page reload and loses app state.
What does RouterLinkActive do and why exact: true for home?
It toggles CSS classes on the link whose URL matches the current route. The root link "/" is a prefix of every URL, so without exact matching it would always be active.
Hash vs path location strategy?
Path strategy gives clean URLs but the server must return index.html for unknown paths; hash strategy puts the route after # and needs no server configuration.

topics.name: Navigation, route and query parameters

beginner.content:
Moving between pages and passing data

• Programmatic navigation means navigating from TypeScript code with router.navigate(), for example after a successful login.
• Route parameters are parts of the path: /users/42 matches users/:id. Query parameters come after a question mark: /search?term=java&page=2. Rule of thumb: identifiers in the path, filters and optional things in the query.
• Optional route parameters are normally query parameters (or matrix params like ;sort=asc).

intermediate.content:
Reading route parameters

Three ways, newest first:
1. Component input binding (withComponentInputBinding(), v16+): route params, query params, data and resolved data are set directly on matching input()s. Cleanest, signal friendly.
2. ActivatedRoute observables: paramMap and queryParamMap emit on every change, required when the component is reused for different ids.
3. Snapshot: route.snapshot.paramMap.get('id'), a one-time read; stale if the component is reused.

Navigation extras

NavigationExtras is the second argument of navigate: queryParams, queryParamsHandling ('merge' or 'preserve'), fragment, relativeTo, replaceUrl (do not add a history entry), skipLocationChange, state (hidden data in history), onSameUrlNavigation. navigateByUrl('/a/b?x=1') takes a full URL string.

expert.content:
Pitfalls and best practices

• Same component, different id: Angular reuses the instance, so ngOnInit does not run again. Use observables, input signals or switchMap from toObservable(id).
• Always URL-encode is automatic for navigate arrays; building URL strings by hand with user text is an injection and bug source. Prefer UrlTree via router.createUrlTree() and guards returning UrlTrees.
• Route params are strings: convert with numberAttribute transform: input({ transform: numberAttribute }).
• Put shareable state (filters, page, sort) in query params: refresh and bookmarks work, and the back button behaves. Do not put secrets or large objects in URLs or state (state is lost on reload in some flows).
• Relative navigation (relativeTo) keeps feature routes movable.

interviewQA: Route parameter vs query parameter?
Route params are part of the path and identify a resource (/users/42), required for matching. Query params follow ? and are optional, used for filters, paging and sorting.
How can a component read route params in modern Angular?
With withComponentInputBinding the param becomes an input. Otherwise inject ActivatedRoute and use paramMap / queryParamMap observables, or the snapshot for one-off reads.
Why does my component not refresh when /users/1 changes to /users/2?
The Router reuses the component instance for the same route config, so ngOnInit does not run again. React to paramMap (or an input signal) changes instead.
Name some NavigationExtras.
queryParams, queryParamsHandling, fragment, relativeTo, replaceUrl, skipLocationChange, state, onSameUrlNavigation.
navigate vs navigateByUrl?
navigate takes a commands array and extras and supports relative navigation; navigateByUrl takes an absolute URL string or UrlTree and is always absolute.

topics.name: Child, nested, redirect and wildcard routes

beginner.content:
Child routes, redirects and not-found pages

• Child routes are routes inside a parent route's children array. The parent component (a layout with a menu) contains its own <router-outlet> where the child appears: these are nested routes. Think of a house (parent) with rooms (children).
• A redirect route sends one URL to another: { path: '', redirectTo: 'home', pathMatch: 'full' }.
• A wildcard route path: '**' matches anything left over; use it for the 404 Not Found page.
• Route ordering: the router takes the first match, so put specific routes first and the wildcard last.

intermediate.content:
Layout routes and pathMatch

• pathMatch: 'full' means the whole remaining URL must equal the path; 'prefix' (default) matches when the URL starts with the path. An empty-path redirect without 'full' would match every URL: infinite redirect.
• A componentless route (no component, only children) groups routes to share guards, data or providers without adding a layout.
• Relative links inside children (routerLink="users") resolve against the parent route.
• A 404 page should also set a proper status when using SSR. A redirect can be a function (v18+): redirectTo: (data) => '/new/' + data.params['id'].

expert.content:
Matching rules and pitfalls

• The router matches depth-first, in config order. A greedy route such as :slug placed before about swallows it. Put static segments before parameterised ones.
• Custom UrlMatcher functions handle patterns like @username that the path syntax cannot express.
• Nested route trees mean many outlets; keep nesting shallow (2-3 levels) for readability. Use feature-level route files (admin.routes.ts) loaded with loadChildren.
• Wildcard inside a lazy child only catches unmatched URLs under that parent; add a top-level ** as well.
• Trailing-slash, case-sensitivity and relative redirect (redirectTo: 'home' vs '/home') are frequent bugs: a leading slash makes it absolute.

interviewQA: What are child routes and how do they render?
Routes in a parent route children array. The parent component hosts a nested router-outlet in which the matched child component renders.
Why does pathMatch full matter on a redirect with an empty path?
With the default prefix, an empty path is a prefix of every URL, so the redirect would match everything and loop. full requires the whole URL to be empty.
How do you build a 404 page?
Add a wildcard route path ** as the last entry that renders a NotFound component (optionally with a title).
Why does route order matter?
The router uses the first matching route, so a generic or parameterised route defined earlier can hide specific ones, and the wildcard must be last.
What is a componentless route used for?
Grouping child routes under one path so they share guards, data, resolvers or providers without a wrapper component.

topics.name: Lazy loading, preloading and routing performance

beginner.content:
Load code only when needed

• By default all code ships in one big file. Lazy loading splits the app into chunks that the browser downloads only when the user visits that route, like ordering food only when you are hungry instead of carrying the whole menu.
• Lazy loading components: loadComponent: () => import('./x').then(m => m.XComponent).
• Lazy loading route configurations: loadChildren: () => import('./admin/admin.routes').then(m => m.ADMIN_ROUTES) loads a whole feature's route tree.

intermediate.content:
Preloading strategies and custom preloading

• Preloading strategies download lazy chunks in the background after the first page is ready. Built in: NoPreloading (default) and PreloadAllModules. Enable with withPreloading(PreloadAllModules).
• Custom preloading: implement PreloadingStrategy and preload only routes marked with data: { preload: true }, or only on fast connections.

expert.content:
Routing performance

• Lazy load every feature that is not on the landing path; check the result with ng build --stats-json and a bundle analyzer. Keep the initial bundle small.
• Avoid importing lazy components elsewhere (static imports pull them into the main bundle); share code through a shared file, not through cross-feature imports.
• Use withComponentInputBinding (less subscription code), @defer for in-page chunks, withViewTransitions for perceived speed, and resolvers or skeletons to avoid blank screens.
• Guards and resolvers run sequentially or in parallel depending on type; keep them fast and cache their data. Route-level canMatch prevents downloading a chunk the user may not access.
• Chunks are content-hashed; after a deploy, users with an old tab may fail with a ChunkLoadError: handle it by reloading (global error handler) and by serving old assets for a while.
• Version: functional loadComponent/loadChildren with default exports since v15; PreloadAllModules name remains although modules are optional.

interviewQA: loadComponent vs loadChildren?
loadComponent lazily loads a single standalone component for a route; loadChildren lazily loads a set of child routes (a feature route file) for a path prefix.
What is preloading and why use it?
Downloading lazy chunks in the background after the initial load so later navigation is instant, while keeping the first load small.
How do you preload only some routes?
Write a custom PreloadingStrategy that checks route.data (for example preload: true) or network conditions and returns load() or of(null).
What accidentally defeats lazy loading?
Importing a lazy component or its feature files statically from eagerly loaded code, which pulls them into the main bundle.
How do you reduce routing-related startup cost?
Lazy load features, use canMatch to avoid fetching unauthorised chunks, preload selectively, keep guards and resolvers fast, and analyse bundles with stats.

topics.name: Route guards and protected routes

beginner.content:
Route guards: the bouncers of your app

• A route guard decides whether a navigation may continue. Like a security guard at a door it returns true (come in), false (stay out), or a UrlTree (go there instead, e.g. the login page).
• CanActivate: may I enter this route? CanActivateChild: may I enter any child? CanDeactivate: may I leave (unsaved changes)? CanMatch: should this route even be considered?
• Modern guards are functional route guards: plain functions (CanActivateFn) that use inject(). Class-based guards are legacy and deprecated.

intermediate.content:
The four guard types

GuardWhenTypical use
canMatchWhile matching, before lazy chunk downloadRole/feature-flag based route variants
canActivateBefore entering a routeLogin required
canActivateChildBefore entering any childGuard a whole section once
canDeactivateBefore leavingUnsaved-changes confirmation

Protected routes and role-based navigation

• Protected routes combine canActivate with a login flow: redirect to /login?returnUrl=... and navigate back after success.
• Role-based navigation: put the allowed roles in route data, read them in one reusable guard factory, and hide menu items the user cannot open (UI hint only).

expert.content:
Guard internals and security reality

• Guards may return boolean | UrlTree | Observable | Promise (and RedirectCommand from v18.1+ to control redirect navigation extras). Observables must complete or the navigation hangs: add take(1) / first().
• Order: canMatch then canDeactivate (leaving), canActivateChild (parent to child), canActivate (parent to child). Guards of the same type run in parallel unless runGuardsAndResolvers / async redirects short-circuit; the first false/UrlTree wins.
• Prefer returning a UrlTree to calling router.navigate inside a guard (which cancels the current navigation inconsistently).
• Security: guards are only UX. The JavaScript is in the browser and can be modified. The Spring Boot API must authorise every request (@PreAuthorize, method security). Never rely on a guard to protect data.
• Use canMatch rather than canActivate for lazy features you want hidden; use canActivateChild or a componentless parent route to avoid repeating guards. Class guards (CanActivate interface) are deprecated since v15.2.

interviewQA: What is a route guard and what can it return?
A function/class run by the router to allow or block navigation. It returns true, false, or a UrlTree (redirect), directly or as Observable/Promise.
canActivate vs canMatch?

canMatch runs while the router is matching and can make a route not match at all (so the lazy chunk is not downloaded and another route with the same path can match). canActivate runs after matching to allow or deny entry.
How do you prevent losing unsaved form changes?
Add a canDeactivate guard that asks the component (via an interface) whether it has unsaved changes and shows a confirmation.
Are guards enough to secure an app?
No. They only improve user experience. All authorisation must be enforced by the backend API (for example Spring Security), because client code can be bypassed.
Why prefer functional guards?
Less boilerplate, composable guard factories, use inject() directly, and class-based guards are deprecated.
Why might navigation hang in a guard?
The returned Observable never completes. Use take(1) or first().

topics.name: Resolvers, route data, titles and route providers

beginner.content:
Data, titles and resolvers

• Route data: static information attached to a route with data: { ... }, such as breadcrumb text or required roles.
• Route titles: title: 'Orders' sets document.title automatically for each route.
• A route resolver fetches data before the page shows, so the component never renders half empty. Think of a waiter bringing your meal to the table instead of you cooking it at the table.
codeExamples:
{
  path: 'orders/:id',
  component: OrderDetailComponent,
  title: 'Order details',                       // route title
  data: { breadcrumb: 'Order' },                // route data
  resolve: { order: orderResolver },            // resolver
}

intermediate.content:
ResolveFn and reading resolved data

• ResolveFn<T> is the type of a functional resolver. It may return a value, Promise or Observable (which must complete or emit once).
• Read resolved data with an input of the same name (with withComponentInputBinding) or route.data.
• Dynamic titles use TitleResolveFn or a custom TitleStrategy.

Route-level providers

A route can have a providers array. Angular creates an environment injector for that route (and its children), giving feature-scoped services without a NgModule. Services are created when the route is first activated and live as long as the route config is loaded.

expert.content:
Resolver trade-offs and best practices

• A resolver blocks navigation until it finishes: slow APIs make the app feel frozen, with the previous page staying visible. Often better: navigate immediately and show a skeleton, using a signal/resource in the component. Use resolvers for data the page cannot render without, or when you need to redirect on a 404 before the page appears.
• Resolvers re-run only when params change by default; control with runGuardsAndResolvers: 'paramsOrQueryParamsChange' | 'always'.
• Handle errors: an error thrown in a resolver cancels the navigation (a NavigationError event). Return EMPTY or a RedirectCommand (v18.1+) deliberately.
• Route data merges parent data into children only with paramsInheritanceStrategy: 'always' (withRouterConfig) for componentless/empty-path parents.
• Route-level providers are tree-shakable alternatives to providedIn: 'root' for stateful feature services: state resets when leaving the route tree is destroyed only if the route's injector is destroyed (lazy loaded config injectors live on). For per-visit state, provide in the component's providers.

interviewQA: What is a resolver and when would you use one?

A function run before activation that fetches data the route needs, so the component renders with data ready. Use it when the page cannot render without the data or to redirect on missing data; otherwise prefer loading states.
What is ResolveFn?
The TypeScript type of a functional resolver: (route, state) => T | Observable<T> | Promise<T>.
How does a component receive resolved data?
Through route.data (ActivatedRoute) or, with withComponentInputBinding, as an input named like the resolve key.
How do you set a dynamic page title?
Use title as a function or ResolveFn on the route, or provide a custom TitleStrategy.
What are route-level providers?
A providers array on a route that creates an environment injector scoped to that route subtree, so feature services need no NgModule.

topics.name: Router events, navigation lifecycle and testing

beginner.content:
Router events and the navigation lifecycle

• The router announces what it is doing through an observable, router.events. Typical use: show a loading bar while navigating.
• Navigation lifecycle in short: NavigationStart, route recognised, guards run, resolvers run, ActivationStart, components activate, NavigationEnd (or NavigationCancel / NavigationError).

intermediate.content:
Events in detail and router testing

Order of events: NavigationStart, RoutesRecognized, GuardsCheckStart, ChildActivationStart, ActivationStart, GuardsCheckEnd, ResolveStart, ResolveEnd, ActivationEnd, ChildActivationEnd, NavigationEnd (v17+ adds NavigationSkipped). Filter with filter((e): e is NavigationEnd => e instanceof NavigationEnd).
Router testing: use provideRouter(routes) and RouterTestingHarness (v15.2+) to navigate and get a fixture for the routed component. Use provideRouter([]) with a stubbed Router for isolated unit tests.

expert.content:
Lifecycle details worth knowing

• Navigation is transitional and cancelable: a new navigation cancels the previous one (NavigationCancel with a code), so make guards and resolvers cancellation friendly (observables get unsubscribed).
• Phases: parse URL, apply redirects (applyRedirects), recognize, run guards (canMatch, canDeactivate, canActivateChild, canActivate), resolve data, activate routes (create or reuse components), update the URL (urlUpdateStrategy: 'deferred' by default, after success), scroll.
• router.events is a Subject: subscribe before navigation happens (the constructor of the root component). Use router.navigated and router.url only after NavigationEnd. For scroll restoration and anchors use withInMemoryScrolling.
• In tests, prefer the harness; avoid RouterTestingModule (deprecated). Asynchronous guards need await or fakeAsync+tick.
• Signals: toSignal(router.events.pipe(filter(...))) gives a signal of the latest event; a "currentUrl" signal from NavigationEnd is a common pattern for breadcrumbs.

interviewQA: How do you detect when navigation starts and ends?
Subscribe to router.events and check instances of NavigationStart and NavigationEnd (also NavigationCancel and NavigationError to hide a spinner reliably).
Describe the navigation lifecycle.
URL parsed and redirects applied, routes recognised, guards run, resolvers run, components activated, URL updated, NavigationEnd emitted. Failures emit NavigationCancel or NavigationError.
How do you test a route guard end to end?
Configure TestBed with provideRouter(routes) and stub services, create a RouterTestingHarness, navigate to the protected URL and assert the resulting router URL or rendered component.
What happens when a new navigation starts during an ongoing one?
The router cancels the earlier navigation (NavigationCancel) and processes the latest, unsubscribing from in-flight guards and resolvers.

interviewQA: How should I use this checklist?
Work through the lessons in order, tick each item once you can explain it and write a small example from memory. The last column tells you which lesson to revisit.

topics.name: Template-driven vs reactive forms

beginner.content:
Two ways to build forms

• Forms in Angular connect HTML inputs to TypeScript data, track whether the data is valid, and report errors.
• Template-driven forms: you write the form mostly in HTML with ngModel. Quick for small forms (like filling a paper form: the form defines itself as you write it). Needs FormsModule.
• Reactive forms: you build the form object in TypeScript (FormGroup, FormControl) and bind the HTML to it with [formGroup] and formControlName. More code, but explicit and testable (like an architect's blueprint first). Needs ReactiveFormsModule.

intermediate.content:
Choosing between the two

AspectTemplate-drivenReactive
ImportFormsModuleReactiveFormsModule
Source of truthTemplate (directives create controls)Component class (explicit model)
Data flowAsynchronous (model updated after change detection)Synchronous, immutable-friendly
ValidationDirective attributes (required, email)Validator functions
Dynamic fieldsHardEasy (FormArray, add/remove controls)
TestingNeeds renderingPlain unit tests
Best forSmall, simple formsAnything non-trivial, enterprise forms
Both can live in one app, but not on the same input. Reactive forms are the default recommendation for real projects.

Wiring modules in a standalone app

Standalone components import the pieces they use: FormsModule (ngModel, ngForm), or ReactiveFormsModule (formGroup, formControlName, formControl, formArrayName). Importing the module gives you the directive set; no provide... call is needed.

expert.content:
Under the hood

• Both approaches use the same model classes: the template-driven directives (NgModel, NgForm) create FormControl/FormGroup instances for you, asynchronously (a microtask later), which is why you cannot read form.controls in ngOnInit with template-driven forms.
• Each control is wired to the DOM element through a ControlValueAccessor (DefaultValueAccessor, CheckboxControlValueAccessor, SelectControlValueAccessor...), the same mechanism you use for custom controls.
• Reactive forms are observable-based: valueChanges and statusChanges are streams, perfect for RxJS operators like debounceTime. Template-driven forms expose the same on the generated model.
• Angular forms have no built-in signal API yet (as of v20, signal forms are experimental/in development); convert with toSignal(control.valueChanges, { initialValue }).
• Version note: NgModel two-way binding [(ngModel)] works on signals as well: [(ngModel)]="name" where name is a model() or WritableSignal.

interviewQA: Template-driven vs reactive forms?

Template-driven defines the form in the template with ngModel directives and is asynchronous and simple; reactive defines the model explicitly in TypeScript, is synchronous, observable-based, easier to test and better for complex or dynamic forms.
Which module does each need?
Template-driven needs FormsModule; reactive needs ReactiveFormsModule. In standalone components you import them in the component imports.
Why does form.controls look empty in ngOnInit for template-driven forms?
The controls are created asynchronously by the directives after the first change detection; reactive forms build the model synchronously in code.
Can you mix both approaches?
Yes in the same app, but not on the same control or form element.

topics.name: Form model: FormControl, FormGroup, FormArray, FormBuilder

beginner.content:
The three building blocks

• FormControl = one input (a single cell). It holds the value and state.
• FormGroup = a set of named controls (a form or a section). Its value is an object.
• FormArray = an ordered list of controls or groups (rows). Its value is an array.
• FormBuilder is a helper service with short methods group(), control(), array() so you write less code.

intermediate.content:
Typed forms and NonNullableFormBuilder

• Since v14 reactive forms are typed: FormControl<string | null>, FormGroup<{ name: FormControl<string> }>. form.value is Partial (disabled controls are omitted); getRawValue() includes everything.
• By default reset() sets a control to null, which makes the type string | null. NonNullableFormBuilder (fb.nonNullable) or { nonNullable: true } makes reset() go back to the initial value and types as plain string.
• Use FormRecord for dynamic string-keyed groups and UntypedFormGroup only when migrating.

Working with the model

Common API: setValue() (all fields), patchValue() (some fields), get('address.city'), controls.x, addControl/removeControl, disable()/enable(), valueChanges / statusChanges, reset(value).

expert.content:
Internals and recommendations

• FormControlState: a control emits valueChanges before updating validity; statusChanges after. Options { emitEvent: false } and { onlySelf: true } control propagation. Since v18 a unified control.events stream emits ValueChangeEvent, StatusChangeEvent, PristineChangeEvent, TouchedChangeEvent, FormSubmittedEvent, FormResetEvent.
• Prefer typed forms end-to-end; avoid as any casts. Create the form once as a field, not in a getter (a getter would recreate it on each change detection).
• Map form value to a DTO explicitly (the Spring Boot request class) rather than posting the raw form blindly; handle nulls and number/date conversions in one mapper.
• Do not subscribe to valueChanges without cleanup: use takeUntilDestroyed().

interviewQA: FormControl vs FormGroup vs FormArray?
FormControl holds a single value and its state, FormGroup aggregates named controls into an object, FormArray aggregates an ordered list of controls into an array.
What is NonNullableFormBuilder for?
It creates controls that are non-nullable: reset() restores the initial value instead of null and the types stay plain (string instead of string | null).
setValue vs patchValue?
setValue requires a value for every control of the group and throws if shape differs; patchValue updates only the supplied fields.
value vs getRawValue?
value omits disabled controls; getRawValue includes all controls, enabled or disabled.
What did typed reactive forms (v14) change?
Controls, groups and arrays carry generic types, so value, setValue and controls access are compile-time checked.

topics.name: Form states and built-in validators

beginner.content:
What state is a form field in?

Every control keeps FormControl states (CSS classes ng-valid, ng-dirty... are added automatically):
• pristine / dirty: dirty once the user changed the value.
• untouched / touched: touched after the field loses focus (blur).
• valid / invalid: all validators pass or at least one fails. Also pending (async validation running) and disabled.
Good UX: show an error only when the field is invalid and touched, not as soon as the page opens.
codeExamples:
<!-- signup.component.html -->
<input formControlName="email">
@if (email.invalid && (email.dirty || email.touched)) {
  <small class="error">Please enter a valid email.</small>
}
<!-- component: get email() { return this.form.controls.email; } -->

intermediate.content:
Built-in validators

ValidatorMeaningError key
Validators.requiredValue not empty (required validation)required
Validators.minLength(n) / maxLength(n)Minimum and maximum length of textminlength / maxlength
Validators.min(n) / max(n)Numeric rangemin / max
Validators.emailEmail validation (simple format check)email
Validators.pattern(regex)Pattern validation with regular expressionpattern
Validators.requiredTrueCheckbox must be truerequired
Validators.compose / composeAsyncCombine validators-
Using them in both styles
codeExamples:
<!-- template-driven: the same rules as attributes -->
<input name="username" ngModel required minlength="3" maxlength="20" #u="ngModel">
<input name="email" ngModel required email>
<input name="pincode" ngModel pattern="[0-9]{6}">
@if (u.errors?.['minlength']; as e) { <small>Need {{ e.requiredLength }} chars, you typed {{ e.actualLength }}</small> }

expert.content:
Details and gotchas

• Validators.required treats '', null, empty arrays as missing; 0 and false are valid values. minLength ignores empty values (combine with required).
• Validators.email is intentionally lax (e.g. accepts a@b); use a stricter pattern or server validation for real checking. A pattern string is anchored automatically with ^ and $; a RegExp is used as is.
• Validity propagates upward: the group is invalid if any child is. updateValueAndValidity() re-runs validators (needed when another field affects validity). markAllAsTouched() on submit reveals all errors.
• Status values: VALID, INVALID, PENDING, DISABLED. Disabled controls are excluded from validation.
• Use the updateOn: 'blur' | 'submit' option to validate less often. Browser novalidate on the form avoids double native validation bubbles (Angular adds it automatically).

interviewQA: Difference between touched and dirty?
Touched means the field has been focused and blurred; dirty means its value has been changed by the user. They are independent.
Which built-in validators exist?
required, requiredTrue, min, max, minLength, maxLength, email, pattern, plus compose and composeAsync helpers, and null validator.
When should validation messages be displayed?
When the control is invalid and (touched or dirty) or the form was submitted, so users are not shown errors before interaction.
Why does minLength not make a field required?
Length validators ignore empty values; add Validators.required to enforce presence.
How do you show all errors on submit?
Call form.markAllAsTouched() (and check form.invalid) before submitting.

topics.name: Custom, cross-field and async validation, error messages

beginner.content:
Your own rules

• A custom validator is a function that receives a control and returns null when valid or an object describing the error: { noSpaces: true }.
• Cross-field validation compares several fields (password and confirm password); attach it to the group.
• Form error messages: translate error keys to friendly text in one place.

intermediate.content:
Parameterised, async validators and error messages

• A validator with parameters is a factory returning a ValidatorFn.
• Asynchronous validators (AsyncValidatorFn) return an Observable or Promise, e.g. "is this username taken?". While running, status is PENDING. They run only after all sync validators pass. Use debounceTime via timer and switchMap, and updateOn: 'blur' to limit requests.

Validation strategies and server-side errors

• Form validation strategies: (1) show errors on blur/touched (default recommendation), (2) on submit only (updateOn: 'submit' or a submitted flag), (3) immediately while typing (password strength meters). Pick per form; consistent across the app.
• Server-side validation errors: the backend remains the authority. Map its field errors (Spring Boot returns e.g. { "errors": { "email": "already registered" } }) to controls using setErrors().

expert.content:
Design notes

• Validators must be pure and fast; they run on every value change. Return the same error shape consistently ({ key: details }). Never mutate the control.
• A group-level validator marks the group (not the field) invalid; to display it on the field, either read form.errors in the template or setErrors on the child inside the validator (a documented but frowned-on side effect). Another option: validator returns the error and you show it near the confirm field.
• Async validators: always handle errors (catchError(() => of(null))), debounce, and cancel previous requests with switchMap (cancellation is automatic as Angular unsubscribes from the previous pending validation). Check on the server too (race conditions between check and insert).
• Server errors set via setErrors are cleared on the next validity recalculation (value change). That is correct behaviour; do not persist them manually.
• Template-driven custom validators need a directive implementing Validator and provided with NG_VALIDATORS; reactive validators need nothing extra. Share validators between both through a small wrapper directive.
• Version note: control events (v18) and { nonNullable: true } options; ValidatorFn typing stays the same across v14-v20.

interviewQA: How do you write a custom validator?
A function (control) => ValidationErrors | null. Return null for valid and an object like { myError: true } for invalid; parameterised validators are factories returning that function.
How do you validate two fields together?
Attach a validator to the parent FormGroup that reads both controls (for example password and confirm) and returns an error on the group.
How do async validators work and what is PENDING?
They return Observable/Promise of errors; while waiting, the control status is PENDING. They run only if sync validators pass, and a new value cancels the previous pending validation.
How do you display backend validation errors?
Map the error response fields to controls with control.setErrors({ server: message }) and render them like normal validation messages; the backend remains the source of truth.
How do you centralise error messages?
Use a map from error key to message function and a helper or pipe/component (for example app-field-error) used everywhere.
When should errors appear?
Usually after blur (touched) or on submit attempt; immediate feedback only for helpful hints such as password strength.

topics.name: Dynamic, nested and conditional forms, submit and reset

beginner.content:
Forms that change shape

• Nested forms: a FormGroup inside a FormGroup (address inside user). In HTML use formGroupName.
• FormArray for dynamic fields: a list the user can grow, like adding phone numbers. Use push() to add and removeAt() to remove.
• Conditional form fields: show or require a field depending on another value (e.g. "Company name" only if "I am a business").
• Form submission: (ngSubmit) on the form, then read the value. Resetting forms: form.reset().
codeExamples:
@for (item of items.controls; track item; let i = $index) {
}

intermediate.content: Conditional fields, submission and reset

Dynamic forms from metadata

A dynamic form is generated from a description (JSON from a Spring Boot endpoint or a config object): loop over field definitions, create controls and render the right input per type.

expert.content:
Pitfalls and architecture

• track by control identity (track item) in FormArray loops; tracking by $index misrenders when removing rows in the middle.
• reset() does not shrink a FormArray; clear it yourself (clear()). reset() also marks the control pristine and untouched, and with nonNullable restores the initial value (the one given at construction); to change the baseline, use reset(newValue).
• Disabled controls are missing from form.value; use getRawValue() or enable before sending, and send exactly what the backend DTO expects.
• Toggling validators requires updateValueAndValidity(); prefer disabling hidden controls: disabled controls are excluded from validation, which keeps hidden required fields from blocking submit. Use emitEvent: false to avoid loops when you update controls inside valueChanges handlers.
• Prevent double submit: disable the button while saving, use exhaustMap for the submit stream.
• Large dynamic forms: build reusable "sub-form" components receiving a FormGroup as input (typed), or use ControlContainer with viewProviders to nest templates without passing the group around.
• Version: typed forms (v14), FormRecord for dynamic keys; FormArray.push accepts options such as { emitEvent: false } (v18+).

interviewQA: How do you build a list of repeating fields?
Use a FormArray of FormGroups or FormControls; render it with @for over array.controls inside formArrayName, and add/remove via push() and removeAt().
How do you make a field conditionally required?
Subscribe to the controlling field valueChanges and add or remove validators (or enable/disable the control), then call updateValueAndValidity().
How do you handle submission correctly?
Use (ngSubmit), check form.invalid and call markAllAsTouched(), disable the button while the request runs, map the form value to the DTO, and reset on success.
What does form.reset() do?
Sets values back to null or the nonNullable initial value and marks controls pristine and untouched. It does not remove FormArray items.
How are nested forms bound in the template?
formGroupName for nested groups, formArrayName plus an index-bound formGroupName for arrays, formControlName for leaf controls.
Why track by control rather than index in FormArray loops?
Index tracking recycles DOM for the wrong row after removal; tracking by control object keeps DOM and state aligned.

topics.name: Custom form controls and ControlValueAccessor

beginner.content:
Your own input component

• A custom form control is a component (a star rating, a date picker, a tag input) that can be used with formControlName or [(ngModel)] just like a normal input.
• The glue is ControlValueAccessor (CVA): an interface that tells Angular how to write a value into your component and how your component reports changes. Think of it as an adapter plug between the forms system and your component, like a Java interface that lets any class be used as a Comparator.

intermediate.content:
Making it production ready

• Register with NG_VALUE_ACCESSOR and multi: true. forwardRef is needed because the class is referenced before it is defined.
• Alternative without providers: inject NgControl with @Self() and set ngControl.valueAccessor = this in the constructor. This gives access to the control (for validation state and CSS classes).
• Call onTouched() on blur; call onChange() only for user changes, not inside writeValue (that would loop and dirty the form).
• Implement Validator too (NG_VALIDATORS) when the control has built-in rules.
• With OnPush, call cdr.markForCheck() in writeValue and setDisabledState, or keep value in a signal.

expert.content:
Details

• writeValue may be called with null (reset) and before the view exists; code defensively. registerOnChange is called once per binding; never call the callback before registration.
• Do not duplicate form state in your own internal state if you can derive it; the form control is the source of truth. For compound values (an address editor), pass an object and treat it immutably.
• Accessibility is your job: label association (aria-labelledby), keyboard support, roles, aria-invalid from ngControl.invalid.
• Version notes: Angular does not yet ship a signals-native CVA replacement (signal forms were being previewed in v20+); also consider simply using a model()-based component when no integration with forms validation is needed. Libraries like Angular Material use CVA for all their controls (MatFormFieldControl adds the form-field integration).
• Test a CVA through a host component with a real FormControl: set a value, assert the DOM, interact, assert control value and touched.

interviewQA: What is ControlValueAccessor?
An interface (writeValue, registerOnChange, registerOnTouched, setDisabledState) that bridges Angular forms and a DOM element or component so it can work with ngModel and reactive forms.
How do you register a custom control?
Provide NG_VALUE_ACCESSOR with useExisting forwardRef(() => Component) and multi: true, or inject NgControl and assign valueAccessor = this.
When must the control call onChange and onTouched?
onChange when the user changes the value (never from writeValue), onTouched when the user leaves or finishes interacting.
Why forwardRef?
The provider references the class inside its own decorator before the class is defined; forwardRef defers resolution.
How does a custom control show validation state?
Inject NgControl (self) to read invalid/touched, or let the parent show messages; apply aria-invalid and styles accordingly.

topics.name: Form accessibility, testing and performance

beginner.content:
Accessible forms

• Every input needs a visible label tied by for/id (or wrapping the input). Placeholders are not labels.
• Mark invalid fields with aria-invalid="true" and connect the error text with aria-describedby; announce errors with role="alert" or aria-live.
• Use proper input type and autocomplete, keep keyboard order logical, and on a failed submit move focus to the first invalid field.
codeExamples:
<label for="email">Email</label>
<input id="email" type="email" formControlName="email" autocomplete="email"
       [attr.aria-invalid]="email.invalid && email.touched"
       [attr.aria-describedby]="email.invalid && email.touched ? 'email-err' : null">
@if (email.invalid && email.touched) { <small id="email-err" role="alert">Enter a valid email address</small> }

intermediate.content:
Form testing

• Test validators as plain functions. Test form components with TestBed: set values, dispatch input events, call detectChanges, and assert errors and submitted payloads.
• Reactive forms are easy to unit test without a DOM because the model lives in the class.

expert.content:
Form performance

• Validators and valueChanges handlers run on every keystroke. Use updateOn: 'blur' (control or whole form) for heavy validation, debounceTime for searches, and avoid method calls in templates that iterate big FormArrays.
• For large forms (hundreds of controls) use OnPush sub-components that take a typed FormGroup, track in loops, and @defer for sections. Disable emission when patching many values: patchValue(v, { emitEvent: false }) and call updateValueAndValidity() once.
• Prefer form.valid as a template read over a function; ensure async validators are debounced.
• Memory: complete valueChanges subscriptions with takeUntilDestroyed; controls created dynamically and removed are garbage collected once unreferenced.
• Accessibility checks (axe, Lighthouse) belong in CI; add a test that each input has a label.
codeExamples:
form = new FormGroup({ search: new FormControl('') }, { updateOn: 'blur' });     // validate/emit only on blur
bulk() { this.form.patchValue(bigObject, { emitEvent: false }); this.form.updateValueAndValidity(); }

interviewQA: How do you make a form accessible?
Associate labels with inputs, use correct types and autocomplete, set aria-invalid and aria-describedby for errors, announce errors with role=alert, and manage focus on failed submit.
How do you unit test a validator?
Call it as a function with a FormControl or group holding test values and assert it returns null or the expected error object.
How do you reduce validation cost on big forms?
Use updateOn blur or submit, debounce async validators and searches, batch updates with emitEvent false, use OnPush sub-forms and track in loops.
How do you simulate user input in a component test?
Set the element value, dispatch an input event, then call fixture.detectChanges(); alternatively set the control value directly for model-level tests.

interviewQA: How should I use this checklist?
Work through the lessons in order, tick each item once you can explain it and write a small example from memory. The last column tells you which lesson to revisit.

topics.name: Reactive programming, Observables and Observers

beginner.content:
Streams over time

• Reactive programming means describing what should happen when data arrives, instead of asking for it. Compare a Java List (all values exist now) with a stream of events (values arrive over time): clicks, keystrokes, HTTP responses.
• RxJS (Reactive Extensions for JavaScript) is the library that models these as Observables. Angular uses it in HttpClient, Router, forms and more.
• An Observable is a lazy stream, like a YouTube channel: nothing happens until someone subscribes. The Observer is the subscriber with three callbacks: next (a value), error (failed) and complete (finished). A Subscription is the handle you get back; unsubscribe() cancels.

intermediate.content:
Creating observables and how execution works

Creating observables usually uses creation functions rather than new Observable:
codeExamples:
import { of, from, fromEvent, interval, timer, defer, range, throwError, EMPTY } from 'rxjs';

of(1, 2, 3);                               // emits 1,2,3 then completes
from([10, 20, 30]);                        // from array / Promise / iterable
from(fetch('/api/ping'));                  // from a Promise
fromEvent(document, 'click');              // DOM events (infinite)
interval(1000);                            // 0,1,2,... every second (infinite)
timer(2000);                               // one value after 2s
timer(0, 1000);                            // start immediately, then every second
range(1, 5);                               // 1..5
defer(() => of(Date.now()));               // create a fresh source per subscriber
EMPTY;                                     // completes immediately

intermediate.content:
Observable execution

• Each subscribe() runs the producer function again (for cold observables): two subscribers means two executions, e.g. two HTTP requests.
• The contract: zero or more next, then at most one of error or complete. After error or complete nothing else is emitted and resources are released.
• The function you return from the producer is the teardown logic, called on unsubscribe, error or complete.

expert.content:
Cold versus hot

• Cold observable: the producer is created inside the Observable, per subscriber (HttpClient, of, interval). Like Netflix: each viewer starts their own playback.
• Hot observable: the producer lives outside and values flow whether or not someone listens (DOM events, WebSocket, a Subject). Like live TV: you see what is airing now.
• Convert cold to hot with share(), shareReplay() or by pushing through a Subject. Beware: two subscribes or two | asyncs on a cold HTTP observable fire two requests.

Internals and rules

• Observables are lazy and unicast by default; Subjects are multicast. subscribe(fn) with a single function is shorthand for { next: fn }. In RxJS 7 the deprecated signature with three positional callbacks still works but prefer an observer object.
• Synchronous observables (of) emit during subscribe(); the observable contract does not promise asynchronous delivery. observeOn/subscribeOn change the scheduler.
• Observable vs Promise: Promise is eager, single value, not cancellable, always async; Observable is lazy, many values, cancellable, sync or async. Java parallels: CompletableFuture (Promise-like), java.util.stream.Stream (pull, one use) vs Reactor Flux / Mono (push, very similar to Observable).
• RxJS 7 (Angular 13-20 era) and 8 (in preview, removes some deprecated APIs). Import operators from 'rxjs' (since v7.2), not 'rxjs/operators'.

interviewQA: What is an Observable and how does it differ from a Promise?
An Observable is a lazy stream that can emit many values over time, is cancellable and runs per subscription. A Promise is eager, resolves one value once and cannot be cancelled.
What are Observer and Subscription?

The Observer is the set of callbacks (next, error, complete) that receives notifications. The Subscription is the object returned by subscribe() that represents the running execution and offers unsubscribe().
Cold vs hot observable?

Cold creates its producer per subscriber, so each subscription runs separately (HTTP). Hot shares one producer that emits regardless of subscribers (DOM events, Subjects). share/shareReplay turn cold into hot.
Which ways exist to create observables?
new Observable, of, from, fromEvent, interval, timer, range, defer, EMPTY, throwError, plus Subjects and framework sources like HttpClient.
When does an observable stop emitting?
After error or complete, or when the subscriber unsubscribes; teardown logic then runs.

topics.name: Subjects: Subject, BehaviorSubject, ReplaySubject, AsyncSubject

beginner.content:
Subjects: an observable you can push into

• A Subject is both an Observable (others subscribe) and an Observer (you call next()). Think of a radio station: one broadcaster, many listeners; listeners only hear what is broadcast after they tune in.
• Subjects are multicast: all subscribers share one execution. Typical use: a service that broadcasts events to components.

intermediate.content:
The four kinds

TypeBehaviourUse for
SubjectNo memory; late subscribers miss earlier valuesEvents, commands
BehaviorSubjectNeeds an initial value; holds the current value (.value); new subscribers get it immediatelyState: current user, theme, selected item
ReplaySubject(n)Replays the last n values (optionally within a time window) to new subscribersHistory, late-joining consumers
AsyncSubjectEmits only the last value, and only when it completesOne final result (like a Promise)
A tiny state service

expert.content:
Best practices and traps

• Never expose the raw Subject; expose asObservable() so only the owner can call next.
• Subjects are hot and stay alive: complete them or unsubscribe subscribers, otherwise leaks. A Subject that errors is dead for everyone.
• Do not call next inside a subscriber of the same subject without care: reentrancy can overflow the stack. Emit with a clean flow (operators like scan) rather than shared mutable state.
• BehaviorSubject.getValue() in business logic is a code smell mirroring mutable state; prefer derived streams. For state in new code prefer signals (Module 13), keeping BehaviorSubject where streams and operators are needed.
• ReplaySubject(1) vs BehaviorSubject: Replay has no initial value and does not emit until first next; use it when "not yet known" must be expressed by absence. shareReplay({ bufferSize: 1, refCount: true }) is often a safer alternative to a hand-written ReplaySubject cache.
• Java parallels: BehaviorSubject ~ Reactor Sinks.many().replay().latest(); Subject ~ Sinks.many().multicast().

interviewQA: Subject vs BehaviorSubject?

Both multicast. BehaviorSubject requires an initial value, always holds the current value and gives it to new subscribers immediately; a plain Subject has no memory so late subscribers miss earlier emissions.
When would you use ReplaySubject?
When late subscribers must receive the last N values (or those in a time window), such as event history or cached emissions.
What does AsyncSubject emit?
Only the last value, after complete(); nothing if it errors.
Why expose asObservable() from a service?
To prevent consumers from calling next/complete on your Subject, preserving encapsulation of the state owner.
Why do Subjects need care about memory?
They are long-lived and hold references to subscribers; undisposed subscriptions leak and keep callbacks running.

topics.name: Operators: categories and everyday operators

beginner.content:
Operators: tools on an assembly line

• An operator is a function that takes an Observable and returns a new one. You chain them in pipe() like stations on an assembly line; the source is not modified.
• Operator categories:
Creation operators make streams (of, from, interval, timer, fromEvent).
Transformation operators change values (map, scan, switchMap, mergeMap).
Filtering operators drop values (filter, take, debounceTime, distinctUntilChanged).
Combination operators join streams (combineLatest, merge, forkJoin, concat, withLatestFrom).
Utility operators support the flow (tap, delay, startWith, timeout).
Error-handling operators (catchError, retry, finalize) are in the error lesson.

intermediate.content: map, filter, tap, take, startWith

debounceTime and distinctUntilChanged: the search-box pair

• debounceTime(ms) waits until the source is quiet for ms milliseconds, then emits the last value. Perfect for typing.
• distinctUntilChanged() drops a value equal to the previous one (pass a comparator for objects).

expert.content:
Practical details

• tap is for side effects only; do not mutate values in it. It accepts an observer object too: tap({ next, error, complete, subscribe, unsubscribe, finalize }) (RxJS 7.3+) which is excellent for debugging lifecycle.
• debounceTime delays the final emission; throttleTime emits the first and ignores the rest for a period (scroll/resize); auditTime emits the last at the end of each period; sampleTime samples periodically. Choose by whether you need the first, last or periodic value.
• take(1) vs first(): first() errors with EmptyError if the source completes without emitting; take(1) just completes. Use first(pred, default) for defaults.
• distinctUntilChanged uses ===; for objects pass a key selector (distinctUntilKeyChanged('id')) or compare function; mutable objects defeat it.
• startWith is ideal with combineLatest so the combined stream emits before every source has emitted.
• Pipeable operators (functions) replaced the old prototype-patching .map() chain; a custom operator is simply a function (source: Observable<T>) => Observable<R>.
• Order matters: filter before expensive map; debounceTime before switchMap; distinctUntilChanged right after debounce.

interviewQA: What is an operator and what is pipe()?
An operator is a function from Observable to Observable. pipe() composes operators left to right, leaving the source untouched.
List the main operator categories with examples.

Creation (of, from, interval), transformation (map, scan, switchMap), filtering (filter, take, debounceTime, distinctUntilChanged), combination (combineLatest, merge, forkJoin), utility (tap, delay, startWith), error handling (catchError, retry).
What does tap do?
Runs a side effect for each notification without changing the stream, useful for logging or setting flags.
debounceTime vs throttleTime?
debounceTime emits the latest value after a quiet period; throttleTime emits the first value then ignores others for the period.
Why combine debounceTime and distinctUntilChanged for search?
Debounce reduces requests while typing; distinct avoids repeating the same query when the text returns to the same value.
take(1) vs first()?
first() throws EmptyError when the source completes empty; take(1) simply completes.

topics.name: Higher-order observables: switchMap, mergeMap, concatMap, exhaustMap

beginner.content:
Streams that start other streams

• A higher-order observable is an observable whose values are themselves observables, for example "for every search term, start an HTTP call". You rarely handle it by hand: the flattening operators switchMap, mergeMap, concatMap and exhaustMap subscribe to the inner observable and flatten the results.
• They differ in how they treat a new outer value while an inner one is still running:
switchMap: cancel the old, start the new (latest wins).
mergeMap: run all at once (concurrent).
concatMap: queue, one after another (order preserved).
exhaustMap: ignore new ones until the current finishes.

intermediate.content:
When to use which

OperatorConcurrencyOrderUse for
switchMap1, cancels previousLatestSearch-as-you-type, route param changes, load details for selected id
mergeMapMany (limit via 2nd arg)Completion orderIndependent fire-and-forget calls, batch upload
concatMap1, queuedStrict source orderSaving edits in order, sequential API calls
exhaustMap1, drops othersFirst winsLogin or submit button (prevent double click)
Examples with HTTP

expert.content:
Cancellation, HTTP cancellation and pitfalls

• Observable cancellation: unsubscribing runs the teardown. Flattening operators unsubscribe the inner observable when switched away, when the outer completes/unsubscribes, or on error.
• HTTP request cancellation: unsubscribing from HttpClient aborts the in-flight XHR/fetch (the browser cancels it). With switchMap the old request is aborted automatically. Caveat: the server may already have processed it, so never use switchMap for non-idempotent writes (POST payments): use concatMap or exhaustMap.
• Do not nest subscribe inside subscribe ("callback hell"): flatten with an operator, which also gives you cancellation and error propagation.
• Errors: if an inner observable errors, the outer chain dies. Put catchError inside the flattening function to keep the outer stream alive.
• mergeMap without a limit can flood a backend; pass concurrent. Results arrive in completion order; use concatMap or forkJoin if order matters.
• For a click-driven stream use exhaustMap; for "latest request only" use switchMap; switchMap is also the default choice for GET with changing inputs. Newer helpers: mergeScan, switchScan (RxJS 7.x).

interviewQA: Explain switchMap, mergeMap, concatMap and exhaustMap.

All map a value to an inner observable and flatten. switchMap cancels the previous inner, mergeMap runs all concurrently, concatMap queues them in order, exhaustMap ignores new values while one inner is active.
Which operator for typeahead search and why?
switchMap after debounceTime and distinctUntilChanged, because only the latest query matters and earlier requests are cancelled.
Which operator prevents double submits?
exhaustMap on the click stream, since extra clicks are ignored until the request finishes.
What is a higher-order observable?
An observable that emits observables. Flattening operators subscribe to the inner ones and merge their output into a single stream.
Does unsubscribing cancel an HTTP request?
Yes, the browser request is aborted, but the server may already have processed it, so be careful with non-idempotent operations.
Where to place catchError with switchMap?
Inside the inner pipe, so a failing request does not terminate the outer stream.

topics.name: Combining streams and sharing results

beginner.content:
Joining streams

• combineLatest([a$, b$]): whenever any source emits, emit the latest values of all (after each has emitted once). Like a dashboard showing the latest of several gauges.
• forkJoin([a$, b$]): wait until all complete, then emit the last values once. Like Promise.all for HTTP calls.
• merge(a$, b$): interleave values from all, as they come.
• concat(a$, b$): run a$ fully, then b$.
• withLatestFrom(b$): when the main stream emits, also take the latest value of b$ (b$ alone does not trigger).

intermediate.content: Typical patterns

Sharing: shareReplay

shareReplay multicasts one execution and replays the last value(s) to late subscribers. Use it for cached lookups so several components or async pipes do not repeat the HTTP call.

expert.content:
Choosing and avoiding bugs

• combineLatest never emits until every source has emitted at least once, and never completes until all complete; infinite sources (valueChanges) need startWith. forkJoin needs finite sources, emits nothing if any completes empty, and errors fail all (catch per source). For polling or never-ending streams use combineLatest not forkJoin.
• zip pairs values by index (1st with 1st); race takes the first source to emit. combineLatest and forkJoin accept arrays or object maps (named results, v7+); the multi-argument form is deprecated.
• merge has concurrent limit; concat waits for each source to complete (infinite first source blocks the rest).
• shareReplay pitfalls: shareReplay(1) without refCount: true keeps the source subscription alive forever after the last subscriber leaves (a leak for infinite sources, but good for HTTP that completes). Cached errors: the source is not re-subscribed after error unless you reset; use share({ connector: () => new ReplaySubject(1), resetOnError: true, resetOnComplete: false, resetOnRefCountZero: true }) for exact control (RxJS 7). Cache invalidation needs an explicit refresh trigger, e.g. refresh$.pipe(startWith(null), switchMap(() => http.get(...)), shareReplay(1)).
• Because an HttpClient observable is cold, two | async in a template trigger two requests: share, or bind once with @if (data$ | async; as data) (or toSignal).

interviewQA: combineLatest vs forkJoin?

combineLatest emits every time any source emits (after all have emitted once) and works with infinite streams. forkJoin waits for all sources to complete and emits their last values once, like Promise.all.
merge vs concat?
merge subscribes to all sources at once and interleaves emissions; concat subscribes to the next source only after the previous completes.
What does withLatestFrom do?
On each emission of the main stream it combines the latest value of another stream; emissions of the other stream alone do not trigger output.
Why does combineLatest sometimes emit nothing?
One source has not emitted yet. Add startWith for sources like valueChanges that emit only on change.
What does shareReplay do and what is its main risk?
It shares one subscription and replays the latest N values to late subscribers. Without refCount it keeps the source alive forever and can cache stale data or errors.
How do you load several HTTP calls in parallel on init?
forkJoin with an object of observables, handling errors per call if partial results are acceptable.

topics.name: Error handling, completion and subscription management

beginner.content:
Errors and ending streams

• Error handling: an error notification ends the observable. Unhandled, it reaches the subscriber (or is thrown as an unhandled error). Handle it with catchError (give a fallback), retry (try again), finalize (cleanup code that always runs).
• Subscription management: infinite streams (interval, fromEvent, Subjects) never end, so you must end them. Memory leak prevention = every long-lived subscription has an owner that closes it.
• Tools: take, takeUntil, takeUntilDestroyed, unsubscribe(), the async pipe.

intermediate.content: catchError, retry, finalize in more detail
Stopping streams: take, takeUntil, takeUntilDestroyed

Observable to Promise: firstValueFrom and lastValueFrom

firstValueFrom(obs$) resolves with the first emission; lastValueFrom(obs$) waits for completion and resolves with the last. They replace the deprecated toPromise() and enable async/await. Both reject with EmptyError if the stream completes without a value, unless you pass { defaultValue }.

expert.content:
Details and recommendations

• Error semantics: the subscriber error callback is terminal. catchError replaces the failing source with another observable, so the downstream sees a normal continuation. To keep a long-lived stream (a valueChanges pipeline) alive, catch inside the inner observable, not on the outer.
• retry resubscribes to the whole upstream chain (cold sources re-execute, e.g. re-send an HTTP request): never retry non-idempotent POSTs blindly. Add back-off (retry({ delay })) and jitter; for HTTP combine with an interceptor. retryWhen is deprecated.
• finalize runs on complete, error and unsubscribe, making it ideal for spinners; its position matters (put it last in pipe to also cover downstream unsubscription, but before takeUntil if you want it to run when takeUntil triggers).
• takeUntil position: put it as the last operator, after switchMap/mergeMap, otherwise inner subscriptions can leak.
• Unhandled errors with no error callback are reported asynchronously through reportUnhandledError (RxJS 7), reaching Angular's ErrorHandler.
• What does not need manual unsubscribe: completing HttpClient calls, async pipe, toSignal, first()/take(n) that complete. What does: interval, fromEvent, valueChanges, router events, Subject-based buses, WebSockets.
• Detect leaks with browser memory profiler (growing detached DOM nodes / listeners) and by logging with tap({ finalize }). A lint rule (eslint-plugin-rxjs-angular, no-ignored-subscription) helps.
• toPromise() is deprecated (removed in RxJS 8): always use firstValueFrom/lastValueFrom.

interviewQA: How do you handle errors in RxJS?
Use catchError to supply a fallback observable or rethrow, retry for transient failures (with delay/back-off), the subscriber error callback as last resort, and finalize for cleanup.
Where to put catchError in a switchMap chain?
Inside the inner observable so the outer stream survives an error; at the end of the chain it would end the stream.
How do you prevent memory leaks from subscriptions?
Use async pipe, toSignal, take/first for finite needs, takeUntilDestroyed or takeUntil(destroy$) placed last in the pipe, or a Subscription container unsubscribed in ngOnDestroy.
What is takeUntilDestroyed?
An Angular rxjs-interop operator completing a stream when the injection context (component, directive, service) is destroyed; takes an optional DestroyRef.
firstValueFrom vs toPromise?
firstValueFrom/lastValueFrom are the replacements for the deprecated toPromise, with explicit semantics and EmptyError or defaultValue handling.
When does finalize run?
On complete, on error and on unsubscribe.

topics.name: AsyncPipe, Signals interop, testing and choosing operators

beginner.content:
AsyncPipe: subscribe from the template

• AsyncPipe (| async) subscribes to an Observable (or Promise) in the template, shows the latest value and unsubscribes automatically when the component dies. It also triggers change detection for OnPush components.
• Use @if (data$ | async; as data) to subscribe once and get a local variable.

intermediate.content:
RxJS with Angular Signals

• toSignal(obs$, { initialValue }) turns an observable into a signal (auto-unsubscribes).
• toObservable(signal) turns a signal into an observable (emits asynchronously through an effect), the bridge to switchMap.
Both come from @angular/core/rxjs-interop (stable in v17+; developer preview in v16). Details in Module 13.

Choosing the right operator

I want to...Use
Change each valuemap
Drop some valuesfilter, take, skip, distinctUntilChanged
React once typing pausesdebounceTime
Call an API per value, latest onlyswitchMap
Call an API per value, keep orderconcatMap
Call an API per value, in parallelmergeMap
Ignore triggers while busyexhaustMap
Wait for several callsforkJoin
Latest of several live streamscombineLatest
Combine an event with current statewithLatestFrom
Recover from errorscatchError, retry
Share an HTTP resultshareReplay
Stop on destroytakeUntilDestroyed

expert.content:
RxJS marble testing

Marble testing describes streams as ASCII diagrams run on a virtual clock via TestScheduler: - is one frame (1 ms), letters are values, | complete, # error, (ab) same-frame group, ^ subscription point in hot observables, ! unsubscription. Time progression such as debounceTime(30) is then tested without real waiting.

Interop details and AsyncPipe internals

• AsyncPipe is impure; it holds the subscription, calls markForCheck on emission (so it works with OnPush), and returns null before the first value (so guard with @if ... as or use ?? default). Each | async is a separate subscription: share cold sources.
• toSignal subscribes immediately, unsubscribes on owner destroy, throws on read if the observable errored, and needs an initialValue (or requireSync: true for synchronous sources like BehaviorSubject) otherwise the type includes undefined. It must run in an injection context (or pass injector). toObservable emits through an effect, so rapid sequential sets are coalesced and the first emission is asynchronous.
• Prefer signals for state, RxJS for events and async flows (debounce, cancellation, retry, websockets). Angular's own httpResource/resource() (Module 13) cover many simple cases that once required switchMap wiring.
• Avoid manual subscribe in components where the async pipe or toSignal fit; if you subscribe, own the cleanup.
• Version note: RxJS 7.8 ships with Angular 16-20; RxJS 8 will remove deprecated APIs (toPromise, the old subscribe(next, error, complete) form, retryWhen) so migrate now.

interviewQA: What does the AsyncPipe do and why is it recommended?
It subscribes to an Observable/Promise in the template, renders the latest value, unsubscribes automatically on destroy and marks the view for check, avoiding manual subscriptions and leaks.
What is toSignal and what must you provide?
It converts an Observable to a Signal and unsubscribes automatically. Provide initialValue (or requireSync) or accept undefined; call it in an injection context.
How do you bridge a signal into an RxJS pipeline?
toObservable(signal) then operators like debounceTime and switchMap, optionally converting back with toSignal.
What are marble diagrams?
A textual notation for streams over virtual time (- frames, letters values, | complete, # error) used with TestScheduler to test timing-based operators deterministically.
How do you choose between switchMap, concatMap, mergeMap and exhaustMap?
Latest only: switchMap. Ordered queue: concatMap. Parallel: mergeMap. Ignore while busy: exhaustMap.
Signals or RxJS for state?
Signals for synchronous state and derived values; RxJS for event streams, time-based operators, cancellation and complex async orchestration. Interop functions connect them.
