topics.name: Signals basics: signal(), set(), update(), asReadonly()

beginner.content:
Introduction to Signals

• A signal is a box holding a value that tells Angular when the value changes. Like a spreadsheet cell: change A1 and every cell using it recalculates automatically.
• Creating signals: signal(initialValue). Reading signal values: call it like a function, count(). Updating signal values: count.set(5) or count.update(c => c + 1).
• Signals in templates: write {{ count() }}; Angular updates only that spot when it changes. No pipes, no subscriptions.

Signals vs Observables

SignalObservable
ValueAlways has a current valueValues arrive over time (maybe none)
ReadSynchronously: s()Subscribe
CleanupAutomatic (garbage collected)Must unsubscribe unless async pipe
Best forUI state, derived valuesEvents, HTTP, time-based flows
Push/PullPush notification, lazy pull of valuesPush

intermediate.content:
Writable, read-only, and signals in components

• set() replaces; update(fn) derives from the previous value. For objects and arrays always create a new reference: items.update(list => [...list, x]).
• asReadonly() returns a read-only view so a service can keep set private and expose state safely (like a Java getter without a setter).
• Signals in components: declare state as signal fields; the template reads them by calling. They work with OnPush and zoneless change detection because Angular knows what to refresh.

expert.content:
How signals work

• A signal is a node in a reactive graph. Reading one inside a reactive context (template, computed, effect) records a dependency; setting it marks consumers dirty and schedules them. The graph is push-pull: notification is pushed, values are pulled lazily and cached.
• Templates are reactive contexts: a component with OnPush is marked for check only when a signal it read changed. This is the foundation for zoneless change detection (provideZonelessChangeDetection(), stable in v20.2, experimental from v18).
• Signals are not deep reactive: user().name = 'x' mutates silently and nothing updates. Use immutable updates (or copy-on-write helpers). Signal arrays of signals are possible but make code hard to reason about; prefer one signal of an immutable structure and derive slices with computed.
• Reading a signal in a plain method called outside a reactive context just returns the current value; no tracking occurs. untracked(() => sig()) reads without creating a dependency.
• Version: signals stable from v17 (developer preview v16); signal inputs v17.1, model v17.2, signal queries v17.2, output() v17.3, linkedSignal and resource v19 (experimental through v19-20; check release notes), zoneless from v18 (experimental).

interviewQA: What is a signal?
A reactive wrapper around a value. You read it by calling it, change it with set/update, and Angular tracks consumers (templates, computed, effects) so only dependents update.
set vs update?
set replaces the value; update takes a function receiving the current value and returning the new one.
Why use asReadonly()?
To expose state without letting consumers modify it, keeping write access inside the owner (encapsulation).
Signals vs Observables?
Signals hold a current synchronous value and suit UI state; Observables model asynchronous streams over time with operators. They interoperate.
Why does mutating an object inside a signal not update the view?
Signals detect change by reference equality (Object.is). Mutation keeps the same reference; replace the object or array with a new one.

topics.name: computed(), effect(), equality and dependencies

beginner.content:
computed() and derived state

• Derived state is anything you can calculate from other state (totals, filtered lists). Do not store it separately; compute it.
• computed() creates a read-only signal from a formula. Like a spreadsheet formula cell: it recalculates when its inputs change, and caches the result otherwise.
• effect() runs code (a side effect: logging, saving, calling a library) whenever the signals it reads change.

intermediate.content:
Dependencies, equality and effects in practice

• Signal dependencies are tracked dynamically at runtime: only the signals actually read in the last run count. In flag() ? a() : b() only one of a or b is a dependency at a time.
• Signal equality: a signal notifies only if the new value is not equal (Object.is) to the old one. Pass { equal: fn } to signal or computed for custom comparison.
• effect() must be created in an injection context (constructor or field initialiser), runs asynchronously during change detection, and is destroyed with its owner. Use it for syncing with the outside world (localStorage, analytics, canvas, third-party widgets), not for deriving state.

expert.content:
Rules, pitfalls and version notes

• computed is lazy and memoised: the function runs on first read and again only if a dependency changed. It must be pure: no side effects and no writes to signals (Angular throws).
• effect timing: component effects run during change detection before the component's template check (v19 changed timing: effects are tied to the component tree and run in the "mark for check" phase; root effects run in microtask-like flush). Do not rely on exact order; do not read DOM state in effects: use afterRenderEffect / afterNextRender.
• Writing signals inside effects is disallowed by default (error NG0600) because it creates loops; v19 removed allowSignalWrites as a requirement, but prefer computed or linkedSignal for derivations. Use untracked() to read signals without subscribing.
• Avoid effects for state propagation chains (A sets B sets C): hard to debug. Use computed or event handlers.
• effect outside an injection context: pass { injector }. Manual destroy: const ref = effect(...); ref.destroy().
• Conditional reads: if the effect returns early before reading a signal, that signal is not tracked in that run; read all dependencies you need first.
• Java mapping: computed ~ a memoised getter; effect ~ a listener/observer registered for you.

interviewQA: computed vs effect?
computed derives a read-only, lazily evaluated and memoised value and must be pure. effect performs side effects whenever its dependencies change and returns nothing.
How does Angular know a computed or effect depends on a signal?
It tracks signals read during execution (dynamic dependency tracking) and re-evaluates when any of them changes.
What is signal equality?
A signal updates dependents only when the new value differs from the old one by Object.is, or by a custom equal function you provide.
Why avoid using effect to set other signals?
It hides data flow, can cause loops and extra change detection. Use computed for derivation or linkedSignal for resettable state.
Where can you call effect()?
In an injection context such as a constructor or field initialiser (or pass an injector); it is auto-destroyed with the owner.

topics.name: Signal-based components: input(), model(), output()

beginner.content:
Signal-based component API

• Input signals: name = input<string>() or input.required<string>(); read with name(). Replaces @Input().
• Output functions: saved = output<User>(), emit with this.saved.emit(user). Replaces @Output() + EventEmitter.
• Model signals: value = model(0) is a writable input plus an automatic output, enabling [(value)] two-way binding.
• Signal-based component communication: parent sets inputs, child emits outputs, siblings share a signal service.

intermediate.content:
Derive from inputs and share signal state

Inputs are signals, so derived values are plain computed (no ngOnChanges). input() accepts { alias, transform }, e.g. numberAttribute or booleanAttribute.

Signal-based state management in a service

A root service with private writable signals, public readonly signals, computed selectors and methods for actions is enough for most apps.

expert.content:
Details and migration

• Signal inputs are read-only inside the component and can be read only after construction (not in the constructor body before inputs are set; use computed/effect or ngOnInit). Required inputs throw if read before binding.
• transform functions must be pure and statically analysable. Use input<T, TRaw> generics for transforms.
• output() is not an Observable (no pipe) but supports outputToObservable / outputFromObservable in rxjs-interop. Emitting during change detection or in the constructor is not allowed. It cleans up its subscribers automatically.
• model() can be bound with [(x)] or with [x] plus (xChange). Parent must pass a writable signal for true two-way sync; model.required() exists.
• Signal queries: viewChild(), viewChildren(), contentChild(), contentChildren() replace decorator queries and return signals (fixes timing problems).
• Schematics migrate automatically: ng generate @angular/core:signal-input-migration, output-migration, signal-queries-migration.
• inject()-based services plus signals give a lightweight store; when you need devtools, undo, effects orchestration at scale, consider NgRx Signal Store (Module 15).

interviewQA: How do input signals differ from @Input?
input() returns a read-only signal, can be required, supports transform and alias, and integrates with computed/effect so ngOnChanges is unnecessary.
What does model() do?
It creates a writable signal that is both an input and an output (xChange), enabling two-way binding with [(x)].
How do you emit events with output()?
Declare name = output<T>() and call name.emit(value); parents listen with (name)="handler($event)".
How can siblings communicate with signals?
Through a shared service that owns signals (private writable, public readonly) and exposes methods to change them.
Can you read input signals in the constructor?
Not meaningfully, they are not set yet; use computed, effect or ngOnInit.

topics.name: linkedSignal() and resource()

beginner.content:
Two newer helpers

Version note: linkedSignal() and resource() arrived in Angular 19 as experimental/developer-preview APIs and may be stabilised or renamed in later versions (resource gained params instead of request in v20, and httpResource was added in v19.2). Check the docs of your version before relying on them.
• linkedSignal: a writable signal whose value is reset automatically when a source signal changes, yet the user can still set it. Example: the selected size resets to the first option when the product changes.
• resource(): loads async data driven by signals, exposing value(), isLoading(), error() and status() as signals.

intermediate.content:
Using them in real components

• linkedSignal({ source, computation }) gives access to the previous value so you can keep a selection when still valid.
• resource aborts the previous load when the request changes and exposes reload(), set(), update() for local edits, and status(): idle, loading, reloading, resolved, error, local.
• rxResource (rxjs-interop) takes an Observable loader. httpResource() (v19.2+, experimental) wraps HttpClient so interceptors apply.

expert.content:
Guidance and caveats

• Use linkedSignal instead of an effect that writes to a signal when another changes (the classic "reset selection" bug-prone pattern).
• resource() is for reads, not mutations: use HttpClient + a method for POST/PUT/DELETE and then resource.reload(). Resource does not retry or cache by default; add your own cache or keep using a service for shared data.
• Reading value() of an errored resource throws in newer versions; check hasValue()/error(). During reload the previous value is kept (status "reloading"), which avoids flicker.
• Because these APIs are experimental in some releases, isolate them behind a service, and keep an RxJS (switchMap + toSignal) fallback in mind. Argument names changed between 19 and 20; follow the migration notes of your version.
• SSR: resource loaders run on the server; avoid browser-only APIs inside loaders.

interviewQA: What problem does linkedSignal solve?
A writable state derived from another signal that must reset when the source changes (selected item, current page) without hand-written effects.
What does resource() provide?
Signal-driven async loading: value, isLoading, error and status signals, automatic reload when its request/params signal changes and abort of stale loads.
Are linkedSignal and resource stable?
They were introduced as experimental in Angular 19; stability and some option names changed by v20, so verify against your version documentation.
resource vs RxJS switchMap?
resource covers simple load-on-change cases with built-in loading and error state; RxJS remains better for debounce, retries, combination and complex streams.
Should resource be used to save data?
No, it models reads. Perform writes with HttpClient or services and then reload or set the resource.

topics.name: Signal interop with RxJS: toSignal() and toObservable()

beginner.content:
Bridging two worlds

• Signal interop with RxJS lets you use signals for the view and RxJS for async flows.
• toSignal(observable$) subscribes and exposes the latest value as a signal (and unsubscribes automatically).
• toObservable(signal) makes an observable that emits when the signal changes.

intermediate.content: Typical flow: search

Options

• toSignal options: initialValue, requireSync: true (for BehaviorSubject-like sources that emit synchronously), injector (outside injection context), manualCleanup, rejectErrors.
• Without initialValue the signal type is T | undefined.

expert.content:
Gotchas

• Errors: if the observable errors, reading the signal rethrows the error. Handle with catchError upstream.
• toObservable uses an effect internally, so emissions are asynchronous and glitch-free: if the signal is set several times quickly, only the final value is emitted. Do not use it for synchronous event ordering.
• Injection context: both functions need one (constructor/field), otherwise pass { injector }; do not call toSignal repeatedly in methods, as each call creates a new subscription (leak until the owner dies).
• toSignal on a cold HTTP observable fires the request immediately on creation, even if the template never reads the signal.
• toSignal does not replace the async pipe in every case: the async pipe subscribes only when rendered (lazy), toSignal is eager.
• outputToObservable(output) and outputFromObservable(obs$) bridge component outputs; takeUntilDestroyed comes from the same package.
• Version: stable since Angular 17 (preview in 16); the rejectErrors option arrived in v19+.

interviewQA: How do you convert an Observable to a Signal?
toSignal(obs$, { initialValue }) from @angular/core/rxjs-interop; it subscribes immediately and unsubscribes when the owner is destroyed.
Why does toSignal need initialValue?
A signal always has a value but the observable may not have emitted yet; without initialValue the type includes undefined, or use requireSync for synchronous sources.
How do you use a signal with switchMap?
Convert with toObservable(signal), apply operators, then toSignal for the result.
Is toObservable synchronous?
No, it emits through an effect, so changes are batched and asynchronous.
What happens to errors in toSignal?
The error is thrown when the signal is read; catch errors in the pipeline.

topics.name: Signal performance, testing, mistakes and best practices

beginner.content:
Common signal mistakes

• Forgetting the parentheses: {{ count }} shows a function; use {{ count() }}.
• Mutating objects or arrays inside a signal instead of replacing them.
• Using effect to compute values (use computed).
• Writing to signals in computed.
• Storing the same data twice (a signal and a derived duplicate).
• Reading a signal in the constructor and expecting it to update.

intermediate.content:
Signal testing

Signals are plain synchronous values, so tests are simple: set, read, assert. Effects need change detection: call TestBed.flushEffects() (older versions) or TestBed.tick() / fixture.detectChanges() in newer ones. Inputs of a component are set with fixture.componentRef.setInput('name', value).

expert.content:
Signal performance and best practices

• Fine-grained: with signals only the exact template bindings that read a changed signal are refreshed; combined with OnPush or zoneless, big trees are not rechecked. computed memoises, so move heavy calculations into computed instead of template method calls.
• Keep computed functions small and free of I/O; break large ones into several computed signals to limit recomputation (each caches independently). Use equal to stop propagation when results are equivalent.
• Avoid signals of signals and giant objects updated frequently; prefer normalised, immutable structures (Module 15) so unchanged slices keep identity (use computed selectors to project them).
• Do not create signals or effects in loops, methods or template-called functions; create them as fields once.

Best practices

• State as private writable signal, expose asReadonly() or computed. Name signals as plain nouns, observables with $ suffix.
• Prefer computed over effect, linkedSignal over effect-setters, input/model/output over decorators, toSignal over manual subscribe in components.
• Use effects only at the edges (storage, logging, DOM/third-party integration) with onCleanup for resources.
• Migrate incrementally with the Angular schematics; signals and zone-based change detection can coexist.
• Debug with Angular DevTools (signal graph view in recent versions) and by logging inside effect.

interviewQA: What are the most common signal mistakes?

Forgetting to call the signal, mutating values in place, using effect for derived state, writing signals inside computed, and creating signals/effects outside a stable place like fields or constructors.
How do you test signal-based code?
Read and set signals synchronously; use fixture.componentRef.setInput for inputs and detectChanges (or TestBed.tick/flushEffects depending on version) to run effects.
Why do signals improve performance?
Angular knows exactly which bindings depend on which signals, so it updates only those, and computed values are memoised.
When is effect appropriate?
For side effects at the boundary: persistence, logging, analytics, imperative DOM or library integration, always with cleanup.
How would you structure signal state in a service?
Private writable signals, public readonly signals or computed selectors, and methods that perform immutable updates.

interviewQA: How should I use this checklist?
Work through the lessons in order, tick each item once you can explain it and write a small example from memory. The last column tells you which lesson to revisit.

topics.name: HTTP, REST and JSON fundamentals

beginner.content:
HTTP, REST and JSON in plain words

• HTTP fundamentals: the browser sends a request (method, URL, headers, optional body) and the server answers with a response (status code, headers, body). HTTP is stateless: every request stands alone, like sending separate letters.
• REST architecture: design the API around resources (nouns): /api/employees, /api/employees/7. The method says the action. If you know Spring Boot, a @RestController exposes exactly this.
• JSON request and response: data travels as JSON text: { "id": 7, "name": "Asha" }. Angular converts JSON to objects for you.
codeExamples:
// Angular (client): GET /api/employees/7  ->  200 OK  { "id": 7, "name": "Asha" }
this.http.get<Employee>('/api/employees/7').subscribe(e => console.log(e.name));

beginner.content:
Methods and status codes

MethodPurposeIdempotentSpring annotation
GETReadYes@GetMapping
POSTCreateNo@PostMapping
PUTReplace whole resourceYes@PutMapping
PATCHChange some fieldsUsually no guarantee@PatchMapping
DELETERemoveYes@DeleteMapping

HTTP status codes: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content; 301/302 redirect; 400 Bad Request (validation), 401 Unauthorized (not logged in), 403 Forbidden (not allowed), 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict, 422 Unprocessable; 500 Internal Server Error, 503 Service Unavailable.

intermediate.content:
Designing the contract

• Use plural nouns, nested resources sparingly (/api/orders/5/items), query parameters for filter/sort/page, and consistent error bodies.
• Respond with proper codes: 201 + Location header on create, 204 on delete, 400 with field errors for validation, 404 for missing resources. In Spring Boot use ResponseEntity and a @RestControllerAdvice for error shaping.
• JSON mapping: Jackson converts DTO classes to JSON with the same property names. Dates travel as ISO strings (2025-03-01T10:00:00Z) and become strings in TypeScript; convert with new Date(...) or the date pipe. Java Long beyond 2^53 loses precision in JavaScript: send as string.

expert.content:
Expert notes

• Idempotency drives retry safety: retry GET/PUT/DELETE freely; POST only with an idempotency key header the server honours.
• 401 vs 403: 401 means unauthenticated (try refresh token or log in), 403 authenticated but not permitted (show forbidden page). Clients should not treat both the same.
• HTTP/2 multiplexing makes many small requests cheap; HTTP caching headers (ETag, Cache-Control) can save bandwidth: browsers cache GET responses unless told otherwise; use If-None-Match flows for large lists.
• Keep contracts typed: generate TypeScript clients from OpenAPI (springdoc-openapi + openapi-generator) so Spring DTO changes break the Angular build instead of production.
• Prefer JSON everywhere; XML or form-encoded only for legacy endpoints (application/x-www-form-urlencoded via HttpParams body).

interviewQA: What does REST mean in practice?
Resource-oriented URLs, HTTP methods as verbs, stateless requests, representations such as JSON, and meaningful status codes.
PUT vs PATCH?
PUT replaces the whole resource and is idempotent; PATCH sends only changed fields.
401: the client is not authenticated or the token is invalid; 403: authenticated but not authorised for the action.
Which status code after a successful POST that creates a resource?
201 Created, ideally with a Location header and the created resource in the body.
Which methods are idempotent and why does it matter?
GET, PUT and DELETE (and HEAD/OPTIONS); repeating them has the same effect, so they are safe to retry. POST is not.

topics.name: HttpClient setup and CRUD requests

beginner.content:
Setting up HttpClient

• Configuring provideHttpClient() in the application config registers the HttpClient service. Add features such as withInterceptors([...]) and withFetch().
• Inject with inject(HttpClient) and call get/post/put/patch/delete. Each returns an Observable that sends the request only when subscribed (cold). Without subscribe (or async pipe) nothing is sent!

intermediate.content:
Using the service in a component

GET for reading, POST for creating (the object is the request body, sent as JSON automatically), PUT to replace, PATCH to update parts, DELETE to remove. Request bodies may be objects (JSON), FormData, strings, Blob or HttpParams for form-encoded.

Response types and observe options

• Response types (responseType): 'json' (default), 'text', 'blob', 'arraybuffer'.
• observe: 'body' (default) returns the body; 'response' returns the whole HttpResponse (status, headers); 'events' returns progress events.

expert.content:
Internals and good practice

• Cold observables: subscribing twice sends two requests. Responses of successful calls complete after one emission, so no unsubscribe is needed; but unsubscribe cancels in flight.
• provideHttpClient() replaced HttpClientModule (legacy). Use withFetch() (uses the Fetch API; recommended for SSR), withInterceptorsFromDi() to keep old class-based interceptors, withXsrfConfiguration(), withJsonpSupport().
• Order: interceptors listed run in order for requests and reverse for responses.
• Put HTTP in services, not components. Components deal with state (loading, data, error); the service returns observables mapped to domain types.
• Do not build URLs by string concatenation of user input; use HttpParams or encode (encodeURIComponent).
• Mutations followed by reads: after POST/DELETE, update local state or refetch; avoid reading stale cached lists.
• Angular 19.2+ httpResource() offers a signal-first read API on top of HttpClient (experimental).

interviewQA: Why is my HttpClient call not sending a request?
HttpClient returns a cold Observable; the request is sent only on subscribe (or async pipe / toSignal). Nothing happens without a subscriber.
How do you register HttpClient in a standalone app?
Add provideHttpClient() (with features like withInterceptors) to the application providers.
How do you read the status code or headers?
Pass { observe: "response" } so the observable emits HttpResponse with status, headers and body.
Do you need to unsubscribe from HttpClient calls?
Usually no, they complete after the response; unsubscribe only to cancel an in-flight request (switchMap and takeUntilDestroyed handle it).
What does withFetch() do?
It makes HttpClient use the Fetch API instead of XMLHttpRequest, useful for SSR; note it does not support upload progress events.

topics.name: Parameters, headers and typed services

beginner.content:
Sending data in the URL and headers

• Path parameters are inside the path: /api/employees/7 (Spring @PathVariable).
• Query parameters follow ?: /api/employees?dept=IT&page=0 (Spring @RequestParam).
• HTTP headers carry metadata like Authorization and Content-Type.
• These are all kinds of request parameters, alongside the request body.
codeExamples:
this.http.get<Employee>('/api/employees/' + id);                            // path parameter
this.http.get<Employee[]>('/api/employees', { params: { dept: 'IT', page: 0 } });   // query: ?dept=IT&page=0
this.http.get<Employee[]>('/api/employees', { headers: { 'X-Trace-Id': 'abc' } });  // header

intermediate.content:
HttpParams and HttpHeaders (immutable)

HttpParams and HttpHeaders are immutable: every set/append returns a new object, so reassign. They also encode values safely.

Typed API responses and a generic API service

Always pass the generic type so the compiler knows the shape (typed API responses). Remember: TypeScript types are erased at runtime, so they are not validation. A generic API service removes CRUD repetition.

expert.content:
Notes

• Forgetting to reassign HttpParams is the classic bug (params.set(...) alone does nothing).
• HttpParams encodes with its own codec which leaves some characters such as + unencoded; for exotic characters pass new HttpParams({ encoder: ... }) or fromObject with a custom HttpParameterCodec.
• Boolean/number values in the object form are converted to strings; undefined/null values may be skipped or stringified depending on the Angular version; filter them yourself.
• Typed responses can lie: a backend rename leads to undefined at runtime. Use generated clients, or runtime validation (zod) at critical boundaries, and map DTOs to domain models in the service (adapter pattern): parse dates, rename fields.
• Prefer composition (a small ApiClient wrapper per resource) over deep inheritance if endpoints diverge. Keep Content-Type automatic: setting it manually for FormData breaks the multipart boundary.
• Headers like Authorization belong in an interceptor, not repeated per call.

interviewQA: Path vs query parameters?
Path params identify a specific resource (/employees/7); query params provide optional filters, paging and sorting (?dept=IT&page=0).
Why is HttpParams immutable and what is the usual bug?
Each set/append returns a new instance, so you must reassign it; calling params.set without assignment silently does nothing.
How do you type an HttpClient response?
Use the generic argument, e.g. http.get<Employee[]>(url). It is compile-time only; there is no runtime validation.
Why create a generic CRUD service?
To avoid repeating list/get/create/update/delete for each resource while keeping type safety through generics.
Should you set Content-Type manually for FormData?
No, the browser must set multipart/form-data with the boundary; setting it manually breaks the upload.

topics.name: Interceptors, errors, retry, timeout and loading

beginner.content:
Interceptors: one place for cross-cutting rules

• An HTTP interceptor sits between your code and the network and can inspect or change every request and response, like a servlet Filter or Spring HandlerInterceptor.
• Functional interceptors are plain functions HttpInterceptorFn registered with withInterceptors([...]); class-based HttpInterceptor is the legacy style.
• Typical interceptors: add an authentication token, show a loading indicator, handle errors globally, log, set base URL.

intermediate.content:
Global error handling, HTTP error responses, retry and timeout

• HTTP error responses arrive as HttpErrorResponse with status, error (the body) and message. Status 0 = network/CORS failure. 4xx/5xx errors go to the observable error channel.
• Global error handling: one interceptor translates errors (401 to login, 403 to forbidden page, 5xx to a toast) and rethrows for local handling.
• Retry strategies: retry only transient failures (network, 503) on idempotent calls, with back-off. Request timeout: RxJS timeout().

Request and response transformation, and loading indicator

Clone the request to modify it; map the HttpResponse body to transform responses (for example convert ISO date strings). A counter of active requests drives a global spinner.

expert.content:
Pitfalls and architecture

• Immutability: HttpRequest and HttpResponse are immutable; always clone. Interceptor order = array order for requests, reverse for responses. Place error handling and retry inside auth when you refresh tokens.
• Token refresh pattern: on 401, perform one refresh using exhaustMap/shareReplay shared with other waiting requests, then replay the original request; protect against infinite loops by skipping the refresh URL itself.
• Interceptors see every request including those to third-party hosts: attach tokens only to your own API origin to avoid token leakage. Use HttpContextToken to pass per-request flags (skip auth, disable retry) without magic headers.
• Retry only idempotent requests; combine with exponential back-off and jitter. Do not retry 4xx. Each retry re-runs the downstream chain including your loading counters; keep finalize outside retry to count once.
• timeout throws TimeoutError (not HttpErrorResponse) and cancels the request.
• The loading counter must decrement in finalize else a cancelled request leaves the spinner on.
• DI note: functional interceptors run in an injection context, so use inject() at the top of the function. Legacy class interceptors: provideHttpClient(withInterceptorsFromDi()) and the HTTP_INTERCEPTORS multi token.

interviewQA: What is an HTTP interceptor and why use it?
A function or class that handles every HttpClient request/response, used for auth headers, logging, error handling, loading indicators and URL/body transformation in one place.
How do you write a functional interceptor?
Define an HttpInterceptorFn (req, next) => next(req.clone(...)), use inject() inside, and register with provideHttpClient(withInterceptors([fn])).
Why clone the request?
HttpRequest objects are immutable; clone creates a modified copy with new headers, url or body.
How do you implement a global loading indicator?
Count active requests in a signal service, increment in the interceptor, and decrement in finalize so success, error and cancellation are all covered.
What does HttpErrorResponse status 0 mean?
The browser could not reach the server: network down, DNS failure or CORS blocked, no HTTP response was received.
How should retries be done safely?
Only for idempotent requests and transient errors, with limited count and exponential back-off.

topics.name: File upload, download and progress events

beginner.content:
Sending and receiving files

• File uploads: put the selected file into a FormData and POST it. The browser sets the multipart header itself. In Spring Boot this arrives as MultipartFile.
• File downloads: request with responseType: 'blob' and create a temporary URL to trigger the browser download.
• Progress events: with reportProgress: true and observe: 'events' you receive upload/download progress for a progress bar.

intermediate.content: Download and progress

Filename from the server

Use observe: 'response' to read Content-Disposition (Spring: ResponseEntity with HttpHeaders.CONTENT_DISPOSITION). For CORS you must expose it: exposedHeaders("Content-Disposition").

expert.content:
Constraints and security

• Validate on the client (type, size) for UX but enforce on the server: spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size, content-type sniffing, virus scan, random server-side file names, storage outside web root.
• Large files: Blob in memory is limited; for very big downloads prefer a direct link with a short-lived signed URL, window.open or streaming (StreamingResponseBody) instead of loading into JS memory. For huge uploads consider chunked/resumable uploads.
• withFetch() does not report upload progress (Fetch limitation); keep XHR-based HttpClient for upload progress.
• Always revoke object URLs. Cancelling the observable cancels the transfer. Use HttpEventType.DownloadProgress with responseType: 'blob' for download bars (needs Content-Length).
• Multiple files: mergeMap(file => upload(file), 3) to limit concurrency. Never set Content-Type yourself for FormData.
• For authenticated downloads you cannot use a plain <a href> (no Authorization header): use HttpClient blob download, or a one-time token in the URL.

interviewQA: How do you upload a file from Angular to Spring Boot?
Build a FormData with the File under the field name expected by @RequestParam/@RequestPart (MultipartFile) and POST it; do not set Content-Type manually.
How do you download a file?
GET with responseType blob, create an object URL, click a temporary anchor with the download attribute, then revoke the URL.
How do you show upload progress?
Use reportProgress true and observe events, handle HttpEventType.UploadProgress (loaded/total) and HttpEventType.Response.
Why might progress events not appear?
Using withFetch(), which lacks upload progress, or a server not sending Content-Length for downloads.
Which checks belong on the server?
Size, type, content validation, safe file naming, storage location, authorisation, virus scanning.

topics.name: Pagination, search, cancellation, parallel and cached calls

beginner.content:
Common API patterns

• Pagination: ask for one page at a time: ?page=0&size=10. Spring Data returns a Page JSON with content, totalElements.
• Sorting and filtering: ?sort=name,asc&status=ACTIVE.
• Search with debounce: wait until the user stops typing, then call the API.
• API cancellation: abandon outdated requests. Parallel API requests: independent calls together. Sequential API requests: when one needs the result of another. Caching API responses: avoid asking again for unchanged data.

intermediate.content: Paged, sorted, filtered list with a single stream
Parallel, sequential and cancellation

expert.content:
Design considerations

• Server-side paging, sorting and filtering for any data set that can grow: never load everything and filter in the browser. Spring Data's Pageable maps page, size, sort automatically. For large offsets or live data consider keyset (cursor) pagination.
• Keep the query state (page, sort, filters) in URL query params so refresh, back button and sharing work: read from ActivatedRoute, write with router.navigate([], { queryParams, queryParamsHandling: 'merge' }).
• Race conditions: without switchMap an older slow response can overwrite a newer one. forkJoin fails entirely if any call fails: catch per call. forkJoin on a never-completing stream never emits.
• Caching options: shareReplay in a service, an interceptor-based cache keyed by URL with TTL (GET only), signals/stores holding loaded entities, HTTP cache headers (ETag, Cache-Control) honoured by the browser, and stale-while-revalidate (emit cache, then refresh). Invalidate after mutations.
• Avoid duplicated parallel calls for the same resource (several components requesting simultaneously): share in-flight requests (shareReplay/Map of in-flight observables).
• Dependent calls should be batched on the backend where possible (aggregation endpoint) to avoid waterfalls.

interviewQA: How do you implement search-as-you-type properly?
valueChanges (or signal via toObservable) with debounceTime, distinctUntilChanged and switchMap to the API, handling errors inside the inner observable.
Why use server-side pagination?
To keep payloads and memory small and make large data sets usable; the client sends page, size, sort and filters, and Spring Data returns a Page.
Parallel vs sequential requests: which operators?
Parallel: forkJoin (or combineLatest for live streams). Sequential/dependent: switchMap/concatMap; ordered independent: concat.
How do you cancel an outdated request?
Unsubscribe; switchMap does it automatically when a new value arrives, and takeUntilDestroyed on destruction.
How can you cache API responses in Angular?
shareReplay in a service, a TTL cache interceptor for GET requests, store entities in signals, and rely on HTTP cache headers; invalidate after writes.

topics.name: Environments, CORS, testing and Spring Boot integration

beginner.content:
Environments, CORS and wiring to Spring Boot

• Environment-specific API URLs: development talks to http://localhost:8080, production to https://api.example.com. Keep the base URL in a config, never hard-coded in services.
• CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing): browsers block a page from calling another origin (scheme + host + port) unless the server allows it. Angular on localhost:4200 calling Spring on localhost:8080 is cross-origin. The server answers with Access-Control-Allow-Origin.
• Connecting Angular with Spring Boot: Spring exposes /api/**; Angular calls it via a dev proxy or an allowed CORS origin.

intermediate.content: Environment files and runtime config
Spring Boot side: CORS and a full vertical slice

expert.content:
API integration testing with HttpTestingController

Unit-test services without a server: provide provideHttpClient() and provideHttpClientTesting(), call the service, then use HttpTestingController to assert the request and flush a fake response.

CORS and deployment notes

• Preflight: for non-simple requests (JSON content type, Authorization header, PUT/PATCH/DELETE) the browser first sends an OPTIONS request; the server must answer with allowed origin, methods and headers. Errors show as status 0 with a console CORS message: fix the server, not Angular.
• allowedOrigins("*") cannot be combined with credentials. Never reflect arbitrary origins in production; list exact origins per environment.
• Best production setup: serve Angular and the API under the same origin (reverse proxy such as Nginx routing / to static files and /api to Spring Boot) so no CORS is needed; or serve the built Angular files from Spring Boot static resources with a forward of unknown paths to index.html.
• Runtime configuration (a config.json fetched at start with provideAppInitializer/APP_INITIALIZER) lets one build be deployed to many environments without rebuilding.
• Test levels: service unit tests with HttpTestingController, component tests with stubbed services, and real end-to-end tests (Playwright/Cypress) against a Spring Boot test instance or MockServer/WireMock.

interviewQA: What is CORS and how is it solved?

A browser security rule blocking cross-origin calls unless the server sends Access-Control-Allow-* headers. Solve with server CORS configuration (Spring CorsRegistry / Security cors()), a dev proxy, or serving both under one origin via a reverse proxy.
How do you manage different API URLs per environment?
environment files with fileReplacements, an InjectionToken for the base URL, or runtime config loaded at startup; never hard-code URLs.
What is a preflight request?
An automatic OPTIONS request the browser sends before cross-origin requests that are not simple; the server must approve method, headers and origin.
How do you test an HTTP service?
Use provideHttpClient plus provideHttpClientTesting, call the service, assert with HttpTestingController.expectOne, flush responses or errors, and verify() in afterEach.
What does the dev proxy do?
ng serve forwards /api calls to the backend (target), so the browser sees the same origin and CORS is not needed in development.
How do you wire Angular with Spring Boot end to end?

Define the REST controller and DTOs with validation, enable CORS or a proxy, mirror DTOs as TypeScript interfaces (or generate from OpenAPI), call through services with HttpClient and interceptors, handle errors uniformly and deploy behind one reverse proxy.

interviewQA: How should I use this checklist?
Work through the lessons in order, tick each item once you can explain it and write a small example from memory. The last column tells you which lesson to revisit.

topics.name: State fundamentals: local, shared, service, RxJS and Signals state

beginner.content:
What is state?

• State is the data that decides what the screen shows: the logged-in user, items in the cart, whether a menu is open. State management is deciding where that data lives and how it changes.
• Local component state: used by one component only (is the dropdown open?). Keep it in the component as a signal.
• Shared application state: needed by several components (cart, user). Put it in a service that components inject (like a Spring singleton bean).
• Rule: keep state as local as possible and share only what must be shared.

intermediate.content:
Service-based state: two styles

Service-based state management = a root service that owns the state and exposes read-only access plus methods for changes.
RxJS-based state: BehaviorSubject inside the service, exposed as an observable (classic, good with operators).
Signals-based state: signal + computed (modern, simplest).

expert.content:
Design rules for service stores

• One store per domain/feature (cart, auth, products) rather than one giant service; stores can depend on each other through inject() but avoid cycles.
• Expose state read-only; mutate only through named methods ("actions"). That gives you a single place to log, validate or persist changes, similar to Redux without the ceremony.
• Choose scope deliberately: providedIn: 'root' lives for the whole app; providers on a route or component gives a store whose lifetime matches that feature, and a fresh instance per visit.
• Do not use services as a communication bus for everything: server data belongs in a cache layer (see Module 14), UI-only state belongs in components.
• Server state vs client state: data fetched from the API (a cache that can go stale) behaves differently from client state (selected tab). Keep them distinct, using resource/query-style tools for server data.
• RxJS stores shine for event-heavy logic (debounce, retry, websockets); signal stores shine for synchronous UI state. You can combine: toSignal(store.items$).
• Java parallel: a root service is a singleton bean; a route-level provider is like a prototype/request-scoped bean.

interviewQA: What is local vs shared state and where should each live?
Local state belongs to one component (signal field). Shared state is needed by multiple components and belongs in an injectable service (or store) scoped appropriately.
How do you implement a simple store with Signals?
A service with a private writable signal, a readonly exposure via asReadonly, computed selectors and methods that update immutably.
BehaviorSubject store vs signal store?
BehaviorSubject integrates with RxJS operators and async flows; signals are simpler for synchronous UI state and read without subscription. Both can be combined via interop.
Why expose state read-only?
So only the store can change state, which keeps updates traceable and prevents accidental mutation from components.
What is the difference between server state and client state?
Server state is remote data that is cached and may become stale; client state exists only in the UI (filters, open panels). They need different tools and lifecycles.

topics.name: Immutable updates, normalization, derived, loading and error state

beginner.content:
Four habits of clean state

• Immutable state updates: never change an object in place; create a new one. Change detection and signals notice new references only.
• Derived state: do not store what can be calculated (the total of a cart); compute it.
• State normalization: store each item once, by id, and refer to it by id. Like a database: a foreign key instead of copying the whole row.
• Loading and error states: every remote request has phases: idle, loading, success, error. Model them explicitly so the UI can show spinners and messages.

intermediate.content: Normalized state and loading status

expert.content:
Why and when

• Immutability enables cheap change detection (reference comparison), OnPush, memoised selectors, undo/redo and time travel. For deep trees consider helper libraries (immer, or structuredClone for copies), or NgRx Signal Store's patchState with partial updates. Large arrays copied on every keystroke can be costly: batch updates.
• Normalize when entities are shared by many views or updated often (chat messages, users, products referenced from orders). Keep nested only when data is read-only and exclusive to one view. NgRx EntityAdapter normalizes for you (ids + entities).
• Derived state should be computed in selectors (computed/createSelector) so it is memoised and always consistent. Avoid redundant booleans (isLoading, isError, hasData that can contradict); one status union prevents contradictions.
• Keep stale data visible during reloads (status "reloading") and show errors without throwing away previous data; separate per-request status for lists vs details to avoid global spinners masking everything.
• Optimistic updates: change state first, send the request, roll back on error; for correctness keep a copy of the previous state.

interviewQA: Why must state updates be immutable?
Angular, signals and selectors detect changes through reference comparison; mutation leaves the reference unchanged so nothing updates, and it breaks OnPush, memoisation and debugging.
What is state normalization?
Storing entities once in a lookup by id and referencing them by id elsewhere, avoiding duplication and inconsistent updates.
How do you model loading and error state?
With an explicit status (idle, loading, success, error) preferably as a discriminated union, so contradictory combinations are impossible.
What is derived state and why not store it?
A value computable from other state (totals, filtered lists). Storing it risks inconsistency; compute with computed or selectors.
What is an optimistic update?
Applying the change in the UI immediately and reverting if the server request fails.

topics.name: Authentication state, persisting state and browser storage

beginner.content:
Authentication state and saving state

• Authentication state = who is logged in: the user, their roles and the token. It is a classic shared state: put it in one AuthStore that guards, interceptors and menus use.
• Persisting state means keeping it after a refresh by saving to the browser: LocalStorage (stays until cleared, shared across tabs) or SessionStorage (until the tab closes).
• Both store strings only: use JSON.stringify / JSON.parse.

intermediate.content: An auth store with persistence
A safe storage helper

expert.content:
Security and limits of browser storage

• Never store secrets (passwords, long-lived tokens) in LocalStorage/SessionStorage: any XSS can read it. Prefer HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies set by Spring Security for session or refresh tokens, and keep the access token in memory (a signal) with silent refresh. If you must store a token, keep it short-lived.
• Storage is synchronous, limited (about 5 MB), same-origin, per-browser, can be disabled or throw (private mode, quota). Always wrap in try/catch and tolerate missing or corrupted data. Version stored shapes ({ v: 2, data }) so releases can migrate old data.
• Cross-tab sync: listen to the storage event (fires in other tabs) to update the state on logout in another tab.
• SSR: localStorage does not exist on the server; guard with isPlatformBrowser or wrap behind an injection token (STORAGE) with a no-op server implementation, which also helps testing.
• Persist only what is worth persisting (preferences, drafts, filters), not server data that can be refetched. For larger data use IndexedDB.
• Remember: client-side auth state is for display. The server validates every request. Guards and interceptors read this state (Module 16 covers the full security model).

interviewQA: LocalStorage vs SessionStorage?
LocalStorage persists until cleared and is shared across tabs of the same origin; SessionStorage lasts for one tab session. Both store strings and are synchronous.
Where should the authentication state live?
In a dedicated auth store/service (signals) exposing user, roles and isLoggedIn, consumed by guards, interceptors and templates.
Is LocalStorage a safe place for tokens?
Not for sensitive long-lived tokens, because XSS can read it. Prefer HttpOnly secure cookies or in-memory short-lived access tokens.
How do you persist state safely?
Serialise to JSON in try/catch, version the shape, persist only needed parts, and abstract storage behind a token for SSR and tests.
How can you sync logout across browser tabs?
Listen to the window storage event and clear the in-memory state when the key is removed.

topics.name: NgRx fundamentals: Store, actions, reducers, selectors

beginner.content:
NgRx fundamentals

• NgRx is Angular's implementation of the Redux pattern: one predictable, central Store and a strict one-way loop. Think of a bank: you do not edit the ledger yourself; you fill a slip (action), the clerk (reducer) updates the ledger by fixed rules, and you read balances through statements (selectors).
• The loop: component dispatches an Action to the Store; a Reducer (pure function) returns the next state; Selectors read slices; components re-render. Effects handle side effects such as HTTP.
• Install: ng add @ngrx/store (plus @ngrx/effects, @ngrx/entity, @ngrx/store-devtools).

intermediate.content:
Actions, reducers, selectors for a feature

• Actions describe events, named "[Source] Event", with a typed payload (createActionGroup reduces boilerplate).
• Reducers are pure: no HTTP, no randomness, no mutation; same input, same output.
• Selectors (createFeatureSelector, createSelector) are memoised functions that read and derive state.

expert.content:
Principles and details

• Store is an Observable of state plus dispatch. Use store.select(selector) (Observable) or store.selectSignal(selector) (Signal, v16+). Prefer signals in components.
• Reducers must be pure and fast. Runtime checks (strictStateImmutability, strictActionImmutability, serializability) are on in development and freeze state to catch mutation. Keep state serializable: no class instances, Dates (use ISO strings), Maps/Sets or functions.
• Selectors memoise by input reference: composing small selectors gives precise recomputation. A selector that returns a new object/array each time defeats memoisation downstream. Use projector to unit test selectors without a store.
• Actions are the audit log: model events ("Order Placed"), not setters ("Set Order Flag"); good action names describe what happened, not what to do. Avoid reusing one action for many sources.
• NgRx adds files and indirection. It pays off with big teams, complex cross-feature workflows, strict traceability or undo/redo; not for a to-do app. Compare with a signal service in the last lesson.
• Version: standalone APIs (provideStore, provideState, provideEffects) from NgRx 15+; createFeature v12+; class-based StoreModule is legacy; on-based reducers since v8.

interviewQA: Explain the NgRx data flow.

Components dispatch actions; reducers (pure functions) compute the new immutable state in the Store; selectors expose slices to components; effects handle async side effects and dispatch further actions.
Why must reducers be pure?
So state transitions are predictable, testable and replayable (time travel, DevTools); side effects belong in effects.
What are selectors and why memoised?
Functions to read and derive state; memoisation recomputes only when input slices change, saving work and avoiding extra renders.
What are the three ways to read state in a component?
store.select (Observable with async pipe), store.selectSignal (Signal), or subscribe manually (discouraged).
How should actions be named and designed?
As events that happened with a [Source] prefix, such as [Products Page] Load, describing the origin and intent rather than generic setters.

topics.name: NgRx effects, entities, feature state and DevTools

beginner.content:
Effects: where side effects live

• Effects listen to the stream of actions, perform side effects (HTTP calls, navigation, storage) and dispatch new actions with the result. They keep reducers pure and components thin.
• Feature state: state split per feature, registered with provideState on a lazy route, so the code and its slice load together.
• Entity management: @ngrx/entity manages collections as normalised ids + entities with ready-made add/update/remove methods.
• Store DevTools: a browser extension view of every action and state, with time-travel.

intermediate.content: Entity adapter
Dispatching and reading in a component; DevTools setup

expert.content:
Effects in depth

• Choose the flattening operator deliberately: switchMap (latest wins, loads), concatMap (ordered writes), mergeMap (parallel independent), exhaustMap (ignore duplicates, login). Put catchError inside the inner pipe, or the effect dies after the first error (NgRx resubscribes effects up to 10 times by default but do not rely on it).
• Non-dispatching effects (navigation, logging): { dispatch: false }. Effects can read state with concatLatestFrom (or withLatestFrom(store.select(...))) to avoid races.
• Avoid the "effect chain" anti-pattern where effect A triggers action that triggers effect B for a simple sequence; and avoid effects that only map one action to another (do it in the reducer or selector).
• Entity: use selectId for custom keys and sortComparer only when needed (sorting cost). Selectors from getSelectors() are memoised; combine with feature selectors.
• Feature state: register with provideState at route level so a lazy chunk brings its reducer; avoid cross-feature direct state access, expose public selectors/facades. The state key must be unique.
• DevTools: use maxAge to bound memory, logOnly in production, sanitize large or sensitive actions/state (actionSanitizer, stateSanitizer), never expose tokens. Features: time travel, action replay, state diff, import/export.
• Facade pattern: wrap Store access in a feature service/facade so components do not know about NgRx; eases migration to Signal Store or services.

interviewQA: What are effects used for?
Handling side effects outside reducers: HTTP calls, navigation, storage, analytics. They react to actions and dispatch result actions.
Why put catchError inside switchMap in effects?
So an error in one request does not complete the outer actions stream and kill the effect.
What does EntityAdapter provide?
A normalised ids/entities state and ready-made reducer helpers (addOne, setAll, updateOne, removeOne) and memoised selectors (selectAll, selectEntities).
What is feature state?
A slice of the store owned by one feature, registered with provideState (often on a lazy route) so its reducer and effects load with the feature.
What do Store DevTools offer?
Inspection of dispatched actions and state diffs, time travel, replay and import/export of sessions; configure sanitizers and logOnly for production.

topics.name: NgRx Signal Store

beginner.content:
NgRx Signal Store: the light version

• NgRx Signal Store (@ngrx/signals) is a signal-based store with far less boilerplate than the classic Store: define state, computed values and methods in one place.
• Building blocks: signalStore(), withState(), withComputed(), withMethods(), patchState(), withHooks().
• Think of it as a well-structured service with a standard shape, so every team writes stores the same way.

intermediate.content:
Async methods, entities and hooks

• rxMethod (from @ngrx/signals/rxjs-interop) turns an RxJS pipeline into a method that accepts a value, signal or observable: ideal for loading with switchMap.
• withEntities() from @ngrx/signals/entities provides normalised collections. withHooks({ onInit, onDestroy }) runs setup and cleanup.
• Add status with a custom feature (signalStoreFeature) to reuse loading/error handling across stores.

expert.content:
Design and caveats

• State is exposed as deep-readonly signals; updates go through patchState only (state itself is not writable from outside), keeping encapsulation. State must be a plain object; each top-level property becomes a signal (nested objects can be deep signals).
• Scope: providedIn: 'root' for global, or provide on component/route for per-feature lifecycle (a fresh instance per visit, destroyed with it, with withHooks cleanup).
• Compared with classic NgRx: no actions/reducers/effects, no DevTools by default (community withDevtools feature exists: @angular-architects/ngrx-toolkit), less ceremony, less audit trail. Great default for feature-level state; classic Store for app-wide event-sourced logic.
• Extend with signalStoreFeature (reusable slices: loading status, pagination, undo-redo), withProps (v19+) for injected dependencies and observables, and withLinkedState (v20) for linkedSignal-based state; check your @ngrx/signals version because the API grew quickly (v17 introduced it, stable from v18/19).
• Use getState(store) for snapshots and watchState to observe changes; keep derived data in withComputed. Do not put non-serialisable things in state if you plan to persist or debug it.
• NgRx Signal Store pairs naturally with Angular signals and zoneless apps; keep HTTP inside rxMethod with switchMap or exhaustMap chosen deliberately.

interviewQA: What is the NgRx Signal Store?
A lightweight signal-based store from @ngrx/signals defined with signalStore, withState, withComputed and withMethods, updated through patchState, without actions and reducers.
How do you do async loading in a Signal Store?
With rxMethod and an RxJS pipeline (tap, switchMap, tapResponse) that patches loading, data and error state.
Signal Store vs classic NgRx Store?
Signal Store is simpler, local or feature-scoped, with direct method calls; classic Store enforces actions/reducers/effects for global, auditable, DevTools-friendly flows at the cost of boilerplate.
How do you reuse logic across Signal Stores?
Create custom features with signalStoreFeature (for example withLoadingStatus) and compose them.
Can a Signal Store be scoped to a component?
Yes, omit providedIn root and add it to the providers of a component or route, so each instance gets its own store which is destroyed with it.

topics.name: State management testing and choosing an approach

beginner.content:
Choosing a state approach

SituationUse
UI state of one componentLocal signal
Shared by a few components, simpleSignal service store
Stream-heavy (websocket, polling, debounce)RxJS service (BehaviorSubject) with toSignal
Feature with loading, entities, many methodsNgRx Signal Store
Large app, many teams, cross-feature workflows, audit, time travelNgRx Store + Effects + Entity
Server data fetch and cacheresource/httpResource or a data-fetching layer with caching
Start simple (signals in services) and escalate only when a real problem appears.

intermediate.content:
State management testing

• Signal service store: instantiate via TestBed, call methods, assert signals (synchronous).
• NgRx reducer: pure function: call with state and action, compare result. Selector: call .projector or with a mock state. Effect: provide actions as a stream (provideMockActions) and mock the API, assert emitted actions. Component with Store: provideMockStore({ initialState, selectors }) and spy on dispatch. Signal Store: TestBed.inject(Store), call methods, read signals; mock the injected API.

expert.content:
Decision factors and migration

• Evaluate: team size and experience, need for traceability/undo/time travel, number of cross-feature interactions, amount of async orchestration, testing culture, bundle size, and onboarding cost. NgRx brings strong conventions (valuable across large teams) and cost (boilerplate, learning).
• Hide implementation behind facades or store services so components depend on an interface (signals, methods), enabling later swaps (service to Signal Store to classic NgRx).
• Avoid anti-patterns: global store for everything (form input state, hover flags), duplicated server data in many places, state in the URL ignored (filters, paging belong in route/query params), subscriptions in components that copy store data into fields.
• Server state libraries: Angular resource/httpResource and community TanStack Query for Angular provide caching, refetching and invalidation which stores do poorly by hand.
• Testing strategy: unit-test pure logic (reducers, selectors, computed), integration-test effects and stores with fake APIs, and a few end-to-end tests for critical flows. Test behaviours (state after actions), not implementation details.
• Java mapping: signal service ~ singleton Spring bean with state; NgRx ~ event sourcing / CQRS with an event log; Signal Store ~ a typed state holder with command methods.

interviewQA: How do you choose between services, Signals and NgRx?

Start with local signals, then signal services for shared state, Signal Store for richer feature state, and classic NgRx when you need strict conventions, auditability, DevTools and large-scale team coordination.
How do you test a reducer and a selector?
Reducers are pure: call with state and action and assert the result. Selectors: test projector functions or run against a mock state.
How do you test an NgRx effect?
Provide a mock actions stream (provideMockActions), mock the injected API, run the effect in an injection context and assert emitted actions.
What is a facade in this context?
A service wrapping store access so components use simple signals and methods without knowing whether NgRx, Signal Store or plain services are underneath.
Name state management anti-patterns.
Putting everything in a global store, duplicating server data, mutating state, storing derived values, copying store data into component fields via subscribe, and ignoring URL state.
