topics.name: Authentication, JWT and token storage

beginner.content:
Who are you, and what may you do?

Think of a hotel. At reception you show your passport and get a key card: that is authentication (proving identity). The key card then opens only your room and the gym: that is authorization (permissions). Java developers know the same split in Spring Security: AuthenticationManager versus hasRole() rules.
• Login: the user sends username and password over HTTPS, the server checks them and answers with a token or session cookie.
• Registration: a form creates a new account; the server validates, hashes the password (BCrypt) and stores it. The browser never hashes for security; the server does.
• Logout: the client forgets the session and the server invalidates it.

What is a JWT?

A JWT (JSON Web Token) is like a stamped ticket: anyone can read it, but only the issuer can produce a valid stamp. It has three Base64URL parts separated by dots: header (algorithm), payload (claims such as sub, roles, exp) and signature. Important: the payload is encoded, not encrypted, so never put secrets in it.

intermediate.content:
Access tokens, refresh tokens and where to store them

• An access token is short-lived (5-15 minutes) and sent on every API call as Authorization: Bearer .... A leaked one is useful to an attacker only briefly.
• A refresh token is long-lived and used only against one endpoint (/auth/refresh) to get a new access token. Good designs rotate it on every use and revoke the whole family if an old one is replayed.
• Token storage trade-offs:
  - localStorage/sessionStorage: easy, survives reload, but readable by any script on the page, so a single XSS hole leaks the token.
  - In-memory (a signal in a service): invisible to other scripts and lost on reload; pair it with a refresh cookie to silently get a new token at startup.
  - HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite cookie: JavaScript cannot read it (XSS cannot steal it), but you then need CSRF protection.
• A common solid pattern: access token in memory, refresh token in an HttpOnly SameSite cookie scoped to the refresh path.

Secure logout

A secure logout does more than navigate to /login: (1) call the backend so it revokes the refresh token and clears the cookie, (2) clear the in-memory token and user signal, (3) clear any cached user data (state stores, HTTP caches, IndexedDB), (4) cancel in-flight requests, (5) redirect to the login page. On shared computers also consider a sync across tabs via the storage event or BroadcastChannel.

expert.content:
JWT internals and pitfalls

• The server validates the signature (HS256 shared secret, or RS256/ES256 with a public key) plus exp, iss, aud. Spring Boot's resource server does this for you. Reject alg: none and algorithm confusion.
• The Angular app should treat the token as opaque. Decoding the payload for UI hints (name, roles) is fine, but never trust it for security: a user can edit their own copy.
• JWTs cannot be revoked before exp unless you keep a deny list or short lifetimes; this is why access tokens are short and refresh tokens are server-tracked.
• Handle refresh races: when several requests get 401 at once, queue them behind a single refresh call (see the interceptor lesson).
• Do not put PII or secrets in the payload; tokens end up in logs, proxies and browser history if misplaced in URLs. Never send tokens in query strings.

Session cookies versus JWT (Spring perspective)

Spring Security's classic JSESSIONID session is a server-side session with an HttpOnly cookie: simple, instantly revocable, but needs sticky sessions or a shared store (Redis) when scaled. JWT is stateless, scales horizontally and suits mobile and microservices, but is harder to revoke. For a browser-only Angular + Spring app, a cookie-based session or BFF (backend for frontend) pattern is often safer than putting JWTs in JavaScript-reachable storage. Choose consciously, not by fashion.

interviewQA: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?

Authentication verifies who the caller is (login, token validation). Authorization decides what that identity may do (roles, permissions). A 401 means not authenticated; a 403 means authenticated but not allowed.
What are the three parts of a JWT and is it encrypted?

Header, payload and signature, Base64URL-encoded and joined by dots. A normal JWT (JWS) is signed, not encrypted: anyone can read the payload, so it must hold no secrets. The signature only guarantees integrity.
Why use both access and refresh tokens?

The short-lived access token limits damage if stolen. The refresh token lets the user stay logged in without re-entering credentials; it is stored more safely, used only at one endpoint, and can be rotated and revoked server-side.
Where should an Angular app store tokens?

localStorage is simple but exposed to XSS. A better approach is keeping the access token in memory and the refresh token in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie (which then needs CSRF defense). There is no free lunch; the right choice depends on threat model.
What should happen on logout?
Revoke the refresh token on the server, clear the in-memory token, user state and caches, notify other tabs, cancel pending requests and redirect to login.

topics.name: Interceptors, guards, RBAC and backend authorization

beginner.content:
Doorman, bouncer and the real vault

Imagine a bank. The interceptor is the clerk who stamps every request slip with your ID. A route guard is the sign on a door saying "Staff only": it saves honest people from wandering in. But the backend authorization is the vault itself, which checks your key every time.

Important note: route guards are not a substitute for backend authorization. Anyone can open DevTools, edit JavaScript or call your API with curl. The Spring Boot APIs must enforce permissions independently on every endpoint (@PreAuthorize, hasRole). Guards and hidden buttons only improve user experience.

intermediate.content:
Authentication interceptor with 401 handling

A functional HTTP interceptor attaches the token to API calls only (never to third-party URLs) and handles 401 by refreshing once and retrying. A shared refresh observable prevents a stampede of refresh calls.

Role-based access control and permission-based UI

RBAC maps users to roles (ADMIN, MANAGER, USER). Permission-based UI is finer: the backend returns permissions like order:delete and the UI shows controls accordingly. Use a role guard factory for routes and a small helper for templates. Again: this only hides things; Spring must still return 403.

expert.content:
Guards, sessions and error handling in depth

• Use canMatch for role-based lazy routes so unauthorized users do not even download the chunk, and canActivateChild to protect a whole subtree. Guards can return boolean | UrlTree | Observable | Promise; prefer returning a UrlTree over calling router.navigate inside the guard.
• Authentication error handling: map 401 to refresh-or-login, 403 to a "not allowed" page (do not log the user out), 400/422 to form messages, network errors to a retry banner. Show generic login errors ("Invalid email or password") to avoid account enumeration.
• Secure session management: set an absolute lifetime and an idle timeout, rotate the session id/refresh token after login and privilege changes, use cookies with HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax/Strict, and offer "log out everywhere". Re-check the session when the tab regains focus.
• Do not read roles from a stale token: if permissions change, force a refresh or fetch /me.
• Test guards as plain functions inside TestBed.runInInjectionContext.

Backend authorization checklist (Spring Boot)

Every endpoint: authenticate (resource server validates JWT), authorize by role and by ownership (an ordinary user must not read /orders/99 that belongs to someone else: this is the classic IDOR/BOLA bug), validate inputs, and return 401/403 correctly. Treat the Angular app as an untrusted client always.

interviewQA: Why are route guards not enough for security?

Guards run in the browser, which the user controls. They can be bypassed by editing code or calling the API directly. Only server-side authorization (Spring Security rules) is trustworthy; guards just improve UX.
How do you attach a JWT to requests in modern Angular?
With a functional interceptor registered via provideHttpClient(withInterceptors([...])). It clones the request with an Authorization: Bearer header for your own API URLs only.
How do you avoid multiple refresh calls when several requests return 401?
Share one in-flight refresh observable (shareReplay or a subject/lock). Other requests wait for it, then retry with the new token. If refresh fails, log out once.
What is the difference between 401 and 403 and how should the UI react?
401: not authenticated or token expired, try refresh then login. 403: authenticated but forbidden, show a no-access message without logging out.
What is canMatch and why use it for roles?
canMatch decides whether a route definition matches at all, so with lazy loading the code chunk is not even fetched for unauthorized users, and another route with the same path can match instead.
What is IDOR and how does it relate to frontend checks?
Insecure direct object reference: a user changes an id in the URL to access another user data. Only the backend ownership check prevents it; hiding links in Angular does not.

topics.name: XSS, CSRF, CSP and Angular sanitization

beginner.content:
Attacks in plain language

• Cross-Site Scripting (XSS): an attacker gets their JavaScript to run on your page (for example inside a comment you display). It then runs with the user's powers: reads data, calls APIs, steals tokens in localStorage.
• Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF): the attacker's site tricks your browser into sending a request to your bank; because the browser attaches your cookies automatically, the bank thinks it was you. CSRF only matters when authentication relies on cookies, not on a manually attached Bearer header.
• Content Security Policy (CSP): a response header that tells the browser "only run scripts from these sources", a safety net that limits XSS damage.
Good news: Angular treats every value in a template as untrusted and escapes it for you. Trouble starts only when you bypass that.
codeExamples: {{ comment.text }}

intermediate.content:
Angular template security and sanitization

Angular defines security contexts: HTML, Style, URL and Resource URL. For each binding it picks the right treatment: interpolation is HTML-escaped; [innerHTML] goes through the built-in sanitizer that removes <script>, inline event handlers and javascript: URLs; unsafe URLs get a unsafe: prefix; resource URLs (iframe src, script src) are blocked unless trusted. In dev mode you see a console warning when something is removed.
• Safe DOM manipulation: prefer template bindings. If you must touch the DOM use Renderer2, setProperty or textContent, not elementRef.nativeElement.innerHTML = ... (this skips sanitization entirely).
• Avoiding unsafe HTML: the bypassSecurityTrustHtml/Script/Style/Url/ResourceUrl methods on DomSanitizer switch protection off. Use them only on content you fully control, never on user input, and review each usage like a security bug.

CSRF with Angular and Spring

If you use cookie-based authentication, protect state-changing requests. Spring Security's CookieCsrfTokenRepository.withHttpOnlyFalse() sets an XSRF-TOKEN cookie. Angular's HttpClient automatically copies it into the X-XSRF-TOKEN header for mutating requests to the same origin. Add SameSite=Lax/Strict cookies as a second layer. If you use a Bearer token from JavaScript memory, classic CSRF does not apply (but XSS does).
codeExamples:
// app.config.ts
provideHttpClient(withXsrfConfiguration({ cookieName: 'XSRF-TOKEN', headerName: 'X-XSRF-TOKEN' }))   // defaults; for cross-origin APIs add the header manually

// SecurityConfig.java
http.csrf(csrf -> csrf.csrfTokenRepository(CookieCsrfTokenRepository.withHttpOnlyFalse()));

expert.content:
Content Security Policy for Angular

A strict CSP reduces XSS impact. Angular specifics: inline styles added by components historically needed style-src 'unsafe-inline'; use a nonce instead: set ngCspNonce attribute on the root element (or provide the CSP_NONCE token) so Angular adds the nonce to styles it injects. Avoid 'unsafe-eval' (AOT compiled apps do not need it; JIT does). Newer Angular (v19+) supports hash-based strict CSP for inline scripts via the build option. Roll out with Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only first.
codeExamples:
# Example header set by Nginx or Spring (one line)
Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'nonce-RANDOM'; style-src 'self' 'nonce-RANDOM'; img-src 'self' data:; connect-src 'self' https://api.example.com; frame-ancestors 'none'; base-uri 'self'

<!-- index.html (server injects a fresh nonce per response) -->
<app-root ngCspNonce="RANDOM"></app-root>

expert.content:
Pitfalls

• Angular's protection covers templates, not your own document.write, eval, new Function, third-party widgets, or server-rendered HTML you inject elsewhere.
• Never build templates from user strings at runtime (template injection); never use JIT with user input.
• Sanitizing on the server (Java: OWASP Java HTML Sanitizer) plus encoding on output is defense in depth. Sanitization of [innerHTML] strips style and some attributes: expect that rich text may lose formatting.
• XSS makes tokens in localStorage worthless as a secret, which is why storage choice and CSP belong together.
• SSR note: transferred state serialization is escaped by Angular; do not put unescaped user data into hand-written <script> blocks in server templates.

interviewQA: How does Angular protect against XSS by default?

It treats all template values as untrusted: interpolation is HTML-escaped and property bindings are sanitized according to their security context (HTML, Style, URL, ResourceURL). Dangerous content like script tags and javascript: URLs is removed.
What is bypassSecurityTrustHtml and when is it dangerous?

A DomSanitizer method that marks a string as trusted so Angular skips sanitization. If the string contains user-controlled content it creates an XSS vulnerability. Use only for static or fully trusted content.
When do you need CSRF protection in Angular?

When authentication uses cookies the browser sends automatically. Use SameSite cookies plus the double-submit XSRF-TOKEN cookie/X-XSRF-TOKEN header pattern that HttpClient supports. Bearer-in-header schemes are not vulnerable to classic CSRF.
What does a Content Security Policy do?

It tells the browser which sources of scripts, styles, images and connections are allowed, blocking injected inline scripts and unknown origins. It limits the damage of XSS but does not replace output encoding.
Why is using nativeElement.innerHTML risky?
It writes directly to the DOM and bypasses Angular sanitization. Use bindings, Renderer2 or textContent instead.

topics.name: Transport, configuration and security best practices

beginner.content:
Locks on the doors and windows

• HTTPS encrypts traffic between browser and server like a sealed envelope; without it, Wi-Fi snoopers can read passwords and tokens. Always serve both app and API over HTTPS and redirect HTTP to HTTPS; enable HSTS.
• CORS configuration: browsers block a page from http://localhost:4200 calling an API on another origin unless the API replies with the right Access-Control-Allow-* headers. CORS is configured on the server (Spring), never fixed in Angular.
• Protecting sensitive information: do not put passwords, API secrets or personal data where others can see them: URLs, logs, console, localStorage, or the JavaScript bundle.

intermediate.content:
Secure environment configuration, redirects and dependencies

• Secure environment configuration: everything in environment.ts or a served config.json is public. Put only API base URLs, public client ids and feature flags there. Real secrets (database passwords, private keys, client secrets) live on the server (Spring config, environment variables, a vault). Use runtime configuration so one build deploys to many environments.
• Open redirect prevention: after login, a returnUrl query parameter is convenient but dangerous: /login?returnUrl=https://evil.com would send a user to a phishing site. Only allow internal, relative paths.
• Dependency vulnerability scanning: run npm audit in CI, use Dependabot or Renovate, lock versions with package-lock.json, use npm ci, and update Angular regularly for security patches. Beware of typosquatted packages and install scripts.
codeExamples:
# CI step
npm ci
npm audit --audit-level=high      # fail the build on high/critical issues
npm outdated

expert.content:
Angular security best practices checklist

1. Never trust the client: authorize on the backend. 2. Keep Angular and dependencies up to date. 3. Do not use bypassSecurityTrust* with dynamic data. 4. Avoid direct DOM access and innerHTML. 5. Serve over HTTPS with HSTS and a strict CSP. 6. Prefer HttpOnly cookies or in-memory tokens over localStorage for long-lived credentials. 7. Configure CORS narrowly; no wildcard with credentials. 8. No secrets in bundles or source maps in public production (or restrict source maps). 9. Do not log tokens, passwords or personal data; scrub error reports. 10. Use AOT production builds; never ship JIT. 11. Validate redirects and file uploads (type, size) on the server. 12. Add security headers: X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy, frame-ancestors (clickjacking), Permissions-Policy. 13. Run SAST/dependency scans and periodic penetration tests, including OWASP Top 10 checks against the Spring API.

Subtleties worth knowing

• CORS is not security against non-browser clients; it only instructs browsers. A preflight (OPTIONS) is sent for custom headers such as Authorization; cache it with Access-Control-Max-Age.
• During development, use the Angular dev-server proxy (proxy.conf.json) to avoid CORS locally, but configure real CORS or a same-origin reverse proxy (Nginx) in production. Same-origin deployment also simplifies cookies and CSRF.
• Environment files are compiled in; prefer a runtime /assets/config.json loaded by provideAppInitializer for per-environment values.
• Error messages shown to users should be generic; log details server-side with a correlation id.

interviewQA: What is CORS and where do you fix a CORS error?

Cross-Origin Resource Sharing is a browser mechanism that blocks cross-origin calls unless the server allows the origin through response headers. You fix it on the server (Spring CORS config) or by serving app and API from one origin, not in Angular code.
Can you hide an API key in an Angular environment file?
No. Everything shipped to the browser is readable. Secrets must stay on the server; the frontend calls your backend, which uses the secret.
What is an open redirect and how do you prevent it in a login flow?
Redirecting to an attacker-supplied URL after login. Only accept relative internal paths for returnUrl (or an allow-list) and reject absolute or protocol-relative URLs.
How do you keep dependencies secure?
Lock files and npm ci, npm audit/Dependabot in CI, regular Angular upgrades, review new packages, and avoid abandoned libraries.
Why use HTTPS and HSTS?
HTTPS provides confidentiality and integrity in transit; HSTS tells browsers to always use HTTPS for the domain, preventing downgrade and SSL-strip attacks. Secure cookies require HTTPS.

topics.name: Rendering and change detection

beginner.content:
How does the screen stay in sync?

Think of a whiteboard in a classroom. Change detection is the teacher walking the room to compare the whiteboard with the real data and rewriting whatever is different. The rendering architecture (Ivy) compiles each template ahead of time (AOT) into small instructions: a creation pass builds the DOM once and an update pass later refreshes only the bindings that changed.
• Default change detection: after every trigger (click, timer, HTTP response) Angular checks every component from the root down. Simple and safe, but wasteful in big apps.
• OnPush change detection: a component is checked only when an input reference changes, an event fires in it, a signal it reads changes, or it is marked dirty. Think "wake the teacher only when something relevant happens".

intermediate.content:
Zone.js, zoneless and signals

• Zone-based change detection: Zone.js monkey-patches browser async APIs (events, timers, promises, XHR). When an async task finishes, NgZone emits onMicrotaskEmpty and Angular runs a check. It works with zero effort but runs checks even when nothing changed.
• Zoneless Angular: remove Zone.js and let Angular be told when to check. Triggers: signal changes read in templates, template event listeners, markForCheck(), AsyncPipe, and component creation/removal. Enabled with provideZonelessChangeDetection() (developer preview in v18-19, stable in v20.2; names and status are version dependent). Smaller bundles, better stack traces, faster.
• Signals and change detection: a template that reads a signal registers it as a dependency; when it changes, Angular marks exactly that view for refresh. Signals make OnPush behaviour automatic and are the foundation for zoneless.

Manual control: ChangeDetectorRef

Inject ChangeDetectorRef for manual control. markForCheck() marks the component and its ancestors dirty so the next normal pass refreshes it (use when OnPush state changed outside Angular's knowledge, e.g. a plain callback). detectChanges() runs the check right now on this view and its children (use sparingly, e.g. after dynamically creating views or in tests). detach()/reattach() remove a view from the tree for high-frequency widgets.

expert.content:
Internals and pitfalls

• A check is a depth-first walk of component views; per binding Angular compares old and new value with Object.is and updates the DOM only on difference. In dev mode a second pass throws ExpressionChangedAfterItHasBeenChecked (NG0100) if a value changed during the check: do not mutate parent state from a child's hook or getter.
• OnPush with mutated objects fails silently: the input reference does not change. Use immutable updates or signals.
• In zone apps run noisy work outside Angular with NgZone.runOutsideAngular() (scroll, mousemove, canvas loops) and re-enter only to update state. Libraries that rely on zone patching need care in zoneless apps.
• Zoneless migration checklist: switch components to OnPush, convert state to signals, replace setTimeout-driven updates, use afterNextRender/afterEveryRender for DOM work, test with provideZonelessChangeDetection() in TestBed.
• The signal graph uses reactive contexts: a reactive consumer per template; computed is lazy and memoised. Signal-based inputs plus OnPush give the best default today. Experimental or preview status of zoneless varies by version, so check release notes.

Choosing a strategy

New code: standalone, OnPush (v20 style guides default to it), signals for state, zoneless if all dependencies allow. Keep Default only for legacy components until migrated. Debug with Angular DevTools profiler to see which components are checked and why.

interviewQA: What is the difference between Default and OnPush change detection?

Default checks the component on every cycle triggered anywhere. OnPush checks only when an input reference changes, an event originates in the component or its children, an async pipe/signal it reads emits, or it is marked via markForCheck.
What does Zone.js do and what changes with zoneless Angular?

Zone.js patches async APIs so Angular knows when to run change detection. Zoneless removes it; Angular is notified by signals, template events, markForCheck, AsyncPipe and similar. Result: smaller bundle, fewer redundant checks.
markForCheck vs detectChanges?

markForCheck schedules the view and its ancestors to be checked in the next cycle. detectChanges runs a check synchronously on that view subtree immediately and can cause performance or recursion issues if overused.
Why does an OnPush component not update after I mutate an array?
The input reference did not change, so OnPush sees nothing new. Create a new array/object (immutable update) or use signals.
What causes ExpressionChangedAfterItHasBeenChecked?

A binding value changed between the check and the dev-mode verification pass, typically because a child or lifecycle hook modified parent state. Fix by moving the logic earlier, using signals/computed, or restructuring.
How do signals improve change detection?
Templates track which signals they read, so Angular refreshes only affected views, works naturally with OnPush and enables zoneless operation.

topics.name: Dynamic components, DI and reactive abstractions

beginner.content:
Building UI at runtime

Normally the template decides which components appear. Sometimes you only know at runtime (a dashboard with user-chosen widgets, a modal service). Dynamic component rendering creates them in code. A ViewContainerRef is a "parking spot" in the DOM where you can insert components, and the ComponentRef is the "remote control" returned: it gives access to the instance, lets you set inputs and destroy it.
Content projection is the opposite direction: the parent hands pieces of markup to the child with <ng-content> (like slots in a card or dialog).

intermediate.content:
Providers, injection context and advanced DI

• Custom providers tell the injector how to build a dependency: useClass (swap implementation), useValue (constant/config), useFactory (build with logic and deps/inject()), useExisting (alias), multi: true (collect many, e.g. validators or interceptors).
• Advanced Dependency Injection: injectors form a hierarchy (element injector -> environment injector -> root -> platform). Use resolution modifiers via inject(Token, { optional: true, self: true, skipSelf: true, host: true }). Scope services at route level (providers in a route) or component level to get one instance per feature/instance.
• Injection context: inject() works only while Angular is constructing something: constructor, field initialisers, a provider factory, a functional guard/interceptor/resolver, or inside runInInjectionContext. Calling it later in a click handler throws NG0203. Save the injector (inject(Injector)) and use runInInjectionContext or assertInInjectionContext in helpers.

Content projection and custom decorators

Use multi-slot projection with select, and ngTemplateOutlet when the parent supplies a template with context. Custom decorators are TypeScript functions (@Memoize(), @Log()). Note that Angular's own decorators are compiled specially; custom member/class decorators use the standard (or experimental, depending on experimentalDecorators) TypeScript proposal, are not understood by AOT metadata, and cannot add DI or template behaviour. In modern Angular prefer functions, directives, host directives and DI tokens over custom decorators.
codeExamples:
<!-- card.component.html -->
<header><ng-content select="[card-title]" /></header>
<section><ng-content /></section>
<ng-container *ngTemplateOutlet="footerTpl() ?? defaultFooter; context: { $implicit: data() }" />
<ng-template #defaultFooter>Default footer</ng-template>

expert.content:
Custom reactive abstractions and RxJS interoperability

Wrap recurring reactive patterns into custom reactive abstractions: small functions that return signals or observables and use inject() internally (like React hooks, but with injection context rules). Interop bridges the two worlds: toSignal(obs$, { initialValue }) subscribes and unsubscribes with the injection context; toObservable(signal) emits via an effect (so values are coalesced, not synchronous); takeUntilDestroyed() auto-completes streams; rxResource/httpResource (v19+, experimental in 19-20) turn request streams into signal state. Keep Observables for events, cancellation and time; signals for state.

Pitfalls

• toSignal throws if the observable errors and read; handle with catchError or rejectErrors. Without initialValue the type includes undefined (or use requireSync for BehaviorSubject-like sources).
• Do not call toSignal inside effects or event handlers repeatedly (it creates subscriptions); create it once in a field.
• Prefer ComponentRef.setInput() over assigning properties, so OnPush and signal inputs update. Always destroy dynamic refs you create manually; inputs of ngComponentOutlet accept an ngComponentOutletInputs object.
• Provider scope bugs ("my service is not a singleton") usually mean a component-level or route-level provider created a second instance.

interviewQA: How do you create a component dynamically?

Get a ViewContainerRef (viewChild with read: ViewContainerRef), call createComponent(Type), set inputs with ref.setInput, and destroy via ref.destroy() or container.clear(). The declarative alternative is *ngComponentOutlet.
Explain useClass, useValue, useFactory, useExisting and multi.

useClass substitutes a class, useValue gives a constant, useFactory runs a function (often with inject()), useExisting aliases another token, and multi:true collects several providers of the same token into an array.
What is an injection context and why does inject() fail outside it?

It is the synchronous time window when Angular is instantiating something (constructor, field initialisers, factories, functional guards). inject() needs the current injector; outside it throws NG0203. Use runInInjectionContext with a saved Injector.
toSignal vs the async pipe?
Both subscribe and clean up automatically. toSignal gives a signal usable in computed/effect and TypeScript code, the async pipe is template-only. toSignal needs an initial value or requireSync.
Why avoid custom decorators in modern Angular?

They are outside Angular compiler knowledge, depend on TS decorator mode, hide behaviour and cannot participate in AOT or DI. Functions, directives and host directives are more transparent and tree-shakable.

topics.name: Routing, errors, interceptors and libraries

beginner.content:
Growing a real application

Bigger applications need patterns beyond components: forms that come from configuration (dynamic forms architecture), layouts nested through advanced routing, one place that deals with failure (error handling architecture), and shared code packaged as Angular libraries with a clear public API. Picture a company: the router is the building map, the error handler is the reception that receives all complaints, and a library is a department that offers services through a front desk (the public API), not through its back rooms.

intermediate.content:
Dynamic forms and advanced routing

Dynamic forms architecture: keep a typed metadata model, build the FormGroup from it, render fields by @switch on type (or through a registry mapping type to component with ngComponentOutlet), and let validators be named in metadata. The backend (Spring) can even deliver the schema.
Advanced routing: layout routes with child outlets, auxiliary (named) outlets, custom UrlMatcher, resolvers, withComponentInputBinding() to bind params to inputs, view transitions with withViewTransitions(), and route-level code splitting. Route-level state: route params, query params, data, resolved data, and route-scoped providers (a service instance that lives as long as that route subtree is active).

Error handling layers and global handler

Layer your error handling architecture: (1) local handling where the user can act (form errors, retry button), (2) HTTP interceptor for cross-cutting status mapping (401, 403, 5xx, network), (3) router errors (withNavigationErrorHandler), (4) a global error handler for everything uncaught, (5) reporting to Sentry/ELK with a correlation id. Implement ErrorHandler and register it with provideBrowserGlobalErrorListeners() (v20) or { provide: ErrorHandler, useClass: ... }.

expert.content:
Advanced interceptors and libraries

Advanced HTTP interceptors compose in order: request goes through the array first-to-last, response comes back last-to-first. Typical stack: correlationId -> auth -> loading -> cache -> retry(backoff) -> error mapping. Use HttpContextToken to pass per-request flags (skip loading, skip auth, cache TTL). Keep interceptors pure and single purpose; avoid circular DI (an interceptor injecting a service that injects HttpClient: use inject(Injector) lazily).
Reusable component libraries / Angular libraries: ng generate library ui-kit creates a project built with ng-packagr into partial-Ivy output (APF format). Use standalone components with ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush, theme with CSS custom properties, avoid depending on app services, document with Storybook, version with semver and changelog.
Public API design: export only what consumers need in public-api.ts (components, tokens, provideXxx() functions, types); keep internals unexported (secondary entry points for big libs); prefer provideUiKit(config) functions and InjectionToken configuration; deprecate before removing; breaking changes follow major versions. Think of it as a Java module's exported packages.

Pitfalls

• A global handler must never throw and should avoid loops (reporting failing triggers reporting). Zone/async errors in zoneless apps still reach ErrorHandler for framework-run callbacks, but plain setTimeout errors need provideBrowserGlobalErrorListeners (v20) or window listeners.
• Do not catch an error in an interceptor and return EMPTY silently: callers hang waiting for a value.
• Library peerDependencies: Angular packages are peers, not dependencies, or you ship duplicate copies and break DI.

interviewQA: How would you design dynamic forms?

Describe fields in typed metadata (possibly from the backend), build FormGroup/FormArray from it, render with @switch or a component registry, map named validators, and keep submission typed. Keep layout separate from the schema.
Where should global error handling live?

A layered approach: local UI handling, an HTTP interceptor for status mapping, router navigation error handler, and a custom ErrorHandler for uncaught errors with logging/reporting and a generic user message.
In which order do interceptors run?
In array order for requests and in reverse order for responses, like servlet filters. Order matters, e.g. auth before retry, error mapping last.
What belongs in a library public API?
Only stable, documented components, services, tokens, provide functions and types exported from public-api.ts. Internals stay private so they can change without breaking consumers.
What are route-level providers useful for?
They scope a service instance to a route subtree, creating fresh state per navigation context instead of a root singleton, and enable lazy loading of the service code.

topics.name: Monorepos, microfrontends and real-time channels

beginner.content:
One repo, many apps, live data

A monorepo keeps several apps and libraries in one Git repository, like one building with many offices sharing a canteen. Angular workspace management: one angular.json lists projects (applications and libraries); shared libraries are imported through path mapping in tsconfig.json (@shop/ui). Tools like Nx add caching and dependency-graph rules.
Browsers can also do background and live work: Web Workers (heavy calculation off the UI thread), WebSockets (two-way live channel, chat) and Server-Sent Events (one-way live feed from the server, notifications).
codeExamples:
# create a workspace without a default app, then add projects
ng new shop --create-application=false
cd shop
ng generate application storefront
ng generate application admin
ng generate library ui-kit

// tsconfig.json
"paths": { "@shop/ui-kit": ["projects/ui-kit/src/public-api.ts"] }

intermediate.content:
Web Workers, WebSockets and SSE

Web Worker: ng generate web-worker heavy creates a worker file and the tsconfig. Messages are copied (structured clone) or transferred; the worker has no DOM.
WebSocket: use RxJS webSocket() for a typed stream with reconnect logic (retry with delay). Spring: WebSocketHandler or STOMP over SockJS.
Server-Sent Events: browser EventSource gives automatic reconnects and works over plain HTTP/2; wrap it in an Observable. Spring: SseEmitter or Flux<ServerSentEvent>. SSE cannot set custom headers (so no Bearer header): use cookies or short-lived tickets in the URL.

expert.content:
Microfrontends and monorepo pitfalls

Microfrontend architecture splits a large UI into independently built and deployed apps (per team/domain). In Angular the common route is Module Federation (Webpack, or Native Federation with esbuild via @angular-architects/native-federation): a shell loads remotes at runtime (loadRemoteModule) and shares singleton libraries (Angular, RxJS) with version ranges. Alternatives: iframes, Web Components (Angular Elements), or server-side composition.
Trade-offs: much higher complexity (shared dependency versions, consistent design system, routing contracts, auth sharing, E2E testing, observability) in exchange for team autonomy. Do not adopt microfrontends for a small team; a well-structured monorepo with libraries and enforced boundaries (Nx enforce-module-boundaries, ESLint rules) usually suffices.
Monorepo advice: keep libs layered (feature, ui, data-access, util), forbid circular imports, use affected-only builds in CI and caching, keep one version of Angular for the whole repo.

Real-time channel advice

• Run worker messaging and socket callbacks so that state lands in signals (zoneless-safe). In zone apps, high-frequency sockets can flood change detection: use runOutsideAngular and batch/throttle updates (bufferTime, auditTime).
• WebSocket needs heartbeat/ping, reconnect with exponential backoff, resubscribe after reconnect and authentication on connect. SSE reconnects itself and supports Last-Event-ID for resume. Choose SSE for one-way streams (simpler, proxy friendly), WebSocket for bidirectional or binary.
• Terminate workers (worker.terminate()) and close sockets in DestroyRef.onDestroy. Angular CLI bundles workers separately.

interviewQA: What is a monorepo and what are its benefits in Angular?

One repository containing multiple applications and libraries. Benefits: shared code via libs, atomic changes across projects, unified tooling and versioning; with Nx or the CLI you also get caching and affected builds.
When would you choose microfrontends?

When many independent teams must deploy parts of one product separately. They bring operational complexity (shared deps, consistency, testing), so avoid them for small teams; start with modular monorepo libraries.
WebSocket vs Server-Sent Events?

WebSocket is a bidirectional full-duplex protocol; SSE is one-way server to client over HTTP with built-in reconnect and event ids. SSE is simpler for notifications; WebSocket for chat, games, binary data.
Why use a Web Worker in Angular?
To run CPU-heavy tasks without blocking the main thread (parsing big files, crypto, sorting large data). Workers cannot access the DOM and communicate through messages.
How does the Angular CLI help with workspaces?
It manages multiple projects in angular.json, generates apps and libraries, and builds each with ng build <project>. Path mapping lets apps import libraries by alias.

topics.name: Internationalization, accessibility and architecture

beginner.content:
Software for everyone

• Internationalization (i18n) means designing the app so it can work in many languages (no hard-coded text, flexible layouts). Localization (l10n) is the work of providing a specific language and format (Marathi, German, dates, currency).
• Accessibility (a11y) means people using keyboards, screen readers or magnifiers can use the app: semantic HTML, labels, contrast, focus visibility.
• A design system is a shared set of colours, spacing, components and rules so every screen looks and behaves consistently.
codeExamples:
Welcome to our shop

Hello, {{ name }}!

intermediate.content:
i18n workflow and accessibility basics

Angular's compile-time i18n: add @angular/localize, mark text with i18n, run ng extract-i18n to produce XLF/XLIFF, translate it, configure locales in angular.json and build one bundle per locale (fast at runtime, but one deployment per language). Runtime libraries such as Transloco or ngx-translate switch language without rebuilding. Use ICU expressions for plurals, and locale-aware pipes (date, currency, number) with LOCALE_ID.
Accessibility basics: use real button/a/label elements, alt text, a logical heading order, visible focus, sufficient contrast, aria-live for dynamic status messages, and @angular/cdk/a11y (LiveAnnouncer, FocusTrap, cdkTrapFocus).
codeExamples: You have {count, plural, =0 {no messages} =1 {one message} other {{{count}} messages}}

# commands
ng add @angular/localize
ng extract-i18n --output-path src/locale
# angular.json: "i18n": { "sourceLocale": "en-US", "locales": { "mr": "src/locale/messages.mr.xlf" } }
ng build --localize

expert.content:
Architecture best practices

• Structure: feature folders, lazy-loaded feature routes, thin core (singletons, interceptors) and shared (dumb UI), enforce boundaries with lint rules.
• Smart/presentational split: containers fetch and hold state, presentational components take input()/output() and are OnPush and pure.
• State: signals in services for most apps, NgRx Signal Store or Store only when complexity warrants.
• Types: strict: true, strict templates, typed forms, DTO interfaces mirroring Spring DTOs (consider generating clients from OpenAPI).
• Performance defaults: OnPush/zoneless readiness, track in @for, lazy routes, @defer.
• Quality: ESLint, Prettier, tests per layer, CI gates, performance budgets, Architecture Decision Records.
• i18n/a11y/design-system as first-class concerns from day one: retrofitting translations or accessibility is costly. Design tokens as CSS custom properties; wrap Material or CDK in your own components so you can replace libraries.

Gotchas

• Compile-time i18n bakes text at build time, so server routing must pick the locale (path /mr/) and each locale is a separate build; runtime i18n lets users switch instantly but costs a translations download. Pick before the project grows.
• Do not concatenate translated strings; word order differs between languages. Always use ICU/parameters.
• Right-to-left languages need logical CSS properties (margin-inline-start).
• Automated a11y tools (axe, Lighthouse) catch only about a third of issues; add keyboard-only and screen-reader manual passes.

interviewQA: Difference between internationalization and localization?

i18n is engineering the app to support multiple locales (externalized text, flexible layout, locale-aware formatting). l10n is adapting it for a specific locale: translations, formats, cultural conventions.
Compile-time i18n vs runtime libraries like Transloco?

Angular built-in i18n produces one optimized build per locale, requires redeployment per language and no runtime lookup. Runtime libraries load translation files dynamically so the language can switch live, at the cost of a lookup and extra requests.
How do you make an Angular component accessible?

Use semantic elements, labels and alt text, ensure keyboard operation and focus management, adequate contrast, ARIA only when native elements cannot express semantics, live regions for updates, and test with axe and a screen reader.
What is a design system and how does it appear in Angular code?

A shared collection of tokens, components and guidelines. In Angular it is typically a library of standalone OnPush components styled with CSS custom properties, documented in Storybook, versioned and consumed by all apps.
Name some Angular architecture best practices.

Feature-based lazy modules/routes, smart vs presentational components, immutable state/signals, strict typing, enforced boundaries, interceptors for cross-cutting concerns, OnPush, tests and CI quality gates.

topics.name: Rendering and change detection performance

beginner.content:
Where does the time go?

Understanding rendering performance: a page update is a pipeline: JavaScript runs, the browser recalculates styles, computes layout, paints and composites. Angular adds its own work, change detection. A slow app is usually doing too much of one of these: too many DOM nodes, too many checks, or heavy JavaScript. Think of a restaurant kitchen: the fix is not a faster waiter but cooking less unnecessary food.
Quick wins: OnPush on components, track in lists, keep template expressions cheap, and let the AsyncPipe handle subscriptions.
codeExamples:
{{ calculateTotal(items) }}

{{ total() }}

intermediate.content:
Change detection optimization with OnPush, signals and memoization

• OnPush strategy + immutable inputs lets Angular skip whole subtrees. Combine with signal inputs: the component re-renders only when the signal values it reads change.
• Signals-based optimization: computed() caches the value until a dependency changes (memoization for free). Prefer it to getters or methods in templates. Use equal option for custom equality on object signals.
• Avoiding unnecessary computations: no sorting, filtering, regex or JSON work inside bindings; move to computed/pure pipes; debounce frequent events (debounceTime, auditTime); run scroll/mousemove handlers outside the zone.
• Pure pipes are memoized by input reference; custom functions can be memoized by a small cache (last-arguments).

AsyncPipe and subscription optimization

The AsyncPipe subscribes on view creation, marks the view for check on emission and unsubscribes on destroy: no leaks. Use one @if (data$ | async; as data) per stream, not many pipes on the same observable (each creates a separate subscription and HTTP call unless shared). Subscription optimization: share expensive streams with shareReplay({ bufferSize: 1, refCount: true }), use take(1)/first() for one-shot reads, takeUntilDestroyed() for manual subscriptions, switch to toSignal, and avoid nested subscribes (use switchMap).

expert.content:
Deeper insights

• Profile before optimising. Use Angular DevTools (Profiler tab) to see which components were checked and how long they took; look for components checked on every mouse move because of a global listener.
• Methods in templates are not always evil (a trivial getter is fine) but an expensive call multiplied by hundreds of rows with Default CD is a classic slowdown.
• Signals avoid the per-view dirty walk: with signal inputs and OnPush the framework refreshes only views that read the changed signal. In zoneless mode, accidental global checks disappear.
• effect() is not a performance tool and can cascade; keep side effects minimal and never derive state in effects.
• Large object graphs in signals are compared by reference (Object.is); create new references for changes or define equal. Mutating arrays in place with mutate no longer exists (removed); use update() with copies.
• Prefer @if/@for control flow (built in, faster than *ngIf/*ngFor, no directive overhead) in v17+.

Rendering cost checklist

Fewer DOM nodes (virtualize, paginate, @defer), avoid layout thrashing (read layout then write, never alternate), use CSS transform/opacity for animation (compositor-only), content-visibility: auto for off-screen sections, avoid forced reflow in ngAfterViewChecked, and keep ngDoCheck hooks cheap.

interviewQA: Why is calling a method in a template potentially slow?

With Default change detection the method runs on every check, even if inputs did not change. Expensive methods multiplied across rows degrade performance. Use computed signals, pure pipes or precomputed fields.
How does OnPush plus signals reduce work?

OnPush skips views unless input references change, events occur or signals read in the template update. Signals identify exactly which views depend on changed state, so unrelated components are not checked.
AsyncPipe benefits and a common mistake?

Auto subscribe/unsubscribe and marks for check. The mistake is applying it several times to one cold observable, causing multiple subscriptions/HTTP calls; unwrap once with @if ... as, or share the stream.
What is memoization and where does Angular give it to you?
Caching a function result for given inputs. computed() signals and pure pipes memoize automatically; others use custom caches or shareReplay for observables.
How do you find the cause of slow rendering?
Use Angular DevTools profiler and the browser Performance tab, locate long tasks and repeated change detection, then fix with OnPush, track, virtualization or moving work off the main thread.

topics.name: Bundles, lazy loading, @defer and images

beginner.content:
Ship less code, ship it later

The smaller the JavaScript the browser must download and run, the faster the first screen. Think of packing for a trip: carry only what you need now.
• Lazy loading and route-level code splitting: each lazy route (loadComponent/loadChildren) becomes a separate file downloaded when the user visits it.
• Tree shaking: the build removes code nobody imports. Import from specific packages, not whole barrels, and prefer ES modules.
• Production builds: ng build uses production configuration by default (AOT, minification, dead-code elimination, hashed file names, no source maps in output).

intermediate.content:
@defer, preloading and bundle analysis

Deferrable views with @defer split part of a template (and the components it uses, which must be standalone) into a lazy chunk with triggers: on viewport, on idle (default), on interaction, on hover, on timer(2s), on immediate or when condition. Add @placeholder, @loading (with minimum time to avoid flicker), @error, and prefetch on ....
Preloading strategies: withPreloading(PreloadAllModules) fetches all lazy chunks after the app is stable; a custom strategy can preload only routes flagged data: { preload: true } or based on network quality (see below).
Bundle size analysis: ng build --stats-json then upload to the esbuild bundle analyzer or webpack-bundle-analyzer; or npx source-map-explorer dist/**/*.js. Look for moment.js, whole lodash, unused icon sets, duplicated libraries.
codeExamples:
@defer (on viewport; prefetch on idle) { } @placeholder (minimum 300ms) {
} @loading (after 100ms; minimum 500ms) { } @error {

Could not load the chart.

}

intermediate.content:
Image optimization and performance budgets

Use NgOptimizedImage (ngSrc): it requires width/height (prevents layout shift), lazy-loads by default, supports priority for the LCP image (adds preload and fetchpriority=high), and generates srcset with a loader (Cloudinary, Imgix, custom). Serve WebP/AVIF, correct sizes, and use a CDN.
Performance budgets in angular.json make the build warn or fail when bundles grow.

expert.content:
Internals and trade-offs

• The new application builder (esbuild + Vite, default since v17) produces ESM with automatic code splitting, faster builds and better tree shaking than the old Webpack browser builder. Use --stats-json to analyze it.
• Tree shaking is defeated by side-effectful imports, require/CommonJS packages (Angular warns about them), huge barrel files and global registrations. Use providedIn: 'root' services (tree-shakable providers) and standalone APIs, import only needed Material components, and replace heavy libraries with lighter ones (date-fns instead of moment).
• Too many tiny chunks hurt HTTP/1 but with HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 it is fine; do not preload everything on slow mobile networks (navigator.connection.saveData).
• @defer dependencies must not be referenced eagerly elsewhere (component imported in imports and used outside the block is no longer deferred). Content in @defer is not in SSR output unless the trigger fires on the server, and with incremental hydration (v19+) hydrate on ... triggers apply.
• Do not defer above-the-fold content: it worsens LCP.
• Budgets should be tuned to your baseline and tightened gradually. Separate budgets for initial, anyScript, anyComponentStyle.

Production-readiness checklist

AOT on, optimization on, sourceMap: false (or hidden source maps uploaded to the error tracker), compression (gzip/brotli) at the server, long-cache headers for hashed files and no-cache for index.html, fonts with font-display: swap (Angular can inline critical CSS and fonts), remove unused polyfills, and keep the third-party script count low.

interviewQA: What is lazy loading and how do you do it in Angular?
Loading code only when needed. Use loadComponent/loadChildren with dynamic import() in route definitions, or @defer in templates. Each becomes a separate chunk.
What does @defer offer compared with route lazy loading?
It lazy loads parts of a page inside a template with triggers (viewport, idle, interaction, timer, condition), placeholders, loading and error blocks, and prefetching.
How does tree shaking work and how can you help it?
The bundler drops unused ES module exports. Help it with ES modules, specific imports, tree-shakable providers, avoiding side effects and CommonJS libraries.
How would you analyze a large bundle?
Build with --stats-json and open it in an analyzer (esbuild analyzer, webpack-bundle-analyzer) or use source-map-explorer, then replace or lazy load heavy dependencies.
Why use NgOptimizedImage?
It enforces width and height, lazy loads, prioritizes the LCP image, generates srcset via loaders and warns about common mistakes, improving LCP and CLS.
What are performance budgets?
Size limits configured in angular.json; the build warns or errors when bundles exceed them, preventing silent regressions.

topics.name: Lists, tables, data and network performance

beginner.content:
Big lists and repeated requests

List rendering optimization: every row is DOM, and DOM is expensive. With @for you must write track: it tells Angular how to recognise an item (by id) so changed lists reuse existing DOM nodes instead of rebuilding them. It is like a teacher recognising students by name instead of re-seating the whole class every time one arrives.
Reducing duplicate API requests: if five components ask for the same data, fetch once and share the result.

intermediate.content:
Virtual scrolling and large tables

Virtual scrolling (@angular/cdk/scrolling) renders only the rows visible in the viewport plus a small buffer, so 100,000 items cost the same as 20. Large table optimization: server-side pagination/sorting/filtering (Spring Pageable), virtual scroll for long client lists, OnPush row components, fixed row height, avoid per-cell pipes and functions, and debounce filter input.
codeExamples: {{ o.id }} - {{ o.customer }}

intermediate.content:
HTTP caching and request de-duplication

HTTP caching has three layers: the browser cache via Cache-Control/ETag headers from Spring, an Angular caching interceptor (Map by URL with TTL), and state in services/stores. Reduce duplicates with shareReplay, the resource()/httpResource() family (experimental in v19/v20), or a keyed in-flight map. Also enable SSR transfer cache (withHttpTransferCacheOptions) so the browser does not repeat server requests, and cancel superseded requests with switchMap.

expert.content:
Workers, network and pitfalls

• Web Workers for CPU work: client-side CSV parsing, big sorts, image processing, crypto. Pass typed arrays by transfer (postMessage(buf, [buf])) to avoid copying. Do not use workers for tiny tasks: the messaging overhead dominates.
• Network performance: enable HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 and brotli compression (Nginx), CDN for static files, preconnect to API/font origins, fetchpriority, avoid request waterfalls (parallel with forkJoin/combineLatest, resolvers vs lazy fetching), batch small calls, return only needed fields from Spring (DTO projections, pagination), and use ETag/304. Cache hashed assets for one year with immutable; never cache index.html.
• A cache needs invalidation: clear on mutation (POST/PUT/DELETE) and logout. Never cache per-user data in a shared (CDN) cache; use Cache-Control: private.
• track $index on a list that reorders or inserts defeats the purpose: rows are reused with wrong data and state. Always track a stable id.
• Virtual scroll requires a known/uniform item size (autosize strategy is experimental) and a viewport with fixed height; it does not combine well with find-in-page or accessibility without extra work.

Large dataset strategy

Prefer server-side work: page, sort and filter in the database (indexes). Client-side virtualization is for lists you truly must hold in memory. For huge tables combine: server paging, fixed-height rows, OnPush cells, and column virtualization only when necessary.

interviewQA: Why is track required in @for?

It provides identity for each item so Angular can move and reuse DOM nodes when the collection changes instead of recreating them. It is required for correctness and speed; track a unique id, not the index for dynamic lists.
How does virtual scrolling work?
The CDK viewport renders only items in view plus a buffer, using a spacer for total height and recycling DOM nodes as you scroll. Cost depends on visible rows, not total rows.
How do you avoid duplicate HTTP requests for the same data?
Share the observable (shareReplay), cache in a service or interceptor with TTL, use resource-style APIs or a store, and for SSR use the HTTP transfer cache.
When should you use a Web Worker?
For CPU-bound work that blocks the UI (large parsing, sorting, calculation). Not for DOM work or tiny tasks.
How would you display a table with one million records?
Do not load them. Use server-side pagination/sorting/filtering; if scrolling is needed use cursor-based pagination with virtual scrolling and keep rows lightweight.

topics.name: Measuring: Lighthouse, Web Vitals, profiling and budgets

beginner.content:
Measure first, then optimise

Guessing is the biggest performance mistake. Measure with real tools:
• Lighthouse performance analysis: built into Chrome DevTools (Lighthouse tab) or npx lighthouse; it scores performance, accessibility, SEO and best practices and lists concrete fixes. Run it in an incognito window on a production build.
• Core Web Vitals are Google's user-focused metrics: LCP (Largest Contentful Paint, how fast the main content appears, aim under 2.5 s), INP (Interaction to Next Paint, responsiveness, under 200 ms; replaced FID in 2024) and CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift, visual stability, under 0.1).
• Browser profiling: the Performance tab records what the CPU did; long tasks over 50 ms are red flags.
codeExamples:
# measure a production build locally
ng build
npx http-server dist/my-app/browser -p 8080 -g
npx lighthouse http://localhost:8080 --view

intermediate.content:
Profiling, memory leaks and tracking vitals in code

Browser profiling: record in the Performance panel, interact, stop, and look at the flame chart: scripting (JS), rendering, painting. Angular DevTools adds a profiler that shows change detection cycles and the components checked. Use performance.mark/measure for custom timings.
Memory leak detection: symptoms are a heap that never shrinks after navigating away. Use the Memory tab: take a heap snapshot, navigate away and back several times, force GC, take another snapshot and compare; search for detached DOM nodes and retained component instances. Typical Angular leaks: unmanaged subscribe(), setInterval/event listeners not removed (window.addEventListener), RxJS subjects in singleton services holding component references, dynamic components not destroyed, and global caches growing without limits.
Report real-user metrics with the web-vitals library.

Performance testing

Performance testing makes performance a regression-proof requirement: Lighthouse CI in the pipeline with assertions (score and metric thresholds), bundle budgets failing the build, Playwright traces for key flows, and load tests (k6, JMeter, Gatling) against the Spring Boot API. Compare against a baseline on the same hardware profile and network throttling.

expert.content:
Interpreting results

• Lab data (Lighthouse) is synthetic and varies; field data (CrUX, RUM via web-vitals) is what Google ranks on. Optimise for the 75th percentile of real users on mid-range phones.
• Typical Angular LCP fixes: SSR/prerender, priority on the hero image, preconnect, defer non-critical JS, avoid render-blocking CSS, trim initial bundle, avoid waterfall of API calls before first paint. INP fixes: break up long tasks, OnPush/signals, move work to workers, scheduler.yield/setTimeout chunking, avoid heavy handlers. CLS fixes: dimensions on images and embeds, reserve space for async content/skeletons, avoid injecting content above existing content.
• Heap snapshot analysis: use the "Comparison" view and "Detached" filter; check retainers to learn which reference keeps the object alive.
• Production profiling needs source maps (hidden) to read stack traces. Dev-mode numbers are misleading: Angular does extra checks in development.
• Beware of measurement bias: Chrome extensions, dev mode, cache state and CPU throttling (use 4x slowdown to emulate mobile).

Performance governance

Define a performance budget (bundle and Web Vitals), track it per pull request, keep a dashboard from RUM, and assign ownership. Fixing one big regression after release costs far more than a failing CI check.

interviewQA: What are the Core Web Vitals?
LCP (loading, under 2.5 s), INP (interactivity, under 200 ms) and CLS (visual stability, under 0.1). They are measured at the 75th percentile of real user visits.
How do you find a memory leak in an Angular app?

Take heap snapshots before and after repeated navigation, compare for growing objects and detached DOM nodes, inspect retainers, then fix unmanaged subscriptions, timers, listeners or retained component references.
What do you check first when Lighthouse reports poor LCP?
Identify the LCP element, then reduce bundle and render-blocking resources, prioritize and size the image (NgOptimizedImage priority), use SSR/prerender, and remove request waterfalls.
How do you prevent performance regressions?
Budgets in angular.json, Lighthouse CI thresholds, bundle size checks in pull requests and RUM dashboards.
Why not trust development-mode performance?
Dev mode includes extra checks, unminified code and no AOT optimizations. Always profile production builds, ideally with throttling.
