topics.name: CSR, SSR, SSG and prerendering

beginner.content:
Three ways to produce a page

• Client-Side Rendering (CSR): the server sends an almost empty index.html and a JavaScript bundle; the browser builds the page. Like receiving flat-pack furniture and assembling it at home. Great interactivity, but a blank page until JS runs, and weak for SEO/social previews.
• Server-Side Rendering (SSR): the server renders full HTML for every request, like a restaurant serving a cooked meal. The user sees content immediately, then Angular hydrates it to make it interactive.
• Static Site Generation (SSG) / prerendering: pages are rendered once at build time and served as static files, like a printed menu. Fastest and cheapest, but content is only as fresh as the last build.
codeExamples:
# add SSR to a new or existing app
ng new shop --ssr
ng add @angular/ssr

# run
ng serve                 # dev server with SSR support
npm run serve:ssr:shop   # run the built Node server

intermediate.content:
Angular SSR setup in practice

Modern Angular (v17+) uses @angular/ssr with the application builder: a server.ts (Express) and main.server.ts plus app.config.server.ts that merges the client config. Enable hydration with provideClientHydration() and withEventReplay() to replay clicks made before hydration. Since v19 you choose the render mode per route with ServerRoute (RenderMode.Server, RenderMode.Prerender, RenderMode.Client) in app.routes.server.ts; availability of this API depends on version (v19+, developer preview in some releases).

Choosing CSR, SSR or SSG

ModeBest forCost
CSRLogged-in dashboards, internal tools, admin panelsCheap static hosting; slower first paint; poor SEO
SSRPublic, dynamic, personalised or frequently changing pages needing SEONode server, CPU per request, caching required
SSG / prerenderMarketing, docs, blogs, product pages that change rarelyRebuild to update; very cheap and fast

Most real apps mix them per route (hybrid rendering).

expert.content:
Internals and trade-offs

• On each SSR request Angular bootstraps a new application instance on the server with a DOM emulation (Domino), renders to a string, waits until the app is stable (pending HTTP, router navigation, PendingTasks) and sends HTML. Long timers or never-completing observables delay or hang responses.
• SSR improves LCP, SEO and link previews but adds server cost, TTFB latency (slow API calls block the HTML) and operational complexity. For authenticated pages it often gives little benefit; use RenderMode.Client for those.
• Prerender cannot depend on per-request data (cookies, headers). Dynamic route params need getPrerenderParams or a crawl of discovered routes.
• Older tooling: @nguniversal/* and ng add @nguniversal/express-engine are legacy; use @angular/ssr. NgModule-based ServerModule is legacy for standalone apps.
• ISR (incremental static regeneration) is not built in; achieve it with CDN caching and short revalidation or an external platform.

Migration tips

Start by enabling SSR on a public route group, fix browser-only code (next lesson), measure TTFB and LCP before/after, and add caching. Avoid SSR just for fashion: if the app is behind a login and not indexed, CSR + good bundles is simpler and cheaper.

interviewQA: What is the difference between CSR, SSR and SSG?
CSR renders in the browser; SSR renders HTML on the server on every request; SSG/prerender renders HTML at build time and serves static files. They trade off freshness, speed, SEO and infrastructure.
What is prerendering in Angular?
Rendering routes to static HTML at build time (SSG) with the SSR engine, configured via RenderMode.Prerender or the prerender option, then served from any static host.
When would you not use SSR?
For authenticated or internal apps where SEO and first paint on public pages do not matter, or when server cost and complexity outweigh benefits.
How do you set up SSR in a new project?
ng new app --ssr or ng add @angular/ssr, which adds server.ts, main.server.ts, server config and hydration providers.
What is hybrid rendering?
Choosing a render mode per route (server, prerender, client) in the same app, using ServerRoute configuration in v19+.

topics.name: Hydration and server vs browser code

beginner.content:
Waking up the server HTML

With SSR the user first sees plain HTML. Hydration is the step where Angular attaches to that existing DOM and makes it interactive, instead of throwing it away and rendering again (which causes flicker and wasted work). Think of a pre-built shop front: hydration plugs in the electricity rather than rebuilding the shop.
On the server there is no real browser: no window, no real document layout, no localStorage, no screen size. Code using them breaks with "window is not defined". These are browser-only APIs.

intermediate.content:
Handling window, document and platform differences

Techniques: (1) afterNextRender() / afterRender() for DOM-touching code (browser only); (2) inject the DOCUMENT token instead of the global document (works on the server for basic DOM operations); (3) isPlatformBrowser(inject(PLATFORM_ID)) guards; (4) wrap storage in an abstraction service with browser and server implementations; (5) the @defer and ngSkipHydration attribute for components that manipulate the DOM directly or are third-party widgets.
codeExamples:
<!-- third-party widget that mutates DOM: exclude from hydration -->
<app-legacy-chart ngSkipHydration />

intermediate.content:
Incremental hydration

Incremental hydration (v19+, developer preview in 19, stable in later releases; check your version) builds on @defer: a deferred block is rendered on the server, stays dehydrated (no JS downloaded) and hydrates only when its trigger fires: hydrate on viewport, on interaction, on idle, on hover, on timer, when, or hydrate never. Enable with provideClientHydration(withIncrementalHydration()).

expert.content:
Hydration mismatches and execution differences

• Hydration expects server and client DOM to match. Mismatches (NG0500-series errors) come from direct DOM manipulation, invalid HTML nesting (e.g. <div> in <p>, <tbody> missing), random/time-based content (Math.random(), Date.now() in templates) and browser-only rendering branches. Use ngSkipHydration sparingly, fix the cause where possible.
• Server and browser execution differences: one process serves many users, so module-level mutable state is shared across requests (a security leak and bug source): keep state in injected, request-scoped services. No layout APIs (getBoundingClientRect returns zeros), no IntersectionObserver/ResizeObserver/matchMedia, timers keep the response waiting, and relative HTTP URLs need an absolute base on the server (use an interceptor or absolute API_URL token).
• Event replay (withEventReplay()) records user clicks before hydration completes and replays them afterwards, improving INP.
• i18n hydration is supported from v18; HttpClient with withFetch() is advised for SSR.
• Avoid setTimeout or setInterval in constructors that run on the server; start them inside afterNextRender.

Library compatibility

Many third-party UI libraries touch window at import time, which crashes SSR before any guard can run. Lazy import them inside afterNextRender with dynamic import(), or render the component only in the browser via @defer (on immediate) or RenderMode.Client routes.

interviewQA: What is hydration?
Reusing the server-rendered DOM: Angular attaches listeners and state to existing nodes rather than destroying and re-creating them, avoiding flicker and duplicated work.
How do you use window or localStorage safely in an SSR app?
Never touch them at import/constructor time on the server. Use afterNextRender, isPlatformBrowser guards, the DOCUMENT token, or a storage abstraction with server-safe fallback.
What is incremental hydration?
Server-rendered @defer blocks stay dehydrated and hydrate on triggers such as viewport or interaction, so less JavaScript runs up front. It is a v19+ feature; check the status for your version.
What causes hydration mismatch errors?

Different DOM on server and client: direct DOM changes, invalid HTML, random or time-based values, or browser-only conditional rendering. Fix the source or use ngSkipHydration for problematic components.
Why is module-level state dangerous in SSR?
A Node process handles many requests; a module-level variable is shared among users and can leak data between requests. Use request-scoped Angular services.

topics.name: SEO and metadata

beginner.content:
Helping search engines and social apps understand pages

SEO fundamentals: crawlers need meaningful HTML at a stable URL. Key ingredients: readable content in the initial HTML (SSR/prerender), unique page titles and descriptions, descriptive links (<a href> via routerLink, not click handlers), semantic headings, fast Core Web Vitals, mobile friendliness, sitemap.xml and robots.txt, and structured data (JSON-LD). Without SSR, Google can execute JavaScript but other crawlers and social previews often cannot.
codeExamples:
<!-- what a crawler wants to see in the first HTML response -->
<title>Angular Course for Java Developers | JavaSchool</title>
<meta name="description" content="Learn Angular step by step with Spring Boot examples.">
<link rel="canonical" href="https://javaschool.example.com/courses/angular">

intermediate.content:
Dynamic metadata with Title, Meta and route titles

Angular provides Title and Meta services (they work on the server too, because they write into the DOM emulation that becomes the HTML). For simple pages use the route title property or a TitleStrategy (to add a suffix). For dynamic pages (product, article) set metadata after loading data, typically in the component or a resolver.

Open Graph and canonical URLs explained

Open Graph metadata (og:title, og:description, og:image, og:url, og:type) controls how a link looks when shared on WhatsApp, LinkedIn, Facebook, Slack; X/Twitter uses twitter:* tags. The preview bot does not run JavaScript, so tags must be in the server-rendered HTML. A canonical URL tells search engines which URL is the master copy when the same content is reachable via several URLs (query strings, trailing slash, http/https, www), preventing duplicate-content dilution.

expert.content:
Details and pitfalls

• Set tags before the app becomes stable on the server; metadata set after a delayed callback is missed by SSR. Fetch data in a resolver or use resource/transfer cache so the server waits for it.
• Use updateTag (not addTag) to avoid duplicates on navigation. Remove stale tags on routes that do not need them.
• Titles ~50-60 chars, descriptions ~150-160 chars, og:image 1200x630 absolute HTTPS URL. Use absolute URLs for canonical and og tags.
• Structured data: inject a <script type="application/ld+json"> element with JSON-LD built from your own data via JSON.stringify; escape the closing script sequence in user-provided strings.
• Use proper status codes: a not-found page should return HTTP 404 from the server (set it on the response via the request-response token in the Express server); a client-only 404 view returns 200 ("soft 404") which hurts SEO. Redirects should be 301/302 at the server level.
• Provide sitemap.xml generated from backend data and robots.txt. Avoid hash-based URLs (useHash), which crawlers ignore.
• Testing: view the "View source" HTML, use Google Search Console URL inspection, the Rich Results test and social debuggers; curl the URL to see what a non-JS bot gets.

Per-route SEO pattern

Store SEO data in route data for static pages and in resolvers for dynamic ones; a single TitleStrategy plus SeoService keeps it consistent and testable. Combine with prerender so each product page is a ready HTML file with correct tags.

interviewQA: Why does SEO need SSR or prerendering for many Angular sites?
Crawlers and social preview bots may not execute JavaScript; with CSR they see an empty shell. SSR/SSG delivers real HTML with content and metadata in the first response.
How do you set page title and description dynamically?
Inject Title and Meta services (or use route title and a TitleStrategy) and update after the data loads, preferably in a resolver so SSR waits for it. Use updateTag to avoid duplicates.
What is a canonical URL?
A link rel=canonical tag naming the preferred URL of a page so duplicates (query params, protocol variants) consolidate ranking signals.
Why are Open Graph tags important with SSR?
Social crawlers read og tags from the initial HTML without running JS. They must be present in the server-rendered output to produce rich previews.
What is a soft 404?
A not-found page returning HTTP 200. Search engines treat it as real content. Return an actual 404 status from the server for missing resources.

topics.name: Server data, caching, security and deployment

beginner.content:
Data, speed and safety on the server

• Server-side data fetching: during SSR the server calls your API (Spring Boot) so the HTML already contains data. The browser must not repeat these calls: Angular's HTTP transfer cache serializes GET responses into the page and reuses them on the client during hydration.
• SSR caching: rendering is CPU work; cache rendered HTML for anonymous pages (CDN or in memory) with short TTLs.
• SSR security: the Node server is now a backend: treat it as part of your attack surface.
• Deployment of SSR applications: you now run a Node process, not just static files.

intermediate.content:
Fetching on the server and caching output

Use HttpClient with withFetch(). On the server, API URLs must be absolute (an API_URL InjectionToken provided differently for server and browser) or an interceptor prefixes them; inside the same network use the internal Spring hostname to avoid public round trips. Pass the user's cookies to the API only for personalised (non-cached) pages and forward them explicitly from the request (REQUEST token).
SSR caching layers: (1) CDN or reverse proxy caches HTML (Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=300); (2) in-memory LRU of rendered pages by URL in server.ts; (3) cache upstream API calls. Never cache responses that depend on cookies or authorization (use Vary or bypass).

expert.content:
SSR security

• Isolation: no per-user data in module-level variables or singletons created outside the request injector; each render gets its own platform injector but static code is shared.
• Secrets: the server can hold secrets (API keys) but never serialize them into transfer state or HTML; the transfer cache embeds responses, so do not fetch secrets in components. Hide cookie/headers: the HTTP transfer cache drops sensitive headers such as Authorization and Proxy-Authorization unless you opt in.
• SSRF: if a URL comes from the request (Host header or query parameter) and is used for fetching, an attacker can make your server call internal addresses. Newer Angular validates the host (allowedHosts in the server config in recent versions, after security advisories in 2025); keep Angular patched and configure an allow-list of hostnames; do not trust X-Forwarded-* blindly.
• XSS in HTML output: Angular escapes templates; custom REQUEST data and JSON-LD scripts need escaping. Apply CSP, helmet headers, rate limiting and timeouts on the Express app. Prefer running Node as non-root in a container.
• Tokens in cookies/localStorage: on the server there is no localStorage, so SSR auth requires cookies, which brings CSRF considerations.

Deployment

Build with ng build (outputs dist/app/browser and dist/app/server), run node dist/app/server/server.mjs under PM2/systemd/Docker, behind Nginx (TLS, gzip/brotli, static asset caching, proxy to Node). Prerendered-only apps need just static hosting. Options: containers (Cloud Run, ECS, Kubernetes), Firebase Hosting with Cloud Functions, Vercel/Netlify adapters, or edge runtimes (check version support). Health check endpoints, graceful shutdown, structured logging, horizontal scaling and a render timeout are production basics. With Spring Boot, either serve Angular SSR from Node and proxy /api to Spring, or keep CSR and serve static files from Nginx/Spring.
codeExamples:
# Dockerfile (outline)
FROM node:22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build
FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
USER node
EXPOSE 4000
CMD ["node", "dist/my-app/server/server.mjs"]

interviewQA: How does the HTTP transfer cache help SSR?
GET responses fetched on the server are embedded into the HTML and reused during hydration in the browser, avoiding duplicate requests and flicker.
How would you cache SSR output safely?
Cache only anonymous, non-personalised pages via CDN/reverse proxy or in-memory LRU with short TTLs and stale-while-revalidate; bypass or vary on cookies and authorization.
What are SSR-specific security risks?
Cross-request state leaks, secrets in transferred state, SSRF via untrusted host headers or URLs, unescaped data in server templates, and exposing the Node server without hardening.
How do you deploy an Angular SSR app?

Build, run the Node server file under a process manager or in a container, put Nginx or a CDN in front for TLS and caching, proxy API calls to Spring Boot, and add health checks. Prerendered-only sites need only static hosting.
Why use absolute API URLs on the server?
There is no browser origin during SSR, so relative URLs have no base. Provide an API base token or interceptor for the server environment.

topics.name: Testing fundamentals and tooling

beginner.content:
Why test?

Software testing fundamentals: tests are a safety net so you can change code without fear, like the seat belt in a car. They run automatically and tell you when behaviour breaks. A good test follows Arrange - Act - Assert: set up, do the thing, check the result. The test pyramid says: many fast unit tests, a medium number of integration tests, and few slow end-to-end (E2E) tests.
• Unit testing: one piece in isolation (a pipe, a service, a validator).
• Integration testing: pieces working together (a component with its template and a fake service).
• End-to-end testing: a robot uses the real app in a real browser, against the real or stubbed backend. For Java developers: JUnit ~ unit, Spring Boot Test ~ integration, Selenium ~ E2E.

intermediate.content:
The tool landscape

Note on tooling and versions: Angular testing defaults vary by version and project configuration. Classic CLI projects use Jasmine (framework: describe/it/expect/spyOn) with Karma (runner that launches real Chrome). Newer Angular versions are moving away from Karma (Karma is deprecated upstream); the CLI offers an experimental Vitest builder (@angular/build:unit-test) and the team's direction is Vitest, while many teams use Jest (jsdom, with jest-preset-angular or the builders). Learn the runner your project actually uses and read its angular.json/package.json.
ToolTypeNotes
Jasmine + KarmaUnit/integration in a real browserClassic default; real browser fidelity, slower; Karma is legacy direction
JestUnit/integration in jsdom (Node)Fast, snapshots, jest.fn, jest.spyOn; no real layout
VitestUnit/integration, Vite-poweredJest-compatible API (vi.fn), fast watch mode; Angular support newer / experimental in some versions
PlaywrightE2E (Chromium, Firefox, WebKit)Auto-waiting, traces, parallel; recommended modern E2E
CypressE2E (+ component testing)Great interactive runner; runs in the browser, one tab model

Code coverage: ng test --code-coverage produces a report (statements, branches, functions, lines). Use it to find untested areas, not as a goal in itself (100 percent coverage does not mean correct).

Continuous Integration testing

Run unit tests headless on every push/pull request, fail the build on test or coverage regressions, run E2E against a deployed preview or docker-compose stack (Angular + Spring Boot + DB), upload reports/traces as artifacts.
codeExamples:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml (excerpt)
- run: npm ci
- run: npx ng test --watch=false --browsers=ChromeHeadless --code-coverage    # Karma/Jasmine project
# or for a Jest/Vitest project: npm test -- --coverage
- run: npx playwright install --with-deps chromium
- run: npx playwright test

expert.content:
Strategy and honest trade-offs

• Jasmine/Karma tests run in a real browser (accurate layout, getBoundingClientRect, CSS) but are slow and need Chrome in CI. Jest/Vitest in jsdom or happy-dom are faster but do not implement layout, IntersectionObserver or many CSS features; stub those, or move such checks to Playwright.
• Migration from Karma: check the official guidance for your version; Jest migration usually means replacing jasmine.createSpyObj/spyOn().and.returnValue with jest.fn/jest.spyOn().mockReturnValue, fakeAsync still works with zone.js (needs zone testing setup) but zoneless/Vitest setups use fake timers (vi.useFakeTimers) and await fixture.whenStable().
• Prefer testing behaviour (what the user sees) over implementation (private methods). Query by role/label/text, not CSS classes.
• Keep unit tests deterministic: no real network, time, randomness; control with fakes and fake timers.
• Balance: pyramid plus a handful of critical E2E journeys (login, checkout). Flaky E2E tests destroy trust; use auto-wait locators, isolated test data, and avoid fixed sleeps.
• Contract testing / Spring Cloud Contract or a mock server (MSW) keeps front and back in sync; real full-stack E2E validates integration with Spring Boot, CORS and security.
• Coverage thresholds in CI (e.g. 80 percent for new code) plus mutation testing (Stryker) give a better quality signal.

Choosing for a new project

Follow the CLI default of your Angular version unless there is a reason. If starting fresh on a recent version, evaluate Vitest (speed, Vite alignment) but confirm it is supported (stable or experimental) for your Angular release; use Playwright for E2E.

interviewQA: What is the test pyramid?
A guideline: many fast unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests in the middle and a few slow end-to-end tests at the top, balancing speed, confidence and maintenance cost.
Jasmine vs Karma?
Jasmine is the testing framework (describe, it, expect, spies). Karma is the runner that launches browsers and executes the tests. Karma is on the deprecation path; many teams use Jest or Vitest.
Jest vs Vitest in Angular?

Both offer Jest-style APIs. Jest runs in Node with jsdom and is mature; Vitest is Vite-based, faster, with ESM focus, and has newer, sometimes experimental, Angular CLI support. Check your Angular version.
Playwright vs Cypress?

Both test the real app in browsers. Playwright supports multiple browsers including WebKit, multiple tabs and contexts, auto-waits and traces; Cypress has an excellent interactive runner and component testing but a different execution model.
Does 100 percent code coverage guarantee quality?
No. It only shows lines executed, not that assertions are meaningful. Use it to find gaps and combine with good assertions and mutation testing.

topics.name: TestBed, components, services and DI

beginner.content:
Angular testing utilities

Angular testing utilities live in @angular/core/testing. TestBed creates a mini Angular environment for a test, like a small stage where you place only the actors (components, providers) you need. ComponentFixture is the handle to the created component: fixture.componentInstance (the class), fixture.nativeElement (the DOM) and fixture.detectChanges() (run change detection so the template updates).
Component testing: create it, change state, detect changes, assert on DOM text.

intermediate.content:
Services, DI, inputs/outputs, lifecycle

Service testing: for a plain service just new it with fakes, or use TestBed when it uses inject(). Dependency Injection testing: override providers ({ provide: Api, useValue: fakeApi }) to isolate the unit; check hierarchical/route scopes with TestBed.inject. Testing inputs and outputs: set inputs with fixture.componentRef.setInput; for output() subscribe with .subscribe(spy) (or an EventEmitter spy), then trigger the DOM event. Testing lifecycle behavior: the first fixture.detectChanges() runs ngOnInit; changes via setInput trigger ngOnChanges; fixture.destroy() runs ngOnDestroy.

Directives and pipes

Testing pipes is the easiest: instantiate and call transform. Testing directives: create a small host component whose template uses the directive, then assert on the host element (classes, attributes, events).

expert.content:
Best practices and pitfalls

• With the default ComponentFixtureAutoDetect off, nothing renders until detectChanges(). For OnPush components, setting a plain property after first detectChanges() does not re-render; use setInput (or a host wrapper) because the fixture's change detection respects OnPush.
• Prefer component harnesses (@angular/cdk/testing, Material harnesses like MatButtonHarness) over CSS selectors for library widgets: they hide DOM details and wait for stability automatically (TestbedHarnessEnvironment.loader(fixture)).
• Shallow vs deep component tests: import child components for realistic integration, or override them (TestBed.overrideComponent with stubs) for isolation. Avoid NO_ERRORS_SCHEMA hiding real template errors.
• Use TestBed.runInInjectionContext(() => ...) for functions using inject() (guards, interceptors, helpers). Call TestBed.resetTestingModule() only if you must; the framework resets between tests. Avoid sharing state between specs.
• Do not test Angular itself (that *ngIf works); test your logic and visible outcomes.
• Zoneless: configure provideZonelessChangeDetection() in tests to match production, and use await fixture.whenStable() instead of relying on automatic zone-triggered detection.
• Keep tests fast: use TestBed only when needed; pure functions do not need it.

Structuring specs

Co-locate *.spec.ts with the file, one describe per unit, builders/factories for test data, shared test providers in a helper, and descriptive names ("shows an error when the email is invalid") so failures read like documentation.

interviewQA: What does TestBed do?
It configures and creates a testing Angular environment: declares or imports components, sets providers, creates components and exposes the injector (TestBed.inject).
What is ComponentFixture used for?
It wraps a created component: access componentInstance, nativeElement/debugElement, run detectChanges, set inputs via componentRef.setInput, and destroy it.
How do you test a component output?
Subscribe to the output (or spy on the EventEmitter) and trigger the DOM event that causes it, then assert the spy was called with the right value.
How do you test a directive?
Create a host test component that uses the directive in its template, detect changes and assert on the host element, simulating events with dispatchEvent.
What are component harnesses?
Abstractions from the CDK that expose a component API for tests (click, getText) independent of the DOM structure, handling async stability automatically.
Why does my OnPush component not update in a test?
Mutating a property after the first detectChanges does not mark an OnPush view dirty. Use setInput, signals, or markForCheck via a wrapper host.

topics.name: Mocking, async, Observables and Signals

beginner.content:
Fakes, spies and waiting

Mocking dependencies means replacing real collaborators (HTTP, router, other services) with controllable fakes so the test checks only your unit. A stub returns canned answers; a spy records how it was called (like Mockito's mock and verify). Asynchronous testing deals with code that finishes later: promises, timers, observables.

intermediate.content:
Asynchronous tests, Observables, Signals, errors

Asynchronous testing options: (1) async/await with await fixture.whenStable(); (2) fakeAsync + tick(ms) / flush() / flushMicrotasks() to control time without waiting (needs zone.js testing; for zoneless use fake timers of the runner); (3) waitForAsync (legacy-ish helper). Testing Observables: convert with firstValueFrom/lastValueFrom and await, or collect emissions; use RxJS TestScheduler marble tests for time-based operators (debounce, switchMap). Testing Signals: signals are synchronous, so write/read them directly; computed recomputes on read; effects run during change detection, so call TestBed.tick() (v20; earlier TestBed.flushEffects()) or fixture.detectChanges(). Testing error handling: make the fake throw (throwError(() => new Error('x'))) and assert the error message, state or fallback.

Marble test example

Marbles describe streams over virtual time: - is a frame, letters are values, | completes, # errors.

expert.content:
Details and pitfalls

• Jest/Vitest equivalents: jest.useFakeTimers() + jest.advanceTimersByTime / vi.useFakeTimers() replace fakeAsync/tick when zone.js testing is not set up; jest.spyOn(service, 'x').mockReturnValue(...) vs Jasmine spyOn(service, 'x').and.returnValue(...). Tests that mix fakeAsync with real timers or pending periodic timers fail with "1 periodic timer(s) still in the queue": call discardPeriodicTasks() or flush().
• Do not use subscribe with done callbacks and forget failures; firstValueFrom is cleaner. An observable that never completes will hang lastValueFrom.
• Spies vs stubs vs fakes: prefer small hand-written fakes (an in-memory repository) for complex collaborators, spies for verifying interactions. Over-mocking couples tests to implementation; verify outcomes first.
• Signal effect() timing: effects are scheduled; in zoneless tests, await fixture.whenStable() flushes them. For toSignal you need an injection context (TestBed.runInInjectionContext).
• Use HttpTestingController or MSW rather than mocking HttpClient itself when the HTTP details (URL, headers, body) matter.
• Always assert that errors are handled without unhandled rejections; Jasmine fails on unhandled promise rejections in newer versions.

Testing strategy for async code

Make time injectable: pass a scheduler or use asyncScheduler override, wrap Date.now in a clock service, and keep timing operators at the edges. Pure signal/computed logic needs no async handling at all, one more reason to keep state in signals.

interviewQA: Spy vs stub vs mock?

A stub supplies canned responses; a spy wraps a function or object to record calls (and can also return values); a mock is a pre-programmed object with expectations (Mockito-style). In Jasmine/Jest, spies cover most needs.
How does fakeAsync work?
It runs the test in a zone that virtualizes timers and microtasks. tick(ms) advances virtual time, flush() runs all pending timers, so time-based code is tested instantly and deterministically.
How do you test an RxJS stream with debounce?
Use fakeAsync/tick or fake timers, or RxJS TestScheduler marble tests with virtual time and assert the expected marble diagram.
How do you test signals and effects?
Read and write signals directly because they are synchronous; for effects trigger scheduling with fixture.detectChanges, TestBed.tick (or flushEffects in older versions) or whenStable.
How do you test error paths?
Have the fake dependency return throwError or reject, then assert that the UI shows the message, state flags are set and no unhandled error is thrown.

topics.name: Forms, guards, HTTP, router and accessibility tests

beginner.content:
Testing the building blocks of real apps

• Testing forms: set a control value, check valid/invalid and the error message shown.
• Testing validators: a validator is just a function; call it with a FormControl.
• Testing HTTP services: never hit the network; use provideHttpClientTesting() and HttpTestingController to intercept requests and answer them with fake data, like a mock server.

intermediate.content:
HTTP, guards, resolvers and router

Provide provideHttpClient() then provideHttpClientTesting(). Use expectOne(url) to find the request, check method/headers/body, flush(data) to answer (or flush(msg, { status: 500, statusText: '...' }) for errors) and finally verify() to be sure no unexpected requests remain.
Testing route guards and resolvers (functional): run them inside TestBed.runInInjectionContext with fake services. Router testing: use RouterTestingHarness (v15+) with provideRouter(routes) to navigate and get the activated component; stub child components or lazy routes as needed.

Accessibility testing

Accessibility testing: run axe-core (via jest-axe, axe-playwright or @axe-core/playwright) on rendered components/pages, assert roles and labels (getByRole), verify keyboard operation (Tab, Enter, Escape), focus return after dialogs, and aria-live messages. Automated tools catch a portion of issues; combine with manual screen-reader checks.

expert.content:
Depth and pitfalls

• Register interceptors in tests with provideHttpClient(withInterceptors([myInterceptor])) to test them through real HttpClient plus the testing backend; assert the cloned request headers on the matched req.request.
• For async validators use fakeAsync + tick; for cross-field validators build a FormGroup and assert errors on the group.
• Resolvers returning Observables: await firstValueFrom(result as Observable<T>). Functions may return value, Promise or Observable; normalise in the test.
• RouterTestingHarness performs real navigation with guards and resolvers, so it doubles as an integration test of route config. Use RouterModule.forRoot mocks only in legacy code.
• http.verify() in afterEach catches forgotten requests; remember expectOne fails if there are two matching requests (use match).
• Testing forms: dispatch real input events to test template-driven ngModel (it updates asynchronously: await fixture.whenStable()); reactive forms can be tested via the model alone, plus a few DOM checks for error messages and disabled buttons.
• Real backend: a handful of E2E tests against Spring Boot (using Testcontainers or a seeded test database) verify CORS, security rules and DTO mapping which front-end unit tests cannot.
• Coverage on guards/resolvers/validators is cheap and high value, because they are pure functions.

Test-suite hygiene

Keep one assertion theme per test, share builders (e.g. buildUser({ role: 'ADMIN' })), do not depend on test order, and clean up with afterEach. Run tests in random order if the runner supports it to expose hidden coupling.

interviewQA: How do you test a service that uses HttpClient?
Provide provideHttpClient and provideHttpClientTesting, call the method, use HttpTestingController.expectOne to assert the request, flush a fake response, and call verify().
What does HttpTestingController.verify() do?
It asserts that no unmatched or unexpected HTTP requests are outstanding, catching forgotten or extra requests.
How do you unit-test a functional route guard?
Configure TestBed with fake services and call the guard inside TestBed.runInInjectionContext, then assert the boolean or UrlTree result.
How do you test routing?
Use RouterTestingHarness with provideRouter(routes): navigateByUrl returns the activated component so you can assert state, with guards and resolvers executed for real.
How do you test a custom validator?
Call the validator function with a FormControl or FormGroup holding test values and assert the returned error object or null; async validators need fakeAsync or await.
What can automated accessibility tests not do?
Axe finds a subset of issues (missing labels, contrast, roles). Keyboard flow, focus management and screen-reader experience still need manual verification.

topics.name: Responsive layout, CSS architecture and encapsulation

beginner.content:
Building screens that fit every device

Responsive UI design means one codebase looks good on a phone, a tablet and a desktop, like water taking the shape of its glass. Start mobile first (simple one-column layout) and add rules for larger screens with media queries. Component-based UI architecture means the screen is a tree of small components (header, card, button), each responsible for one thing and reusable.
Two layout tools: Flexbox arranges items in one direction (a row or a column), Grid arranges in rows and columns at once.

intermediate.content:
Component styling, encapsulation, CSS architecture and variables

Angular component styling: styles in styles / styleUrl apply only to that component. View encapsulation controls it: Emulated (default; Angular adds attributes like _ngcontent-abc to scope rules), None (styles become global), ShadowDom (native Shadow DOM, real isolation). Use :host to style the component's own element, :host-context(.dark) for theme ancestors, and avoid the deprecated ::ng-deep (it still works but is deprecated; prefer CSS variables or exposed classes).
CSS custom properties (--brand) are inherited at runtime and cross encapsulation boundaries, making them the right API for theming components.
CSS architecture (layers): (1) design tokens as variables in :root, (2) global reset/typography in styles.css, (3) layout utilities, (4) component styles co-located, (5) optional utility framework. Use a naming convention (BEM) for global classes and keep specificity low. Use @layer to control order.

Responsive tools in Angular

Use CSS first (media/container queries). When logic needs breakpoints, the CDK BreakpointObserver gives an Observable; convert to a signal with toSignal and branch with @if.

expert.content:
Deeper notes

• Emulated encapsulation does not style child component internals; do not fight it with ::ng-deep globally. Expose variables (--card-bg) from the child. Content projected via ng-content belongs to the parent's scope, so parent styles apply.
• ShadowDom encapsulation blocks global CSS (including Bootstrap/Tailwind) from reaching inside; usually desirable only for widgets (Angular Elements).
• Style budgets matter: big component CSS is duplicated per component instance type only once, but huge style bundles slow parsing; use shared partials via @use (Sass) sparingly and avoid importing large files in every component.
• Prefer logical properties (margin-inline, padding-block) for RTL, rem units for accessibility scaling, container queries (@container) so components respond to their own width rather than the viewport (supported in all modern browsers).
• Avoid layout thrashing and animating width/height; animate transform/opacity. Respect prefers-reduced-motion.
• Flexbox vs Grid: Flexbox for content-driven one-dimensional alignment (toolbars, nav), Grid for page and card layouts; they nest well. Use gap instead of margins.
• Keep component styles small, with no hard-coded colours; consume tokens. Angular's animations package is legacy-ish in v20.2+ in favour of CSS animate.enter/leave (check your version).

Structure of a UI codebase

ui/ (dumb reusable components), features/ (screens using them), styles/ (tokens, mixins, themes). Presentational components accept inputs and emit outputs only, are OnPush, and are visually tested in isolation (Storybook).

interviewQA: Explain Angular view encapsulation modes.
Emulated (default) scopes styles using generated attributes, None makes styles global, ShadowDom uses the browser shadow root for true isolation.
How can a parent theme a child component without ng-deep?
Expose CSS custom properties from the child (var(--card-bg)) and set them on the parent or host; custom properties inherit through encapsulation.
Flexbox or Grid?
Flexbox for one-dimensional alignment and distribution (rows of buttons, navbars); Grid for two-dimensional layouts (page areas, card galleries). Combine them.
What does :host do?
It targets the component host element from inside the component styles, e.g. :host { display: block; }.
What is mobile-first responsive design?
Write base styles for small screens, then enhance with min-width media queries or container queries for larger ones.

topics.name: Angular Material and the CDK

beginner.content:
Ready-made building blocks

Angular Material is the official component library implementing Google's Material Design: buttons, cards, form fields, tables, dialogs, menus. Add with ng add @angular/material. Under it sits the CDK (Component Dev Kit): unstyled behaviour such as overlays, drag and drop, accessibility helpers, virtual scrolling. Think of Material as a furnished flat and the CDK as the plumbing and wiring you can use to build your own flat.
Material components are standalone: import only what you use in imports.

intermediate.content:
Tables, dialogs, forms and navigation

Material tables: mat-table with a MatTableDataSource, matSort, mat-paginator. Material dialogs: inject MatDialog, open(Component, { data }), and read afterClosed(). Material forms: mat-form-field wraps matInput, mat-select, mat-datepicker with mat-label, mat-error and mat-hint; works with Reactive Forms. Material navigation: mat-toolbar, mat-sidenav-container, mat-menu, mat-tab-group, mat-nav-list with routerLink.
codeExamples:
Filter
Name {{ u.name }}

intermediate.content: Dialog service pattern

expert.content:
CDK in depth

• CDK fundamentals: behaviour without styling. Modules/APIs: a11y, overlay, portal, drag-drop, scrolling, table, layout, testing (harnesses), clipboard, menu, listbox, stepper.
• CDK overlays: Overlay.create({ positionStrategy, scrollStrategy, hasBackdrop }) returns an OverlayRef; attach a ComponentPortal/TemplatePortal. Position strategies: global (centered) and flexible connected (anchored to an element with fallbacks). Material dialogs, menus, tooltips, selects and autocompletes are built on it. Always dispose the overlay.
• CDK accessibility: cdkTrapFocus keeps Tab inside a modal; FocusMonitor knows if focus came from keyboard, mouse or program; LiveAnnouncer.announce() speaks text to screen readers; ListKeyManager/ActiveDescendantKeyManager give arrow-key navigation; cdkAriaLive.
• CDK drag and drop: cdkDropList + cdkDrag, (cdkDropListDropped) with moveItemInArray/transferArrayItem; supports handles, previews, placeholders, connected lists (Kanban).
codeExamples:
@for (t of tasks(); track t.id) {
{{ t.title }}
}

expert.content:
Pitfalls and version notes

• Import Material only per component; global MatModule imports are legacy. Material 3 (v18+) theming uses Sass mixins (mat.theme in v19/20) and CSS system variables (--mat-sys-*); older M2 palettes (mat.define-light-theme) are legacy. Theming APIs changed between v17, v18, v19 and v20: read the guide for your version.
• MatTableDataSource is client-side; for server-side paging implement your own DataSource/signal list and drive matSort/mat-paginator events to the API. Many rows: add virtual scroll or paginate.
• Wrap dialog opening in a service so UI code stays testable; use MatDialogHarness in tests. Return focus is handled by default.
• Animations: Material needs provideAnimationsAsync() (or no-op animations) in older versions; newer versions reduce this dependency.

interviewQA: Angular Material vs CDK?

Material is a styled component library following Material Design. The CDK is the unstyled behavioural layer (overlay, a11y, drag-drop, virtual scroll, table) that Material is built on and that you can use to craft your own components.
How do you open a dialog and get its result?
Inject MatDialog, call open(Component, { data }), subscribe to afterClosed() (or convert to a promise). The dialog closes with [mat-dialog-close] or dialogRef.close(value).
How do Material tables support sorting and pagination?
Use MatTableDataSource and attach MatSort and MatPaginator to it for client-side work; for server-side data, listen to sort/page events and fetch from the API.
What is a CDK overlay?
A floating pane rendered at the document body level with a position strategy and scroll strategy, hosting a portal; it powers dialogs, menus, tooltips and selects.
Which CDK utilities help accessibility?
FocusTrap, FocusMonitor, LiveAnnouncer, ListKeyManager, and a11y-focused harnesses; they handle focus and keyboard navigation patterns correctly.

topics.name: Bootstrap, Tailwind, design systems and theming

beginner.content:
Choosing a look and feel

• Bootstrap with Angular: add Bootstrap CSS (or Sass) for grid, utilities and styled components; use ng-bootstrap or ngx-bootstrap for components so you do not rely on Bootstrap's jQuery-style JavaScript.
• Tailwind CSS with Angular: utility classes in templates (class="flex gap-2 p-4"); the build scans files and ships only used classes.
• Reusable UI components: wrap repeated markup (button with spinner, form field with label and error) in a component with inputs/outputs.
• A design system collects tokens, components and guidelines so every team builds consistent screens.

intermediate.content:
Reusable components and theming

A reusable UI component is small, OnPush, driven by input(), communicates by output(), uses content projection for flexibility, hides styling behind variants, and uses tokens. Theming and dark mode: define colours as CSS custom properties; switch by toggling a class or data-theme attribute on <html>; default to prefers-color-scheme and remember the user's choice (localStorage, guarded for SSR). Material 3 themes provide the same via Sass mixins and color-scheme.
Tokens in CSS

expert.content:
Choosing and combining

OptionStrengthWatch out
Angular MaterialAccessible, official, consistent, themeableOpinionated look; major theming changes between versions
Bootstrap (+ ng-bootstrap)Familiar, quick, big ecosystemGlobal CSS, generic look; avoid its JS bundle with Angular
TailwindFast iteration, small CSS, custom designsLong class lists; wrap in components; need headless/CDK for behaviour
PrimeNG / Spartan / othersRich component setsEvaluate license, a11y quality and maintenance

• Mixing Material and Tailwind is common (Tailwind for layout, Material for components); set Tailwind preflight carefully to avoid resetting Material styles.
• Design system practice: tokens (colour, spacing, type, radius, elevation) in a single source (JSON or CSS), components as a versioned library, documentation in Storybook with accessibility checks, visual regression tests (Chromatic/Playwright snapshots), and contribution rules. Build design-system components on CDK primitives to inherit accessibility.
• Dark mode traps: hard-coded colours, images with white backgrounds, insufficient contrast in one theme, flash of wrong theme (set the attribute early via inline script or SSR cookie), third-party widgets ignoring tokens. Test contrast in both themes.
• Do not duplicate Bootstrap's grid and Angular Material layout both: pick one system per concern. Avoid overriding framework internals with !important; use tokens or wrapper components.

Governance

Version the UI library separately, deprecate with codemods or schematics, and test visual changes. A thin adapter layer (ui-button rather than direct mat-button everywhere) lets you swap or update underlying libraries with one change.

interviewQA: How do you add Tailwind to an Angular project?

Install tailwindcss with its PostCSS plugin, configure PostCSS (.postcssrc.json), import Tailwind in styles.css and use utility classes in templates. Exact setup depends on the Tailwind and Angular versions.
Why prefer ng-bootstrap over Bootstrap JS?
ng-bootstrap implements components natively in Angular without jQuery or Bootstrap JS DOM manipulation, so it integrates with change detection and the template system.
How do you implement dark mode?
Define colours as CSS custom properties, switch a data-theme attribute or class on the root element, respect prefers-color-scheme, persist the choice and avoid a flash by applying it early.
What makes a UI component reusable?
Clear inputs and outputs, content projection, no hard-wired services or styles, token-based styling, accessibility built in, OnPush and documentation/tests.
What is a design system?
A set of design tokens, reusable components and usage guidelines shared across products to keep UI consistent and speed development.

topics.name: UI patterns: navigation, dialogs, tables and accessibility

beginner.content:
Everyday UI patterns

• Responsive navigation: a sidebar on large screens becomes a hamburger drawer on phones.
• Modal and popup design: a modal blocks the page for a focused task; a popover or tooltip is lightweight and non-blocking. Always provide a clear close action and Escape.
• Data tables show records; pagination splits them into pages; sorting and filtering help find rows.
• Accessibility and keyboard navigation: everything must work with Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space, Arrow keys and Escape.
• ARIA attributes describe roles and states to screen readers when native HTML is not enough (prefer native elements first).

intermediate.content:
Navigation, tables with server-side paging, dialogs

Responsive navigation: Material sidenav in over mode on handsets and side on desktop. Data tables: semantic <table> with <th scope>, a caption, sticky header, loading and empty states. Pagination, sorting and filtering for large data belong on the server (Spring Pageable: ?page=0&size=20&sort=name,asc&q=ann); keep the state in the URL query params so views are shareable and the back button works.
codeExamples: Home

intermediate.content:
Keyboard and ARIA essentials, focus in dialogs, UI testing

Dialog checklist: role="dialog" (or alertdialog), aria-modal="true", labelled by its title, focus moves inside on open, Tab is trapped, Escape closes, focus returns to the trigger. Use aria-live="polite" for async messages, aria-expanded/aria-controls for disclosure buttons, aria-sort on sorted column headers, aria-current="page" on the active link, and aria-label for icon-only buttons.
UI testing: component tests with harnesses, a11y checks with axe, visual regression with Playwright screenshots or Storybook/Chromatic, E2E for critical flows and responsive viewport tests (page.setViewportSize).
codeExamples: {{ statusMessage() }}

expert.content:
Depth and pitfalls

• First rule of ARIA: do not use ARIA if a native element does it (button, a, select, dialog). Wrong ARIA is worse than none. The native <dialog> element (showModal()) now handles focus trapping and Escape and is a valid base for modals.
• Keyboard patterns follow the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices: tabs use arrow keys with roving tabindex; menus use arrows, Home/End and type-ahead; use CDK ListKeyManager instead of reinventing.
• Never remove focus outlines without a replacement; use :focus-visible. Provide skip links ("Skip to content") and a logical DOM order. Touch targets at least 44x44 px (WCAG 2.2: 24x24 minimum).
• Data tables: avoid putting interactive elements in every cell without labels; for very wide tables allow horizontal scroll in a focusable region (tabindex="0" with label) or switch to card layout on mobile. Announce sort changes and result counts via live regions.
• Pagination vs infinite scroll: pagination is better for orientation, keyboard use and footer access; infinite scroll needs "load more" fallback and focus management.
• Modals: avoid stacking modals; prefer inline editing, drawers or separate routes for complex flows (so the URL and back button work). Use a route-based dialog for deep-linkable screens.
• Test with real usage: keyboard only, 200 percent zoom, screen readers (NVDA, VoiceOver), reduced motion, high contrast. Automated axe covers maybe a third of WCAG issues.
• Filtering with debounce, cancellation (switchMap) and reset-to-first-page on change avoid stale and empty-page bugs.

UI testing pyramid

Unit-test logic (sort/page state), component-test rendering and events with harnesses, visual-regression key states (empty, loading, error, dark mode, mobile), and keep a few Playwright journeys for responsive nav, dialogs and tables against a seeded backend.

interviewQA: How would you implement a data table for 100k rows?

Server-side pagination, sorting and filtering through the Spring API (Pageable), keep state in signals or URL params, debounce and cancel stale requests, show loading/empty/error states, and use virtual scroll only for in-memory lists.
What makes a modal accessible?
Role dialog and aria-modal, accessible name, focus moved in and trapped, Escape closes, focus restored to the trigger, background inert. CDK/Material dialogs or native dialog handle most of this.
When should you use ARIA?
Only when native HTML cannot express the semantics (custom tabs, comboboxes). Use correct roles, states and keyboard behaviour; wrong ARIA harms accessibility.
How do you build responsive navigation in Angular?
CSS for layout plus BreakpointObserver to switch Material sidenav mode (over on mobile, side on desktop), a hamburger toggle, and routerLinkActive for the current page.
How do you test UI in Angular?
Component tests with TestBed and harnesses, axe for accessibility, visual regression snapshots, and Playwright/Cypress for end-to-end flows at multiple viewport sizes.

topics.name: Browser architecture, DOM and storage

beginner.content:
What is inside a browser?

Browser architecture: a browser is many parts working together: a rendering engine (turns HTML/CSS into pixels), a JavaScript engine (V8) with a single-threaded event loop, a networking layer, storage, and security sandboxing per tab/site. Your Angular app lives in one tab's sandbox.
• DOM APIs: the page is a tree of nodes you can find (querySelector) and modify. In Angular you rarely touch it directly: templates and bindings do the work.
• Window and Document: window is the global object (location, history, localStorage, innerWidth); document is the page (document.title, body).
• Storage choices: LocalStorage (stays until cleared), SessionStorage (until the tab closes), IndexedDB (big structured data), Cookies (sent to the server with every request).

intermediate.content:
Using storage properly in Angular

localStorage and sessionStorage: synchronous, string-only (use JSON.stringify), about 5 MB per origin, shared across tabs for local (the storage event notifies other tabs), blocks the main thread and is unavailable on the server (SSR) or throws in private mode / when disabled. Wrap it in a service with a try/catch and an in-memory fallback. IndexedDB: asynchronous, transactional, indexed, stores objects, blobs and files, hundreds of MB; use a wrapper like idb or Dexie. Cookies: sent automatically with requests to matching domain/path, 4 KB each; set by the server (Set-Cookie) or document.cookie.
Access globals the Angular way: inject DOCUMENT, and get window via DOCUMENT.defaultView, so code is testable and SSR-safe. Prefer Renderer2 or template bindings to DOM manipulation.

Cookie security

Cookie security attributes: HttpOnly (JavaScript cannot read it, protects against XSS theft), Secure (HTTPS only), SameSite=Strict|Lax|None (controls cross-site sending, main CSRF defence; None requires Secure), Path/Domain (scope as narrow as possible), Max-Age/Expires (short lifetimes for session cookies), and the __Host- prefix (forces Secure, Path=/, no Domain). Set auth cookies on the server; JavaScript-set cookies cannot be HttpOnly.

expert.content:
Trade-offs and pitfalls

StoreSizeLifetimeReadable by JSSent to server
Cookieabout 4 KBSession or expiryUnless HttpOnlyYes, automatically
localStorageabout 5 MBUntil clearedYesNo
sessionStorageabout 5 MBTab sessionYesNo
IndexedDBLarge (quota based)Until cleared/evictedYes (async)No

• Anything in web storage is readable by any script on the origin: never store secrets, long-lived tokens or sensitive personal data there unaccompanied by XSS defences (see security module). Encrypting in JavaScript does not help if the key sits beside the data.
• Storage is per origin (scheme + host + port); subdomains do not share localStorage. Browsers may evict data under storage pressure; request persistence with navigator.storage.persist() for important IndexedDB data. Safari limits script-writable storage (about 7 days of inactivity for some cases) under ITP.
• Always version stored data ({ v: 2, ... }) and handle migration or invalidation after deployments; validate on read because users and extensions can modify it. Use effect() to persist signals and read once at startup; synchronous large writes can jank, prefer IndexedDB for big data.
• Third-party cookie restrictions: cross-site cookies are increasingly blocked; keep API and app on the same site (or use proper SameSite/CORS credentials) to avoid surprises.
• SSR: localStorage and document.cookie do not exist on the server; read cookies from the request via the Angular SSR REQUEST token, and use storage only in the browser.
• Browser internals worth knowing: the event loop runs one task at a time; long synchronous JS blocks rendering and input (INP), so offload to workers and chunk work.

Choosing quickly

UI preference (theme, table columns): localStorage. Wizard draft for one tab: sessionStorage. Offline data and caches (PWA): IndexedDB. Authentication session: HttpOnly Secure SameSite cookie from the server. Server-only data: not in the browser at all.

interviewQA: LocalStorage vs SessionStorage vs Cookies?

localStorage persists across sessions for an origin; sessionStorage is scoped to a tab and cleared on close; cookies are small, can expire, and are automatically sent to the server with matching requests. Cookies can be HttpOnly, web storage cannot.
When would you use IndexedDB?
For large or structured data, offline-first apps, caching API results or files, since it is asynchronous, indexed and has far larger quota than localStorage.
Explain HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite.
HttpOnly hides the cookie from JavaScript; Secure sends it only over HTTPS; SameSite restricts cross-site sending (Lax/Strict) which mitigates CSRF.
Why is localStorage a bad place for secrets?
Any script running on the page, including injected XSS or compromised third-party code, can read it, and it persists indefinitely.
How do you handle storage in an SSR Angular app?
Never access localStorage on the server; guard with isPlatformBrowser or afterNextRender, use cookies via the request for server-visible state, and wrap storage in an injectable service.
What is the difference between window and document?
window is the global browser object (location, history, storage, size); document, a property of window, represents the loaded page DOM tree.

topics.name: Device and user-interaction APIs

beginner.content:
Talking to the device

Browsers expose powerful features through APIs, usually asking the user for permission first:
• Clipboard API: copy text with navigator.clipboard.writeText() (e.g. a "Copy link" button).
• Geolocation API: navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition() returns latitude and longitude after the user allows it.
• Notifications API: show a system notification after the user grants permission.
• File API: read files the user picked from an <input type="file"> without uploading them first.
• Drag and Drop API: native drag events, including dropping files onto your page.
codeExamples: @if (copied()) { Copied! }

intermediate.content:
Practical usage with Angular

Geolocation: wrap the callback API in a Promise/Observable; handle PERMISSION_DENIED, POSITION_UNAVAILABLE, TIMEOUT; use watchPosition for tracking and clear it on destroy. Notifications: ask in response to a user action, not on page load; Notification.requestPermission() then new Notification(title, options); background push uses Service Workers + Push API (Angular SwPush). File API: File and Blob, FileReader or the modern file.text()/arrayBuffer(), URL.createObjectURL for image previews (revoke afterwards). Validate type and size before upload (and again in Spring). Drag and Drop API: dragover (must preventDefault() to allow dropping), drop with event.dataTransfer.files; for in-app reordering prefer CDK drag and drop.
codeExamples: Drop files here

expert.content:
Pitfalls and design guidance

• Secure context: Clipboard, Geolocation, Notifications and Service Workers require HTTPS (localhost is exempt). Clipboard write needs a user gesture; clipboard.readText() prompts and is not available in all browsers (Firefox restricts it).
• Permission fatigue: request at the moment of need with an explanation (a pre-permission dialog) because a denied permission is hard to reverse (the user must change browser site settings, and you cannot prompt again).
• Geolocation is sensitive personal data: use the lowest accuracy that works, do not store it without consent, send it only over HTTPS, and handle denial gracefully with a manual alternative (type your city). iOS Safari requires a user gesture for notifications and supports web push only for installed web apps.
• File handling: never trust file.type or the name (they come from the client); validate with magic bytes server-side, limit size, scan for malware, and store outside the web root. Revoke object URLs (URL.revokeObjectURL) to avoid leaks. Big files: stream or chunk the upload, use HttpClient with reportProgress. The File System Access API (showOpenFilePicker) is Chromium-only.
• HTML5 DnD quirks: dragenter/dragleave fire on child elements (use a counter or pointer-events: none on children), the API is not touch-friendly and has poor accessibility; always provide a keyboard alternative (the file input, move up/down buttons).
• Test these APIs by injecting thin wrappers (CLIPBOARD token or service) so unit tests can substitute fakes; in zoneless apps ensure results are written to signals.

Wrap native APIs behind services

Create ClipboardService, GeolocationService, NotificationService with SSR-safe checks and typed results (Result = granted | denied | unsupported). Feature components then stay declarative and testable, and you can swap in CDK Clipboard (@angular/cdk/clipboard, with cdkCopyToClipboard) which has a fallback for older browsers.
codeExamples: <button [cdkCopyToClipboard]="inviteLink()">Copy invite</button>     <!-- CDK clipboard: no manual API calls -->

interviewQA: How do you copy text to the clipboard in Angular?
Use navigator.clipboard.writeText() in a click handler on HTTPS, or the CDK Clipboard service/cdkCopyToClipboard directive that includes a fallback; handle failure and give feedback.
What conditions apply to the Geolocation API?
It needs user permission and a secure context, returns async results or errors (denied, unavailable, timeout), and should be requested only when needed with a fallback.
How do you build an image upload preview with the File API?
Read the File from an input or drop event, validate type and size, create an object URL with URL.createObjectURL for the preview, revoke it later, and upload with FormData via HttpClient.
Why call preventDefault on dragover?
The default behaviour disallows dropping; cancelling dragover marks the element as a valid drop target so the drop event fires.
Why should you not trust file.type for uploads?
The MIME type and extension are client-supplied and can be forged; the server must validate content, size and name.

topics.name: Background work, live channels, history and observers

beginner.content:
Doing things in the background and watching the page

• Web Workers: extra threads for heavy computation so the page stays responsive, like hiring a helper for the long calculation.
• WebSockets: a persistent two-way line to the server (chat, live prices).
• Server-Sent Events (SSE): the server pushes updates one-way over normal HTTP (notifications, progress).
• History API: history.pushState changes the URL without reloading; the Angular Router uses it for you, and the browser Back button fires popstate.
• Intersection Observer: tells you when an element enters or leaves the viewport (lazy images, infinite scroll, animations on reveal).
• Resize Observer: tells you when an element's size changes (responsive charts).

intermediate.content:
Angular-friendly wrappers

Wrap observers in Observables so teardown is automatic, and run them outside the zone when they fire frequently. Use SSR guards: these APIs do not exist on the server.
codeExamples:
// history: Angular Router does this for you. Raw API, for reference:
history.pushState({ step: 2 }, '', '/wizard/2');              // add entry, no reload
window.addEventListener('popstate', e => console.log(e.state)); // user pressed Back/Forward
history.replaceState(null, '', '/wizard/3');                  // change URL without a new entry

intermediate.content:
Workers, sockets and SSE in use

Generate a worker with ng generate web-worker; post messages and receive results; terminate on destroy. For live data wrap WebSocket (or RxJS webSocket()) and EventSource in services exposing a signal or Observable, with reconnect and heartbeat. Detailed examples are in the Module 17 real-time lesson; here note browser rules: workers have no DOM or window (use self), data crosses by structured clone, and transferable objects (ArrayBuffer) move without copying.

expert.content:
Details and trade-offs

• Workers: dedicated (one page), shared (multiple tabs, limited support) and service workers (network proxy for PWAs, offline, push). Overhead of message passing means only worthwhile for tasks above roughly 50 ms. Module workers (type: 'module') are supported by the Angular build. Libraries like Comlink give RPC-style calls.
• WebSocket security: browsers do not apply CORS to WebSockets, so the server must validate the Origin header and authenticate the handshake (cookie or short-lived ticket in query; custom headers cannot be set from the browser API). Use wss://, limit message size, and re-authorize on reconnect. Backpressure is poor: slow consumers can accumulate memory.
• SSE: auto-reconnect and Last-Event-ID resume, text only, limited to about 6 connections per domain on HTTP/1.1 (fine on HTTP/2), no custom headers, so token in cookie. Proxies may buffer: disable buffering in Nginx (proxy_buffering off).
• History API: with PathLocationStrategy the server must return index.html for deep links (fallback rule); HashLocationStrategy avoids this but is ugly and bad for SEO. State objects must be serializable. Do not mix manual pushState with the Router; use Location/router.navigate with replaceUrl, skipLocationChange or state.
• IntersectionObserver is asynchronous and cheap compared with scroll handlers; options root, rootMargin, threshold. Disconnect when done. ResizeObserver callbacks can cause "ResizeObserver loop" warnings when you change layout inside the callback; batch with requestAnimationFrame. Both are browser-only (SSR guard) and not available in jsdom unless polyfilled in tests.
• Run high-frequency observer events outside Angular's zone or write results to signals so only affected views update.

Checklist

Cleanup everything (disconnect, close, terminate, remove listeners) on destroy; keep sockets and workers in services scoped as narrowly as needed; guard with isPlatformBrowser; handle offline and reconnection; test through wrapper services.

interviewQA: Why prefer IntersectionObserver over scroll listeners?
It runs asynchronously off the hot path, reports visibility changes without per-scroll layout reads, and is more efficient and simpler for lazy loading and infinite scroll.
What is the difference between a Web Worker and a Service Worker?

A Web Worker runs scripts in a background thread for computation tied to a page. A Service Worker is an event-driven proxy between app and network used for offline caching, push and background sync, living beyond a single page.
WebSocket or SSE for live notifications?
SSE for simple one-way server push (auto reconnect, plain HTTP). WebSocket for bidirectional, low-latency or binary communication. Mind auth: neither lets the browser set custom headers.
How does Angular Router relate to the History API?
The Router uses Location/PathLocationStrategy, which calls history.pushState and listens for popstate, so navigation updates the URL without reloading. The server needs a fallback to index.html.
How do you avoid leaks with observers and sockets?
Disconnect/close/terminate in ngOnDestroy or DestroyRef.onDestroy, or wrap them in Observables with teardown and use takeUntilDestroyed.

topics.name: Compatibility, permissions and secure API usage

beginner.content:
Not every browser is the same

Browser compatibility: a feature may exist in Chrome but not Safari or an older phone. The safe habit is feature detection (ask "does this exist?") rather than guessing by browser name. Check support tables (caniuse.com, MDN).
Browser permissions: sensitive features (camera, microphone, location, notifications, clipboard read) need the user's consent. The user can allow, block or ignore the prompt, and your code must cope with each.
Secure browser API usage: use these powers carefully: ask only when needed, send nothing sensitive over plain HTTP, and never trust data that came from the browser.

intermediate.content:
Compatibility toolchain and Permissions API

Angular targets "evergreen" browsers; the supported list is defined by .browserslistrc (and since v18 the CLI warns when the configuration is outside the supported matrix). The build transpiles syntax (not APIs), so missing APIs need polyfills (add to the polyfills array in angular.json, e.g. core-js modules, not the whole library). Test with BrowserStack/Playwright across Chromium, Firefox and WebKit. CSS: use @supports and autoprefixer (built in). Permissions API: navigator.permissions.query({ name }) returns granted | denied | prompt and a change event; not every name is supported in every browser (Safari partial), so wrap in try/catch.

Secure usage rules of thumb

Request permissions in context and explain why; degrade gracefully on denial; use the least-powerful API; keep everything on HTTPS; do not write secrets to storage, clipboard or logs; validate everything you read back from the browser (storage, URL, postMessage, files); revoke or stop resources (geolocation watch, media streams, object URLs) when done. For window.postMessage always check event.origin and use an exact target origin.

expert.content:
Defense in depth

• Permissions-Policy response header limits which features pages and iframes may use (Permissions-Policy: geolocation=(self), camera=(), microphone=()); iframe sandbox and allow attributes restrict embedded content. Combine with CSP.
• Secure contexts: many APIs are HTTPS-only. Use window.isSecureContext to check. Mixed content is blocked.
• Fingerprinting and privacy: avoid APIs that expose device details unnecessarily; honour Do Not Track/consent laws (GDPR cookie consent applies to non-essential storage). Document what you store and why.
• Third-party scripts run with full page privileges; use Subresource Integrity (integrity=) for CDN files, prefer self-hosting, and isolate untrusted widgets in sandboxed iframes.
• Input trust: location.search, hash fragments, document.referrer, storage and postMessage are all attacker-influenceable; sanitize before use and never feed them to innerHTML, eval or bypassSecurityTrust*.
• Compatibility policy: decide your support matrix with analytics (not assumptions), use progressive enhancement (core function without the fancy API), isolate API access behind services so fallbacks live in one place, and test fallbacks deliberately (disable the API in DevTools or stub it). Keep Angular, browserslist and polyfills updated; check release notes since Angular drops old browsers over time.
• Permission UX: store a "do not ask again" decision, never re-prompt in a loop, and make the feature work without the permission wherever possible.

Testing and observability

Use Playwright to grant or deny permissions per test (context.grantPermissions(['geolocation']), setGeolocation) and run the suite on Chromium, Firefox and WebKit. Log feature-support and permission outcomes (without personal data) to learn which fallbacks users actually hit.

interviewQA: How do you handle browser compatibility in Angular?
Define supported browsers in .browserslistrc, rely on feature detection with fallbacks, add targeted polyfills for missing APIs, and test across Chromium, Firefox and WebKit.
Feature detection vs browser sniffing?
Feature detection checks whether an API exists and works, which is reliable and future-proof. User-agent sniffing is brittle and often wrong.
What are good practices for browser permissions?
Ask in context after a user action with an explanation, handle granted, denied and dismissed states, provide fallbacks, do not re-prompt repeatedly, and use the Permissions API to read state.
How do you secure postMessage communication?
Verify event.origin against an allow-list, specify the exact target origin when sending, and validate the message payload.
What does a secure context mean?
A page served over HTTPS (or localhost) that unlocks powerful APIs like Clipboard, Geolocation and Service Workers; check with window.isSecureContext.
