expert.content:
How to use this module on a real project

• Treat the table as a definition of done: for a production application every row should be a conscious decision (done, deliberately skipped, or planned).
• Java developers: map each item to what you already know from Spring (profiles, filters, Maven, JUnit) and note only the Angular-specific differences.
• Some items are version dependent (Angular 17-20, Spring Boot 3, Spring Security 6); the lessons say so where it matters.

interviewQA: How should I use a module checklist?
As a definition of done: for each item decide whether it is implemented, deliberately skipped or planned, and revisit the list before every release.
Why group topics into lessons rather than learn them one by one?
Items interact (for example CORS, interceptors and JWT all appear in one login flow), so learning them together mirrors how they are used in a real application.
What versions does this module assume?
Modern Angular (v17-20, standalone components, signals, functional guards and interceptors) with Spring Boot 3 and Spring Security 6; version-specific APIs are flagged.

topics.name: Architecture, REST communication, CORS and environments

beginner.content:
Two programs, one conversation

Think of a restaurant. Angular is the dining room (what the customer sees, running in the browser). Spring Boot is the kitchen (business rules and the database). REST over HTTP is the waiter, and JSON is the order slip. They are built, tested and often deployed separately.
• Frontend-backend architecture: the browser downloads static files (HTML, JS, CSS) once, then Angular calls the API for data. The server never renders HTML (unlike JSP/Thymeleaf).
• Angular and Spring Boot integration in development: Angular on localhost:4200 (ng serve), Spring Boot on localhost:8080. Different ports mean different origins, which is why CORS matters.
• REST API communication: Angular HttpClient sends GET /api/employees; Spring returns JSON that Angular turns into typed objects.

intermediate.content:
CORS and the dev proxy

• CORS configuration (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing): the browser blocks Angular on :4200 from reading responses from :8080 unless the server sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin. Configure it once in Spring Security via a CorsConfigurationSource bean and enable it in the filter chain.
• Alternative in development: Angular's proxy forwards /api to :8080 so the browser sees a single origin and no CORS is needed at all.
• Never use allowedOrigins("*") together with allowCredentials(true); list the real origins.

Environment-specific configurations

• Angular: since v15.1 environments are not generated by default; run ng generate environments to create environment.ts (production) and environment.development.ts with fileReplacements in angular.json. Keep only the API base URL there, never secrets (everything in the bundle is public).
• Spring Boot: use profiles: application.yml plus application-dev.yml and application-prod.yml, activated with SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod. Secrets come from environment variables.

expert.content:
Preflight, credentials and the cleanest setup

• Non-simple requests (JSON body, Authorization header, PUT/DELETE) trigger an OPTIONS preflight. Spring's CORS support must run before authentication, otherwise preflights get 401. Using http.cors() in the filter chain guarantees that order; a @CrossOrigin annotation alone is not enough once Spring Security is present.
• The browser, not the server, enforces CORS: curl and Postman ignore it, so "works in Postman" proves nothing.
• Cookies across origins need allowCredentials(true), an explicit origin (no wildcard) and withCredentials: true on the Angular request, plus SameSite=None; Secure cookies.
• Best production design: serve Angular and the API under the same origin (Nginx routes / to files and /api to Spring). CORS then disappears, cookies are first-party and the setup is simpler to secure.
• Version notes: Spring Boot 3 requires Java 17+ and Jakarta (jakarta.*) packages; Angular environment handling above is v15.1+.

interviewQA: Why do I get a CORS error in the browser but not in Postman?
CORS is enforced by browsers only. The server must send Access-Control-Allow-Origin (and answer the OPTIONS preflight); Postman and curl do not check it.
What is a preflight request?
An automatic OPTIONS request the browser sends before a non-simple cross-origin request to ask whether the method and headers are allowed. Spring must answer it without requiring authentication.
How do you avoid CORS entirely?
Make the browser see one origin: use the Angular dev proxy in development and an Nginx reverse proxy (or a single Spring Boot jar serving the Angular files) in production.
How are environments handled in Angular and Spring Boot?
Angular uses environment files replaced at build time (or runtime config loaded at startup); Spring Boot uses profiles and environment variables. Secrets must never live in the Angular bundle.
Why is allowedOrigins("*") with credentials invalid?
The CORS spec forbids a wildcard when credentials are allowed; the server must echo a specific trusted origin.

topics.name: CRUD APIs, DTOs, service layer and error models

beginner.content:
CRUD end to end

CRUD = Create, Read, Update, Delete, mapped to POST, GET, PUT/PATCH, DELETE. In Spring Boot you write a controller (HTTP), a service (business rules) and a repository (database). In Angular you write a service that calls the controller and a component that shows the result.
• A DTO (Data Transfer Object) is the shape you promise to the frontend. Never expose JPA entities directly: you would leak columns, trigger lazy-loading errors and tie the API to the schema.
• JSON mapping: Jackson maps Java field names to JSON keys (camelCase by default, which matches TypeScript conventions).

intermediate.content:
The Angular service layer and generic models

• One Angular service layer class per resource keeps URLs, parameters and types in one place; components never call HttpClient directly.
• Generic API response models: define reusable generics once, Page<T> for paged results and ApiError for failures, so every service is typed without repetition. A generic base service removes CRUD duplication.
• API versioning: put the version in the URL (/api/v1/...) or a header; Angular reads the base from the environment so a v2 migration is a one-line change. Old mobile or cached Angular builds keep working against v1.

Error response handling

Make the server return one consistent error body using @RestControllerAdvice (Spring 6 also offers RFC 7807 ProblemDetail), then translate it in Angular, ideally in one error interceptor.

expert.content:
Contracts, mapping and drift

• Map entities to DTOs with MapStruct (compile-time, fast) rather than hand-written or reflection mappers; keep DTOs per use-case (create, update, summary, detail) so changing one screen does not break another.
• Dates travel as ISO-8601 strings: configure Jackson (spring.jackson.serialization.write-dates-as-timestamps=false) and treat them as strings in TypeScript, converting with DatePipe. Money should be a string or integer minor units to avoid floating-point issues; BigDecimal serialises as a JSON number which JavaScript parses as a double.
• To stop frontend and backend models drifting, generate the TypeScript client from the OpenAPI spec (see the OpenAPI lesson) instead of writing interfaces by hand.
• Avoid returning 200 with an error payload; use correct status codes (201, 204, 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 422, 500). Angular's HttpClient only throws on non-2xx, so status discipline makes catchError work.
• Version policy: additive changes (new optional fields) are backward compatible; renames or removals need a new version. Keep two versions alive during rollout.

interviewQA: Why use DTOs instead of returning entities?
DTOs decouple the API contract from the database model, avoid leaking fields and lazy-loading/serialization problems, and let each use case expose only what it needs.
What does a generic Page<T> model give you?
One typed shape for every paged endpoint; it mirrors Spring Data Page JSON (content, totalElements, number, size) so services and tables are reusable.
How do you return consistent errors from Spring Boot?
Use @RestControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler methods (or ProblemDetail) producing one body with status, message, path and field errors.
How do you version an API consumed by Angular?
Put the version in the URL (/api/v1) or a header, read it from Angular environment config, keep old versions running during migration and only break contracts in a new version.
Why have a service layer in Angular instead of calling HttpClient in components?
It centralizes URLs, typing and error mapping, makes components easy to test with a mock service and lets you change the API without touching the UI.

topics.name: Pagination, search, validation and file transfer

beginner.content:
Big lists, forms and files

• Pagination and sorting: never send 100,000 rows. The client asks for page=0&size=10&sort=name,asc; Spring Data answers with one page plus totals.
• Search and filtering: optional query parameters (?q=ann&department=IT) handled on the server, because only the server sees all the data. In Angular, wait for the user to stop typing (debounce).
• Form validation on frontend and backend: the frontend validates for speed and friendliness; the backend validates because users (or attackers) can bypass the browser. Both are required.
• File upload and download: files travel as multipart/form-data (upload) and as binary blobs (download).

intermediate.content:
Debounced search, validation mirror and file handling

Combine a reactive form control with debounceTime, distinctUntilChanged and switchMap so every keystroke does not hit the server and stale responses are cancelled. For validation on both sides, use the same rules in Validators and in Bean Validation annotations, and display server fieldErrors on the matching control.

expert.content:
Pitfalls and best practices

• Pagination: offset paging (page/size) gets slow on huge tables; use keyset (cursor) pagination for feeds. Whitelist sortable fields on the server to avoid injection through sort parameters. Spring Boot caps size (default max 2000); set spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size. Note Spring Data 3.3+ recommends PagedModel/@EnableSpringDataWebSupport(pageSerializationMode = VIA_DTO) because the raw PageImpl JSON structure is not guaranteed stable.
• Dynamic filters: use Specifications or Querydsl instead of string concatenation; always parameterised queries.
• Validation: never trust client validation; also validate request params with @Validated, and return 422/400 with field errors. Custom cross-field rules need a class-level constraint.
• Files: validate type by content (not just extension or Content-Type), limit size (spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size), store outside the web root, generate your own file names (path traversal), and consider S3-style object storage plus virus scanning. Large downloads should stream.
• Upload progress: with observe: 'events' check HttpEventType.UploadProgress to draw a progress bar.

interviewQA: How does Angular tell Spring Boot which page to return?
It sends page, size and sort query parameters (HttpParams); Spring MVC resolves them into a Pageable that Spring Data applies in the query.
Why debounce a search box?
To avoid one request per keystroke; combined with switchMap the in-flight stale request is cancelled so only the latest term updates the UI.
Why validate on both frontend and backend?
Frontend validation gives instant feedback; backend validation is the security boundary because requests can be crafted without the UI.
How do you upload a file from Angular to Spring Boot?
Send FormData with HttpClient.post (no manual Content-Type) and receive it as @RequestParam MultipartFile; limit size and validate the file server-side.
How do you download a file with Angular?
Request with responseType blob, create an object URL, click a temporary anchor with the download attribute and revoke the URL.

topics.name: Spring Security, JWT, refresh tokens and roles

beginner.content:
Who are you, and what may you do?

• Authentication = proving who you are (login). Authorization = what you are allowed to do (roles).
• Spring Security integration: a filter chain in front of every controller. For a single-page app the API is stateless: no server session, each request carries a token.
• JWT authentication: after login the server returns a signed JSON Web Token (header.payload.signature). Angular stores it and sends Authorization: Bearer <token> on every call. Think of it as a signed wristband at a festival: staff check the signature, not a guest list.
• The payload is only encoded, not encrypted: never put passwords or secrets in it.

intermediate.content:
Stateless Spring Security 6 with a JWT filter

The filter reads the header, validates the signature and expiry, and puts an Authentication with authorities into the SecurityContext. Use a maintained library (Nimbus via spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server is the simplest way to validate JWTs) instead of hand-rolling crypto.

Refresh token design and role-based authorization

• Access token: short life (10-15 min), kept in memory in Angular. Refresh token: long life, in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie and rotated on each use (the old one is invalidated; reuse of an old one means theft, so revoke the family).
• On 401 the Angular interceptor calls /auth/refresh once, queues parallel requests, retries them with the new token, and logs out if refresh fails.
• Role-based authorization: roles go into a claim; Spring enforces with @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')") (enable @EnableMethodSecurity); Angular only hides UI and blocks routes with guards.

expert.content:
Token storage trade-offs and hardening

• localStorage tokens are readable by any XSS; HttpOnly cookies are immune to JS theft but need CSRF defence (SameSite=Strict/Lax, or a CSRF token with Angular's withXsrfConfiguration and Spring CookieCsrfTokenRepository). A common compromise: access token in memory, refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie.
• Use asymmetric keys (RS256/ES256) when several services validate tokens; HS256 needs a secret of at least 256 bits from the environment. Always check exp, iss, aud; reject alg: none. Keep a small clock-skew allowance.
• Store refresh tokens hashed in the database with user, device, expiry and revoked flag, to support logout-all and reuse detection. Logout must revoke the refresh token server side; deleting the browser copy is not enough. Access tokens cannot be revoked before expiry, which is why they are short.
• Do not decode the JWT in Angular to make security decisions; decode only for display (name, roles). Guards and hidden buttons are UX; every endpoint must enforce authorization itself.
• Version note: Spring Security 6 removed WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter; use SecurityFilterChain beans and the lambda DSL. For enterprise SSO consider OAuth2/OIDC (Keycloak, Auth0) with the Authorization Code + PKCE flow instead of custom login.

interviewQA: How does JWT authentication work between Angular and Spring Boot?
The login endpoint returns a signed token; Angular sends it in the Authorization header via an interceptor; a Spring filter validates the signature and expiry and sets the security context.
Why use both access and refresh tokens?
The short-lived access token limits damage if stolen; the refresh token lets users stay logged in without re-entering credentials and can be rotated and revoked server-side.
Where should the JWT be stored in the browser?
No option is perfect: localStorage is exposed to XSS, HttpOnly cookies need CSRF protection. A good pattern is access token in memory and refresh token in an HttpOnly Secure SameSite cookie.
Are Angular route guards enough for authorization?
No. Guards only improve UX; the Spring Boot API must enforce roles itself with authorizeHttpRequests or @PreAuthorize.
What is refresh token rotation?
Each refresh issues a new refresh token and invalidates the old one; if an old token is reused, the server treats it as theft and revokes the whole token family.
Why can CSRF be disabled for a bearer-token API?
Browsers do not attach Authorization headers automatically, so cross-site forms cannot forge authenticated requests; with cookie-based auth CSRF protection must stay on.

topics.name: Database, OpenAPI, testing and production

beginner.content:
Data, docs, tests and going live

• Database-backed applications: Spring Data JPA turns Java entities into tables; the API reads and writes through repositories. Angular never sees the database.
• PostgreSQL/MySQL integration through Spring Boot: add the driver dependency and a few spring.datasource.* properties; Hibernate does the rest.
• API documentation with OpenAPI: springdoc-openapi produces a live Swagger UI at /swagger-ui.html from your controllers.
• Integration testing: test controller plus database together instead of mocks only.
• Production deployment and end-to-end security testing: build both apps, put Nginx in front, then try to break your own login and roles.
codeExamples:
# application-dev.yml (PostgreSQL)
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/hrdb
    username: hr_user
    password: change-me-in-env        # real password comes from env var SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD
  jpa:
    hibernate.ddl-auto: validate      # never 'update' in production; use Flyway migrations
    open-in-view: false
# MySQL: url jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/hrdb and driver com.mysql:mysql-connector-j

// pom.xml additions
// org.postgresql:postgresql, org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-data-jpa,
// org.flywaydb:flyway-core, org.springdoc:springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui

intermediate.content:
Entities, migrations, OpenAPI client and tests

Use Flyway or Liquibase for versioned schema scripts, keep entities out of controllers (DTOs), and test with a real database via Testcontainers. Generate Angular clients from the OpenAPI spec so the contract cannot drift.
codeExamples:
# generate a typed Angular client from the spec (run once per API change)
npx @openapitools/openapi-generator-cli generate -i http://localhost:8080/v3/api-docs -g typescript-angular -o src/app/api
# alternatives: ng-openapi-gen, orval

expert.content:
Production deployment and security testing

• Deployment shape: (a) Nginx serves dist/app/browser and proxies /api to the Spring Boot jar (best separation, same origin); (b) copy the Angular build into src/main/resources/static of the jar (one artifact, simplest, but redeploys everything and needs a forwarding controller for deep links); (c) separate hosts plus CORS. Details are in Module 24.
• Production checklist: ddl-auto=validate, Flyway on, server.forward-headers-strategy=framework behind a proxy, actuator health endpoint for probes, secrets from env or a vault, connection pool sized (HikariCP), HTTPS only, springdoc disabled or protected in prod.
• End-to-end security testing checklist: call every endpoint without a token (expect 401), with a user token on admin routes (403), with an expired and a tampered token, with another user's id (IDOR / broken object-level authorization), with oversized and malicious payloads (validation, SQL injection through filters), check CORS from a disallowed origin, refresh token reuse, logout revocation, response headers (CSP, HSTS), and run OWASP ZAP or Burp plus Playwright/Cypress flows for the login journey. Add @WebMvcTest security slices for authorization rules so they run in CI.
• Do not rely on Angular tests to prove security: security is proved against the running API.

interviewQA: What do you need to connect Spring Boot to PostgreSQL or MySQL?
The JDBC driver dependency, spring.datasource url/username/password, JPA/Hibernate settings and ideally Flyway migrations; the database dialect is auto-detected in Spring Boot 3.
Why not use ddl-auto=update in production?
It changes the schema unpredictably and cannot be reviewed or rolled back; use versioned migrations (Flyway/Liquibase) with ddl-auto=validate.
How does OpenAPI help the Angular team?
springdoc exposes the spec and Swagger UI for exploration, and the spec can generate typed Angular clients so frontend models always match the API.
How do you integration test a Spring Boot API?
Use @SpringBootTest with MockMvc and a Testcontainers database, plus @WithMockUser or real tokens to exercise security rules.
Name tests you would run for end-to-end security.
Missing/expired/tampered tokens, role escalation, accessing another user's resources, CORS from a foreign origin, refresh reuse, input fuzzing and a ZAP scan, in addition to UI journey tests.

beginner.content:

intermediate.content:
Suggested study order

• Lesson 1: Builds, configuration and secrets

Read each lesson in three passes: the Basic tab for the idea, the Intermediate tab to write the code yourself, and the Expert tab for pitfalls and version notes. Then answer the interview questions aloud.

expert.content:
How to use this module on a real project

• Treat the table as a definition of done: for a production application every row should be a conscious decision (done, deliberately skipped, or planned).
• Java developers: map each item to what you already know from Spring (profiles, filters, Maven, JUnit) and note only the Angular-specific differences.
• Some items are version dependent (Angular 17-20, Spring Boot 3, Spring Security 6); the lessons say so where it matters.

interviewQA: How should I use a module checklist?
As a definition of done: for each item decide whether it is implemented, deliberately skipped or planned, and revisit the list before every release.
Why group topics into lessons rather than learn them one by one?
Items interact (for example CORS, interceptors and JWT all appear in one login flow), so learning them together mirrors how they are used in a real application.
What versions does this module assume?
Modern Angular (v17-20, standalone components, signals, functional guards and interceptors) with Spring Boot 3 and Spring Security 6; version-specific APIs are flagged.

topics.name: Builds, configuration and secrets

beginner.content:
Development build versus production build

• The Angular development build (ng serve or ng build --configuration development) is quick to produce: no minification, source maps on, readable code.
• The production build (ng build, since v12 the default configuration) does ahead-of-time compilation, tree-shaking, minification, and adds a content hash to file names (main-A1B2C3.js) so browsers cache safely. Output goes to dist/<project>/browser (v17+ application builder).
• Analogy: development is a rough draft with notes in the margin; production is the printed, proofread book.
codeExamples:
# build commands
ng build --configuration development     # fast, source maps, no optimization
ng build                                  # production (default configuration)
ls dist/my-app/browser                    # index.html, main-HASH.js, styles-HASH.css, media/

intermediate.content:
Build configuration, environments and runtime config

• Build configuration lives in angular.json under configurations: budgets (fail the build if bundles grow), optimization, outputHashing, fileReplacements. You can add staging next to production.
• Environment configuration is baked in at build time (a new build per environment). Simple, but you ship different artifacts, so what you tested is not what you deploy.
• Runtime configuration: build once, load /assets/config.json (or /config.json) before the app starts with provideAppInitializer (v19+; APP_INITIALIZER earlier). The deploy step just writes a different JSON file. This gives true "build once, promote everywhere".

expert.content:
Secrets, artifacts and traceability

• Environment variables and secret management: anything in the Angular bundle (environment files, config.json) is public. Put only non-secret values there (API URL, public client IDs). Real secrets (DB passwords, JWT signing keys, third-party API keys) live in the backend, injected from the CI secret store, Docker/Kubernetes secrets or a vault (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager). If the frontend needs a third-party key, proxy the call through your backend.
• Node-time variables (e.g. NG_BUILD_..., API URL passed to a script that generates environment.ts) exist only during the CI build; they are not runtime variables in the browser.
• Build artifact management: build once in CI, name the artifact with version and commit SHA (app-1.8.2-3f9c1ab.tgz or a Docker image tag), store it (GitHub Actions artifacts, Nexus/Artifactory, container registry) and promote the same artifact dev, staging, production. Never rebuild for production. Keep the last N versions for rollback and keep the source maps privately (upload to the error tracker, do not serve them publicly).
• Cache correctness: index.html must be no-cache while hashed JS/CSS can be cached for a year (immutable). Version notes: Angular 17+ default application builder (esbuild + Vite) replaces the webpack browser builder; output moved to dist/<app>/browser.

interviewQA: What is the difference between a development and production Angular build?
Development keeps code readable with source maps for fast rebuilds; production applies AOT, tree-shaking, minification, hashing and budgets for small, cacheable bundles.
Environment files versus runtime configuration?
Environment files are replaced at build time so you need one build per environment; runtime configuration loads a JSON at startup so one build can be promoted everywhere.
Where do secrets belong in an Angular project?
Not in Angular at all: the bundle is public. Keep secrets in the backend and CI/server secret stores, and expose only non-secret config to the browser.
What are build budgets?
Size limits in angular.json that warn or fail the build when bundles or component styles grow beyond a threshold.
Why version and store build artifacts?
To deploy exactly what was tested, trace production back to a commit and roll back by redeploying a previous artifact.

topics.name: Static hosting, Ubuntu, Nginx, DNS and HTTPS

beginner.content:
Angular is just files

Hosting static Angular applications is easy because after ng build you only have HTML, JS, CSS and images. Any web server (Nginx, Apache, S3 plus CloudFront, Netlify, GitHub Pages, Firebase Hosting) can serve them. The one special rule: for a single-page app, unknown URLs like /employees/5 must return index.html, otherwise a browser refresh shows 404.
Ubuntu server basics you need: connect with ssh user@server, update with sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade, install software with apt install, manage services with systemctl, open ports with ufw, and keep files owned by the right user.
codeExamples:
# first steps on an Ubuntu server
ssh deploy@203.0.113.10
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y nginx ufw
sudo ufw allow OpenSSH && sudo ufw allow "Nginx Full" && sudo ufw enable
sudo systemctl status nginx
sudo mkdir -p /var/www/myapp && sudo chown deploy:deploy /var/www/myapp
scp -r dist/my-app/browser/* deploy@203.0.113.10:/var/www/myapp/

intermediate.content:
Nginx configuration and reverse proxy

• Nginx configuration is a server block per site in /etc/nginx/sites-available (symlinked into sites-enabled). try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html is the SPA fallback.
• Reverse proxy fundamentals: Nginx accepts the browser request and forwards /api/ to Spring Boot on localhost:8080, then returns the answer. The browser sees one origin (no CORS), Spring Boot is not exposed to the internet and Nginx handles TLS, compression and caching.

Domain, DNS and HTTPS

• Domain and DNS configuration: at your registrar create an A record (app.example.com to the server IPv4), an AAAA record for IPv6 and a CNAME for aliases (www to app). Propagation can take minutes to hours; check with dig app.example.com or nslookup. Lower the TTL before a migration.
• HTTPS and SSL certificates: use Let's Encrypt through certbot; it edits the Nginx config, adds a 301 redirect from HTTP and renews automatically (check sudo certbot renew --dry-run). Modern features (service workers, geolocation, clipboard, secure cookies) require HTTPS.

expert.content:
Production Nginx details that bite

• Add proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto and set server.forward-headers-strategy=framework in Spring Boot, otherwise redirects and absolute links come out as http:// behind the proxy.
• Do not apply the SPA fallback to /api: a missing API route must stay a real 404 JSON, and missing static assets (.js) should return 404 rather than index.html, or a stale tab loads HTML as JavaScript and shows a confusing syntax error after a deploy.
• Raise client_max_body_size for uploads (default 1 MB), tune proxy_read_timeout for slow endpoints, use http2 on, enable Brotli if available, and add HSTS (Strict-Transport-Security) once HTTPS is stable.
• For SSE and WebSockets add proxy_http_version 1.1, Upgrade/Connection headers and proxy_buffering off.
• Prefer a non-root deploy user with key-based SSH, PasswordAuthentication no, fail2ban and automatic security updates (unattended-upgrades). A CDN in front gives global caching and DDoS absorption.
• Subpath hosting (/app/) needs ng build --base-href /app/ and a matching location block.

interviewQA: Why does refreshing /employees/5 give 404 on a static server?
The server looks for a file at that path. An SPA needs a fallback (try_files ... /index.html) so Angular's router handles the URL.
What does a reverse proxy do for an Angular plus Spring Boot app?
It serves static files, forwards /api to Spring Boot, terminates TLS and compresses/caches responses; the browser sees one origin so CORS is unnecessary.
Which DNS records do you need to publish a site?
An A record (IPv4) and optionally AAAA (IPv6) to the server, and CNAME records for aliases such as www.
How do you get free HTTPS?
Install certbot, run it with the Nginx plugin to get a Let's Encrypt certificate, redirect HTTP to HTTPS and rely on the auto-renew timer.
How should hashed assets and index.html be cached?
Hashed JS/CSS can use a very long immutable cache; index.html must be no-cache so users get new hash references after each deploy.

topics.name: Git, GitHub workflows, Jenkins and CI/CD

beginner.content:
From laptop to server without hands

• Deployment automation: replace "copy files by hand" with a repeatable pipeline. Same steps, same order, every time.
• Git fundamentals: a commit is a snapshot; a branch is a moving label; merge or rebase combines work; a pull request is a reviewed merge. Basic loop: git switch -c feature/login, git add, git commit, git push, open a PR.
• CI/CD pipelines: CI (continuous integration) builds and tests every push; CD (delivery/deployment) ships the passing build to an environment. Analogy: an assembly line with quality checks at every station.
codeExamples:
git clone https://github.com/acme/hr-portal.git
git switch -c feature/employee-search     # new branch
git add src/app/employee && git commit -m "feat: employee search with debounce"
git push -u origin feature/employee-search
git fetch origin && git rebase origin/main  # keep history linear before the PR
git tag v1.4.0 && git push --tags            # tag a release

intermediate.content:
GitHub workflows

A workflow is a YAML file in .github/workflows. Jobs run on runners; steps use actions (actions/checkout, actions/setup-node) or shell commands. Secrets are referenced as GitHub expressions and are masked in logs. Use npm ci (reproducible installs from the lock file) and cache npm.
codeExamples:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: ci
on:
  push: { branches: [main] }
  pull_request:
jobs:
  build-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 20, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npx ng test --watch=false --browsers=ChromeHeadless
      - run: npx ng build
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with: { name: dist, path: dist/my-app/browser }
  deploy:
    needs: build-test
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with: { name: dist, path: dist }
      - name: Copy to server
        uses: appleboy/scp-action@v0.1.7
        with:
          host: ${{ secrets.SSH_HOST }}
          username: ${{ secrets.SSH_USER }}
          key: ${{ secrets.SSH_KEY }}
          source: dist/*
          target: /var/www/myapp-new

intermediate.content:
Jenkins fundamentals

Jenkins is a self-hosted automation server. A Jenkinsfile in the repository defines a declarative pipeline of stages; credentials are stored in Jenkins and bound with withCredentials. Use it when you must stay on-premises or already run Jenkins; for new projects GitHub Actions or GitLab CI is lighter to maintain.

expert.content:
Designing a trustworthy pipeline

• Order stages fast-to-slow: install, lint, unit tests, build, e2e, publish artifact, deploy. Fail early. Run Angular unit tests in headless Chrome (Karma ChromeHeadlessCI with --no-sandbox in containers) or your project's runner (Jest/Vitest); testing tools vary by version.
• Build once, then deploy the same artifact to staging and production, with a manual approval gate before production (GitHub environments with required reviewers, Jenkins input step).
• Deploy atomically: upload to a new release folder, then switch a current symlink (see rollback lesson) so users never see a half-copied site.
• Branching: trunk-based with short-lived branches and feature flags tends to beat long-lived develop branches. Protect main (required checks, reviews, no force-push). Use conventional commits and semantic-release for automatic versioning if desired.
• Security: pin actions to a version or SHA, use least-privilege GITHUB_TOKEN permissions, store secrets only in the secret store, use OIDC to cloud providers instead of long-lived keys, scan dependencies (npm audit, Dependabot, Trivy for images), and never print secrets.
• Speed: cache ~/.npm, parallelise jobs (lint, unit tests, backend tests), and use Nx or Turborepo affected-only builds in monorepos. Backend (Spring Boot) gets its own parallel job: ./mvnw verify.

interviewQA: What is the difference between CI and CD?
CI builds and tests every change automatically; CD delivers (or deploys) the passing build to an environment, optionally after approval.
Why use npm ci instead of npm install in a pipeline?
It installs exactly what package-lock.json specifies, fails on mismatches and is faster and reproducible.
Merge versus rebase?
Merge preserves history with a merge commit; rebase replays your commits on top of the target branch for a linear history. Never rebase shared public branches.
GitHub Actions or Jenkins?
Actions is hosted, YAML-based and integrated with GitHub; Jenkins is self-hosted, highly extensible and suits on-prem constraints but needs maintenance.
How do you keep secrets safe in a pipeline?
Use the platform secret store or OIDC, reference secrets only in steps that need them, restrict who can trigger deploys and never echo them or bake them into artifacts.
What is a good deployment gate?
Passing lint, tests and build on main, then a manual approval for production with the same artifact that passed staging.

topics.name: Docker, Compose, containers and cloud

beginner.content:
Ship the whole kitchen, not just the recipe

• Docker fundamentals: an image is a read-only package of an app plus its runtime; a container is a running instance; a registry (Docker Hub, GHCR, ECR) stores images; layers are cached so rebuilds are fast. "Works on my machine" becomes "works in the container".
• Dockerizing Angular applications: a multi-stage build: stage 1 uses Node to run ng build; stage 2 copies only the static output into a tiny Nginx image. The final image has no Node and no source code.
codeExamples:
# Dockerfile (Angular)
FROM node:20-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci                      # cached layer unless package files change
COPY . .
RUN npx ng build

FROM nginx:1.27-alpine
COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
COPY --from=build /app/dist/my-app/browser /usr/share/nginx/html
EXPOSE 80
# build and run:  docker build -t hr-web:1.0.0 .   then   docker run -p 8080:80 hr-web:1.0.0

# .dockerignore
node_modules
dist
.git
.angular

intermediate.content:
Docker Compose and container deployment

Docker Compose describes several containers in one YAML file: Angular/Nginx, Spring Boot and PostgreSQL, with a private network, volumes for data, health checks and environment variables from an .env file (not committed). Container deployment on a single server: CI pushes ghcr.io/acme/hr-web:1.4.0, the server runs docker compose pull && docker compose up -d.
codeExamples:
# docker-compose.yml
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: hrdb
      POSTGRES_USER: hr_user
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE: /run/secrets/db_password
    secrets: [db_password]
    volumes: [dbdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data]
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U hr_user -d hrdb"]
      interval: 10s
  api:
    image: ghcr.io/acme/hr-api:1.4.0
    environment:
      SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: prod
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/hrdb
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME: hr_user
    depends_on:
      db: { condition: service_healthy }
    restart: unless-stopped
  web:
    image: ghcr.io/acme/hr-web:1.4.0
    ports: ["80:80"]
    depends_on: [api]
    restart: unless-stopped
volumes: { dbdata: {} }
secrets:
  db_password: { file: ./secrets/db_password.txt }

# Spring Boot image (Dockerfile.api) - layered, non-root
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
RUN useradd -r app
USER app
COPY target/hr-api.jar /app/hr-api.jar
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/app/hr-api.jar"]

intermediate.content:
Cloud hosting fundamentals

• IaaS (a VM such as EC2, a droplet): you manage the OS. PaaS/containers (Azure App Service, Cloud Run, Elastic Beanstalk, Render, Fly.io): you provide an app or image. Kubernetes (EKS, AKS, GKE): many services at scale.
• Typical low-cost layout: Angular static files on object storage plus a CDN (S3 + CloudFront, Azure Static Web Apps, Firebase Hosting, Netlify); Spring Boot in a container; managed database (RDS, Cloud SQL) with automated backups; secrets in the provider vault; a load balancer with TLS.
• Think about regions, scaling, cost, and shared responsibility (you secure your app and data, the provider secures hardware).

expert.content:
Container best practices and pitfalls

• Pin base image versions (not latest), run as a non-root user (nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged), keep images small (alpine/distroless), scan with Trivy or Docker Scout and rebuild regularly for patches.
• Order Dockerfile layers by change frequency (package files before source) for cache hits; use BuildKit cache mounts for npm. Never copy .env or secrets into images: image layers are readable by anyone with the image.
• Runtime config in containers: generate config.json at container start from environment variables with an entrypoint script (envsubst) so the same image runs in every environment.
• Add a HEALTHCHECK, graceful shutdown (Spring server.shutdown=graceful), resource limits and log to stdout/stderr, not files. The database must use a named volume and must not be exposed publicly. In Compose, depends_on with service_healthy only orders startup; the app still needs DB retry logic.
• Zero-downtime on one host: run two replicas behind Nginx, or use blue/green with a proxy switch; on Kubernetes use rolling updates with readiness probes.
• Angular SSR images need Node at runtime (node dist/app/server/server.mjs), unlike the static Nginx image above.

interviewQA: Why a multi-stage Docker build for Angular?
The Node build stage compiles the app; only the static output is copied into a small Nginx image, so the final image is small, fast and contains no build tools or source.
Image versus container?
An image is an immutable template with the app and its dependencies; a container is a running instance of an image.
What does Docker Compose add?
It defines and runs multi-container applications (web, API, database) with networks, volumes, environment and health checks from a single file.
How do you handle secrets with Docker?
Keep them out of images and source: use Docker/Compose secrets, orchestrator secrets or environment injection at runtime from a vault.
How would you host Angular plus Spring Boot in the cloud cheaply?
Angular static files on object storage with a CDN, Spring Boot as a container on a PaaS, and a managed PostgreSQL with backups.

topics.name: Operations: monitoring, rollback, backup and hardening

beginner.content:
Keeping it running

• Logging and monitoring: logs say what happened (Nginx access/error logs, Spring Boot application logs), monitoring says how healthy it is now (uptime, CPU, memory, response times). Start with tail -f /var/log/nginx/error.log and docker logs -f api; add Spring Boot Actuator /actuator/health and an uptime checker.
• Error monitoring: browser errors never reach your server logs unless you send them. Tools like Sentry capture exceptions with stack traces (readable through uploaded source maps).
• Rollback strategies: the ability to go back to the previous working version within minutes.
• Versioned deployments: every release has a version number and its own folder or image tag.
• Backup and recovery: copies of the database, regularly, stored elsewhere, and tested by restoring.

intermediate.content:
Release folders, rollback and backup scripts

Deploy each release into /var/www/myapp/releases/<version> and point Nginx at the current symlink. Rolling back is re-pointing the symlink (instant); keep the last five releases. With Docker, roll back by redeploying the previous image tag. Backups use pg_dump from cron with retention and an off-server copy.
codeExamples:
#!/bin/bash
# deploy.sh - atomic release with instant rollback
set -euo pipefail
VERSION=$1
BASE=/var/www/myapp
mkdir -p $BASE/releases/$VERSION
tar -xzf /tmp/app-$VERSION.tgz -C $BASE/releases/$VERSION
ln -sfn $BASE/releases/$VERSION $BASE/current      # nginx root is /var/www/myapp/current
sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl reload nginx
ls -1dt $BASE/releases/* | tail -n +6 | xargs -r rm -rf   # keep the last 5

# rollback.sh
PREV=$(ls -1dt /var/www/myapp/releases/* | sed -n 2p)
ln -sfn $PREV /var/www/myapp/current && echo "rolled back to $PREV"

# backup.sh (cron: 0 2 * * *)
pg_dump -U hr_user -h localhost hrdb | gzip > /backups/hrdb-$(date +%F).sql.gz
find /backups -name "*.sql.gz" -mtime +14 -delete
# restore test: gunzip -c hrdb-2025-01-10.sql.gz | psql -U hr_user -h localhost hrdb_restore

expert.content:
Troubleshooting runbook and hardening

Production troubleshooting go layer by layer: (1) does DNS resolve (dig)? (2) is the port reachable and TLS valid (curl -vI https://...)? (3) Nginx up and config valid (nginx -t, error log)? (4) is the right release deployed (version endpoint, current symlink, image tag)? (5) API health and logs (/actuator/health, correlation id)? (6) database connectivity and disk space (df -h)? (7) browser: Network tab status codes, Console errors, stale cache or service worker? Typical culprits: SPA fallback missing, old cached index.html referencing deleted hashed files, CORS/mixed content, expired certificate, wrong environment config, out-of-memory kills.
Security hardening:
• Send headers: Strict-Transport-Security, Content-Security-Policy, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, and frame protection via CSP frame-ancestors. Hide the Nginx version (server_tokens off).
• Expose only 80/443 (and SSH from known IPs); database and Spring Boot listen on localhost or a private network. SSH keys only, no root login, fail2ban, automatic security updates.
• Least privilege for service accounts and database users; rate-limit login routes (limit_req); rotate secrets; keep dependencies patched (npm audit, Dependabot).
• Monitoring in production: structured JSON logs with request ids, Actuator plus Prometheus/Grafana for metrics, alerts on error rate, latency, disk and certificate expiry, and Real User Monitoring for Core Web Vitals.
• Recovery objectives: define RPO (how much data you can lose) and RTO (how long you can be down), rehearse restores, and store backups in another region or provider, encrypted.

interviewQA: How do you roll back an Angular deployment?
Keep immutable versioned releases and switch the current symlink (or redeploy the previous image tag); keep the previous artifact available and make database migrations backward compatible.
Why do users see a blank page or JS errors right after a deploy?

A cached index.html references hashed files that no longer exist (or the fallback returns index.html for missing JS). Serve index.html with no-cache, keep old assets for a while and return real 404s for missing assets.
What belongs in a backup strategy?
Automated scheduled database dumps or snapshots, retention, off-site encrypted copies, defined RPO/RTO and periodic restore tests.
How do you monitor frontend errors?
Install a global ErrorHandler that reports to a tool such as Sentry, tagged with the release and with source maps uploaded privately.
Name key hardening steps for the server.
Open only 80/443, SSH keys and no root login, security headers (HSTS, CSP), hidden server version, rate limiting, patching, least-privilege accounts and secrets from a vault.
What is your first step debugging "site is down"?
Work through layers: DNS, TLS/port, proxy status and logs, deployed version, API health, database/disk, then the browser console and network tab.

Suggested study order

Read each lesson in three passes: the Basic tab for the idea, the Intermediate tab to write the code yourself, and the Expert tab for pitfalls and version notes. Then answer the interview questions aloud.

expert.content:
How to use this module on a real project

• Treat the table as a definition of done: for a production application every row should be a conscious decision (done, deliberately skipped, or planned).
• Java developers: map each item to what you already know from Spring (profiles, filters, Maven, JUnit) and note only the Angular-specific differences.
• Some items are version dependent (Angular 17-20, Spring Boot 3, Spring Security 6); the lessons say so where it matters.

interviewQA: How should I use a module checklist?
As a definition of done: for each item decide whether it is implemented, deliberately skipped or planned, and revisit the list before every release.
Why group topics into lessons rather than learn them one by one?
Items interact (for example CORS, interceptors and JWT all appear in one login flow), so learning them together mirrors how they are used in a real application.
What versions does this module assume?
Modern Angular (v17-20, standalone components, signals, functional guards and interceptors) with Spring Boot 3 and Spring Security 6; version-specific APIs are flagged.

topics.name: Angular CLI: creating projects and generating code

beginner.content:
The ng command is your power tool

The Angular CLI is a command-line program (npm install -g @angular/cli). Like Maven archetypes plus code generators for Java: it creates projects, generates correctly wired files, runs the dev server and builds. Most used commands: ng new, ng serve, ng generate (alias g), ng build, ng test, ng update, ng add, ng version.
Creating projects: ng new hr-portal asks for style format, SSR and so on. Modern Angular creates standalone applications by default (no NgModule).
codeExamples:
ng new hr-portal --routing --style=scss --ssr=false   # create a project
cd hr-portal
ng serve -o                                             # dev server on http://localhost:4200, opens browser
ng version                                              # CLI and framework versions
ng add @angular/material                                # install and configure a library with schematics

intermediate.content:
Generating code

Generated files follow the official style guide and add a spec file. Useful flags: --dry-run (preview), --skip-tests, --inline-template, --inline-style, --change-detection OnPush, --flat. Since Angular 20 the generated files use the new naming (for example employee-list.ts without the .component suffix); the style guide change is version dependent, so check your CLI version.
codeExamples:
ng g c employee/employee-list --change-detection OnPush --inline-style   # component
ng g s core/api                   # service (providedIn: 'root')
ng g d shared/highlight           # attribute directive
ng g p shared/initials            # pipe
ng g guard core/auth              # asks which type: CanActivate etc. (functional guard)
ng g interceptor core/auth        # functional HttpInterceptorFn
ng g environments                 # environment.ts and environment.development.ts + fileReplacements
ng g interface models/employee    # plain TypeScript interface
ng g c ui/card --dry-run          # show what would be created without writing

expert.content:
Schematics, defaults and migrations

• Every generator is a schematic. Set project-wide defaults in angular.json under schematics (for example OnPush and skipTests for all components) so the team generates consistent code. You can write custom schematics for company-specific templates.
• ng update @angular/core @angular/cli runs automated migrations between versions; update one major version at a time, commit between steps and read the update guide at update.angular.dev. ng generate @angular/core:standalone, :control-flow and :inject migrate old code to modern syntax.
• Cache and analytics: the CLI caches in .angular/cache (delete it when builds behave strangely); ng analytics disable turns off prompts in CI; NG_CLI_ANALYTICS=false is a common CI variable.
• Use npx @angular/cli@latest new to try a version without installing globally, and pin the CLI version in devDependencies so CI and teammates match.

interviewQA: What does ng generate do and why use it?
It runs a schematic that creates correctly named, wired files (and specs) following the style guide, saving time and keeping consistency.
How do you preview generated files without creating them?
Add --dry-run to the ng generate command.
How do you upgrade Angular safely?
Use ng update one major version at a time with the update guide, run the provided migrations, test and commit between steps.
What does ng add do?
Installs a package and runs its schematic to configure the project (for example @angular/material or @angular/pwa).
How do you set default options for generated components across a team?
Configure schematics defaults in angular.json (for example OnPush and style), so every ng g c follows them.

topics.name: Builds, dev server, compiler and AOT

beginner.content:
Serve, build and what the compiler does

• Development server: ng serve compiles in memory, serves on port 4200 and reloads the browser on save. Change the port with --port, expose to the network with --host 0.0.0.0, proxy the API with --proxy-config.
• Build commands: ng build writes to dist/; --configuration development or production; --watch rebuilds on change; --stats-json creates data for bundle analysis.
• Production builds optimize and hash files.
• The Angular compiler translates your templates and decorators into efficient JavaScript instructions. AOT (ahead-of-time) does this at build time, so the browser downloads ready code, errors are found before release and no compiler ships to users. (Old JIT compiled in the browser.)
codeExamples:
ng serve --port 4300 --host 0.0.0.0 --proxy-config proxy.conf.json
ng build --configuration development --watch
ng build --stats-json                 # then analyse dist/.../stats.json

intermediate.content:
Build configuration, template type checking and source maps

• Build configuration: angular.json has architect targets (build, serve, test) each with options and named configurations. Pick one with -c.
• Template type checking: enable strictTemplates in tsconfig.json (angularCompilerOptions) so the compiler verifies every binding, pipe argument, event type and @for variable. It catches typos at build time that would otherwise appear at runtime.
• Source maps map minified bundles back to TypeScript. They are on in development; in production you can generate them ("sourceMap": true or { "scripts": true, "hidden": true }) and upload them privately to your error tracker rather than publishing them.

expert.content:
Under the hood: builders, Ivy and AOT details

• Angular 17+ projects use the application builder (esbuild for bundling plus the Angular compiler plugin, Vite for the dev server). It is much faster than the earlier webpack-based browser builder, supports SSR/prerendering in one pipeline, and outputs to dist/<app>/browser (and server). Migrate with ng update's builder migration. Dev-server HMR for styles and templates works out of the box.
• Ivy (default since v9) compiles each component into locality-friendly instructions (ɵcmp, ɵɵelementStart...). The compiler requires static analysability: templates must be known at build time, which is why template-only logic and strict types help tree-shaking. Libraries are published in partial-compiled form and linked by the app build.
• AOT limitations: no dynamic template strings; decorator metadata must be statically resolvable. ngc still exists for library builds (ng-packagr).
• ng build --verbose, NG_BUILD_DEBUG_CACHE and deleting .angular/cache help diagnose odd builds. Use "budgets" to guard size, and NG_BUILD_MAX_WORKERS to limit CPU in CI.
• Differential loading is gone: Angular targets modern browsers (ES2022); the browserslist file controls support. Version notes: zoneless, signal forms and some builders are experimental in certain releases.

interviewQA: What is AOT compilation and why is it default?
AOT compiles templates to JavaScript at build time. It gives faster startup, smaller bundles, earlier error detection and better security because no template compiler runs in the browser.
What does strictTemplates do?
It enables the strictest type checking of templates so wrong property names, argument types and event payloads fail the build.
Why use source maps and should they be public in production?
They map minified code to TypeScript for debugging. In production generate them hidden and upload them to your error tracker rather than serving them publicly.
What is the difference between ng serve and ng build?
ng serve builds in memory, serves and live-reloads for development; ng build writes files to dist for deployment.
What is the Angular application builder?
The esbuild/Vite-based builder (default in v17+) that builds browser, server and prerendered output faster than the older webpack builder.

topics.name: Code quality: ESLint and Prettier

beginner.content:
Linting and formatting

• ESLint reads your code and warns about mistakes and bad patterns (unused variables, missing track, inaccessible markup). Like Checkstyle/SpotBugs in Java.
• Prettier rewrites the code layout (quotes, spacing, line width) automatically so nobody argues about style, like a Java formatter.
Setup: ng add angular-eslint then npx ng lint. Install Prettier with npm and add a .prettierrc.
codeExamples:
ng add angular-eslint        # adds ESLint with Angular rules and a lint target
npx ng lint                   # run checks
npm install --save-dev prettier eslint-config-prettier
npx prettier --write "src/**/*.{ts,html,scss}"

intermediate.content:
A sensible configuration and automation

Use the flat config (eslint.config.js) that angular-eslint generates, extend recommended rules plus the template-accessibility ruleset, and let eslint-config-prettier disable rules that clash with Prettier (ESLint finds problems, Prettier formats). Run both in a pre-commit hook (Husky + lint-staged) and in CI; Prettier formats, ESLint checks.

expert.content:
Rules that matter and rollout tips

• High-value Angular rules: no-output-native, no-input-rename, template/eqeqeq, template/no-negated-async, template/click-events-have-key-events and interactive-supports-focus (accessibility), prefer-standalone, prefer-signals (newer versions), use-lifecycle-interface. Combine with typescript-eslint's type-aware rules (no-floating-promises, no-misused-promises) for async safety; they are slower, so scope them.
• Introduce lint on a legacy codebase gradually: errors only for new rules on changed files (lint-staged), warnings elsewhere, and auto-fix with --fix in a dedicated commit so blame stays useful. Use .git-blame-ignore-revs for the formatting commit.
• Keep one source of truth: .editorconfig for indentation, Prettier for layout, ESLint for correctness. Do not duplicate stylistic rules in ESLint.
• CI: ng lint and prettier --check fail the build; enforce the same versions via lock file. Version note: ESLint 9 uses flat config by default; older projects have .eslintrc.json. TSLint is dead; ignore old tutorials.

interviewQA: ESLint versus Prettier?
ESLint finds code problems and enforces rules; Prettier only formats layout. Use both and disable formatting rules in ESLint with eslint-config-prettier.
How do you install ESLint in an Angular project?
Run ng add angular-eslint, which adds the configuration and a lint target used by ng lint.
How do you enforce quality before code is merged?
Husky/lint-staged pre-commit hooks for fast checks and CI jobs running ng lint, prettier --check, tests and build as required PR checks.
Which ESLint rules help accessibility in Angular templates?
The templateAccessibility set: alt-text, click-events-have-key-events, interactive-supports-focus, label-has-associated-control and valid-aria.

topics.name: Debugging and profiling tools

beginner.content:
Looking inside the running app

• Browser DevTools (F12): Elements (DOM and CSS), Console (errors, console.log), Sources (breakpoints in TypeScript thanks to source maps), Network (every request), Application (localStorage, cookies, service workers).
• Angular DevTools: a browser extension adding an "Angular" tab with the component tree, inputs/outputs and state, signal values and a profiler.
• Network debugging: check the status code, request payload, response body, headers (Authorization, CORS), timing and the red "blocked by CORS" messages.

intermediate.content:
Profiling, dependency analysis and a debugging workflow

• Performance profiling: in Angular DevTools Profiler record an interaction and see which components were checked and how long each change-detection cycle took. In Chrome's Performance tab look for long tasks; Lighthouse reports Core Web Vitals and bundle warnings.
• Dependency analysis: find what makes bundles large and what depends on what.
• Workflow: reproduce, read the console error, check Network, set a breakpoint, inspect state in Angular DevTools, fix, add a test.
codeExamples:
# bundle analysis
ng build --stats-json
npx esbuild-visualizer --metadata dist/hr-portal/stats.json --open      # treemap of the bundle (esbuild builder)
# older webpack builder:  npx webpack-bundle-analyzer dist/hr-portal/stats.json
npx source-map-explorer dist/hr-portal/browser/main-*.js                # needs source maps

# dependency graph and circular imports
npx madge --circular --extensions ts src/
npm ls rxjs                      # which versions are installed?
npm outdated && npm audit        # stale and vulnerable packages

expert.content:
Debugging production issues

Production builds are minified, so stack traces say at e.t (main-4f2a.js:1:33021). Approach:
• Use an error tracker (Sentry, Application Insights) with the release id and privately uploaded source maps to get readable stack traces plus breadcrumbs (clicks, requests).
• Reproduce with a local production build served statically (npx http-server dist/.../browser -c-1 with a SPA fallback) because AOT, minification and strict CD (e.g. ExpressionChangedAfterItHasBeenChecked appears only in dev) behave differently; check the Network tab for 4xx/5xx and compare the deployed version number.
• Add a correlation id header in an interceptor and log it in Spring Boot so one user action can be traced across both logs.
• Use feature flags and remote logging for hard-to-reproduce issues; capture the user agent, route and app version in every report. Chrome's "Override content" and local overrides let you test a fix against production assets.
• Common production-only bugs: stale cache after deploy, missing SPA fallback, CORS misconfiguration, wrong runtime config, window usage during SSR, differences in locale or timezone, and memory leaks from unsubscribed streams (use the Memory tab heap snapshots; compare snapshots to see detached DOM nodes).
• Source maps stay off the public web server but the browser's DevTools can load them locally when you drop them in (Sources, Add source map).

interviewQA: What does Angular DevTools offer that normal DevTools do not?
A component tree with inputs, state and signals, and a profiler that shows change detection cycles per component.
How do you find why a bundle is big?
Build with --stats-json and open it in a visualizer (esbuild-visualizer or source-map-explorer) to see which libraries and modules dominate, then lazy load or replace them.
How do you debug a production-only error?
Use an error tracker with source maps, reproduce with a local production build, check network responses and the deployed version, and trace with a correlation id across frontend and backend.
How do you spot a memory leak?
Take heap snapshots in the Memory tab before and after navigating; growth in detached DOM nodes or listeners signals unsubscribed streams or retained references.
What can you see in the Network tab for an API bug?
Status code, request URL and payload, headers such as Authorization and CORS, the response body and timing.
