topics.name: Application structure, boundaries, monorepos and microfrontends

beginner.content:
Organise by feature, like Java packages by domain

• Angular application architecture: think in layers: UI components, a layer that holds state and logic (facades/stores), a data-access layer (HTTP), and shared utilities. Dependencies point inward: UI to facade to data access, never the other way.
• Feature-based folder structure: put everything about employees in features/employees (components, routes, services, models), not all components in one folder and all services in another.
• Core and shared concepts: core/ holds app-wide singletons used once (auth service, interceptors, layout shell). shared/ holds reusable, stateless building blocks (buttons, pipes, directives) with no knowledge of any feature.
• Standalone application architecture: no NgModules; each route lazily loads a component or a route array with its own providers.
codeExamples:
src/app/
  core/                    # singletons: auth.service.ts, auth.interceptor.ts, error-handler.ts, layout/
  shared/                  # ui/ (button, modal), pipes/, directives/, util/
  features/
    employees/
      data-access/         # employee.api.ts, employee.store.ts, employee.model.ts
      ui/                  # employee-card.component.ts (presentational)
      pages/               # employee-list.page.ts, employee-detail.page.ts (containers)
      employees.routes.ts  # lazy route array
    billing/ ...
  app.routes.ts
  app.config.ts

intermediate.content:
Lazy feature routes and feature boundaries

Each feature exposes a public API (an index.ts barrel or its route file) and hides the rest. Features should not import each other's internals; shared needs go to shared or a domain library. Enforce feature boundaries with ESLint (@nx/enforce-module-boundaries in Nx, or no-restricted-imports patterns).

Modular architecture

Modular architecture means each feature can be understood, tested, loaded and even owned by a team on its own. In standalone Angular the unit of modularity is the route array plus its components and providers, not an NgModule. Legacy NgModules still work and can be migrated feature by feature.

expert.content:
Monorepos and microfrontends

• Monorepo architecture: one repository with several applications (admin, customer) and libraries (ui, data-access, util) built with the Angular workspace (ng g library, projects/ folder) or Nx (computation cache, affected builds, generators, module-boundary rules). Benefits: atomic changes, shared tooling, easy reuse. Costs: CI tooling, ownership rules, build time without caching. Use path aliases in tsconfig.base.json (@acme/ui).
• Microfrontend design: split a very large product into independently deployed frontends owned by different teams, composed in a shell using Native Federation (@angular-architects/native-federation, works with the esbuild builder) or webpack Module Federation. Share singletons (Angular core, RxJS) carefully, keep a thin shared contract (events, a shared auth token, design tokens), version remotes independently and avoid shared mutable state. Alternatives are simpler: iframes, or just a monorepo with lazy features. Microfrontends add real operational cost (versions, duplicated bundles, cross-app routing); adopt them for organisational scaling, not for code organisation.
• Scalability checklist: single responsibility folders, enforced boundaries, lazy loading by route, shared design system library, consistent naming, automated tests per layer, architecture decision records (ADRs).

interviewQA: Why organise Angular code by feature instead of by type?
Related files change together, features can be lazy loaded and owned by a team, and deleting or moving a feature is simple.
What belongs in core and what in shared?
Core holds app-wide singletons (auth, interceptors, shell) loaded once; shared holds reusable stateless UI, pipes and directives with no feature knowledge.
How do you enforce feature boundaries?
Expose a public API per feature and use lint rules (Nx module boundaries or no-restricted-imports) to forbid deep imports across features.
When would you choose a monorepo?
When several apps share libraries and need atomic changes and common tooling; use Nx or the Angular workspace with caching and affected builds.
When are microfrontends justified?
For large products with many teams needing independent deployment; they add complexity (shared deps, routing, versioning), so use a monorepo with lazy features first.

topics.name: Component patterns and reusable forms

beginner.content:
Smart and presentational components

• A smart (container) component knows about services, loads data and handles events. A presentational (UI) component only receives data with input() and reports user actions with output(). Analogy: the smart component is the chef (decides and cooks), the presentational component is the plate (shows what it is given).
• The container and UI component pattern is the same idea under different names. It makes UI parts reusable, easy to test (no HTTP) and fast with OnPush.

intermediate.content:
Component composition and reusable form architecture

• Component composition: prefer small components combined with content projection (ng-content, slots, ng-template inputs) over deep inheritance or components with 20 inputs. A card, table or dialog exposes slots; the caller composes.
• Reusable form architecture: split large forms into sub-form components that receive a typed FormGroup as input (or implement ControlValueAccessor for single-value widgets such as a date picker). Centralise validation messages and reuse validators in a shared file. Use NonNullableFormBuilder and typed forms.

expert.content:
Rules of thumb and traps

• Presentational components should be OnPush, take plain data, and avoid injecting feature services. If a UI component needs three services, it is probably a container.
• Avoid "boolean explosion" ([showHeader] [showFooter] [compact] [rounded]); use slots or a configuration object. Avoid component inheritance; share behaviour through directives, host directives, services or composition functions.
• Container nesting: avoid containers inside every level (prop-drilling is not evil in Angular; signals and DI make passing data cheap). One container per route page is a good default; use an injected store for deeper sharing.
• Reusable forms: keep the form model separate from the API model (map in the container or an adapter); pass only the sub-group a child needs; expose validation through the group so parents see child errors; use ControlValueAccessor for leaf widgets and avoid two-way plumbing of many values. Typed forms catch rename errors at compile time. Unsubscribe via takeUntilDestroyed.
• Test presentational components with plain inputs, containers with a fake store.

interviewQA: Smart versus presentational components?
Smart components get data and coordinate services; presentational components render inputs and emit outputs only. This improves reuse, testing and OnPush performance.
Why prefer composition over inheritance for components?
Inheritance couples templates, lifecycle and DI; composition with content projection, directives and services is more flexible and easier to test.
How do you make a big form reusable?
Split it into sub-form components taking a typed FormGroup (or ControlValueAccessor for single controls) and share validators and messages.
What is a sign of a component doing too much?
Many inputs/booleans, several injected feature services, mixed HTTP and presentation logic, or hard-to-test behaviour.

topics.name: Design patterns in Angular

beginner.content:
Patterns you already know from Java, in Angular clothes

• Facade pattern: one simple service in front of several complicated ones. Components call employeeFacade.load() and do not care about stores, APIs or caching.
• Repository pattern: a service that hides where data comes from (REST, cache, local storage). Components ask for employees, not for URLs.
• Adapter pattern: converts one shape into another, such as an API DTO into a UI model (rename fields, parse dates).
• Strategy pattern: swap an algorithm at runtime, such as different discount or sorting rules, chosen through DI.
• Observer pattern: built in. RxJS Observable/Subject and signals are observers: subscribers react when the source changes.
• Dependency Injection patterns: Angular's DI is the Spring DI of the frontend.

intermediate.content:
Repository, adapter and strategy with DI

An abstract class (or InjectionToken) is the interface; different providers implement it. Swap implementations per environment, per route, or in tests without touching consumers.

expert.content:
When patterns help and when they hurt

• Facade is valuable when a screen touches several services or a store; do not add a facade that just forwards one call. With signal stores, the store itself often is the facade.
• Repository is worth it when data sources may vary (API plus cache, offline sync) or when you want fakes in tests. For simple CRUD, an HTTP service is already the repository; extra abstraction is premature.
• Adapters belong at the boundary (in the data-access layer) so the rest of the app uses the clean model; this isolates you from backend renames. Keep them pure functions, easily unit tested. Convert dates and money once.
• Observer: pick signals for synchronous state and RxJS for events over time; avoid manual Subject event buses spread across features, which hide dependencies. Always complete or unsubscribe (takeUntilDestroyed, async pipe).
• DI patterns: use providedIn: 'root' for app singletons; component or route providers for scoped instances; InjectionToken with factory for configuration; multi: true for plug-in lists; inject() in functions (guards, interceptors) and in injection contexts only; runInInjectionContext for tests; Optional/Self/SkipSelf for hierarchical lookups. Prefer abstract class tokens over TypeScript interfaces (interfaces vanish at runtime).
• Over-engineering warning: patterns exist to reduce change cost; do not add one without a concrete pressure (testing, multiple implementations, boundary).

interviewQA: What is the facade pattern in Angular?
A service offering a simple API for a screen or feature that hides stores, repositories and side effects from components.
How would you implement the strategy pattern?
Define an interface/abstract class or InjectionToken, provide different implementations (or multi providers) and inject the chosen one where needed.
Why use an adapter between API and UI?
It isolates the UI from backend naming and format, so API changes only affect the mapping function.
How does Angular implement the observer pattern?
Through RxJS Observables and Subjects (subscribers are notified of emissions) and through signals whose consumers update when the value changes.
Why use abstract classes as DI tokens instead of interfaces?
TypeScript interfaces do not exist at runtime; a class or InjectionToken can be used as a DI key.

topics.name: State, service layer, API abstraction and error architecture

beginner.content:
Who owns what

• State management patterns: keep state as local as possible. Component signals for UI-only state, a feature store service for shared feature data, NgRx only for large, complex cross-feature state.
• Service layer design: split services by responsibility: API services (HTTP only), state/store services (hold signals), domain services (pure business rules), UI services (toasts, dialogs).
• API abstraction: components never build URLs or handle HTTP; they call typed methods.
• Error handling architecture: errors are caught at three levels: the HTTP interceptor (network/API), the global ErrorHandler (unexpected exceptions) and the component (expected, recoverable cases).

intermediate.content:
A layered data-access and error pipeline

Create a thin typed API client, error classes that carry meaning, one interceptor that normalises errors and one global handler that logs the unexpected. Components show messages from the store or a notification service, not raw HttpErrorResponse.

expert.content:
Choosing and scaling the approach

• Selection guide: local signal for UI toggles; service + signals (or NgRx Signal Store) per feature; NgRx Store when you need time-travel debugging, strict unidirectional flow, many collaborating effects or large teams; server state caching via httpResource/resource or a query library.
• Keep state immutable, normalised by id when shared, derive with computed, expose read-only signals (asReadonly) and mutate only through store methods (single writer). Avoid pushing derived data into the store.
• Service layering rule: UI depends on state services; state services depend on API services; API services depend only on HttpClient and tokens. Never inject a component into a service; never let API services touch UI services.
• Error architecture: distinguish expected errors (validation, 404) handled inline from unexpected ones (bugs) handled globally; add retry only for idempotent GETs and transient statuses (retry with backoff); correlate with request ids; do not swallow errors in catchError(() => of([])) without telling the user; show friendly text, log technical detail. Handle NG0100-type errors by fixing, not hiding them. For observables inside effects, handle errors in the stream to avoid killing it.
• Version notes: provideBrowserGlobalErrorListeners() and provideZonelessChangeDetection() exist in recent versions; an unhandled promise rejection reaches ErrorHandler in zoneless apps only through those listeners.

interviewQA: How do you decide between service+signals and NgRx?
Start with local signals, then feature services with signals. Adopt NgRx when state is large, shared across many features, needs strict patterns, devtools and complex side-effect orchestration.
What is a good service layering rule?
UI depends on state/facade services; state services depend on API services; API services depend only on HttpClient and configuration tokens.
How do you design Angular error handling?
Interceptor for HTTP errors, a global ErrorHandler for unexpected errors with logging, and component-level handling for expected cases with friendly messages.
What is API abstraction good for?
Components stay independent of URLs and HTTP details, so backend changes and mocks only affect the data-access layer.
Why expose signals as readonly from a store?
Only the store should change state; asReadonly prevents consumers from calling set or update.

topics.name: DDD, clean code, SOLID, reviews and refactoring

beginner.content:
Thinking in the business domain

• Domain-driven design fundamentals: use the same words as the business (the ubiquitous language): Invoice, Enrollment, not DataItem. A bounded context is a part of the system with its own model (Billing and Support may both have a Customer, but with different fields). Entities have identity (Employee 42); value objects are defined by value (Money, DateRange).
• Maintainability and scalability: code you can change cheaply and an app that stays fast and organised as it grows.
• Clean code principles: meaningful names, small functions, one level of abstraction, no duplication (DRY), no magic numbers, comments explain why not what.

intermediate.content:
SOLID in Angular

• Single Responsibility: a component renders, a service fetches, a pipe formats.
• Open/Closed: extend behaviour by adding a provider or directive, not by editing a long switch.
• Liskov: any implementation provided for a token must honour its contract (a fake repository behaves like the real one).
• Interface Segregation: small interfaces/tokens (a component needing only load() should not depend on a 20-method service).
• Dependency Inversion: depend on abstractions (abstract class/token) and let DI supply details.

Code review and refactoring

Code review practices: keep pull requests small, review for correctness, tests, security, readability and boundaries; be kind and specific; automate the boring part (lint, format, tests in CI); use a checklist. Refactoring strategies: change structure without changing behaviour, in small steps, with tests first (the "red-green-refactor" safety net). Typical Angular refactors: extract a presentational component, move HTTP into a service, replace *ngIf/*ngFor with @if/@for, constructor injection with inject(), RxJS state with signals, NgModules with standalone, any with real types.
codeExamples:
# automated refactors provided by Angular
ng generate @angular/core:standalone
ng generate @angular/core:control-flow
ng generate @angular/core:inject
ng generate @angular/core:signal-input-migration        # @Input -> input()  (availability depends on Angular version)

expert.content:
Applying the principles with judgement

• DDD in a frontend is mostly: name things as the business does, split features along bounded contexts (a feature library per context), keep domain rules in pure functions or small classes (testable without Angular) and map API DTOs into domain models at the boundary. Do not mirror the entire backend model; the frontend model serves screens. Use branded types, discriminated unions and exhaustive switch to make invalid states unrepresentable (type Load = { s: 'idle' } | { s: 'loading' } | { s: 'ok'; data: T } | { s: 'error'; e: string }).
• Scalability signals: lazy-loaded features, OnPush plus signals, virtual scrolling, bounded bundle budgets, and a CI that fails on boundary violations. Maintainability signals: low coupling, one reason to change, tests at the right level (many unit, some integration, few e2e), consistent conventions, documented decisions (ADRs), up-to-date dependencies.
• Clean code traps: giant components, business logic in templates, deeply nested subscribes (use higher-order operators), boolean parameters, comment-driven code, premature abstraction (rule of three: abstract on the third repetition).
• Review checklist: Does it follow the layering? Subscriptions cleaned up? OnPush-friendly (immutable updates)? Accessible markup? Types (no any)? Error and loading states? Tests? Security (no innerHTML without sanitising, no secrets)? Naming? Small enough to review in 20 minutes?
• Refactoring at scale: use the strangler approach (new code in the new style, old code migrated when touched), feature flags, codemods and one migration per pull request; measure with bundle size and test coverage; never mix refactor and behaviour change in one commit.

interviewQA: What are ubiquitous language and bounded context?
Ubiquitous language is the shared vocabulary of developers and business used in code and conversation; a bounded context is an area where a given model and terms have one precise meaning.
Give examples of SOLID in Angular.

Single responsibility for components/services/pipes; open/closed with multi providers and directives; dependency inversion with abstract tokens supplied by DI; interface segregation with small tokens; Liskov with faithful fakes.
What belongs in a good Angular code review?
Correctness, tests, layering and boundaries, subscription cleanup, immutability and OnPush compatibility, accessibility, security, error/loading states and naming, in a small PR.
How do you refactor safely?
Cover behaviour with tests, change structure in small steps, use Angular migration schematics, keep refactors separate from feature changes and release behind flags if risky.
Name clean-code habits for Angular templates and components.
Small components, logic out of templates, descriptive names, no magic strings or numbers, typed models, one responsibility each and comments that explain why.

topics.name: Accessibility fundamentals: semantics, ARIA, keyboard, focus, contrast

beginner.content:
Everyone should be able to use your app

Accessibility (a11y) means people with visual, hearing, motor or cognitive disabilities (and people with a broken arm, bright sunlight or a slow connection) can use your app. It is also a legal requirement in many places and improves SEO and usability for all.
• WCAG fundamentals: the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines are organised as POUR: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust. Conformance levels A, AA (the normal target) and AAA.
• Semantic HTML: use the right element. A real <button> is focusable, works with Enter/Space and is announced as a button; a <div (click)> is none of that. Use nav, main, header, headings in order, ul for lists, label for fields.
• Color contrast: text needs at least 4.5:1 contrast (3:1 for large text and UI components) and information must never rely on color alone.
codeExamples:
Save
  • Employees

Employees

...

intermediate.content:
ARIA, keyboard, focus and screen readers

• ARIA roles and attributes: first rule of ARIA is "do not use ARIA if a native element works". Use it for custom widgets: role, aria-label, aria-expanded, aria-controls, aria-live. In Angular, bind with [attr.aria-expanded]="open()".
• Keyboard navigation: every action reachable with Tab/Shift+Tab, activated with Enter/Space, closed with Escape, menus and tabs with arrow keys. Never remove the focus outline without a visible replacement. Add a "skip to content" link.
• Focus management: after a route change move focus to the new page heading; after opening a dialog move focus inside and return it to the trigger on close; after a failed submit focus the first invalid field.
• Screen-reader support: every control needs an accessible name (visible text, label or aria-label); images need alt (empty for decorative); dynamic changes are announced through aria-live regions (the CDK LiveAnnouncer).
• Responsive accessibility: layouts reflow at 320px width and 400% zoom without two-direction scrolling, touch targets at least 24x24 CSS px (44px recommended), do not lock orientation, and respect prefers-reduced-motion.

expert.content:
Deeper points for production apps

• Prefer native elements; when you build custom controls follow the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices patterns (roles, states and key handling) or use Angular CDK a11y (FocusTrap, FocusMonitor, ListKeyManager, LiveAnnouncer) and Angular Material, which implement them. Bad ARIA is worse than none (a wrong role overrides correct native semantics).
• SPA specifics: route changes do not reload the page, so screen-reader users get no cue. Update the document title (route title option) and move focus or announce the navigation. Title must be unique per page (WCAG 2.4.2).
• Do not use tabindex greater than 0. Use tabindex="-1" for programmatic focus targets only. Use inert on background content or CDK focus trap for modals.
• Contrast needs checking for hover, focus, disabled, placeholder and dark-mode states; tokens in CSS custom properties make this auditable. Do not rely on opacity for disabled text.
• Angular specifics: [attr.aria-*] not [aria-*] (ARIA attributes are not DOM properties in most browsers); avoid (click) on non-interactive elements (the ESLint template rules flag it); @for lists should render real ul/li or table markup; keep DOM order equal to visual order. WCAG 2.2 adds focus-not-obscured, target size and accessible authentication criteria; the legal baseline is usually WCAG 2.1 AA (and the European Accessibility Act, ADA/Section 508 elsewhere).

interviewQA: What are the four WCAG principles?
Perceivable, Operable, Understandable and Robust (POUR), with conformance levels A, AA and AAA.
Why use a button instead of a div with a click handler?
A native button is focusable, keyboard-operable (Enter/Space), announced correctly by screen readers and styled for states; a div has none of this unless you rebuild it with ARIA and key handlers.
When should you use ARIA?
Only when native HTML cannot express the widget (tabs, tree, combobox); ARIA changes semantics but adds no behaviour, so you must also implement keyboard support.
How do you manage focus in a single-page app?
Move focus to the new page heading after navigation, trap focus in dialogs and restore it to the trigger afterwards, and focus the first invalid field on failed submit.
What contrast ratio is required for text?
WCAG AA requires at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text and UI components.

topics.name: Accessible forms, validation, dialogs and testing

beginner.content:
Forms people can actually complete

• Accessible forms: every input has a visible <label> linked by for/id (placeholders are not labels, they vanish). Group related fields with fieldset and legend (radio groups). Mark required fields in text, use correct type and autocomplete.
• Accessible validation messages: show the error text next to the field, in text (not only red color), connect it with aria-describedby and set aria-invalid.
• Accessible dialogs: a dialog has role="dialog" (or native <dialog>), an accessible name, traps focus, closes with Escape and returns focus to the button that opened it.
codeExamples:
@if (email.invalid && email.touched) {

Enter a valid email address, for example name@company.com.

}

intermediate.content:
Dialogs and an error summary

Use the CDK/Material dialog (focus trap, Escape, restore focus built in) or the native <dialog> element opened with showModal(). For long forms, add an error summary at the top listing links to each invalid field, and focus it after a failed submit.

Accessibility testing

Automate what can be automated, and test the rest by hand: (1) ESLint template accessibility rules; (2) axe-core in unit/e2e tests (jest-axe, @axe-core/playwright, cypress-axe); (3) Lighthouse accessibility score; (4) manual: keyboard-only pass, 200%/400% zoom, high-contrast mode, and a screen reader (NVDA or JAWS on Windows, VoiceOver on Mac, TalkBack on Android). Automation catches roughly a third of issues, so manual checks are required.

expert.content:
Details that separate good from compliant

• Announce validation at the right moment: validate on blur or submit (not every keystroke), move focus on submit, use role="alert" or an aria-live="polite" region sparingly (multiple alerts at once are noisy). Do not rely on the browser's native bubbles when using novalidate and custom messages.
• Custom form controls built with ControlValueAccessor must forward aria-*, label association (aria-labelledby), disabled and invalid states to an inner native element.
• Dialogs: background must be inert (CDK uses aria-hidden on siblings / the inert attribute), the scroll must be locked, aria-modal="true", and destructive actions need a clear name ("Delete employee", not "OK"). Toast notifications use role="status"/alert and must not disappear before they can be read.
• Authentication (WCAG 2.2 3.3.8): allow password managers and paste; avoid cognitive tests. Provide error identification and suggestions (3.3.1, 3.3.3), and consistent help.
• Put accessibility in the pipeline: lint rule failures and axe violations fail CI, and a design-system component library tests each component once. Include accessibility acceptance criteria in tickets. Accessibility testing cannot be fully automated; schedule an expert/user-testing audit for major releases and publish an accessibility statement.

interviewQA: How do you make form validation messages accessible?
Show text errors next to fields, link them with aria-describedby, set aria-invalid, announce via role=alert or a live region, and move focus to the first error or an error summary on submit.
What makes a dialog accessible?
Role dialog and a name, focus moved in and trapped, background inert, Escape to close and focus returned to the trigger; CDK/Material dialogs do this.
Are placeholders a replacement for labels?
No. They disappear on input, have low contrast and are not reliably announced; use a visible label.
How do you test accessibility?
Combine ESLint template rules, automated axe/Lighthouse checks in CI, keyboard-only testing and real screen reader testing, since automation finds only part of the issues.

topics.name: Internationalization: translation, locales, formats, RTL

beginner.content:
One app, many languages

• Internationalization (i18n) = preparing the app so text, dates, numbers and layout can adapt. Localization (l10n) = the actual translation and regional settings for one language.
• Date and number formatting and currency formatting differ per region: 1,234.56 in English (US), 1.234,56 in German, 12/31/2025 vs 31/12/2025. Angular's date, number, percent and currency pipes format according to the active locale.
• Language switching: let users pick a language; remember it.
codeExamples:
{{ today | date:'longDate' }}

{{ 1234567.891 | number:'1.0-2' }}

{{ price | currency:'INR':'symbol':'1.2-2' }}

{{ 0.256 | percent }}

intermediate.content:
Built-in Angular i18n: mark, extract, translate, build

Translation management with @angular/localize follows a build-time workflow: add i18n attributes to templates (and $localize in code), run ng extract-i18n to create messages.xlf, hand it to translators (XLIFF files go to tools such as Lokalise, Crowdin or Phrase), save messages.fr.xlf and configure locales in angular.json. Each locale gets its own optimized build (fastest runtime, but one deployment per language, and no switching without reload).
Locale configuration: set the source locale and the translation files; for extra locale data (pipes) register it with registerLocaleData and provide LOCALE_ID.
codeExamples:
Welcome to the portal

{count, plural, =0 {No employees} =1 {One employee} other {{{count}} employees}}

expert.content:
Runtime switching, RTL and pitfalls

The built-in approach needs one build per locale. For language switching inside the running app, many teams use a runtime library: Transloco or ngx-translate (JSON files, lazy loaded per feature, plural/ICU support). Pick one approach per project. For right-to-left layouts (Arabic, Hebrew, Urdu) set dir="rtl" on the html element and write CSS with logical properties (margin-inline-start, padding-inline, text-align: start, inset-inline-end) so a single stylesheet serves both directions; flip directional icons; use the CDK Directionality service.

Expert notes

• Never concatenate translated fragments ("You have " + n + " items"); use ICU messages with plural and select so grammar works in every language. Give translators context via the meaning/description in the i18n attribute and stable custom ids (@@id).
• Use the Intl API (Intl.DateTimeFormat, NumberFormat, PluralRules, RelativeTimeFormat, Collator for sorting) for formatting outside templates. Store dates in UTC ISO strings, show in the user's timezone; format currency by its ISO code, never hardcode symbols. Keep amounts from the backend as minor units or strings.
• Layout must tolerate text expansion (German is about 30% longer) and different scripts and fonts; avoid text in images; do not truncate with fixed widths.
• Backend alignment: Spring Boot uses MessageSource / messages_hi.properties and the Accept-Language header for API error messages; send error codes and let the frontend translate when possible. Add an interceptor to send Accept-Language.
• SEO and SSR: with build-time locales use URL prefixes (/hi/) and hreflang links; set the html lang attribute for accessibility. Runtime-library approach with SSR needs the translations loaded on the server too to avoid flashing the default language.
• Version notes: Angular's built-in i18n is stable; runtime translation (loading translations without rebuilds) is possible through loadTranslations() from @angular/localize but is less common; libraries such as Transloco cover it with fewer limits.

interviewQA: What is the difference between i18n and l10n?
i18n prepares the app to support multiple languages and regions (marking text, locale-aware formats); l10n is producing the actual translations and regional settings.
How does Angular built-in i18n work?
Mark text with the i18n attribute or $localize, run ng extract-i18n to produce XLIFF, translate it and build each locale separately via angular.json localize configuration.
Built-in i18n or Transloco/ngx-translate?
Built-in produces fast per-locale builds but needs separate deployments and no runtime switching; runtime libraries switch language without reload and load JSON lazily at a small runtime cost.
How do you support right-to-left languages?
Set dir and lang on the html element, use CSS logical properties instead of left/right, mirror directional icons and use the CDK Directionality service.
Why use ICU plural messages?
Plural rules differ by language; ICU plural/select expressions let translators supply correct forms, unlike string concatenation.
How do date, number and currency pipes know the format?
They use the active LOCALE_ID and the registered locale data; the currency pipe also takes the ISO currency code.

topics.name: Core concepts: architecture, components, binding, lifecycle

beginner.content:
Angular architecture

Q: What are the main building blocks of Angular?
A: Components (UI), directives, pipes, services with dependency injection, the router, forms, HttpClient, and the compiler/runtime that renders templates and detects changes. Modern apps are built from standalone components.

Angular vs React

Q: Main difference between Angular and React?
A: Angular is an opinionated full framework (router, forms, HTTP, DI, CLI, TypeScript by default); React is a UI library where you choose routing, state and data tools.

Components and directives

Q: Component versus directive?
A: A component is a directive with a template. Attribute directives change appearance/behaviour of an existing element; structural directives (and control flow) change the DOM structure.

Standalone components vs NgModules

Q: What is a standalone component?
A: A component that declares its own template dependencies in imports and needs no NgModule; it is the default since Angular 19 and the recommended approach.

Data binding

Q: List the types of data binding.
A: Interpolation {{ }}, property binding [prop], event binding (event), and two-way binding [(ngModel)] or [(value)] with model().

Component communication

Q: How does a parent pass data to a child?
A: Through an input (input() signal or @Input) and the child notifies the parent with output() or @Output EventEmitter.

Lifecycle hooks

Q: Name important lifecycle hooks in order.
A: constructor, ngOnChanges, ngOnInit, ngDoCheck, ngAfterContentInit, ngAfterViewInit, then ngOnDestroy when removed.

intermediate.content:
Angular architecture

Q: A new developer asks how a click ends up on screen. Walk through it.
A: The event listener runs your handler, which updates state (a signal or field). Change detection (triggered by zone.js or by signal notification) re-evaluates the template bindings of affected views and updates the DOM.

Angular vs React

Q: Your team must choose for a large enterprise app. What do you weigh?
A: Consistency and built-in tooling (Angular) versus ecosystem flexibility and hiring (React); team Java/TypeScript background, long-term maintenance, size of team and existing code usually favour Angular for big structured apps.

Components and directives

Q: When would you create a custom directive instead of a component?
A: When behaviour applies to any element without its own template, such as autofocus, tooltip, permission-based visibility or click-outside; use hostDirectives to compose them.

Standalone components vs NgModules

Q: How do you migrate an NgModule app?
A: Run the standalone migration schematic in steps (convert declarations, remove unnecessary modules, bootstrap with bootstrapApplication) and move providers to app config or routes.

Data binding

Q: Why does [(ngModel)] not work and what is the fix?
A: FormsModule/NgModel must be imported into the standalone component; two-way binding is just [ngModel] plus (ngModelChange).

Component communication

Q: Two unrelated components must share data. How?
A: A shared injectable service holding signals (or a BehaviorSubject), or a store such as NgRx; avoid ViewChild and event buses across features.

Lifecycle hooks

Q: Where do you fetch data and why not in the constructor?
A: Use ngOnInit (or signal/resource APIs and route resolvers): inputs are set by then and the constructor should only do dependency injection and trivial initialisation.

expert.content:
Angular architecture

Q: How does Ivy and AOT shape the architecture?
A: The compiler turns each template into component-local instruction functions at build time, enabling tree-shaking, lazy loading and locality; the runtime has no template compiler, and DI is resolved through hierarchical injectors (element and environment).

Angular vs React

Q: Compare their reactivity models.
A: Angular uses zone-based or signal-based change detection with templates compiled ahead of time; React re-renders components using a virtual DOM and hooks. Angular signals now give fine-grained updates similar to Solid/Vue refs.

Components and directives

Q: What are host bindings and host directives?
A: host metadata binds properties, attributes and events on the host element; hostDirectives composes other directives onto a component or directive with exposed inputs/outputs, replacing inheritance.

Standalone components vs NgModules

Q: What do NgModules still do that standalone does not replace directly?
A: Nothing essential; providers use provideX functions and route-level providers, and legacy libraries can still be imported as modules into standalone components.

Data binding

Q: Property versus attribute binding?
A: Property binding sets DOM properties (value, hidden); attribute binding [attr.aria-label] sets HTML attributes, needed when no DOM property exists (aria-*, colspan).

Component communication

Q: What are model inputs?
A: model() creates a signal input plus an output for two-way binding [(value)], making custom two-way components concise.

Lifecycle hooks

Q: What are afterNextRender and afterRender?
A: Hooks registered in injection context that run after Angular finishes rendering, browser-only, for direct DOM work; they replace ad-hoc ngAfterViewInit DOM code and are SSR-safe.

topics.name: DI, providers, pipes, routing and guards

beginner.content:
Services and Dependency Injection

Q: What is dependency injection in Angular?
A: A pattern where classes ask for dependencies (inject(Service) or constructor parameters) and Angular's injectors create and supply them, enabling reuse and testing, like Spring beans.

Providers and injection tokens

Q: What is providedIn root?
A: Registers a tree-shakable singleton in the root injector without listing it in any providers array.

Pipes

Q: What is a pipe?
A: A template function that transforms a value for display, for example date, currency, uppercase, async.

Routing and lazy loading

Q: How do you configure routes?
A: Define a Routes array with path/component entries, register it with provideRouter(routes) and render with router-outlet; navigate with routerLink or Router.navigate.

Route guards

Q: What are route guards?
A: Functions that decide whether navigation proceeds: canActivate, canActivateChild, canDeactivate and canMatch; resolvers fetch data before activation.

intermediate.content:
Services and Dependency Injection

Q: Explain hierarchical injectors.
A: Injectors form a tree: element injectors (component/directive providers) and environment injectors (root, route). A lookup walks up from the requesting node until a provider is found.

Providers and injection tokens

Q: When do you use an InjectionToken?
A: For non-class values such as config objects, strings and function strategies; use useValue, useFactory or useExisting to supply it.

Pipes

Q: Pure versus impure pipe?
A: A pure pipe re-runs only when its input reference changes (cheap, default); an impure pipe runs every change detection cycle, so use it rarely (async is impure by design).

Routing and lazy loading

Q: How do you lazy load a feature?
A: Use loadComponent: () => import(...) for a component or loadChildren for a route array; the bundle is fetched when the route is first activated.

Route guards

Q: How do you protect admin routes?
A: A functional canActivate guard injecting AuthService that returns true or a UrlTree to /login; combine with canMatch so unauthorised users cannot even load the lazy bundle, and enforce roles on the server.

expert.content:
Services and Dependency Injection

Q: How do you get a new instance per component?
A: List the service in the component providers array; each component instance then gets its own instance, destroyed with the component.

Providers and injection tokens

Q: What does multi: true do?
A: Several providers contribute to one token, which then injects as an array; used by HTTP interceptors (legacy), validators and plug-in systems.

Pipes

Q: Why avoid method calls in templates compared with pipes?
A: Template method calls run on every change detection; a pure pipe or computed signal memoises the result.

Routing and lazy loading

Q: How do preloading strategies work?
A: withPreloading(PreloadAllModules) or a custom strategy loads lazy routes in the background after startup so later navigation is instant without a large initial bundle.

Route guards

Q: canMatch versus canActivate?
A: canMatch decides whether a route definition applies at all (useful for role-based alternatives or feature flags); canActivate runs after matching and blocks activation. canMatch prevents lazy code download.

topics.name: Forms and RxJS comparisons

beginner.content:
Template-driven vs reactive forms

Q: Difference between template-driven and reactive forms?
A: Template-driven forms build the model implicitly from directives (ngModel) in the template; reactive forms build an explicit FormGroup/FormControl model in code, which is more scalable and testable.

Form validation

Q: How do you validate required and email fields?
A: Validators.required and Validators.email in the control definition (or required/email attributes in template-driven forms) and display control.errors when touched.

Observables vs Promises

Q: Observables versus Promises?
A: A Promise yields a single value, is eager and cannot be cancelled; an Observable is lazy, can emit many values, supports operators, cancellation (unsubscribe) and retry.

Subject vs BehaviorSubject

Q: Subject versus BehaviorSubject?
A: A Subject multicasts to current subscribers only; a BehaviorSubject stores the latest value, requires an initial value and gives it to new subscribers immediately.

switchMap vs mergeMap

Q: switchMap versus mergeMap?
A: switchMap cancels the previous inner observable when a new value arrives; mergeMap runs all inner observables concurrently.

concatMap vs exhaustMap

Q: concatMap versus exhaustMap?
A: concatMap queues inner observables and runs them one after another in order; exhaustMap ignores new outer values while an inner one is running.

intermediate.content:
Template-driven vs reactive forms

Q: Which would you choose for a dynamic, complex form and why?
A: Reactive forms: programmatic control, FormArray for dynamic rows, typed forms, custom validators and easy unit tests without rendering.

Form validation

Q: How do you validate that password and confirm password match?
A: A validator on the FormGroup (cross-field) returning { mismatch: true }, with errors shown at group level.

Observables vs Promises

Q: How do you convert between them?
A: firstValueFrom/lastValueFrom turn an Observable into a Promise; from(promise) turns a Promise into an Observable.

Subject vs BehaviorSubject

Q: When would you use ReplaySubject?
A: When late subscribers need the last N emissions, such as a log or recent notifications.

switchMap vs mergeMap

Q: Which operator for type-ahead search?
A: switchMap after debounceTime and distinctUntilChanged so outdated requests are cancelled and only the latest result shows.

concatMap vs exhaustMap

Q: Which for a Save button double-click and which for ordered updates?
A: exhaustMap prevents duplicate submits; concatMap guarantees ordered saves such as sequential autosave updates.

expert.content:
Template-driven vs reactive forms

Q: What are typed forms?
A: Since v14 FormControl and FormGroup types give compile-time safety on value and controls; NonNullableFormBuilder avoids null values after reset.

Form validation

Q: How do async validators work and what are the pitfalls?
A: They return an Observable/Promise (e.g. username availability), run only after sync validators pass, put the control in PENDING; debounce them (timer in the validator or updateOn blur) and cancel stale requests.

Observables vs Promises

Q: Why is HttpClient cold and what does that imply?
A: The request is sent per subscription, so two subscriptions send two requests; use shareReplay or signals/toSignal to share, and unsubscribing cancels the in-flight request.

Subject vs BehaviorSubject

Q: Why expose subjects as observables?
A: Use asObservable() or a private subject with a public stream so consumers cannot call next(), preserving encapsulation; signals with asReadonly give the same.

switchMap vs mergeMap

Q: What can go wrong with mergeMap on user input?
A: Responses can arrive out of order and overwhelm the server; results of old requests may overwrite newer ones.

concatMap vs exhaustMap

Q: Rank the four flattening operators by concurrency and cancellation.
A: mergeMap: parallel, no cancel; switchMap: latest wins, cancels older; concatMap: sequential queue; exhaustMap: drop new while busy. Choose by what should happen to overlapping work.

interviewQA: Difference between template-driven and reactive forms?
Template-driven forms build the model implicitly from directives (ngModel) in the template; reactive forms build an explicit FormGroup/FormControl model in code, which is more scalable and testable.
What are typed forms?
Since v14 FormControl<T> and FormGroup types give compile-time safety on value and controls; NonNullableFormBuilder avoids null values after reset.
How do you validate required and email fields?
Validators.required and Validators.email in the control definition (or required/email attributes in template-driven forms) and display control.errors when touched.
How do async validators work and what are the pitfalls?

They return an Observable/Promise (e.g. username availability), run only after sync validators pass, put the control in PENDING; debounce them (timer in the validator or updateOn blur) and cancel stale requests.
Observables versus Promises?
A Promise yields a single value, is eager and cannot be cancelled; an Observable is lazy, can emit many values, supports operators, cancellation (unsubscribe) and retry.
Why is HttpClient cold and what does that imply?
The request is sent per subscription, so two subscriptions send two requests; use shareReplay or signals/toSignal to share, and unsubscribing cancels the in-flight request.
Subject versus BehaviorSubject?
A Subject multicasts to current subscribers only; a BehaviorSubject stores the latest value, requires an initial value and gives it to new subscribers immediately.
Why expose subjects as observables?
Use asObservable() or a private subject with a public stream so consumers cannot call next(), preserving encapsulation; signals with asReadonly give the same.
switchMap versus mergeMap?
switchMap cancels the previous inner observable when a new value arrives; mergeMap runs all inner observables concurrently.
What can go wrong with mergeMap on user input?
Responses can arrive out of order and overwhelm the server; results of old requests may overwrite newer ones.
concatMap versus exhaustMap?
concatMap queues inner observables and runs them one after another in order; exhaustMap ignores new outer values while an inner one is running.
Rank the four flattening operators by concurrency and cancellation.
mergeMap: parallel, no cancel; switchMap: latest wins, cancels older; concatMap: sequential queue; exhaustMap: drop new while busy. Choose by what should happen to overlapping work.

topics.name: Signals, change detection, interceptors and errors

beginner.content:
Signals vs RxJS

Q: What is the difference between signals and RxJS?
A: Signals hold a current synchronous value with automatic dependency tracking; RxJS models asynchronous streams of events over time with operators. Use signals for state, RxJS for events and HTTP flows.

Signals vs traditional component state

Q: Why use signals instead of plain fields?
A: Angular knows exactly which template reads which signal, so only those views update, enabling OnPush-like performance and zoneless apps without manual markForCheck.

Change detection

Q: What is change detection?
A: The mechanism that checks template bindings against the component state and updates the DOM when values changed.

OnPush strategy

Q: What does ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush do?
A: The component is checked only when an input reference changes, an event originates in it, an async pipe or signal read in its template emits, or markForCheck is called.

HTTP interceptors

Q: What is an HTTP interceptor?
A: A function in the HttpClient pipeline that can inspect or transform every request and response, for auth headers, logging, error handling or caching.

Error handling

Q: How do you handle HTTP errors?
A: catchError in the stream (or an error interceptor) mapping HttpErrorResponse to a friendly message and showing it via a notification service.

intermediate.content:
Signals vs RxJS

Q: How do they interoperate?
A: toSignal converts an observable into a signal (with initialValue), toObservable converts a signal to a stream, and rxResource/resource load async data from signals.

Signals vs traditional component state

Q: How do you derive state?
A: With computed(), which depends on other signals, is cached and read-only; avoid effect() for deriving values.

Change detection

Q: What triggers it in a zone-based app?
A: zone.js patches async APIs (events, timers, XHR/fetch, promises) and calls ApplicationRef.tick after they run, checking the component tree from the root.

OnPush strategy

Q: Why does my OnPush component not update after mutating an array?
A: The input reference did not change; replace the object/array immutably (spread, map) or use signals.

HTTP interceptors

Q: How do you write and register a functional interceptor?
A: Export an HttpInterceptorFn (req, next) => next(req.clone(...)) and register with provideHttpClient(withInterceptors([fn])); order in the array is the order for requests.

Error handling

Q: What is the difference between error status 0 and 4xx/5xx?
A: Status 0 means no response reached the app (network down, CORS block, blocked request); 4xx are client errors and 5xx server errors with a response body.

expert.content:
Signals vs RxJS

Q: Why are signals glitch-free and what is computed laziness?
A: The graph is evaluated pull-based: computed values are memoised, recalculated only when read and when a dependency changed, so consumers never see inconsistent intermediate states.

Signals vs traditional component state

Q: What is linkedSignal and when use it?
A: A writable signal that resets from a source signal, such as a selected item that resets when the list changes; it is stable in recent versions, so check your Angular version.

Change detection

Q: What is ExpressionChangedAfterItHasBeenChecked?
A: In development mode Angular runs a second check; if a binding changed during or after its own check (state modified in a child hook or getter), it throws to flag unstable data flow. Fix the data flow, do not silence it.

OnPush strategy

Q: How does OnPush relate to zoneless?
A: Zoneless apps (provideZonelessChangeDetection, experimental/stable depending on version) rely on signals, markForCheck, async pipe and events for scheduling, so OnPush-style discipline is required.

HTTP interceptors

Q: How do you implement refresh-token handling in an interceptor?
A: On 401 call refresh once (shared with shareReplay), retry the failed request with the new token, queue parallel requests, and log out if refresh fails; skip the auth endpoints to avoid loops.

Error handling

Q: Where does ErrorHandler fit?
A: It catches uncaught exceptions in Angular code; override it to log to a service like Sentry. Expected errors are handled locally; unexpected ones globally.

topics.name: Auth, state, performance, SSR, testing and security

beginner.content:
Authentication and JWT

Q: How does JWT authentication work in Angular?
A: Login returns a token; an interceptor adds it as a Bearer header; a guard blocks protected routes; the server verifies the signature and expiry on every request.

State management

Q: What is state management?
A: How an application stores, shares and updates data across components, for example with services, signals or NgRx.

Performance optimization

Q: Name five Angular performance techniques.
A: OnPush/signals, lazy loading, trackBy/track in @for, @defer for heavy views, virtual scrolling, pure pipes, production build with tree-shaking.

SSR and hydration

Q: What is SSR and why use it?
A: The server renders the initial HTML for faster first paint and better SEO/social previews; the browser then takes over.

Angular testing

Q: Which tools test an Angular app?
A: Jasmine/Karma or Jest/Vitest for unit tests with TestBed, HttpTestingController for HTTP, Playwright or Cypress for end-to-end; the default runner depends on the Angular version.

Security vulnerabilities

Q: How does Angular protect against XSS?
A: It escapes interpolated values and sanitises bound HTML/URLs/styles by default; avoid bypassSecurityTrust* and innerHTML with untrusted input.

intermediate.content:
Authentication and JWT

Q: Where would you store tokens?
A: Access token in memory, refresh token in an HttpOnly Secure SameSite cookie; localStorage is exposed to XSS.

State management

Q: When is NgRx justified?
A: Large apps with complex cross-feature state, many side effects, need for devtools time travel and strict patterns; otherwise a service with signals (or NgRx Signal Store) is simpler.

Performance optimization

Q: A list of 5,000 rows is slow. What do you do?
A: Virtual scroll (CDK), track by id, OnPush rows, server-side paging, avoid heavy template functions, and profile with Angular DevTools.

SSR and hydration

Q: What is hydration?
A: The client reuses the server-rendered DOM and attaches listeners instead of re-creating it, avoiding flicker; it requires identical DOM structure on both sides.

Angular testing

Q: How do you test a component that uses a service?
A: Provide a fake service in TestBed (useValue or a spy), create the fixture, set inputs, call detectChanges and assert on the DOM and calls.

Security vulnerabilities

Q: How do you defend against CSRF?
A: For cookie sessions use SameSite cookies and CSRF tokens (Angular reads XSRF-TOKEN and sends X-XSRF-TOKEN); bearer-token APIs are not vulnerable to classic CSRF.

expert.content:
Authentication and JWT

Q: Why are guards not security?
A: Client code can be modified. Authorization must be enforced by the server on every endpoint; guards only improve user experience.

State management

Q: Describe normalised state and why.
A: Store entities by id in a dictionary with an id list, so updates are O(1), duplicates are avoided and derived views are computed.

Performance optimization

Q: How do you measure and enforce performance?
A: Lighthouse and Core Web Vitals in CI, bundle budgets in angular.json, bundle analysis, Angular DevTools profiler, and real-user monitoring.

SSR and hydration

Q: What are common SSR pitfalls?
A: Using window/document/localStorage on the server (guard with isPlatformBrowser or afterNextRender), duplicate HTTP calls (use TransferState/HTTP cache), non-deterministic rendering and per-request state leaks in singletons.

Angular testing

Q: What is a good test pyramid for Angular?
A: Many fast unit tests for logic and services, component tests for templates and interaction, fewer integration tests with routing and HTTP mocks, and a small set of e2e journeys.

Security vulnerabilities

Q: List other web risks relevant to Angular apps.
A: Token theft via XSS, open redirects after login, insecure third-party scripts, vulnerable npm dependencies, sensitive data in the bundle, missing CSP and broken server authorization (IDOR).

topics.name: Tooling, deployment, Spring Boot and real-world debugging

beginner.content:
Angular CLI and builds

Q: What does Angular CLI do?
A: It scaffolds projects and code (ng new, ng generate), serves, builds, tests, lints and updates the app via schematics and builders.

Deployment

Q: How do you deploy an Angular app?
A: Run ng build, upload dist/browser to a static host or Nginx with SPA fallback, serve over HTTPS and proxy /api to the backend.

Angular with Spring Boot

Q: How does Angular call Spring Boot?
A: HttpClient to REST controllers returning JSON DTOs, with CORS configured or a shared-origin proxy.

Debugging real-world problems

Q: The page is blank after deploy. What do you check?
A: Browser console and Network tab (404 for hashed files, MIME type errors), cached index.html, SPA fallback, base href, and the CORS or API errors.

intermediate.content:
Angular CLI and builds

Q: What is AOT and why is it the default?
A: Templates are compiled at build time, giving faster startup, smaller output and compile-time template errors.

Deployment

Q: How do you build one artifact for many environments?
A: Use runtime configuration (config.json loaded at startup) or container entrypoint substitution instead of build-time environment files.

Angular with Spring Boot

Q: Describe a secure login flow with Spring Boot.
A: POST credentials to /auth/login, receive a short-lived access token and a rotating HttpOnly refresh cookie, an interceptor attaches the access token, Spring Security validates it statelessly and enforces roles.

Debugging real-world problems

Q: The app gets slower over time. How do you investigate?
A: Heap snapshots to find leaks (unsubscribed streams, listeners, detached nodes), the Angular DevTools profiler for change detection storms, and the Network tab for duplicate requests.

expert.content:
Angular CLI and builds

Q: What changed with the application builder?
A: esbuild and Vite replaced webpack for builds and the dev server, speeding rebuilds and unifying browser, SSR and prerender output.

Deployment

Q: How do you roll back safely?
A: Deploy versioned immutable releases and switch a symlink or image tag, keep the previous assets available and ensure database migrations are backward compatible.

Angular with Spring Boot

Q: How do you keep frontend and backend contracts in sync?
A: Generate an OpenAPI spec with springdoc and a typed Angular client from it, validate in CI, version APIs and use contract tests.

Debugging real-world problems

Q: NG0100 ExpressionChanged error appears only in development. Meaning and fix?
A: A binding changed after being checked in the same cycle (state mutated in lifecycle hooks or via getters). Fix by deriving state with computed, moving the change earlier, or restructuring data flow; do not hide with setTimeout.

topics.name: Coding exercises with solutions

beginner.content:
How coding rounds work

Interviewers ask for small, complete components in 20-40 minutes (live coding): a counter, a todo list, a debounced search, a parent-child data flow, a custom validator, an interceptor. They look for correct modern syntax, clean structure, handling of edge cases, and your ability to explain choices. Practise typing solutions without autocomplete.
Exercise 1: counter with signals: increment, decrement, reset, and a computed double.
Exercise 2: todo list with add, toggle, remove and a filter. Expect questions about track and immutability.

intermediate.content:
Exercise 3: debounced search with cancellation

Requirement (debounce plus switchMap): call /api/users?q= after 300 ms of silence, ignore duplicates, cancel old requests, handle errors without killing the stream.

Exercise 4: custom validators

A cross-field password match and an async "username available" validator.

Exercise 5: functional interceptor and guard

Attach a token, and redirect unauthenticated users while remembering the target URL.

expert.content:
Exercise 6: parent-child with model() and a reusable pipe

Build a rating widget that works with [(value)], and a pure pipe that truncates text.

Exercise 7: tests, and an RxJS puzzle

Test a service with HttpTestingController; then explain what a nested subscribe does wrong and refactor it.

interviewQA: Implement a counter with signals.
signal(0) for count, update(c => c + 1) for increment, computed for derived double, and call count() in the template.
How do you implement a type-ahead search?
FormControl valueChanges with debounceTime, distinctUntilChanged and switchMap to the HTTP call, catching errors inside the inner observable, then toSignal or async pipe.
How do you write a cross-field validator?
A ValidatorFn on the FormGroup that reads both controls and returns an error object or null, applied through the group validators option.
How do you test an HTTP service?
Provide provideHttpClient and provideHttpClientTesting, call the method, use HttpTestingController.expectOne, assert method/url, flush a response and verify no outstanding requests.
What is wrong with nested subscribes?
They leak, skip cancellation, scatter error handling and are hard to read; use a flattening operator such as switchMap and share via signals or the async pipe.

expert.content:
How to use this module on a real project

• Treat the table as a definition of done: for a production application every row should be a conscious decision (done, deliberately skipped, or planned).
• Java developers: map each item to what you already know from Spring (profiles, filters, Maven, JUnit) and note only the Angular-specific differences.
• Some items are version dependent (Angular 17-20, Spring Boot 3, Spring Security 6); the lessons say so where it matters.

interviewQA: How should I use a module checklist?
As a definition of done: for each item decide whether it is implemented, deliberately skipped or planned, and revisit the list before every release.
Why group topics into lessons rather than learn them one by one?
Items interact (for example CORS, interceptors and JWT all appear in one login flow), so learning them together mirrors how they are used in a real application.
What versions does this module assume?
Modern Angular (v17-20, standalone components, signals, functional guards and interceptors) with Spring Boot 3 and Spring Security 6; version-specific APIs are flagged.

topics.name: Beginner projects (1-7)

beginner.content:
How to use the beginner projects

Build these in order. Each project is small enough to finish in a weekend and trains one cluster of ideas. For every project: (1) sketch the screens, (2) write the data model first, (3) build the smallest working version, (4) add features one at a time, (5) commit after each step. Compare your solution with the key code only after you tried.

Project 1: Personal Portfolio

Goal. Build a responsive one-page portfolio (about, skills, projects, contact) from reusable components, deployed as a static site.
Features.
  • Header with smooth-scroll navigation and active link highlight
  • Skills section rendered from an array with progress bars
  • Project cards with filter by tag
  • Contact form with validation (no backend)
  • Dark mode toggle remembered in localStorage
Angular concepts practised. Module 3 (CLI, setup), Module 4 (components, input()), Module 5 (@for, @if, binding), Module 11 (simple form), Module 21 (responsive CSS, theming), Module 24 (static hosting).
Backend. None needed: data is kept in memory and localStorage or a static JSON file.
Extend it.
  • Add a blog section with routes and markdown
  • Translate to two languages (Module 27)
  • Add Lighthouse CI and reach 95+ accessibility
  • Pre-render with SSG (Module 19)
Samples below: (1) suggested folder structure, (2) key data model, (3) the heart of the project.

src/app/
  layout/header.component.ts, footer.component.ts
  sections/hero/, skills/, projects/, contact/
  shared/section-title.component.ts
  data/portfolio.data.ts        # skills and projects arrays
  core/theme.service.ts

export interface Skill { name: string; level: number; }          // level 0-100
export interface PortfolioProject { id: number; title: string; description: string; tags: string[]; repoUrl: string; imageUrl: string; }

beginner.content:
Project 2: Calculator

Goal. Create a calculator with keyboard support and history, with the arithmetic logic separated from the UI so it can be unit tested.
Features.
  • Digits, operators, decimal, clear, backspace
  • Keyboard input with host listeners
  • Division by zero and overflow handling
  • History panel of the last 10 calculations
  • Unit tests for the calculation engine
Angular concepts practised. Module 2 (TypeScript types, unions), Module 4 (component), Module 5 (event binding, @for), Module 6 (host listener), Module 13 (signals, computed), Module 20 (unit tests).
Backend. None needed: data is kept in memory and localStorage or a static JSON file.
Extend it.
  • Scientific mode with parentheses and a tokenizer/parser
  • Persist history
  • Memory keys (M+, M-, MR)
  • Theme and accessibility (aria-live for the display)

Project 3: To-Do List

Goal. A task manager with add, edit, complete, delete, filters and persistence: the classic first state-handling project.
Features.
  • Add task with Enter key, inline edit on double click
  • Complete and delete with immutable updates
  • Filters: all, active, completed with counters
  • Persist to localStorage
  • Drag to reorder (CDK) as a stretch goal
Angular concepts practised. Module 4 (components, outputs), Module 5 (@for track, class binding), Module 13 (signals, computed, effect), Module 15 (local state, persistence), Module 20 (tests).

  • Sync with a Spring Boot API (project 10)
  • Categories with route-based filters
  • Undo and redo stack

beginner.content:
Project 5: Employee Directory

intermediate.content:
Build order and quality checklist (beginner)

• Order inside each project: model, service/store, container component, presentational components, styling, tests, polish.
• Checklist: strict TypeScript with no any, standalone components, @for with track, signals for state, labels on every input, keyboard usable, responsive at 360px width, at least three unit tests (engine or store logic), lint and format clean.
• Publish to GitHub Pages or Netlify with ng build and write a README with screenshots: it becomes your portfolio.

expert.content:
Reviewing your own beginner projects like a senior

• Is logic outside the template and testable (calculator engine, store)? Are updates immutable? Could the component be OnPush-safe? Is persisted data validated when read (corrupt localStorage must not crash the app)?
• Accessibility: real buttons, focus order, live region for the calculator display, error messages linked to inputs.
• Refactor pass: extract presentational components, move constants out, replace magic strings with union types, add a route-level lazy load for the heaviest page. Write down one trade-off per project.

interviewQA: Which beginner project teaches signals best?
The to-do list and expense tracker: signals for state, computed for filtered lists and totals, effect for persistence.
How do you keep calculator logic testable?
Put arithmetic in pure functions in a separate file and let the component only handle input and display.
What do you practise with the registration form project?
Typed reactive forms, nested groups, FormArray, built-in and custom validators, cross-field checks and accessible errors.
Why separate smart and presentational components in the product listing?
The page handles filters and the cart service; cards only render inputs and emit outputs, which makes them reusable and OnPush-friendly.

intermediate.content:
Build order and quality checklist (intermediate)

• Order: API contract (DTOs, errors), Angular models and API service, store, pages, validation and error states, auth, tests, Docker Compose.
• Checklist: feature folders with lazy routes, functional guards and interceptors, one error format end to end, loading/empty/error UI everywhere, server-side validation mirrored in forms, CORS or proxy configured, HttpTestingController tests for each API service, integration tests with MockMvc and Testcontainers, Swagger UI available, secrets in environment variables.
• Security checks: test every endpoint without token and with the wrong role; remember guards are UX only.

expert.content:
Expert review points (intermediate)

• Consistency: one place for URLs, one error mapper, one pagination model. Idempotent GET retries only; double-submit protection with exhaustMap on writes.
• Concurrency: add optimistic locking (@Version) and handle 409 in the UI; cancel stale requests with switchMap; clean up SSE or sockets with teardown logic.
• Token design (project 12): refresh in an HttpOnly cookie, rotation, a single shared refresh, logout everywhere. File handling (project 15): validate content, never trust names, stream large files.
• Observability: correlation id header, structured logs, Actuator health, and frontend error reporting. Deploy through the pipeline from Module 24 and practise a rollback.

interviewQA: What should project 10 (CRUD with Spring Boot) demonstrate?
Typed Angular service, DTOs, Bean Validation with field errors in the form, global error handling, CORS or proxy, and Docker Compose with a database.
How does project 12 avoid a refresh storm?
The interceptor shares one in-flight refresh observable (shareReplay) so concurrent 401s wait for the same new token and then retry.
Why keep search state in the URL in project 14?
Pages become shareable and bookmarkable, back/forward works and state survives refresh; the query params become the single source of truth.
How do you secure uploads in project 15?
Validate size and content type on the server, generate stored names, store outside the web root, authorize downloads and consider scanning.
SSE or WebSocket for notifications in project 17?
SSE is simpler for one-way server push with automatic reconnect; WebSocket is needed for bidirectional traffic such as chat. EventSource cannot set headers, so authenticate by cookie or ticket.

beginner.content:
How to use the advanced projects

These are architecture exercises. Do not try to build every feature: slice vertically. Deliver a thin end-to-end path first (login, one list, one write), then deepen. expert.content:
Architecture trade-offs to defend in an interview

• Monolith first: a modular monolith backend plus a well-bounded Angular monorepo beats premature microservices and micro frontends; adopt federation only for independent team deployment.
• State: signals and feature stores by default; NgRx for the cart, exams and chat where event traceability and complex concurrency matter.
• Real time: SSE for server push, WebSocket/STOMP for bidirectional; always plan reconnection, ordering, duplicates (client ids) and backpressure. Time and exams: server authority, client display only.
• Rendering: prerender content, SSR dynamic pages, CSR for authenticated apps; transfer cache to avoid double fetches; never touch window on the server.
• Operations: idempotency keys on payments and orders, retries only on idempotent calls, circuit breaker at the gateway, tracing across services, feature flags for safe rollout. Version note: zoneless, afterRenderEffect, route render modes and incremental hydration depend on Angular 19-20+; check your version.

interviewQA: How would you structure the e-commerce project?

An Nx workspace with catalog, cart, checkout, orders and admin domain libraries (feature, data-access, ui), SSR for the public catalog, a signal store for the cart and a modular monolith Spring Boot backend.
Why must the exam timer use server time?
Client clocks can be changed; the server issues the deadline, the client shows a countdown adjusted by an offset and the server rejects late submissions.
What makes chat reconnection robust?
Exponential backoff, a queue of unsent messages, client-generated ids for de-duplication and optimistic UI reconciled by server echoes, plus history catch-up after reconnect.
How do you make an SSR site SEO friendly?
Prerender or SSR content pages, set title, description, canonical and Open Graph per route, return real 404 status, provide sitemap and robots, optimise images and Core Web Vitals.
When are micro frontends the right choice?
When separate teams must deploy parts of a very large product independently; otherwise use a monorepo with lazy feature libraries.
What proves the enterprise portal is production ready?
Green quality gates in CI, enforced boundaries, accessibility and i18n coverage, security tests, observability, documented runbooks and a rehearsed rollback.

cheatNotes: @Component - Decorator that marks a class as an Angular component
Interpolation {{ }} - Display a component property's value in the template
[property] - Property binding, sets a DOM element property
(event) - Event binding, calls a method on a DOM event
[(ngModel)] - Two-way binding between a form input and a property
*ngIf - Structural directive, conditionally renders an element
*ngFor - Structural directive, repeats an element per collection item
@Injectable - Marks a class as available for dependency injection
providedIn: root - Registers a service as a singleton for the whole app
Constructor injection - Angular supplies service instances via the constructor
RouterModule - Enables client-side routing between components
routerLink - Directive for SPA navigation without full page reload
router-outlet - Placeholder where the routed component renders
ActivatedRoute - Service to read route parameters and query params
Module (@NgModule) - Groups related components, directives, and services
Pipe - Transforms displayed values in a template, e.g. {{ date | date }}
Lifecycle hooks - ngOnInit(), ngOnDestroy(), etc. run at specific component stages
RxJS Observable - Stream of async values used throughout Angular (HTTP, forms, router)
HttpClient - Angular's built-in service for making HTTP requests
Standalone components - Components that don't require an NgModule (modern Angular)
